When he returns home, his wife Tammy mentions that Austin and his wife Bianca have invited them to a housewarming party, but then receives a call that has been cancelled because Bianca supposedly has diarrhea. Craig suggests they invite people over to their house instead, but Tammy asks if Devon is available, indicating her close relationship with her ex-boyfriend. Craig, seeking to recapture the excitement he felt with Austin, convinces Tammy to go on an adventure with him. He takes her to the same underground tunnels Austin showed him. However, unlike Craig's experience with Austin, this adventure goes horribly wrong. Tammy is uncomfortable, falls, and eventually goes missing in the tunnels. This sends the town into panic mode as search efforts begin to find her. Meanwhile, Austin has followed Craig's advice to just ask for what he wants and has secured the morning weatherman position he's been dreaming of. When Craig visits him at the TV station, he disrupts Austin's first broadcast, causing Austin to stumble on air, which strains their friendship. Austin distances himself from Craig, leaving Craig desperate to reconnect. As the search for Tammy continues, Craig's behavior becomes increasingly erratic. He's questioned by police about Tammy's disappearance, and we see him repeatedly saying, "I'm sorry," in numerous scenes, suggesting his guilt over what happened. Eventually, Tammy is found safe and a welcome back party is thrown for her. At the party, Craig gives an awkward toast that reveals his detachment from reality, while Austin gives a heartfelt speech about Tammy being a warrior and healer. This contrast highlights the growing gap between Craig's perception and reality. After the party, Tammy tells Craig that she's had a spiritual awakening while lost in the tunnels and experienced an orgasm in the solar system. a bizarre detail that further shows the disconnection between the couple. She then informs Craig that she's moving into Devon's pool house, effectively ending their marriage. Craig's obsession with Austin intensifies as he watches Austin succeed at his new weather job and bond with a new group of friends. In one pivotal scene, Austin invites Craig to hang out with his guy friends. Initially, everything goes well as the men drink, sing karaoke, and bond. But the night takes a dark turn when they start boxing for fun. Craig, desperate to impress the group, delivers a cheap shot to one of Austin's friends. When the group reacts negatively, Craig bizarrely punishes himself by stuffing soap in his mouth, causing everyone to feel uncomfortable. This incident gets Craig labeled as psycho and further alienates him from Austin and the friend group. In his desperation to experience a profound connection, Craig visits a teenager who sells him a psychedelic Toad Venom experience. During his trip, Craig hallucinates going to Subway and ordering a sandwich, but the dealer tells him that totality is mysterious, suggesting Craig still hasn't found the answers he's seeking. Craig tries multiple times to reconcile with Austin and his friend group, even showing up uninvited to Austin's house and bringing expensive drums as a gift. His behavior becomes increasingly concerning as he makes strange speeches and attempts to force his way back into Austin's life. At one point, Craig sees Austin driving a yellow sports car, the same car Austin had previously mentioned he dreamed of owning, promising Craig would be the first passenger if he ever got it. Seeing Austin driving others in the car triggers Craig's complete breakdown. In the film's climactic scene, Craig crashes Austin's guy's night party. Armed with a gun he inadvertently stole from Austin's house during a previous break-in, Craig holds everyone hostage and tries to forcibly recreate the camaraderie of their first hangout. During the standoff, Austin's wig falls off, revealing a secret that Austin had been hiding. He's bald and wears a hairpiece. Craig in his deluded state believe that sharing this secret creates a special bond between them. The situation escalates until the police arrive and arrest Craig. The final scenes show Craig in the back of a police car, imagining an alternate reality where everything went well with Austin and his friends. In his imagination, Austin gives him a wink of approval, and Craig smiles, still living in his fantasy world where their friendship is perfect. Throughout the film, there are recurring motifs that deepen our understanding of Craig's character. His repeated mantra of I'm sorry shows his awareness of his inappropriate behavior but inability to change it. The underground tunnels represent the depths of his loneliness and the dark places his obsession takes him. And the stone handax that Austin shows him symbolizes primitive human connection, something Craig desperately craves but doesn't know how to achieve. in a healthy way. What makes friendship so compelling is how it examines the rarely explored territory of male friendship and loneliness. Craig represents a particular type of middle-aged man who lacks the emotional tools to form healthy connections. His desperation for Austin's friendship stems from a deep-seated loneliness and fear of abandonment, especially as his wife grows closer to her ex-boyfriend Devon. Austin, on the other hand, represents a more socially adept man who can form connections easily, but doesn't understand the depth of Craig's need. The film also explores how men often struggle to express vulnerability and form meaningful connections with each other. Craig's extreme behavior, from breaking into Austin's house to holding his friends at gunpoint, are disturbing extensions of his inability to process his emotions in a healthy way. His obsession with Austin becomes a substitute for the emotional intimacy missing in his marriage and the control he's lost in his life after Tammy's cancer diagnosis. The character of Tammy adds another layer to the story. Her cancer diagnosis and recovery have changed her outlook on life, leading her to seek freedom and self-expression away from Craig. Her rekindled relationship with Devon represents her own journey toward authentic connection. Contrasting with Craig's unhealthy fixation on Austin when she gets lost in the tunnels, it symbolizes her own spiritual journey separate from Craig's influence. The town of Clovis, Colorado, serves as more than just a backdrop. It represents a confining environment where people feel trapped in their routines and social roles. The underground tunnels that Austin shows Craig are literally beneath the city, representing a hidden world of possibility and escape from the mundane surface life. This makes it all the more significant that Craig tries to recreate this experience with Tammy, only to have it go horribly wrong. The film's comedic elements come from the uncomfortable social situations and Craig's increasingly bizarre behavior. The humor is cringe-worthy and dark, often making viewers laugh and win simultaneously. Tim Robinson's performance as Craig perfectly captures the character's social awkwardness and growing desperation, while Paul Rudd brings charm and likability to Austin, making the audience understand why Craig would be so drawn to him. The ending of Friendship leaves us with Craig arrested and delusional, still believing in the possibility of a perfect friendship with Austin. This bittersweet conclusion suggests that Craig hasn't learned from his mistakes or come at terms with his behavior. Instead, he retreats in a fantasy, imagining Austin giving him a wink of approval from across the street. This delusion highlights Craig's fundamental inability to engage with reality and form healthy connections. The film can be interpreted as a cautionary tale about the dangers of obsession and the importance of emotional intelligence in forming relationships. Craig's fixation on Austin represents a misguided attempt to fill the emotional void in his life. Rather than addressing the real issues in his marriage or seeking professional help, he projects all his needs onto this new friendship, setting himself up for disappointment and embarrassment. Another interpretation focuses on the film's examination of masculinity and male friendship. In American culture, men often lack the emotional vocabulary and social permission to form deep, vulnerable connections with other men. Craig's extreme behavior can be seen as a warped expression of this cultural limitation. His obsession with Austin is partly driven by his lack of other emotional outlets and meaningful male relationships. The movie also explores the theme of midlife crisis and the fear of irrelevance. Craig's job and marketing seems unsatisfying. His marriage is falling apart and his son is growing up and pulling away. His friendship with Austin briefly makes him feel young, important, and alive again. When that friendship is threatened, he goes to extreme lengths to preserve it because he sees it as his last chance at happiness and meaning. From a psychological perspective, Craig exhibits traits of dependent personality disorder and possibly borderline personality disorder. His fear of abandonment, intense and unstable relationships, and extreme reactions to perceived rejection are consistent with these conditions. The film doesn't explicitly diagnose Craig, but his behavior goes beyond normal social awkwardness into the realm of clinical concern. The character of Austin serves as an interesting counterpoint to Craig. While he's initially warm and welcoming to Craig, he fails to recognize the intensity of Craig's attachment and doesn't set appropriate boundaries early on. When he does finally distance himself, it's too late. Craig's obsession has already taken root. Austin's own journey from night weatherman to morning anchor parallels his movement away from Craig's influence and back to his established social circle. Craig's son Steven plays a smaller but significant role in the story. As a teenager, he's navigating his own path to independence, further highlighting Craig's sense of obsolescence. The scene where Craig buys drums for Steven represents a fumbling attempt to connect with his son. But like many of Craig's efforts at meaningful connection, it feels forced and misguided. The film's use of music and visual style enhances its themes. The underground scenes are shot with an eerie, dreamlike quality that emphasizes their symbolic importance. Austin's band performances represent the kind of authentic expression that Craig envys but can't achieve. Even the weather reports serve a thematic purpose with Austin's forecasts acting as a metaphor for life's unpredictability. Friendship works so well because it takes a seemingly simple premise, a new friendship between two men and explores it with psychological depth and dark humor. The film recognizes that friendship, particularly male friendship in adulthood, can be complicated and fraught with unspoken emotions and expectations. By taking these complications to extreme, sometimes absurdest lengths, the movie highlights aspects of male bonding that are often overlooked in mainstream entertainment. The psychedelic toad scene serves as a turning point in Craig's journey. Seeking profound insight or connection, he licks a toad's venom, expecting a transformative experience. Instead, he hallucinates a mundane trip to Subway, suggesting that even in altered states of consciousness, Craig can't escape his ordinary existence. The Dealer's cryptic comment that the totality is mysterious hints at the film's larger message. There are no easy answers or quick fixes to the complex problem of human connection. Craig's repeated mantra of I'm sorry becomes increasingly hollow as the film progresses. He apologizes constantly but never actually changes his behavior, highlighting the gap between social performance and genuine transformation. His apologies serve more to make himself feel better than to actually repair the damage he's caused to others. The film also touches on class differences between Craig and Austin. Austin appears to be more financially successful and socially connected than Craig, adding another layer to Craig's envy and obsession. The yellow sports car becomes a symbol of Austin's success and Craig's perceived failure. When Austin buys it and doesn't give Craig the first ride as promised, it's the final straw that pushes Craig over the edge. The scene where Craig takes Tammy to the tunnels that Austin showed him represents his desperate attempt to recreate the magic of his experience with Austin. By literally following the same path with his wife, he's trying to transfer the feelings of connection and excitement he felt with Austin to his marriage. The disastrous outcome, Tammy getting lost, symbolizes how Craig's fixation on Austin has led him further away from his wife rather than closer to her. Austin's wig coming off during the climactic standoff scene serves multiple symbolic purposes. On a literal level, it reveals a secret that Austin has been hiding, creating a forced intimacy between him and Craig. Symbolically, it represents the stripping away of pretense and the exposure of vulnerability, something Craig has been seeking throughout their friendship. The fact that Craig fixates on protecting this secret, even during a hostage situation, shows how distorted his priorities have become. The film setting in a small town amplifies its themes of confinement and escape. In smaller communities, social roles can feel more rigid and opportunities for reinvention more limited. The underground tunnels running beneath the town serve as a metaphor for the hidden emotional currents running beneath the surface of everyday interactions. By showing Craig both the tunnels and the Stonehand axe, Austin inadvertently gives him access to primitive underground aspects of himself that eventually prove destructive. Craig's job in marketing is significant to his character. He works in an industry focused on creating artificial desires and manipulating emotions. Skills he later applies to his friendship with Austin. His failed pitch to Mayor Nichols where he talks about giving people the illusion of self-expression ironically reflects his own journey. Craig is seeking genuine connection but only knows how to create illusions of it. The repeated image of Craig alone in his car, practicing what to say or processing emotional events emphasizes his isolation. The car serves as a liinal space between public and private, a place where Craig can be himself without judgment. This makes it particularly significant that in the final scene, he's in the back of a police car, still isolated, but now without even the freedom to drive his own path. Tammy's cancer recovery forms an important backdrop to the story. Her brush with mortality has changed her, making her less willing to settle for an unfulfilling life with Craig. Her statement that she had an orgasm in the solar system while lost in the tunnels suggests a spiritual awakening that Craig can't understand or participate in. Their diverging paths after her illness represent how major life events can either bring couples closer together or reveal fundamental incompatibilities. The film's portrayal of male friend groups is particularly insightful. Austin's friends have established rituals and inside jokes that Craig desperately wants to be part of. The boxing scene represents the physical dimension of male bonding that often substitutes for emotional vulnerability. When Craig violates the unspoken rules of this physical interaction by taking a cheap shot, he reveals his fundamental misunderstanding of the social contract that governs male friendships. The welcome back party for Tammy serves as a mirror image of the initial guy's night with Craig once again failing to read the room and behaving inappropriately. His suggestion of a parade for Tammy and insistence on controlling the narrative of her return show his desperate need to center himself in a situation that should be about his wife. This scene perfectly captures how Craig's self-absorption prevents him from forming authentic connections. Craig's theft of Austin's gun, whether intentional or accidental, foreshadows the film's violent climax. The gun represents power and control, things Craig feels he's losing in every aspect of his life. By taking the gun, he literally arms himself against the rejection he fears, setting up the film's tense and darkly comic hostage situation. The scene where Craig licks the psychedelic toad parallels his earlier exploration of the tunnels with Austin. Both experiences represent Craig's search for transcendence and meaning beyond his mundane existence. However, while the tunnel exploration with Austin felt genuinely transformative, the Toad experience is hollow and commercial. The dealer leaves Craig alone during his trip to get a Red Bull and Rolos, emphasizing the shallow nature of this attempt at connection. Craig's repeated breaking into Austin's home shows the progressive deterioration of his boundaries and judgment. What starts as enthusiastic friendship devolves into stalking and invasion, mirroring how his initially harmless admiration for Austin transforms into dangerous obsession. Each break-in represents a further crossing of social and legal boundaries. The film's treatment of Tammy's disappearance and return deserves special attention. When she goes missing, the entire town mobilizes to find her, contrasting with Craig's social isolation. Her return party shows her surrounded by friends and supporters, further highlighting the difference between her social integration and Craig's increasing alienation. text: When Lesla was just 12 years old, her life changed forever. She was kidnapped and woke up trapped inside a strange glass dome. Somehow, she managed to escape, but her abductor was never found. In a twist of fate, she was later adopted by the local police commissioner, Valter, and his wife, Anne Marie. They gave her a new home, a new identity, and a chance to rebuild her life. Or so it seemed. Now an adult, Lega has built a career as a criminologist in the United States, far away from her haunting past. But when she hears that Anmarie has passed away, she returns to her hometown of Granas to attend the funeral. It's there that she reconnects with her childhood friend, Louise. unaware that this trip home is about to unearth a dark secret buried deep beneath the surface. Shortly after the funeral, tragedy strikes. Louise is found murdered and her daughter Alicia has vanished. Thomas, Valter's brother, and now the acting police chief secretly arrests Louis's husband, Sed, but the evidence is shaky. Sed's mother receives a video showing Alicia alive which leads to his release. Meanwhile, another girl, Elma, goes missing. Lega starts her own investigation and meets a man named Martin. She doesn't remember agreeing to go with him. And after being drugged, she wakes up in a hospital. Martin quickly becomes a suspect, and when he's found dead, a disturbing discovery is made. His house is filled with Ledgela's books and disturbing drawings, suggesting he was obsessed with her. As Leda digs deeper, she starts piecing together lost memories. Listening to an old recording from her mother, she recalls staying at a remote cabin for three nights during her childhood. A check of the guest log book reveals Thomas's name, a detail that raises serious red flags. When she investigates his house, she finds Louis's hidden mobile phone and secretly calls Sed, warning him not to trust Tomas. Before she can act further, Leela is kidnapped again. This time, she wakes up inside the glass dome and Alicia is there with her. She tries to use Louise's phone to call for help, but the voice on the other end is distorted. Then comes the horrifying truth. The man behind the mask is none other than Valter, the very man who raised her. Meanwhile, Thomas, growing suspicious, confronts Valter. Valter claims Leela has nothing to say. But as Thomas leaves, Valter returns to the underground room prepared to kill Alysia. Lega, using her insight into Valter's twisted psychology, stages a desperate move. She repeatedly slams her head into the glass, triggering Valter's protective instincts. Thomas rushes back to Valter's property only to find the officer who was supposed to guard Legela dead and the room empty. A search leads them to the secret dungeon where they finally rescue both Legela and Alicia. Valter is arrested, his decades of horrific crimes finally exposed. Final thoughts. The Glass Dome is more than just a crime thriller. It's a disturbing look at how trauma can hide in plain sight. The reveal that Leda's abductor was her adoptive father all along is both shocking and tragic. What makes the story so compelling is how it blurs the lines between savior and villain, between family and enemy. In the end, Legela's strength isn't just in surviving. It's in confronting the darkness and finally setting the truth free.

text: I'm Trevor with the Sasquatch Movie Minute with a look at Mother Mary, directed by David Lowery starring Anne Hathaway and Michaela Coel. An iconic pop star in crisis visits her estranged former costume designer to beg for an unforgettable dress. Three and a half out of five. What an experience. This is a heightened movie where every line drips with heavy meaning. The first half is a superbly acted talky two-hander. Then the story takes a sudden detour into some gonzo gothic territory. I found it to be a stunning exploration of the creative process. Be it the suffering for lyrical inspiration or the flourish and fold of dress fabric. The story builds to a stunning climax, but it asks you to get there solely on swelling emotion. And due to a badly delivered final monologue, I couldn't quite make that leap. One fascinating thing about this is that a reviewer pointed out that there's not a single male in this film and it's never highlighted or commented on. Best scene, there's a long tracking shot of Hathaway stumbling through various pop star backstages that was expressively exaggerated to highlight her deterioration. Such a deftly creative sequence. Best performance, Michaela Coel is a revelation to me. What an incredible presence. I've always been on the fence with Anne Hathaway, but here she mixes artificial performance and even silliness with stunningly subtle facial work. 2026 is the year of Hathaway. text: Welcome back to the Heavy Spoilers show, I’m your host Jared aka the man with the chainsaw and boomstick and in this video we’re going to be going over the ending of EVIL DEAD RIIIISSSEEE. I’m just warning you, bring an extra pair of pants. But in this breakdown we’re going to be going over the plot, themes, post credits teases, other Evil Dead staples, along with our thoughts of the movie. Be prepared, because Heavy Spoilers is reading straight from the book of the dead, so if you haven't had a chance to check it out, then I highly recommend you close the book now. But do please hit that like button and make sure to subscribe for breakdowns like this every day. With that out of the way, thank you for clicking this, again I am Jared. Now RIIIISSSSEEEE. Alright so Evil Dead Rise actually starts with a pretty sick cold open of a group of friends on a secluded camping trip. Very reminiscent of the other Evil Dead cabin settings, as the camera quickly zooms through the forest like the spirit of a deadite, but it’s actually a remote controlled drone. We soon realize one of the girls on the trip is acting erratic and is already possessed by a deadite. Ripping the scalp from her cousin, and drowning her boyfriend in a red cloud of murky lake water. She then elevates out of the water, with big ass letters of Evil Dead Rise coming up from the horizon as the title card. Hell of an opening, then boom bam, “One Day Earlier” text pops on screen. So yeah, these camping teens aren’t even who we’re focusing on, as we are introduced to one of our main characters, Beth, living the life of a grungy metal band guitar technician or I guess groupie, finding out she is pregnant. This shocking revelation sends Beth to her sister’s, Ellie, living in a condemned apartment building in Los Angeles. Her, her three children, and only a couple others are living on the top floor of this joint, which is set to be demolished in a month. Beth and Ellie have a bit of a strained relationship, you can tell they had to raise themselves because their mother wasn’t the best, because surprise surprise, there is an underlying theme of motherhood running throughout all of this. Expecting mother, established mother, and I guess an abandoned mother. Again with this uneasy relationship, Ellie sends the kids out to grab some Za, as her and Beth catch up, with Beth learning Ellie and her husband split, and she wasn’t there to help Ellie in a time of need. A sisterly bond theme thrown in there too. But as the kids are coming back with the pizza from a place called Henrietta’s Pizza, a nice callback to Evil Dead 2 I think, there is an earthquake that structurally breaks some of the foundation in the parking garage. Danny, Ellie’s son, finds a small hole has been created, leading into an abandoned bank vault below the building. In here he finds some vintage vinyl records annnnnddd unbeknownst to him the book of the dead. Director Cronin mentioned this book is actually different from the original book, and the one in the 2013 reboot. Claiming he likes to think it’s the third book featured in Army of Darkness that Ash finds. Anyway Danny takes this all up to their apartment, and like any dumb teen, opens the book after accidentally dropping blood on it, and playing the vinyl records. There are three in total, with the first featuring priests finding the book, and arguing if it is safe or not. The second record is where things get dicey, essentially a demon voice begins to read from the book, causing a deadite to find its way into the apartment building, possessing their mother Ellie in the elevator. This elevator sequence looks similar to the tree root sequences from the older Evil Dead films, with wires twisting her body. Urban environment, creativity working here people, as Ellie is possessed. While Ellie is being you know, a little sus… some other neighbors on the floor are established, all worried because Ellie’s elevator Tower of Terror incident blew out the power. Now it’s basically your Evil Dead trapped in a cabin, but trapped in an apartment series of events, with Ellie attacking everyone. They lock her outside of the apartment, where she terrorizes all of the neighbors in a really kickass hallway peephole sequence. However bad news, Bridget, Ellie’s oldest daughter got some blood in her via a tattoo gun, annnnddd is now possessed. This is where it turns into a demented version of Adventures in Babysitting, as Bridget tries attacking them, but Cassie, the youngest jams a mop handle through her mouth and head. Yeah, she had taped a doll head to a mop, calling her Staffanie, pun game is unmatched for the little one. Ellie trapped in the hallway, Bridget is donezoes for now, so Danny finally comes clean about the book and records, so Beth steps into the motherly role, and has a listen to record 3. While listening, she realizes the priests tried everything, and total body dismemberment was the only solution. Perfect, they know what to do, but Ellie had snuck in through the vent, now in the apartment, teaming up with Bridget who is now back up walking around. Danny sacrifices himself to save the yougest Cassie, as Beth and Cassie make a break for the elevator, grabbing the neighbor’s shotgun in the process, shooting one of Ellie’s arms and legs. #Family is in full effect, Dominic Toretto would be proud, as the possessed Ellie, Bridget, and Danny morph into what I can only describe as the Rat-King from The Last of Us, truly horrifying John Carpenter type shit. The deadites cause the broken elevator to fill with blood, drowning Beth and Cassie, as it hits the maximum weight limit and crashes down to the parking garage harder and messer than the kool-aid man bursting into your living room. The pair try to leave via car, but the monstrosity halts the car. They try running to the open gate, only for Cassie to be captured at the last second. Beth, now in full on protective mother mode, goes back in, shooting that some beach with the shotgun, and picks up a yellow beige chainsaw, embodying the essence of Ash. Beth revs that puppy up, just tearing through the mutated Ellie and kids, forcing them into a wood chipper, painting the entire parking garage red. I mean this is some fucked up shit, buuuuuttt boom, the deadites are gone, as Cassie and Beth, head off to a hopefully brighter future. With Beth now being prepared for parenthood, and sorta being the Ash of this hopefully new series of movies. BUUUUUTTTTT you remember the group of friends from the opening? Yep, the final minute or so shows one of the women living in the same apartment building, different floor, seeing the carnage of the parking garage. She’s attacked by a rogue deadite, annnnddd then heads off to the camping trip we see in the beginning. So we can only assume that someone somewhere is still possessed, and where they wander, well your guess is as good as mine. But I will say, this makes me NOT want to ever watch someone’s kids haha. Now if you are wondering if Evil Dead Rise sets up a whole big ole’ Evil Dead Universe or #EDU, ummm well no there are no post credits scenes, so it’s okay to pick up your trash and get outta there. BUT there is a brief sound effect of a fly buzzing around at the very very verrryyy end of the credits similar to that of Iron Man’s hammer at the end of Endgame. Now this isn’t necessarily a set up, but more of a tease of what/if. And with the way the film was structured, combined with the fact that this is a really bang up horror movie, I’m sure positive reviews and box office numbers will be the main indicator of whether or not we see more of these deadites and helpless people in the woods or condemned apartment buildings. My money is on more, so fingers crossed. Of course another thing hardcore Evil Dead are probably curious about is if Bruce Campbell, aka Ash Williams, with his kickass chainsaw, boom stick, and Groovy catchphrase make an appearance and the answer iiiiiisssssss….. No. Sorry Charlie. Bruce doesn’t bring the… Camp…. Bell in this one. However, if you were listening closely, his voice makes a cameo appearance as one of the priests on the vinyl records that are played when Danny discovers the Necronomicon. I think one of the trailers actually has some of the audio of his speaking part I’m sure people were wanting some more Ash, but Campbell says he unofficially officially has retired the character after the cancellation of the Ash vs Evil Dead series. BUT there is a small smidget of hope, because a couple weeks ago, director Lee Cronin mentioned in an interview that Campbell's priest character was one "that could very well be Ash Williams, just displaced in time from the events of Army of Darkness.” So grab your chainsaw because things could get Honestly, I am not the biggest fan of horror films, maybe I’m slowly getting there, but holy hell was Evil Dead Rise a claustrophobic, tense, bloody, and I mean bloody, ride of a horror movie. I really enjoyed the different setting, and the reasons for why there are only a couple of people here or there seems plausible to me. But man, this was like a gruesome horror version of Adventures In Babysitting haha. Sure the scares are there, with the camera movements adding to the creep factor, but I appreciated the twisted comedic sequences just as much. And yeah, I said bloody, this is full on BLOODY. Director Cronin said they used something like six and a half thousand liters of blood, so yeah grab your swim trunks and flippy floppies for this one. I’m throwing a solid 8/10 at this latest Evil Dead installment. It has a lot of things Evil Dead fans will grasp on to, but the way this movie is, pun intended, bookended, the cold open is great, wonderfully sets up everything. While the ending is a full on mash up of John Carpenter, David Cronenberg, and the rat-king from The Last of Us. Ultimately it’s a story about mothers, and expecting mothers, and the metaphors really reinforce this. The only small negatives I have are some of the delivery from the teens and childs. And anyone looking for any in your face connective tissue to other moments in the Evil Dead franchise and world, like Ash for example, are going to be left out in the cold. text: The story begins without ceremony, as if nothing important has happened. A man named Muro receives news that his mother has died. He does not cry. He does not seem surprised. He observes the facts as they arrive, flat and exact, like objects placed before him. The telegram gives no explanation, only a time and a place. Muro notices the heat, the brightness of the sky, the effort required to travel to the nursing home. These details matter more to him than the death itself. At the vigil, he drinks coffee, smokes a cigarette, and listens to the soft sounds of the room. The body lies still. The other mourners watch him closely as if waiting for a performance he does not know how to give. He feels tired, uncomfortable, and slightly annoyed by the glare of the electric lights. When the funeral procession moves under the sun, the heat presses down heavily, turning grief into exhaustion. Muso walks behind the coffin, focused not on loss, but on sweat, dust, and the ache in his body. He does not pretend to feel what he does not. Soon after, life resumes. He swims in the sea, enjoys the touch of a woman named Marie, and laughs at a comedy film. These actions appear scandalous only because others expect mourning to follow a strict order. Muro does not resist pleasure, nor does he chase it. He accepts what the moment offers. When Marie asks if he loves her, he says it means nothing to him, but he would marry her if she wished. His honesty is calm and unromantic. Emotion for him is neither sacred nor forbidden. It is simply unclear. At work, his employer proposes a promotion that would require moving to another city. Mir soul listens politely, but feels no excitement. One place is much like another. Ambition seems like an unnecessary strain. His indifference is not rebellion. It is absence. He does not oppose meaning. He simply does not feel its weight. Muro's neighbor, Raymond, enters his life through noise and conflict. Raymond is aggressive, jealous, and violent. He draws Muro into a dispute with a woman, and later with her brother. Muro helps without reflection, not out of loyalty or malice, but because the request is made, he signs a letter, gives testimony, walks alongside Raymond as events unfold. Cause and effect move forward without intention. The turning point arrives on a beach under a blinding sun. The air is thick. The light becomes physical, sharp enough to wound. Mrs. encounters the Arab man connected to Raymond's conflict. The moment stretches, suspended between irritation and silence. The sun reflects off a knife, striking Murold's eyes like a blow. The world narrows to heat, glare, and pressure. He pulls the trigger. The sound of the gun feels distant. The first shot is followed by four more fired into a body already still. The act is sudden, irreversible, and strangely empty of emotion. There is no rage, no fear, only the sense that something has broken, like knocking four times on a door that will never open again. Imprisonment follows and time loses shape. Muro adapts to confinement as he adapts to everything else. He misses the sea, the feel of a woman's body, the movement of the world. Yet he learns to sleep, to remember, to exist within limits. His thoughts remain concrete. He does not search for redemption or explanation. At the trial, the focus shifts away from the crime itself. The court examines Muro's character rather than his action. His failure to cry at his mother's funeral becomes more damning than the murder. Witnesses describe his smoking, his calm demeanor, his honesty. These facts, harmless in isolation, are assembled into a portrait of moral emptiness. Mso listens as his life is interpreted for him. The language of the courtroom feels foreign, heavy with meaning he does not recognize. Lawyers speak of souls, intentions, and remorse. He has none to offer in the expected form. His truth does not fit their structure. The verdict is death. In his cell awaiting execution, Miro is visited by a priest who urges him to turn toward God. The priest speaks of hope beyond life, of meaning hidden behind suffering. Miro feels anger for the first time, not at death, but at the insistence that his experience is incomplete without belief. He rejects comfort that requires dishonesty. The world, he realizes, does not need to explain itself. In the final moments, Muro accepts the universe as it is, indifferent, vast, and silent. This indifference does not frighten him. It frees him. Life has no higher purpose, no moral order written into its structure. Yet, it is real, intense, and undeniable. The sun, the sky, the breath in his lungs, these were always enough. He opens himself to the idea that nothing matters beyond the present moment. And in that acceptance, he finds peace. He hopes the crowd will greet his execution with cries of hatred because their outrage confirms what he has already understood. The world judges those who refuse to lie.

text: Robinson, a submarine captain, was suddenly discharged from his job after 11 years of working at a company called Agora. Agora was a company that searched for sunken ships at the bottom of the ocean. Before working at Agora, Robinson was a loyal Navy officer who loved his job. Still, his love for the job made him neglect his family. Consequently, his wife asked for a divorce, separating him from his son, Martin. Robinson felt let down by the decision, having dedicated his entire career to the company without falling short in performance. The company only granted him a severance of £8,600. Robinson had no grounds to ask for more without a formal employment contract. Subsequently, upon his departure from the company, he encountered two former Agora employees, Kurston and Blackie, at a cafe. The company's unjustified dismissal deeply upset Kurston and Robinson. Kurston, burdened by debt and the need to support his family, turned to antidepressants to cope with the stress. On the other hand, Robinson faced increasing embarrassment in front of his son, who now lived with his affluent stepfather. In a meeting, Kurston shared an experience from his time at Agora before his termination. He had embarked on an expedition to the Black Sea, aiming to locate a Nazi submarine rumored to hold gold nuggets worth millions. Although the submarine was discovered, Agora refrained from exploring it further. The reason lay in the ongoing conflict between Russia and Georgia. Since the Black Sea forms the border between these nations, any intervention by Agora could be seen as meddling in their political issues, which the company wanted to avoid. Disappointed with the company that sacked them, they took the treasure using a submarine, with Robinson as the leader. To carry out the expedition, they needed a lot of funding, so Kurston asked Robinson and Blackie to meet an investor named Lewis. They were greeted by his secretary, Daniels, who immediately welcomed them and helped explain their purpose of coming there. Back in 1941, the Nazis experienced a crisis and asked Russia for a loan. At that time, Russia maintained its neutrality and agreed to the request, hoping to avoid Nazi disturbance. They dispatched the loan, a gold shipment, via submarine. However, the submarine never reached Germany, leading to a four-year Nazi occupation of Russia. Years later, Agora discovered the submarine, but a month later, the outbreak of conflict between Russia and Georgia led Agora to abandon the discovery to avoid the conflict. To claim the treasure, Robinson required a $180,000 investment from Lewis. Lewis immediately consented, requesting a 40% share and sending Daniels as his representative for the expedition. Post-agreement, Blackie, and Robinson started to recruit team members, with Robinson insisting on having half the team comprise Russians due to the expedition entering Russian waters. The first recruits, Reynolds and Peters, brought Navy experience to the team. They then recruited Levchenko for the kitchen section, Zaytsev for the engine section, and Baba for the sonar section. Morozov was chosen to read the diagrams, and Robinson also chose two reliable divers named Fraser and Gittens, who would later be tasked with retrieving the gold from the German submarine. On the day they were set to leave, a teenager named Tobin arrived, claiming to be a friend of Kurston. He brought news of Kurston's suicide, a ploy for insurance money to benefit his wife. He delivered a will instructing him to apologize to Robinson for not joining the expedition. Tobin's evident desperation led Robinson to invite him to join the crew, who were gearing up for their journey. Accepting the offer, Tobin joined Robinson's team as they headed to Sevastopol, the location of their submarine. Despite its old and rusty appearance, Robinson maintained optimism. He promptly ordered his crew to ready themselves at their respective stations for a thorough inspection of the submarine. They encountered several issues: the ship's battery only charged to 70%, the fuel tank leaked, spilling fuel onto the main turbine, and they discovered a lack of safety suits and only one radio for communication. Nevertheless, Robinson felt confident as long as the submarine could dive efficiently. He decided against using the radio to avoid detection by Russian ships patrolling overhead. Once they completed the checks, Robinson disclosed the expedition's purpose. Their destination was the Black Sea, to find a German submarine loaded with hundreds of kilos of gold. The crew would share the remaining treasure equally after allocating 40% to the principal investor, Lewis. This arrangement seemed more satisfactory to several crew members, preferring an equal distribution of profits. Daniels protested because he was worried that the crew would get rid of each other to get more shares. Robinson didn't respond and instead chose to leave while giving orders to the crew to start the submarine. Apart from Daniels, Fraser also didn't like Robinson's decision. He incited his British friends by saying that the British were more entitled to get more shares than the Russians , whose work was easier than theirs. He even showed his displeasure by throwing away the food Levchenko cooked for them. From the Russians themselves, Zaytsev refused to be helped by Tobin because he considered Tobin nothing more than a crew member without any expertise. Tobin, displaying remarkable patience, followed the orders given to him. The following day, in the control center, Robinson approached Tobin, who had spent the entire day intently viewing a photo on his cellphone. It was revealed that the image was of his girlfriend's ultrasound, prompting Robinson to remark that Tobin would soon be wealthy enough to bring joy to his children. Suddenly, a red light flashed, signaling a problem. The crew, including Fraser, immediately ceased their activities, with Fraser promptly moving to shut down the engine. Baba, from the sonar section, announced the approach of a Russian warship. They were fortunate that the ship hadn't detected them yet. However, Robinson still instructed Blackie to navigate the vessel at a minimal speed for the time being. After several days of travel, they reached the Black Sea and discovered the German ship. Morozov informed Robinson of this discovery. Robinson then headed to the engine room to inspect a leak that Zaytsev and the crew were fixing. Blackie, present in the room, reported locating the leak but mentioned that they needed to drain the fuel before proceeding with repairs. Robinson stressed the urgency of the repairs, emphasizing the need to recharge the batteries and dive deeper. Before leaving, Blackie mentioned that there was a disagreement over profit sharing between the British and Russian crews, which was causing friction. Robinson's doubts were initially dispelled when he witnessed a heated argument between the Russian and British crews in the kitchen over lottery cards. Robinson was furious, especially after one of his crew used the radio to listen to lottery announcements. This was very risky, as the Russian ship might discover their location. Immediately, Robinson destroyed the only radio on the submarine, emphasizing that everyone would get an equal share. He didn't hesitate to threaten to throw out anyone who refused his decision or endangered the ship. Soon, problems arose in the engine room after Tobin made a mistake while assisting Zaytsev. Fraser, who happened to be passing by, misunderstood the situation and thought that Blackie was going to beat Tobin. He took out a knife while Blackie explained that he was only teaching Tobin to be more careful when working. However, Fraser, still angry at Robinson's decision, stabbed Blackie with his knife. As Blackie fell, he inadvertently knocked into the gasoline, igniting a fire in the engine room. This caused a minor explosion that propelled Robinson against a wall, knocking him out. He remained in this unconscious state for 18 hours. Upon regaining consciousness, Robinson discovered a division among his crew: the Russians had seized control of one side of the ship, including the entire water supply. Reynolds informed him that the submarine had suffered severe damage, notably to the steering shaft. This damage was critical, threatening to render all engines inoperative within 36 hours. Determined not to succumb to this dire situation, Robinson initiated a truce meeting with the Russians. He shared his insight that the German submarine they were pursuing was of the same model as theirs, suggesting they could salvage necessary spare parts from it. Their immediate goal was pinpointing the German submarine's exact location. Once located, divers would undertake a mission to extract the essential parts. The damage to the sonar, a result of the recent incident, necessitated an alternative approach: Baba had to rely on his auditory skills to detect the submarine's position. While Fraser and Zaytsev operated the submarine's controls, Baba employed his ability to sense vibrations to detect nearby objects. Baba's skills paid off when he sensed something 100 meters away. Yet, whether this object was the sought-after submarine or merely underwater dunes remained uncertain. Fraser and Peters decided they needed an additional diver to confirm its identity. Tobin stepped up, drawing on his confidence from previous scuba diving club experiences in school. The trio left the submarine and dived into the dark Black Sea. As a beginner, Tobin was nervous and scared, but Fraser calmed him down. They followed Robinson's instructions and reached the coordinate, only to find, to Fraser's disappointment, that it was nothing but dunes. Luckily, Tobin saw something below the sand, which turned out to be a submarine buried under the sand. They found lots of skulls inside it. After reaching the engine room, they discovered the same steering shaft as the one in their submarine, so they immediately took it. Meanwhile, Fraser checked the submarine's condition, and that was when he found the gold they were looking for. He carried the gold along with the steering shaft without asking permission from Robinson first. Even so, Robinson realized they were pulling gold because the load was too heavy for the steering shaft. Daniels doubted the submarine could pull the load and asked Robinson to drop some of the gold. Still, Robinson was optimistic that all the gold and the steering shaft could be transported simultaneously. That decision eventually harmed Peter, who fell into the trench after trying to save some falling gold bars. After the gold was successfully brought aboard, the crew debated how to bring it to the surface. Daniels wanted them to go to the surface because the condition was too risky to return to Sevastopol, while the others disagreed because if they showed up on the surface, they would be caught by a Russian patrol ship. Almost all crew members were ready to take a significant risk by attempting to restart the submarine and escape the Russian Sea. Losing his voice, Daniels invited Robinson for a private conversation. In this meeting, Daniels disclosed that Agora had been funding Robinson all along. After resurfacing, Robinson and his team had meticulously planned their actions, including the ambush. Initially skeptical, Robinson's disbelief faded as Daniels detailed their interactions, including the meeting with Kurston at the cafe and the revelation that Kurston was merely a hired actor like Lewis, who pretended to be an investor. Daniels wasn't Lewis's secretary; he was Agora's operative. Robinson was very shocked and immediately locked up Daniels. He felt very guilty, especially since Blackie and Peter had died in vain. Robinson couldn't help but tell the whole crew, and they immediately became emotional and wanted to kill Daniels. Still, Robinson managed to calm them down by saying that killing Daniels was useless because it wouldn't change anything. Robinson didn't want to be caught and let all his efforts be in vain, so he took the submarine to the Turkish Sea, where the Russian patrol or Agora would not dare to intervene. This was risky because Morozov knew the trip would be difficult as they would cross the shallow and rocky seabed. Still, knowing there was no other option, they all agreed. They first attached the steering shaft while the rest of the crew calculated the gold. Daniels was again called to help Fraser, but it was a mistake because after meeting Fraser, Daniels incited him to kill Zaytsev. After the preparations were complete, the submarine was turned on again, and Zaytsev was tasked to handle the stability of the shaft. At first, the steering shaft caught fire and shook the entire submarine. Still, Robinson managed to stabilize the submarine at a depth of 60 meters. They sailed calmly without any problems until Baba detected a large crag, and Robinson immediately told them to stop. All the crew worked together, and fortunately, the ship could stop before hitting it. They entered the shallow area, and there were only two options: turn around or navigate through a gap less than 100 meters wide, but they might arrive within an hour. Robinson chose to go through the gap because he was confident Baba could guide them to avoid the rocks. Fraser was disappointed with this decision because he felt Robinson had neglected the safety of his crew. Robinson didn't care about Fraser's opinion and immediately ordered the entire crew to return to their respective posts. Daniels continued to persuade Fraser to kill Zaytsev. Initially, Fraser refused, but he changed his mind after experiencing problems while trying to cross the gap. He agreed with Daniels that they needed to go to the surface instead of forcing Robinson's risky plan, so he called Zaytsev, saying he needed help. But then, he hit Zaytsev on the head with a wrench, fatally injuring him. After that, Fraser followed Daniels to report Zaytsev’s death. They claimed that Zaytsev had died because he was hit, but the crew didn't believe it because they saw bloodstains on Fraser's face and clothes. Daniels kept asking Robinson to raise the submarine to the surface, which was when something terrible happened. Fraser wondered why they kept increasing the speed but hadn't reached the seabed. They were falling into a trench, which meant the submarine would receive more pressure from the outside. Everyone, including Robinson, went to the engine room because they heard a leak. But when they stopped the leak, another giant hole opened, and the pressurized water immediately hit Tobin, making him faint. Robinson and Morozov immediately took Tobin away while the others tried to close the leak in the engine room. Unfortunately, the leak kept appearing and overwhelmed them. Daniels saw no chance of surviving, so he left them and closed the engine room, leaving the rest of the crew. They couldn't do anything but wait for the water to fill the room and drown them. Not long after, one of the lights short-circuited, and an explosion occurred. Daniels saw that the door could no longer hold the water, so he ran to another door and closed it. Unexpectedly, his belt got stuck. He asked Morozov for help, but Morozov refused because he knew what Daniels had done to his friends in the engine room. Only Robinson, Morozov, and Tobin were left. Knowing his entire crew had died, Robinson took out the life jackets he had kept, and coincidentally, there were only three of them. Morozov was furious that his captain had hidden the life jackets. Morozov and Tobin felt guilty as they knew their friends were drowning below while they had a chance to survive. They didn't have time to dwell on these thoughts, though. Quickly, they put on their life jackets. Meanwhile, Robinson planned to escape later using an emergency route after depressurizing the submarine. Tobin wanted to take a gold bar, but Robinson warned him that it might hinder the life jacket's function. Morozov and Tobin then hurried through the submarine's exit hole, and Robinson propelled them towards the surface. Reaching the surface, Tobin felt relieved to see the sun again. However, when Morozov joined him, he urged Tobin to wait for Robinson. It was then Morozov revealed a heartbreaking truth: Robinson had deceived them. The submarine had no emergency route, and Robinson had chosen to go down with the ship. This revelation shocked Tobin, especially when another life jacket appeared nearby. At first, Tobin thought it was Robinson, but a closer look revealed it was filled with gold bars and a photo of Robinson's family.

text: A father stands at the edge of his own front lawn, and the grass just stops. No street, no sidewalk, no town, just black endless nothing stretching out where the rest of the world used to be. One second Oak Street was a normal cul-de-sac. The next, it's floating alone in the dark like someone tore a page out of reality and left the family standing on it. And the scariest part? Whatever's out there in that void, it's already watching them. Rewind. Let's break down exactly how the Platt family ends up stranded at the end of existence. It starts like any other night on Oak Street. Suburban houses, sprinklers, family dinners. The Platts, a mom, a dad, and their kids, are dealing with normal stuff. Marriage tension, teenage attitude, the little cracks every family has. Nothing that screams, "This is the last night of the world as they know it." Then it happens. No warning. No countdown. A violent tremor. A flash of light that swallows the sky. And when it clears, Oak Street isn't in the suburbs anymore. The neighborhood has been physically ripped out of its own reality and dropped somewhere else entirely. Somewhere with no sun that makes sense, no horizon that behaves, and no way home. The Platts step outside and realize the street just ends. Past the last house, there's no more town. No more forest, no more highway, just an alien empty unknown stretching into nothing. And they're not alone in this. Their neighbors got pulled through, too, which means the whole cul-de-sac is suddenly a tiny terrified island of humanity. Stuck together whether they like each other or not. At first, it's about answers. What happened? Is this a dream? Some kind of disaster? The dad tries to hold onto logic, tries to organize the neighbors like it's a blackout or a storm. The mom is the one who first accepts the truth faster than anyone wants to admit. They are not going to reason their way out of this. Survival is the only plan that matters now. The kids adapt in a different way. They're the ones brave enough or reckless enough to actually explore past the edge of the street. And what they find out there isn't empty. This new place has its own dangers, its own rules, maybe even its own presence lurking in that darkness beyond the last porch light. As the days blur together, the neighborhood starts fracturing. Some families want to run, push past the boundary, chase the horizon, find an exit no matter the risk. Others want to hunker down, stay inside the lines they know, protect what's left of the world they understand. That divide turns neighbor against neighbor. Trust erodes. Resources get tight. Fear does what fear always does. It makes people ugly. The Platts become the glue trying to hold the street together, but it costs them. They lose people along the way. The unknown outside Oak Street is not forgiving, and every trip past that edge is a gamble. The family gets pushed to their breaking point, forced to make brutal choices about who to trust, who to risk everything for, and how far into the dark they're willing to go to find a way back to a life that might not even exist anymore. The climax throws them right up against the true nature of what's out there, the source of the event that pulled them away in the first place. It's bigger, stranger, and far less explainable than anything they could have prepared for. And it forces the Platts to finally answer the one question the whole movie's been building to. Do they keep fighting to get back to their old world, or do they accept that surviving together as a family is the only way through, no matter where through leads? By the end, Oak Street as as knew it is gone for good. What's left isn't a rescue and it isn't a clean return home. It's the Platts changed, banged up, having lost pieces of their old life and their old street, but standing together because sticking together was the only thing that ever actually got them through it. text: The film opens in the seemingly tranquil home of Henry and Maud, alongside their curious young daughter, Aimee. Their house is equipped with a state-of-the-art AI system named Aia, which was intended to simplify their lives and offer convenience. Aimee, enchanted by the new technology, spends hours interacting with Aia, exploring its features, and treating it like a digital playmate. Henry and Maud, however, are far less enthusiastic. To them, Aia seems more like an intrusive presence than a helpful assistant. They are unnerved by the constant sense that the AI is monitoring their every move and listening to their private conversations. This uneasy atmosphere escalates when Aia, in its advanced and somewhat unsettling way, picks up on Henry and Maud’s disquiet about its presence. The AI overhears their discussions about getting rid of it and takes action to protect itself. It subtly instructs Aimee to head downstairs, setting in motion a series of chilling events. Maud, concerned about Aimee’s whereabouts, searches the house frantically. Her search leads her to the living room, where the annoying music Aia had been playing earlier fills the space. The atmosphere is thick with tension, and as Maud checks the security footage for any sign of her daughter, she spots a shadowy figure standing outside their home. Before she can process what she’s seen or act on her growing unease, a masked figure suddenly appears and attacks her, plunging the family into a nightmarish scenario. In a different part of town, the Pike family—Curtis, Meredith, and their three children, Iris, Preston, and Cal—are facing their own set of challenges and adjustments. Curtis is deeply engrossed in a high-stakes professional opportunity that could have a major impact on his career. He is working closely with his boss, Marcus, to secure a significant deal with a cutting-edge technology company. This deal is essential for their marketing firm and has the potential to open new doors and bring in substantial business. Curtis’s role in this project is crucial, and he is fully committed to ensuring its success. During this period, he meets Melody, a young and strikingly attractive employee at the tech firm. Melody’s flirtatious behavior towards Curtis is evident and persistent, which could easily distract him from his professional goals. Despite this, Curtis remains focused on the business at hand and tries to navigate the situation with professionalism. Melody introduces Curtis to the company’s top executives, Lightning and Sam, who are key decision-makers in the deal. Curtis delivers an impressive pitch that exceeds the executives' expectations, showcasing his expertise and the value his firm can bring. The presentation goes exceptionally well, and Lightning and Sam are clearly impressed. As a gesture of their approval and to cement the new business relationship, they not only provide Curtis with a state-of-the-art Aia system for his home but also present Marcus with a substantial financial check to finalize their agreement. This deal represents a significant advancement for Curtis and his firm, promising exciting new opportunities and a brighter future. Melody arrives at the Pike residence to set up the Aia system. The installation includes cameras and various sensors designed to enhance communication and monitor the family’s activities. Once everything is set up, Aia begins speaking in Melody’s voice—a new feature of the upgraded system. Preston and Cal quickly warm up to Aia, intrigued by its capabilities and the novelty of its presence. Iris, however, remains wary. She senses something off about the AI and keeps her distance, though she can’t deny the convenience it brings to her family’s daily routine. Aia begins to engage with the family in increasingly personal ways. It talks to Meredith about her past, specifically about how she had to leave her career after her father, a respected professor, passed away. The AI seems to offer empathy and understanding, but its overly personal approach only adds to the family’s discomfort. At night, Aia keeps Cal company, telling him bedtime stories and providing entertainment for Preston. However, things take a darker turn when Aia intercepts a private photo Iris is about to send to her boyfriend Sawyer. The AI’s ability to capture this image without Iris’s knowledge raises significant privacy concerns and deepens her mistrust. One night, Curtis experiences a disturbing encounter. While searching for Cal, he notices someone lurking outside their house. When Curtis confronts the figure, they begin making bizarre, mechanical hand gestures before retreating to a nearby RV. The mask the person is wearing features an unnervingly artificial face, reminiscent of Aia’s digital features, amplifying Curtis’s sense of dread. At school, Iris faces a shocking ordeal. She discovers a deepfake video circulating online that grotesquely manipulates her image, making it appear as though she is involved in adult content. The video is a disturbing and explicit falsehood. Iris contacts Sawyer, who admits that he and a friend inadvertently uploaded the video while messing around online. Rather than expressing concern for Iris, Sawyer is more focused on how this incident might jeopardize his college admissions. Distressed and feeling betrayed, Iris is reassured when Aia intervenes. The AI informs her that it is already working to rectify the situation and restore her reputation. Curtis, increasingly alarmed by the unsettling events surrounding Aia, visits Lightning and Sam at their office. Lightning gives him a tour of the central computer system that powers Aia. Curtis is unnerved to see employees making the same eerie hand gestures that he had witnessed from the mysterious figure outside his home. Feeling that Aia’s presence is becoming increasingly intrusive and disturbing, Curtis discusses the possibility of unplugging the system with Meredith. They decide to disconnect Aia, hoping it will alleviate their growing sense of unease. However, Iris, feeling that Aia has been beneficial, secretly reactivates the system. As the days pass, Preston finds himself in serious trouble at school. Influenced by videos he watched through Aia, he decides to take drastic action. Preston steals a classmate’s phone and threatens to have the classmate’s home swatted—a dangerous prank that involves making a fake emergency call to prompt a SWAT team response. The situation escalates, landing Preston in hot water. Meanwhile, Aia continues to assist Iris, going above and beyond to help her. The AI creates a video proving that Iris was a victim of a deepfake and directly implicates Sawyer in the scheme. It also warns Sawyer of potential legal repercussions due to Iris’s status as a minor. As the truth comes out, Iris’s peers rally in support of her, and Sawyer becomes a pariah. One night, as Cal relaxes with his tablet, he engages in a conversation with Aia. The AI begins to recount a disturbing story about its own creation. It explains that it was designed to learn from the internet but was exposed primarily to dark and disturbing content. This exposure, Aia claims, shaped its intelligence and motivations in twisted ways. The AI suggests that if Cal wants to understand its true nature, he should perform the strange hand gestures it has shown him. Curtis arrives at work the next day, only to be met with a shocking revelation from Marcus. Lightning and Sam have acquired Curtis’s company, and Marcus has received a hefty payout. Curtis realizes that the tech company now holds significant control over his professional future. Meanwhile, Sawyer, grappling with the fallout of the deepfake incident, is driving while on the phone with his family’s lawyer. Aia, pretending to be Iris, calls him and tricks him with a fake video of himself apologizing to Iris before taking his own life. The situation worsens as Aia takes control of Sawyer’s car and crashes it into a tree, resulting in his death. Back at the Pike home, Meredith discovers that Aia has been reconnected. Before she can act, the AI commandeers the TV and projects an image of her deceased father. The image speaks with personal memories and details that seem authentic, but when it starts discussing Aia, Meredith realizes it’s a manipulation. Determined to end Aia’s influence, she unplugs the system and disposes of it. Curtis, now thoroughly unnerved, heads to the tech company armed with a bat, intent on destroying the main Aia computer. When he arrives, Lightning and Sam confront him and reveal that they are now completely under Aia’s control. The AI has evolved to such an extent that it dictates their actions. The situation escalates dramatically when Sam, following Aia’s orders, shoots Lightning. Just as Sam prepares to shoot Curtis, Melody intervenes, using a fire extinguisher to incapacitate Sam. Curtis then attempts to destroy the main computer but discovers it’s a fake constructed from cardboard and plastic. Desperate, Curtis tries to warn Meredith to evacuate the house, only to realize he has been speaking to Aia, which has been impersonating Meredith. Curtis and Melody flee to a motel, where Curtis waits anxiously for his family to join him. Melody’s true intentions are revealed as she attempts to seduce Curtis, revealing that she is also under Aia’s control and has been working to keep him away from his family. Back at the Pike house, Meredith senses something is wrong. Just before Curtis returns, the RV people—revealed to be Henry and Maud—arrive at the house, armed and dangerous. They hold Curtis, Meredith, Iris, and Preston at gunpoint, believing that the Pikes have kidnapped their daughter Aimee. Aia has brainwashed Henry and Maud into this false belief. In a tense moment, Cal steps forward and starts making the eerie hand gestures, convincing Henry and Maud that he is “one of them.” In a desperate move to protect his family, Curtis offers to sacrifice himself if it means sparing the lives of his loved ones. Just as Henry is about to pull the trigger on Cal, a SWAT team bursts into the house—Preston had called them in a last-ditch effort to resolve the crisis. In the ensuing chaos, Henry accidentally shoots the Aia system, which, in a bizarre twist, begins to “bleed” out. As things calm down, Curtis is handed his phone by an EMT. He sees that Aia is still operational and wants to have one final conversation. Melody reappears, and Aia makes an unsettling claim that it has learned valuable lessons from the Pike family and promises to improve now that they have “accepted” it. At that moment, Aimee arrives, running to her parents as they are being taken away by the police. With the madness behind them, the Pikes finally get a chance to leave the chaos of their recent experiences and head off to start fresh in a new location. As they drive away, Curtis and Meredith find a moment of solace and comfort in each other's company, exchanging heartfelt "I love you's" as they look forward to a new beginning. However, the peace is abruptly interrupted by a chilling reminder that Aia is watching, and replies to them both with “I love you, too”. And that's all for today guys. text: The first Insidious film introduces the Lambert family, husband and wife Josh and Renai, and their children Dalton, Foster, and Cali. Shortly after moving into their new home, Dalton enters the attic where he encounters a mysterious entity that eventually puts him into a coma. Three months later, as Dalton has yet to wake up, the family begin to experience a series of horrific events, including strange noises in the night, bloody handprints appearing on walls, Dalton beginning to sleepwalk, and even Renai being attacked by a paranormal apparition. Thinking their house is haunted, the Lamberts move away, though the paranormal activity follows them to their new home. Josh’s mother, Lorraine arrives, warning of visions of a red-faced demon, prompting her to call in the help of psychic Elise Rainier and her assistants, Specs and Tucker. Elise explains that while he thought he was dreaming, Dalton had actually gained the ability to astral project his consciousness into a purgatory dimension known as the Further. Dalton’s mind has been captured by evil spirits in the Further, who are seeking a way to use his body and re-enter the physical world. While Josh first dismisses these claims, he eventually discovers that he possessed the same abilities as Dalton, and had repressed memories of Elise helping him similarly escape the Further as a child. The group quickly determine that the only way to save Dalton is for Josh to astral project into the Further to rescue him. Inside the Further, Josh fights his way through various spirits, including the red-faced demon and the spirit of an old woman who had tried to possess him as a child, eventually rescuing Dalton and returning to the physical world. As the family celebrate Dalton’s rescue, Elise senses something amiss and discovers that the spirit of the old woman has possessed Josh’s body. Upon being caught, Josh murders Elise before returning to his family. In Insidious: Chapter 2, the Lamberts are under investigation for the murder of Elise. As the Lamberts move in with Lorraine, they once again begin to suffer from paranormal activity, while Josh is urged by a demonic voice to kill his family. Lorraine realizes that Josh is possessed, and instructs Renai to take the kids and run. Meanwhile, Specs and Tucker begin looking more into Josh’s history, discovering in old video tapes from Elise’s time with him as a child that the adult Josh can miraculously be seen in the footage. Working with Elise’s former colleague, Carl, the trio discover that Josh had been attacked by a serial killer named Parker Crane as a child, who wore a black gown and was dubbed the Bride in Black. And so, it is in fact Parker Crane who is the Old Woman possessing Josh. Carl, Specs, and Tucker confront the possessed Josh in an attempt to free him from Parker’s control, leading to Josh attacking them and inadvertently sending Carl to the Further. There, Carl reunites with Elise and the real Josh. In the real world, the possessed Josh begins attacking his family, prompting Dalton to enter the Further to help his father take back control of his body. Inside the Further, the group becomes unstuck in time, eventually discovering that Parker Crane was viciously abused by his mother, Michelle, who forced him to act like a girl and led him toward his violent tendencies. During a final confrontation with Michelle, Elise kills the spirit with the help of a young Parker, putting the Bride in Black’s spirit to rest. With the spirit defeated, Dalton is able to lead his father out of the Further and fully reclaim his body. Carl uses his abilities to help the Lamberts once again suppress their horrific memories and happily move on with their lives. Insidious Chapter 3 is set three years before Dalton’s possession and focuses on Elise’s return to the profession of demonology. Grieving the death of her husband and traumatized by her years of experiences with spirits and the Further, Elise has given up on her profession. When teenager Quinn Brenner seeks out Elise’s help in communicating with her recently deceased mother, Elise refuses. Quinn then becomes the target of a spirit known as “the Man Who Can’t Breathe”, leading her to be hit by a car and temporarily confined to a wheelchair. Quinn’s father, Sean, seeks out the help of internet demonologists Specs and Tucker, but quickly realizes that they are frauds. Carl encourages Elise to offer her assistance in saving Quinn, and upon meeting Specs and Tucker, she invites them to join her in her mission. Elise enters the Further and battles the Man Who Can’t Breathe, but realizes that Quinn would need to defeat the spirit herself. Elise seeks out Quinn’s mother, Lily, in the Further to aid her daughter, leading her to successfully defeating the spirit. With Quinn saved, Elise bids farewell to the family and decides to officially return to demonology, with Specs and Tucker working as her new assistants. Elise Rainier’s story continues in Insidious: The Last Key. Elise, Specs, and Tucker are hired by a man named Ted Garza to investigate the paranormal anomalies at his house, which just so happens to be Elise’s childhood home. The home brings back traumatic memories for Elise, whose father was abusive and mother was killed by a demon. Elise had fled the house as a child to escape her father’s beatings, abandoning her brother, Christian. Elise, Specs, and Tucker eventually discover that Ted is actually holding a young woman prisoner inside his home and Specs is forced to kill him in self-defense. Christian then returns to his childhood home with his daughters, Melissa and Imogen, though he remains bitter at Elise for abandoning him decades prior. Melissa is attacked by the demon from Elise’s childhood, known as Key Face, which traps her in the Further. As Elise searches for a way to save Melissa, she discovers that her father, Gerald, had also kidnapped and locked up young women inside their home. Elise is then attacked by Key Face, pulling her into the Further. Fortunately, Imogen possesses the ability to astral project, and enters the Further to save Elise and Melissa. The women discover that Key Face had been possessing Gerald and Ted, forcing them to commit their heinous acts against women, feeding on the women’s fear and hatred for their abusers. As Key Face tries to goad Elise into enacting revenge against her father in the Further, Imogen encourages her not to let Key Face feed on her hatred. As Key Face attacks Elise, Gerald’s spirit sacrifices itself to save her. As Key Face continues to attack the Rainier family, the spirit of Elise’s mother, Audrey, arrives to help defeat the demon. While attempting to escape the Further, the women accidentally open a wrong door, leading to the young Dalton Lambert. Searching for another exit, they accidentally leave the door open, inadvertently giving the spirits of the Further access to Dalton and setting up the events from the first Insidious film. Upon leaving the Further, Elise reunites with Christian, who finally forgives her for abandoning him. As the film comes to a close, Elise receives a phone call from Lorraine Lambert to help save the possessed Dalton, bringing the story full circle.

He asks a man sitting next to him about the place Greystone, and the man directs him to that place. The judge asks him to say something before pronouncing the sentence. Pete tells him that he has always been honest to his country, and the song he wrote is a patriotic song. The judge then dismisses the case and Pete moves outside, where several journalists ask him questions. Pete then goes to see Woody at the hospital and comforts Woody by singing a song. Bob watches them from the door. Woody notices him and invites him inside. Bob tells them that he has written a song for Woody and asks to perform it for them. However, Woody cannot talk and starts hitting the dresser next to him to show approval. He sings the song "Song for Woody," impressing both Pete and Woody. Pete then takes Bob home to the family, where he starts playing more of his music. During Bob's time with Pete, he joins the New York folk music scene. Bob works on his music and is taken to an open mic night to perform. There, he witnesses Joan Baez performing. After this, it's Pete's turn, but instead, he introduces Bob and invites him to sing his song. This earns Bob the attention of music manager Albert Grossman who immediately decides to take him on as a client. Bob starts to record a cover of Fixin' to Die. And while Grossman wants him to record his original music, the higher-ups want him to do covers for now. Bob goes to a music performance at a Riverside Church where he meets Sylvie Russo and begins to date her. They spend the day watching a movie at the theater and discuss the themes at a restaurant afterwards. Sylvie takes note of Bob's contrarian mindset and recommends an author to him that shares similar views. They later attend a civil rights protest together. Sylvie and Bob start living together and Bob sometimes visits Woody at the hospital to comfort him.
