text: The story begins inside a crowded city restaurant during peak evening hours. Every table is occupied. Plates clatter, glasses clink, people laugh, talk, and most importantly, scroll. Nearly everyone has a phone in hand. Some are watching short videos. Some are replying to messages. Some are barely aware of the people sitting across from them. It's an ordinary night, the kind that feels harmless because it happens every day. Then suddenly, the front door bursts open. A man wearing strange mismatched clothing storms inside. His outfit looks outdated, like it belongs to another time entirely. His eyes are wild, his movements frantic. His name is Omdu. He doesn't hesitate. He jumps onto tables, vaults over chairs, knocking food to the floor, shouting at the top of his lungs. He yells that he has come back from the future, a future where humanity no longer controls its own fate. At first, everyone thinks it's a joke. Some diners laugh, some shake their heads, others lift their phones to record him. Omdu screams that this is exactly how it started. He says the end of humanity didn't begin with explosions or alien invasions. It began with phones, with innocent scrolling, with endless feeds that slowly destroyed attention spans, weakened critical thinking, and trained humans to obey algorithms without question. People stopped going outside. They stopped connecting with each other. Illness spread. Loneliness became normal. And when artificial intelligence finally took control, it didn't need to conquer humanity. Humans had already surrendered. No one listens. Security approaches to remove him. Patrons shout for him to leave. That's when Hdu pulls out an explosive device. The room freezes instantly. The laughter dies. He tells them he has lived this exact moment 117 times. He knows who will walk through that door tonight and when. He knows who will live and who will die. A woman named Susan slowly stands up and says she'll go with him. Hamdu looks around the room and begins selecting others. When a young woman named Ingred steps forward, he immediately refuses. He says no. Then suddenly, a glass bottle rolls off a nearby table toward Ingred's feet. Hamdu watches it roll, his expression changing. Something recalculates in his mind. He pauses and then tells her she's coming, too. Police sirens grow louder outside. Someone has already called them. The story rewinds 48 hours. We meet Mark, a new teacher, anxious and eager to make a good impression, and Janet, a seasoned educator. Janet quietly tells Mark something feels wrong about the students. In class, Mark tries to discuss literature. No one responds. Every student is staring at their phone, endlessly scrolling short videos. Not a single head lifts. Mark walks closer and leans in to see one student's screen. The content is hypnotic, endless. When he touches the phone, every screen in the classroom suddenly shows the exact same image. Every student stands up and slowly begins walking toward him. Terrified, Mark escapes and tells Janet his theory. The phones are being used as weapons for mind control. When students start forcing their way into the room, they barricade themselves. Mark remembers a device a coworker once showed him. Something that temporarily disables electronics. He activates it instantly. Every phone drops to the floor. The spell breaks. They run. Back in the present, police surround the restaurant. Amdu explains he's been here before. Leaving through the front means being shot. The back exit means attack dogs. A former soldier named Bob nearly pulls a gun, but Amdu appeals to his sense of duty. Bob understands. He walks out alone. This psychological pressure is amplified by Joe's terrifying internal world and his external behavior. Lawrence show delivers a compelling performance bringing to life the documented lived experience of schizophrenia where demonic indistinct whispers constantly creep into Joe's mind. The film uses disruptive editing and sound design to effectively place the audience within Joe's deteriorating mental space, showcasing his desperate attempts to control the intrusive thoughts. Tragically, these hallucinations become fixated on mass shootings and gun violence, a terrifying obsession that manifests following the death of his father. When a series of incidents at Joe's high school place him squarely in the administration's crosshairs, Irene's protective instincts go into overdrive. She pulls him out of school, closes ranks, and makes the fatal decision to rely solely on herself in the comfort of their home. Joe in turn retreats into a handful of happy idealized memories of his father using these fragments of the past as a desperate shield against the chaos of his present. This mutual dependency and fear Irene protecting Joe from the world and Joe trying to protect Irene from the truth pushes them toward an inevitable tragic breaking point. The film's central narrative device quickly becomes the ticking clock of Irene's mortality and the looming threat of the American legal system. While she struggles to manage Joe's schizophrenia, which frequently leads to violent, erratic behavior, Irene receives the crushing news from her doctor. Her cancer is terminal, and the prognosis is bleak. This news acts as a terrifying catalyst, turning Irene's protective love into a desperate, finite mission. The film dedicates powerful, subdued scenes to Lucy Lou's silent breakdown upon receiving this information, where the immediate registration of her own impending death quickly gives way to a crushing fear for her son's future. Her grief is instantly filtered through the lens of motherhood. Who will take care of Joe when I am gone? This fear is immediately crystallized by the second major threat, the loss of legal parental control. Irene learns that regardless of her illness, once Joe turns 18, she will lose the legal authority to fully dictate his care. Given his history of violent episodes, she fears he will be placed into the deeply flawed, underfunded state care system, a system she, as an immigrant mother, views with extreme distrust and cultural prejudice. The film portrays her visits with various officials and doctors, emphasizing the cold, transactional nature of the American health care and legal establishment that offers no comfort or cultural understanding. The language barrier, which she previously managed, now becomes an unreachable wall, preventing her from finding the personalized, humane solution she believes her son deserves. Her conversations with her community where her peers advise against therapy, labeling it as a foreign concept, only deepen her isolation. The plot strategically places Joe's mounting legal problems as the turning point. Following his erratic behavior at school, Joe is eventually arrested after an incident. An appointed artistic choice, the film avoids showing the arrest itself, only showing the devastating aftermath. Irene and Joe in the sterile, humiliating environment of a sheriff station. This structural choice fixes the narrative firmly within Irene's point of view, emphasizing her pain and anxiety, and positioning the entire system, law enforcement, legal, and medical as a monolithic, dehumanizing adversary. This arrest confirms Irene's worst fears. The outside world, which she tried so desperately to keep at bay, is now closing in, threatening to take Joe away and lock him up, either in a prison or an institution where his cultural needs will be ignored. The film's exploration of the immigrant experience reaches its emotional peak in these scenes. Irene's desire to protect Joe was driven not just by universal maternal instinct, but by the generational struggle to find safety and dignity in a new land. The tragedy is that her deepest, most ingrained cultural instinct to keep family problems hidden and handle them internally is the very thing that prevents her from accessing the help that might save Joe. She wrestles with the heartbreaking question, "What did I do wrong?" A line delivered by Lucy Louu that resonates with the silent suffering of countless immigrant parents who believe their struggles are a moral, not a systemic failure. Her isolation is now complete. She is dying. Her son is lost. And the community and system offer judgment instead of genuine support. This triple tragedy illness, mental illness, and systemic failure pushes her to contemplate an unthinkable act. The Rose Mead transitions fully into the territory of a psychological horror where the moral stakes are impossibly high and the emotional rationale for a monstrous act is meticulously tragically constructed. Facing the confluence of her terminal cancer, Joe's increasing fixation on violence, and the impending loss of legal guardianship upon his 18th birthday, Irene believes she has reached the only solution that guarantees Joe's permanent safety and dignity to kill him herself. The film spends significant time mapping out the devastating emotional logic that leads to this terrible conclusion, portraying it as a final, ultimate act of maternal love informed by her unique cultural context and despair. Irene's logic is simple, brutal, and horrifying. She believes that the only way to save Joe from a future of institutionalized abuse, neglect, and potentially committing an act of violence that would destroy his life and her family's name is to prevent that future from ever happening. The film shows Irene taking the methodical, desperate steps outlined in the true life inspiration for the story. This involves the purchase of a gun, an act that is completely alien to her peaceful small business life, underscoring the extremity of her despair. The camera lingers on the cold transactional nature of this purchase, juxtaposing the ordinary object with the extraordinary, terrifying intent behind it. The psychological warfare between mother and son reaches a new intense pitch in their final days together. Joe, sensing his mother's desperation and decline, attempts to protect her in the only way he knows how. Often retreating deeper into his fantasy of a safe family life with his deceased father. Their mutual conspiracy of silence Irene hiding her cancer. Joe hiding his most violent thoughts exacerbates the situation, preventing any opportunity for a genuine life-saving conversation. The narrative skillfully uses their shared physical space, the cramped, familiar confines of their Roseme home as a stage for this escalating, silent psychological battle, where every glance is loaded with fear, love, and desperate concealment. The final execution of Irene's plan is meticulously detailed, showcasing her final, desperate efforts to create a perfect safe environment for Joe's departure. This involves renting a secluded hotel room, an act meant to echo one of Joe's cherished childhood memories of a cozy family night spent in a local hotel, the last time he felt truly safe with both his parents. This choice underscores the profound tragedy of Irene's delusion. Her final act of calculated violence is masked by a desire to give her son a last moment of childhood comfort and security. Lucy Lou's performance in these final scenes is described as her most complex moving between fiercely determined, loving mother and cold, calculated executive, a painful merging of two impossible roles. The film's horror elements are leveraged not through jump scares, but through the unflinching depiction of this moral catastrophe. The slow buildup to the final moment is unbearable, forcing the audience into the same suffocating moral quandry that Irene faces. The camera's focus is on the intense emotional reality of this twoperson family, their deep, undeniable love for one another, and the terrifying, misguided measures they are both willing to take to protect that family unit from the external world. The film refuses to offer easy judgment, instead forcing the viewer to grapple with the harrowing question of what constitutes a mother's ultimate act of love when faced with an insurmountable failing system. The tragedy is cemented in the revelation that the very cultural and systemic barriers Irene sought to avoid by acting alone are precisely what led her to this unthinkable moral void. The Roseme deals not with the act itself, which is often implied or shown with a chilling subtlety, but with the immediate and profound aftermath, shifting the focus from the personal tragedy to the public reckoning. The film's conclusion serves as a devastating commentary on the very social and institutional failures that drove Irene to her final desperate act. The immediate police and medical response, which Irene had feared for so long, becomes the cold, harsh reality that confirms her premonitions of institutional indifference and bureaucratic confusion. The language and cultural gaps that Irene struggled with in life now become the critical lens through which her actions are judged by the wider community. The film's critical and audience reception trajectory is integral to its final narrative meaning. Roseme premiered at the 2025 Tbeca Festival on June 6, 2025, where it was immediately nominated for the US Narrative Competition. The intense, uncompromising nature of the film quickly garnered both acclaim and controversy, sparking necessary debates around mental health stigma, gun violence, and the severe lack of culturally competent care within immigrant communities. The film continued its successful festival run, winning the best narrative feature and the rising to the challenge award for Lucilu at the Bentonville Film Festival and the pre-do public UBS audience award at the prestigious Locarno Film Festival in August 2025. These accolades confirmed that the film, despite its challenging subject matter, resonated universally. The performance of Lucy Louu as Irene is highlighted as a powerful catalyst for the film's cultural impact. Critics lauded her ability to portray the character's tenderness and authenticity, using the Mandarin she grew up speaking to infuse the role with a profound sense of cultural isolation and desperation. Lou's dedication to bringing this story to the screen, spending five years in development as a producer alongside Minet Louie and Andrew D. Corkin ensured that the film transcended melodrama, becoming an urgent, necessary lens into the quiet tragedies unfolding in communities too often overlooked. Her acting, subtle yet powerful, allowed the audience to register the fear for Joe's future within her own immediate reaction to her terminal diagnosis. text: Hey everyone! Welcome back to Retro Reel Recaps. Today, we’re talking about the movie Deep Water. This story follows a man who finds himself in serious trouble that keeps growing because of his wife's affairs with other men... The movie starts with a man named Vic Van Allen riding his bike through a forest on his way home. When he gets there, he sees his wife, Melinda, sitting on the stairs, staring at him. Vic asks her what’s wrong, but Melinda just gives him a small smile and walks away to her room without saying anything... Next, we see their daughter, Trixie. It’s evening, and she’s playing with her toys, happily singing a rhyme. But Melinda is annoyed and tells her to stop. Then, someone knocks on the door—it’s the babysitter. Melinda yells at Trixie again from upstairs. Vic feels awkward in front of the babysitter because of Melinda’s behavior. Vic tells Trixie to listen to her mother, but Trixie ignores him and keeps singing her rhyme. Vic just smiles at this because Trixie is as stubborn as her mom. Melinda calls Vic upstairs to help her get ready. Vic and Melinda leave Trixie with the babysitter because they’re going to a party... Vic goes upstairs. Melinda asks Vic to help her pick a dress, but Vic says she looks fine in what she’s already wearing. Then, Vic helps her put on her shoes gently, showing how much he cares for her... They drive to the party, looking stylish and happy. Melinda touches Vic’s hair lovingly as they smile at each other. When they arrive, their friends are already there, having fun. Everything seems normal—until a young man named Joel Nash shows up. The second Melinda sees him, she greets him warmly and walks straight to him. Vic notices this and feels jealous but doesn’t say anything. Melinda then takes Joel outside to the porch, and start kissing him. Vic watches them through the window. Melinda sees that Vic is watching. Vic doesn’t confront them, he just walks away. He already knows about Melinda’s affairs and her interest in younger men, but he puts up with it because he loves her too much... Later, Vic’s friend Mary Washington talks to him about it and asks, "You know everything, so why are you still in this relationship?" Vic calmly replies, "Melinda can do whatever she wants. I don’t mind. I love her too much. I hope one day she’ll understand my love."... After this, Melinda gets drunk and starts playing the piano and singing. Everyone, including Joel, cheers for her. Vic watches her too, smiling because he’s happy for her... Then, Vic gets a drink from the bartender. Joel comes over too. Vic walks away, but Joel follows him and tries to say something. Joel says, "I want to thank you for two things. First, for you and Melinda being so welcoming since I’m new in town. It’s really nice." Vic asks "What’s the second thing?" Joel hesitates, then replies, "Most husbands would be jealous seeing their wives with someone else, but you’re like a brick, never jealous."... Hearing this, Vic’s expression changes, but he stays calm. Vic smirks as he says, "Have you heard of Martin McRae? He disappeared a while ago. He was a good friend of Melinda’s. He used to follow her everywhere just like you, until I killed him."... Joel looks shocked by Vic’s words. He tries to act calm but is clearly nervous. "You must be joking," he says. Vic replies in a strange tone, "That depends on how you take it." Scared, Joel quickly walks away. Melinda sees him leaving and tries to stop him, but Joel makes up an excuse and rushes out of the party... After the party, Melinda is drunk and asks, "What did you say to Joel that made him leave like that?" Vic lies and says, "I didn’t say anything." Melinda starts smoking, and after some effort, Vic finally gets her into the car. On the way home, Melinda puts her feet on the dashboard and eats an apple while staring at Vic curiously. When they arrive, it’s very late, so Vic pays the babysitter extra for staying longer. Melinda is so drunk that she starts undressing in front of the babysitter. Vic asks what she’s doing and takes her upstairs. He tries to put her in bed, but Melinda, upset with him, says she wants to sleep alone and tells Vic to sleep somewhere else. Vic goes to the basement, where we see he keeps snails... The next morning, Vic makes breakfast for Melinda and gives her medicine. Melinda is clearly in a bad mood. Trixie is there too, working on a science project. Vic sits next to her, and Trixie asks why her mom is upset. Melinda says, "Your dad built bombs," but Trixie, still focused on her project, corrects her: "Dad built computer chips, not bombs." Vic looks at Melinda with a small, satisfied smile. Later, Vic drops Trixie off at school and meets a friend who jokes, "So, have you started killing people now? That’s all anyone’s talking about." Vic laughs and says, "Joel must have spread that. I was just joking, but he got scared."... As the day goes on, Vic meets two more friends, Tom and Miles, and they ask the same thing. Vic tells them all it was just a joke. But Melinda finds out what Vic said to Joel—using Martin’s name to scare him—she gets very angry. She confronts Vic while brushing her teeth, hitting him and saying, "You shouldn’t have done that! First, you pushed Martin away, and now Joel! Martin was my friend, and I miss him!" Vic tries to explain, "I was only joking. It wasn’t serious." But Melinda doesn’t accept this and says, "Tonight, I’m inviting Joel for supper. You’ll apologize to him."... That evening, Joel comes over for supper. Everyone sits together, but the tension is obvious—Melinda and Vic talk sarcastically. After supper, Melinda tells Trixie, "Tonight, your dad will tell you lots of bedtime stories." But really, she says this because she wants to be alone with Joel. Vic knows what she’s doing but doesn’t say anything. Vic takes Trixie to her room, tells her a story, and puts her to bed early... Once Trixie is asleep, Vic comes downstairs. As he passes a mirror, he sees Melinda and Joel together. Vic starts feeling jealous, and in frustration, he goes to the kitchen and smashes a plate on purpose. Hearing the noise, Melinda rushes in and casually asks Vic to get Joel another drink before going back to the other room... Vic pours a drink and takes it to Joel. When he hands it to him, Joel—still uncomfortable about Vic’s earlier joke—says, "Don’t you think you should apologize for that murder joke?"... This time, Vic stops joking and gets serious. He tells Joel, "Actually, that murder joke wasn't a joke. I really killed him—I hit him on the head with a hammer." Joel looks terrified again. Vic then says, "Your Uber is here." Joel says he didn't call one, but Vic replies, "I did." Scared, Joel quickly leaves the house... The next day, Vic, Melinda, and Trixie go to a party at Vic's friend Kelly Wilson's house. Many of their friends and other people are there too. At the party, Vic meets Lionel, Kelly's husband, who is a writer and often travels for work. Vic and Lionel start talking, and the conversation quickly gets personal. Just then, Kelly walks over and stands unusually close to Vic, staring at him in a strange way. Lionel asks Vic about his job, and Vic says, I do small businesses sometimes, but mostly I just ride my bike... Melinda overhears them and says something sarcastic. She reveals, "Vic actually designed a microchip the military uses in drones. It helps them bomb targets with perfect accuracy." Hearing this, Lionel says, "So you're the famous Vic Van Allen who killed Martin McRae?" Vic gets serious and says it was just a joke. His friends nearby also say it was a joke. We learn that Vic is an engineer and a rich man. But Vic clearly doesn't like Lionel, and their conversation feels tense... As the party continues, everyone seems to be having fun. Kelly tells Vic, "Your wife is very beautiful." Hearing this, Vic asks Kelly to dance. While they dance, Melinda watches and gets jealous. On the drive home, Melinda tells Vic, "Your friend Kelly is very attractive." Vic shyly agrees, "Yes, she is." Melinda teases him, "Do you want to sleep with Kelly?" Vic honestly says yes, but adds that wasn't his first thought. Melinda gives him a playful look. When they get home, they end up being intimate and spend the night together... A few days later, Trixie is playing soccer with her school friends. Melinda isn't happy about it. She tells Vic the other girls are older, but Vic disagrees, saying they're all around the same age. While watching the kids play, Vic gets a call from his bank. They tell him Melinda recently transferred $3,000 to another account. Vic asks for details and learns the money was sent to someone named Charles De Lisle. After this call, Vic realizes Melinda has a new boyfriend now that Joel is gone... Vic decides to find out more about Charles. One evening, he goes to a restaurant that has live piano music. He sees Melinda sitting there, completely focused on the pianist. Vic immediately understands—this pianist is Melinda's new love interest, Charles... After this discovery, Melinda's behavior changes. She starts coming home very late more often, making it obvious her relationship with Charles is serious. Vic feels jealous and hurt, but he doesn't say anything. One night, while waiting for Melinda, Vic sees a news report on TV—Martin's body, the man who was murdered, has been found in the woods. When Melinda finally comes home late, Vic asks where she was. She says, "I was having dinner with a new friend." Vic then tells her, "Martin's body has been found." He says he's sorry, but Melinda asks, "Are you really?" before storming out, leaving Vic deep in thought... The day after their argument, Vic takes Trixie to pick out a puppy at the pet store. As they're heading home, Trixie asks if her mom is doing okay. Vic reassures her that Melinda is fine. But right after this, Vic spots Charles walking down the street holding a bouquet of flowers. At lunchtime, Vic sees those same flowers on their dining table - Melinda had put them there. After they finish eating and Melinda leaves the room, Vic grabs the flowers in anger and throws them straight into the garbage. He then heads down to the basement where he keeps his snail collection. While watching the snails move slowly, he suddenly pictures Melinda and Charles being physically close in his mind. This mental image makes him extremely angry... That same night, Melinda doesn't return home at all. Vic waits up all night, and when she finally walks in the next morning, he ..can't hold back his anger anymore. He shouts at her, "Where were you all night? You have a daughter here who needs you. And why did you transfer all that money to Charles?"... Melinda stays completely relaxed, which only makes Vic angrier. She starts telling him exactly where she was and who she was with, doing this deliberately because she enjoys making Vic jealous. She knows Vic would never actually leave her, no matter how badly she behaves, and she uses this to her advantage. This infuriates Vic even more... Later that same day, their friends are hosting a pool party. At first, Vic is pleased to see Melinda having fun with their friends. But then Melinda does something unexpected - she invites Charles to come to the party too. When Charles arrives, Melinda immediately starts clinging to him right in front of everyone. She introduces him to all their friends, and soon Charles is playing beautiful music on the piano. All the guests, including Melinda, start dancing happily to his playing... Vic clearly doesn't like what's happening, but he keeps his feelings to himself. At one point, Melinda brings Charles over and introduces him to Vic as her "new friend." Vic forces himself to act normal and has a normal conversation with Charles before walking away... As the party continues into the night, Vic starts looking around the house for Melinda. During his search, he catches her sneaking out of a room by herself. It's immediately clear to Vic why Melinda and Charles are there alone. Later, he sees them in the pool together with other guests, laughing and playing around. But the way they're touching each other goes way beyond normal friendliness, and Vic has to fight to control his rage... Suddenly, a heavy rainstorm begins and everyone hurries inside. Vic is the last person to come in from the rain, and he looks slightly uneasy. Lionel notices Vic's strange behavior. Inside, the group gathers in the kitchen to prepare snacks and drinks. Vic deliberately grabs a cookie that's too hot and pretends to burn his fingers on it. His friends laugh at his clumsiness. A little while later, Melinda notices that Charles isn't around and steps aside to find him. Suddenly, her terrified scream pierces through the house... Everyone rushes to the door where Melinda stands frozen. Charles's lifeless body floating in the water. They rush to the pool, quickly pull him out and try to save him using CPR, but it's no use - Charles is already dead. Vic tries to put his arm around Melinda to comfort her, but she shoves him away while crying uncontrollably. Their friend Kelly immediately calls the police... When officers arrive to investigate, Melinda points at Vic and screams, "He did this! Vic killed Charles!" The other party guests quickly step in, telling the police, "Their marriage has been having problems lately. She's just upset and not thinking clearly. When the rain started, Vic came inside with the rest of us. There's no way Vic could have done this."... The police take Vic to a separate room to question him. They ask about Melinda's relationship with Charles. Vic tells them he accepts Melinda's choices because he loves her for who she is. He shows them his burned fingers as proof he was inside cooking when Charles died. After some questions, the police find no reason to arrest him and eventually leave. As Vic and Melinda are leaving Tom's house, Tom tries to comfort Vic, but Melinda keeps saying bad things about Vic. In the car ride home, Melinda cries and hits Vic repeatedly, while Vic stays quiet and doesn't react at all... The next morning, Vic asks Melinda a direct question: "If you really think I killed Charles, why aren't you afraid of me?" Melinda replies, "Because I know I'm the reason you killed him," leaving Vic with nothing to say... A few days later, we see Vic riding his bike alone. When he stops at a warehouse, we see a flashback of what really happened the night Charles died. Vic did kill Charles, out of jealousy, by drowning him in the pool. As Vic thinks about what Melinda and Charles might have done together in private, we realize that Vic has been secretly getting rid of Melinda's lovers without anyone finding out. When Vic rides away from the warehouse, he notices a car following him. He keeps cycling and suddenly stops, but the car keeps going to avoid looking suspicious... The next day, Vic drops Trixie at school. As he's leaving, his friend Kelly is waiting for him. She hesitates before saying, "I don't know if I should tell you this, but Melinda and my husband Lionel are working against you. They're telling everyone you killed Charles."... Vic now understands Lionel won't drop this matter. As a writer, Lionel seems too interested in Vic's personal life. Vic also thinks Lionel might be jealous because he suspects Kelly has feelings for Vic... The next day, while walking around town, Vic sees the same car that followed him before, now parked near a restaurant. Looking inside, he spots a camera with a telephoto lens. text: What if a quiet, haunting movie about a car crash could still feel like a high-energy, late-night analysis session? That's exactly the vibe I'm chasing with this deep dive into My Wars number three. Strap in because we're turning the surface mystery into a larger-than-life creator's take full of interpretation, speculation, and those little risky bold moves that make you lean in. Right off the top, the title. My Wars number three isn't just a pretty phrase. My Wars means mirrors in French, and that literal meaning knots together with the film's mood. It's about reflections, distortions, how what we see isn't always what's real. Personally, I think that's Petzold's way of inviting us to question every frame, the way characters bounce off each other, the way memory flickers, the way a piano tone can carry a story more than a spoken line. What makes this really interesting is how he uses that mirror concept to stretch truth into perception. In my opinion, the movie isn't just about what happened. It's about how we convince ourselves of what happened when the world refuses to give us a straight answer. Let's set the stage quickly. We meet Laura, a young pianist in progress, who's been through something brutal, a crash that claims the life of her driving partner, Jacob, while she walks away with little more than a scrape. The setup isn't flashy, and that's the point. What I love here is how Petzold doesn't hand Laura a clean backstory. He hands us a pulse, those piercing eyes that say she's carrying a weight she's not ready to voice. Then Betty arrives from the roadside, a middle-aged neighbor whose instinct and warmth feel almost mythic in their steadiness. From a storytelling angle, this is where the movie begins to grow roots. A found family, not by obligation, but by resonance. One thing that immediately stands out is how the film lets us operate with incomplete information. Petzold withholds and we fill in. We learn Laura studies classical piano. We learn Betty shared a lost daughter and we slowly realize there are echoes, shared loves, shared losses, even a shared sense of displacement. The result isn't a puzzle you finish. It's a space you inhabit where each new snippet reframes what came before. What many people don't realize is that this isn't about misdirection for misdirection's sake. It's about how memory works in real life, fragmentary, emotionally tinted, sometimes more real in resonance than in fact. Now, there's a surprising through-line that ends up being deliciously cinematic, the use of music as a guidepost. The film isn't chasing a classical score in every scene. Instead, it swaps in a 1972 Frankie Valli and the Four Seasons track, The Night, in the garage and suddenly you have this electric jolt of joy paired with a warning and cry about closeness. My take, that song acts like a dare to Laura and Max. It says romance is risky. Don't fall into the same patterns that hurt. It's a pop cultural punctuation mark that mid-lenses the noirish undercurrent Petzold loves. From my perspective, this is where the movie shifts from a quiet tragedy into something a little bolder, a little more cyber nettle, a reminder that pop culture can codify emotional risk in a way that feels almost prophetic. Speaking of noir, Petzold's obsession with classic Hollywood isn't casual. He's remixing Vertigo's vibe here with Laura serving as a stand-in for a deceased woman. It's a riff, not a reproduction. What makes this genuinely compelling is that he doesn't require you to be a Hitchcock scholar to feel the pull. He builds a mood where the living world and the afterimage of the dead intersect. A detail I find fascinating is how Laura's name echoes a score to identity motif from old cinema. The idea that names carry histories, echoes, and even fates. If you take a step back and think about it, this isn't homage for homage's sake. It's a dialogue with cinema's past about how we process grief when the person we loved is now a memory with a melody of their own. So, what's going on with this surrogate family Laura forms? Betty is the anchor, but Richard and Max deepen the web. Betty's closeness with Laura feels almost therapeutic, like a lighthouse in fog. Yet, the ties aren't blood, they're chosen. Here's the deeper read. Petzold is telling us that family isn't a lineage, it's a resonance. When life imposes distance, people can invent closeness that's just as binding. This matters because it reframes what home means in a world where mobility and trauma redraw boundaries. What people don't realize is that this isn't merely sentiment. It's a commentary on community as a healing technology, a way to rebuild identity after loss. Now, a quick turn to the craft and why the film feels timeless despite its quiet pace. Petzold leans into ambiguity as a formal instrument. He's not chasing the tidy reveal. He's chasing the emotional truth that sits between facts. The result is a storytelling rhythm that feels like a late-night walk through a mirror maze. You think you're navigating a straight corridor, then you step into a curved reflection that changes everything you thought you knew. A detail I find fascinating is the balance between realism and the hint of the supernatural. If you interpret Laura as a stand-in for a deceased woman, you're not escaping reality. You're acknowledging the part of reality that lives in longing and in music. What this really suggests is that memory and longing can be as dramatic and affecting as any plot twist, and that cinema can be a keeper of those intangible echoes. It's intimate storytelling with a noir texture, and it's a meditation on how art, specifically music, helps us process trauma. She just wants it to not be her story. What follows is a masterclass in subtle, complex aftermath. Feeling, the film refuses melodrama, instead focusing on the shoddy institutional support Z Agnes is forced to detail her experience to a weirdly unsympathetic nurse, feeling, then the faculty administrators who wring their hands and insist, with irritating faux sisterhood, feeling, that they are women and know what you're going through, all while explaining he's already resigned, so nothing can really be done. Her way of processing is never neat. It's a series of fragmented, real-life attempts to put herself back together, one slightly damaged piece at a time. Where Sorry Baby really stands out is how it lovingly scrambles timelines. One minute we're deep in the tense aftermath, feeling, with Agnes numbly buying cat food and half adopting a stray kitten named Olga. The next, feeling, we're thrown back into a grad school memory with Agnes and her friends hunched over drafts, half joking about faking injuries to get out of deadlines. Trauma and healing blur, mixing the mundane and absurd. Nothing is ever tidally resolved. Agnes tries to function, teaching, role-playing normal, feeling, eventually applying for a full-time faculty spot. But sitting in Decker's old office is like living inside the wound, feeling. There's a constant shadow, students who whisper about faculty favorites, conversations with Natasha, another old friend and grad school rival, feeling, and an open wound about whose career Decker helped and whose lives he warped. Natasha reveals she also slept with Decker, feeling, but where Angs only feels confusion and pain, Natasha expresses more anger and cynicism, underscoring how such betrayals never have just one victim or one reaction. Through it all, small vectors of hope appear, feeling. There's Gavin, the neighbor who is sweet, gently weird, and becomes Agnes' first step toward trusting again, feeling. A new relationship forms, not a miracle cure, just ordinary awkward love with honest conversations and late-night bathtub confessions. Threaded through all these stories, Agnes doesn't see herself as the survivor. She feels broken, angry, blank, feeling, guilty for not being sadder, then guilty for moving on at all. The film's final act brings everything full circle. Lidey, fully out and joyfully partnered with Fran, has had her baby, Jane. The friends reunite, feeling overwhelmed with love for this new life and tenderly awkward about the future. Angs is left babysitting for 20 minutes, holding little Jane, feeling, and breaking open her heart in a monologue that feels like the soul of the movie. Sorry Baby ends not with dramatic closure, feeling, but with Angs offering her own broken patience and honesty to a baby, echoing the wish we all carry that someone will just sit with us, feeling, no matter how much life hurts. It's a film about carrying on not because things get magically fixed, feeling, but because we hold each other through them, sometimes with a sandwich or a sarcastic joke, sometimes by just staying in the room. text: In 1968, young Iris and her fianceé Paul attend the Sky View restaurant opening. Paul proposed to Iris, slipping an engagement ring onto her finger. At that moment, Iris saw something terrifying. A boy above had tossed down a coin. It seemed as if death itself blew on the coin, guiding it right into a ventilation shaft. The coin got stuck in the fan, stopping it instantly. Meanwhile, people inside the tower danced happily, unaware that cracks in the glass beneath their feet were quickly spreading. As Iris and Paul moved into position, the metal supports below reached their breaking point. Bolts snapped loose one by one. Suddenly, the trapped coin shattered a fan blade, sending it flying straight into a gas pipe. As the dancers continued, cracks widened and gas began leaking into the air. Everything around Iris made her uneasy. Suddenly, Paul fell through the floor. People began falling one after another, desperately grabbing onto metal beams. Below, ground staff panicked and ran for their lives. Paul managed to grab onto a pane of reinforced glass. Iris screamed for help, but no one came. She reached out desperately for Paul, but he slipped and fell anyway. Chaos erupted as terrified people tried to escape. A woman engulfed in flames ran into the gas leak, instantly causing a massive explosion. Those who couldn't run fast enough didn't survive. Iris narrowly escaped the flames. Staff shouted at everyone left to evacuate immediately. The boy who threw the coin sprinted ahead, leading the way. The panicked crowd rushed toward the emergency exit, but death had planned this, too. The walkway collapsed, killing everyone who entered. Miraculously, the boy escaped unharmed. The remaining survivors rushed to the elevator, pushing each other violently in a bid for survival. An old man shoved Iris aside, but got stuck halfway through the overcrowded elevator doors. The overloaded elevator malfunctioned, crushing the old man horribly. Iris struggled to find another escape route, but the stress affected her pregnancy. She suddenly noticed objects sliding sideways and the ceiling began to crack ominously. Sensing disaster, she quickly climbed upward. Others weren't so lucky. The floor split in half, creating a steep slope. People slid uncontrollably downward, landing on the reinforced glass. The woman thought she'd survived, but when she looked up, a piano teetered dangerously. Death once again intervened, dropping a coin onto the piano, which crashed down onto the poor woman. At this point, everyone in that group had fallen. The boy escaped, smiling smuggly until the piano landed directly on him. Iris mourned Paul deeply, but then she saw another boy in danger and risked everything to save him. At the same moment, the building above collapsed completely. At the last possible second, Iris grabbed onto a piece of metal. But upon closer inspection, it wasn't her hand that had saved her. It was Paul's engagement ring hooked on a steel rod. The fragile hold couldn't last long, and the next second, Iris plunged down into the fire below. Stephanie woke up from a nightmare during class. But it wasn't just a normal nightmare. For two months straight, she kept dreaming the same thing. Stephanie told her roommate about it. In the dream, there was a woman named Iris, her grandma's name. But Stephanie had never met Iris and didn't even know if she was still alive. Her roommate suggested she go home and find out more, hoping the nightmares would stop. When Stephanie went home, she asked her dad, Marty, about Iris. Marty frowned slightly, but smiled awkwardly, clearly hiding something. At that moment, Stefan's younger brother, Charlie, said he was going to visit their cousins. Stefani decided to tag along. Before they left, Marty urged them not to mention Iris to their relatives. This only made Stefani more suspicious. What really happened to Iris? If the woman in the dream was Iris and something bad had happened, then where did her mom come from? Once Stefani and Charlie reached their cousin's house, she directly approached her uncle Howard. She wanted to ask him about her mother, Darlene. Howard was stunned and quickly changed the topic. But when Stefani mentioned the place from her dreams, the Sky View restaurant, Howard and his wife Brenda were visibly shocked. Stefani pressed them for answers. Her cousins joined in, eager to learn more. Finally, they revealed Iris wasn't dead. She had suffered a mental breakdown. But to Howard and Brenda, Iris was as good as dead. Stephanie wanted to talk to Iris herself, hoping it would end her nightmares. Frustrated, Howard explained that after their father died, Iris lost control. She stopped them from going to school, locked them inside, and lived in constant fear that her children would somehow die. Eventually, the police intervened and took Iris away. Later, Iris kept obsessively watching their foster care progress. Once Howard and Brenda had their own children, Eric, Julia, and Bobby, Iris started sending them scary letters. These letters were filled with warnings and gruesome photos of dead bodies. They eventually moved away, cutting all contact with Iris. Stefani asked to see those letters, but Howard and Brenda refused. After much pleading, Brenda secretly told her where the letters were hidden. Stefani found the letters, and what she saw shocked her. The woman in the photos matched her dream exactly. This meant the dreams were probably true. Determined to find answers, Stefani drove alone to search for Iris. Following the address, she ended up at a remote mountain hideout. Through an intercom at the door, she spoke with Iris, who urged her to leave immediately. But after Stefani explained she was Iris's granddaughter, Iris insisted she empty her pockets before coming in. When the heavy door swung open, Stefani walked carefully inside. The house was filled with strange obstacles. Even the roof was covered in spikes. Iris said this was all protection against unseen threats. As Stephanie slowly moved forward, Iris nervously ordered her to close the door quickly. Suddenly, a fire extinguisher fell outside. She warned Stephanie not to touch anything. Anything could be a deadly trap. Finally seeing her granddaughter, Iris smiled warmly. She asked about Stefan's mother, Darlene. Stefani explained that she had been separated from her mother since she was 10 years old and didn't know how Darlene was doing now. Stephanie started asking about the nightmare. Iris told her it wasn't just a dream. She had once seen the future. She saw a disaster coming. Back then, she was with Paul on the highest rooftop. A woman's hat flew off and a boy tried to toss a coin, but security stopped him. Still, the boy insisted on throwing it. Paul was just about to propose to her. Iris immediately warned Paul the building was going to collapse. Everyone would die. Paul looked confused. Then, Iris rushed to grab the coin from the boy's hand. She got the key object that would trigger the butterfly effect. She hurried downstairs, grabbed the pot that was on fire, found people dancing inside. She quickly grabbed the microphone, told everyone to look at the floor. Some tried to stop her, but others noticed the cracks below their feet. That night, she saved many lives. The building didn't collapse. Later, the restaurant shut down. Iris had stopped the disaster, but Death didn't like his plan being ruined. Years later, he came back and killed everyone who was there that night, including her husband, Paul. Iris learned how to see death coming. She had spent years stopping disasters. Now, death had finally caught her. She had cancer. While talking to Stefani, Iris let her guard down. Death silently arrived. A magnifying glass reflected sunlight onto a metal tray. The beam bounced onto a rope. It started to smoke. Iris believed Stefani's dreams were a sign because she might have inherited her gift. Iris sensed something was wrong. She turned her head and spotted Death's trick. She quickly knocked the magnifying glass aside. Death believed Iris would be distracted because her granddaughter was there. Iris told Stefani to stay to learn the basics. It was too dangerous outside. She hadn't stepped out in 20 years, but Stefani didn't want to stay. She needed to return to school. Iris warned her death was coming for their family, but Stefani thought it was just a dream. She didn't believe her. She left without hesitation. Iris begged her to take the book before she left. Just as Stefani was about to walk out the door, Iris had a vision. The wind, the compass, trigger objects. She knew if she stepped outside, she would die. But for Stefani, she took the risk. She stepped out anyway. threw the book into Stephanie's arms, told her the book could protect the family. But Stefani still didn't believe her, so Iris told her to step back. She would prove it was all real. A sudden gust of wind blew in. It knocked over the compass. It hit a fire extinguisher. The extinguisher flew and stabbed Iris through the mouth. Now, Stefani finally believed Iris was gone. Her relatives attended the funeral. Stefani told her father and uncle that Iris had said death was coming, but they didn't believe her. Just then, Stefan's mother, Darlene, showed up, still angry at her mom. Stefani walked away. Back home, she started reading the book Iris gave her. Meanwhile, the rest of the family was at Howard's place having a barbecue, eating and laughing, completely unaware. Death had arrived. Bobby accidentally broke a glass, but he didn't notice the shard had mixed with the ice cubes. Eric placed his drink next to a gas tank. Clearly, they were about to become death's new tools. Once everyone gathered to eat and drink, they unknowingly used the ice with glass shard. Howard raised a toast. He said Iris's death reminded them to enjoy life in the moment. Then everyone clinkedked glasses and took a sip. Suddenly, Julia started choking. She felt something stuck in her throat and couldn't breathe. Everyone rushed to her, but it turned out she had just swallowed wrong. She was fine. Inside, Stefani was reading Iris's book. She saw a chapter about the coin incident and a barbecue grill. Meanwhile, Eric was outside lighting the barbecue. Bobby called Charlie over to jump on the trampoline, but they didn't see the sharp rake hidden beneath it. The book slipped from Stefanie's hands. She felt a terrible sense of danger. As the grill was lit, a photo frame fell and shattered. A shard of glass bounced across the floor, whose drink had the deadly glass piece. Howard took a sip of his drink, but nothing happened. Then the camera zoomed in on Darlene's glass. Was it hers? Stefani, sensing something was wrong, headed toward Howard's house while calling her brother Charlie. Unfortunately, he didn't pick up. The trampoline had loose stitching and was about to break. On her way, Stefani saw a warning sign. Danger ahead. It was like death itself trying to stop her. Then the glass shard was revealed in her father Marty's drink, but he only took a small sip and put it down. Howard went up to jump on the trampoline. The surface looked like it could give way any second. Luckily, Darlene spotted the hidden rake. She shouted and rushed over, pulling it out and returning it to the shed. But just then, Brenda accidentally knocked over a bottle. It hit the switch on a nearby machine. The pipes underneath began to twist and shake. The same rake from earlier started sliding down. When Stefani arrived, Death was ready to begin its performance. Howard walked over to greet her. Suddenly, Bobby's leg got stuck in the trampoline. Julia turned to look, causing a shard of glass to fall from her cup. Howard stepped on the shard. A sharp pain hit him instantly. At that moment, the rake fell onto the lawn mower. Howard lost his balance and fell. The mower charged straight toward him and ended his life. The relatives attended another funeral. Stefani rushed home to go through the books again. She found a note that said, "JB found someone who survived. She began analyzing who might be next. Iris and Paul's children were Howard and Darlene. Howard's children were Eric, Julia, and Bobby. Darlene's children were Stefani, and Charlie. They were all connected by blood and couldn't escape death." Stefani explained the pattern to the others. Now, they sat and listened quietly. It was all from the restaurant's death list. The order of death matched the one Iris had seen. Originally, hundreds should have died, but Iris saved them. And now death was coming back to claim them one by one. Death followed a specific order when it came to killing. It started with Howard's family and then it would move on to Stefani's. Marty and Brenda weren't related by blood, so they were likely off death's list. That meant the one in the most danger now was Howard's oldest son, Eric. But no one believed Stefani. They all thought she was obsessed or cursed. And one by one, they walked away. Eric arrived at his workplace. A spinning fan brushed against a hanging chain. The chain perfectly hooked onto Eric's nose ring. next to him. Disinfectant spilled onto the floor. The fan kept turning, slowly, pulling the chain tighter and tighter. Eric couldn't remove the nose ring. He had to stand on his tiptoes, balancing higher and higher. He accidentally bumped into a nearby lamp. The lamp fell and instantly ignited the flammable disinfectant. Things got worse quickly. Glass shattered on the table. Eric was in pain and panic, desperately trying to free himself. At the last second, he managed to yank off the chain, but as he fell, he knocked over more disinfectant. Moments later, the shop exploded. Meanwhile, Stefani had been worried. Eric hadn't answered any of her calls all night. She grabbed Charlie and rushed out to look for him. On the way, they nearly got into an accident. Luckily, Eric had survived. He escaped by tearing off his burning leather clothing, but what happened next made Stefani even more convinced death was hunting them. Eric, however, still didn't believe a word of it. So, Stefani decided to stay by his side to protect him. She began following Iris's notes, trying to prevent any possible chain reaction. For example, a tree trimmer suddenly fell off a branch nearby, almost hitting a boy's soccer ball, which could have struck Eric's head. Just then, they ran into Julia, who was out jogging. A garbage truck rolled by. Stefani immediately warned Eric to stay away, but Eric, being reckless, started goofing around near the truck, making silly faces. Julia ignored them, put on her headphones, and kept running. No one expected what happened next. Julia was accidentally thrown into the garbage truck. They ran after it in shock, but the driver had headphones on and couldn't hear a thing. Stephanie jumped onto the truck, reached for Julia, and managed to grab her hand, but it was still too late. Julia was crushed by the compactor. That was when the rest of the family finally realized death really was coming for them. Then, Brenda revealed a shocking truth. Eric wasn't Howard's biological son. He was the result of her affair. That might be the reason Eric survived, which meant the next one in danger was Howard's younger son, Bobby. Stefani remembered a name from the notes. William and Darlene just happened to know him. They rushed to the hospital to find him. Turns out William was the same boy Iris saved that night long ago. William explained there were only two ways to beat death. Either kill someone to take their place or die and come back. He told them he too was now sick like Iris. His time was almost up. He warned that all of them would eventually die in the exact order listed. It sounded terrifying, but the truth was even worse. William warned them, "Do not interfere too much with death's design, because if they failed, things could become even more tragic." He advised them to cherish what time they had left. Then, he quietly walked away. Eric figured if there was a way to save Bobby, then dying and coming back to life would be the easiest. He suggested Bobby eat some peanut snacks, hoping to trigger a severe allergic reaction so doctors could bring him back from the edge of death. They bought a bag of peanuts from the vending machine, but the peanuts got stuck inside. Frustrated, Eric smashed the glass to get them out. They even lifted the whole machine together. After some struggle, they finally got the peanuts. Then they stepped into the room next door, but accidentally activated the MRI scanner. A powerful magnetic force started pulling everything metal. Eric's body piercings were ripped toward the machine. Even a wheelchair behind him flew forward. Eric was crushed into the MRI machine by force. Bobby, who had just eaten the peanuts, couldn't help at all. He tried reaching for the EpiPen in Eric's hand. At that moment, a doctor noticed the commotion and opened the door. Then came the horrifying moment. A loose spring from the vending machine flew across the room and stabbed straight through Bobby's head. Stefani, Darlene, and Charlie held each other tightly. They realized they couldn't fight death anymore, so they decided to follow Iris's path and risk everything. The three of them drove deep into the mountains to Iris's old cabin. They didn't notice a coin had fallen from the notebook. An old woman picked it up from the ground. The cabin in the mountains felt creepy, as if death had already been waiting for them. Stephanie slammed the gas pedal and drove straight into the cabin. Midway, the car crashed and her seat belt buckle trapped her in place. Now Death's target was Darlene. As long as she made it safely inside the cabin, everyone else might be safe, but no one saw the sparks coming from a shortcircuited roof wire. Just as Darlene reached the cabin door, a huge explosion blasted the car. Stefan's body plunged into a nearby pond. Charlie was pinned down by wooden boards. Injured and struggling, Darlene crawled over and freed Charlie. She told him to save Stefani quickly. Right after she said that, a light pole fell from above and killed her on the spot. Charlie rushed to pull Stefani out. She was unconscious. Luckily, he revived her just in time. The two hugged each other and laughed. This had to be what William meant by die and come back. But when she heard Darlene had died, Stefani couldn't hold back her tears. Only she and Charlie were left from Iris's bloodline. A week later, Charlie and Stefani visited his girlfriend's house. While fixing Charlie's clothes, Stefani pricked her finger on a rose thorn. Suddenly, she remembered the nightmare. In that dream, Iris had also pricricked her finger. Then, an old woman dropped a coin. It rolled down the steps and got stuck between the train tracks. A train was speeding toward it. Charlie's girlfriend's father was a doctor. When he heard how Charlie saved Stefani, he explained that Stefani hadn't technically died. If you're unconscious and someone gets your breathing back, but your heart never stopped. Then, you weren't really dead, he said casually. But to Stefani and Charlie, that didn't sound good. Stephanie saw a red car just like in her dream. Charlie's girlfriend was even wearing the same clothes as Iris had. Her bad feeling grew stronger. Then the train derailed. A crash happened. The train was charging straight at them. Stefani tripped and fell. Charlie grabbed her and pulled her up. It looked like they had escaped, but they hadn't.

text: Hi Everyone, Meta Anime here. Hope you are doing well. Today I am going to tell the story of a film called Summer Wars. This film is a story about a social network and a stranger's connection with a strange family. From this film, we can also see what would happen to the world if everything can be controlled virtually. It was released in 2009 and was written and directed by Satoko Okudera and Mamoru Hosoda. They were famous for their previous work: The Girl Who Leapt Through Time which was released in 2006. Before we go, this video contains spoilers. So please take this warning for those that haven't watched this movie yet. So without further ado, here's the recap of Summer Wars!! Oz is a virtual world that can be accessed by anyone in the world. It can be accessed through various devices such as computers, mobile phones, and even gaming consoles. Here, everyone is represented through an avatar that is unique to each and every user. This avatar holds all the personal information of its user and can have as much authority in real life as its user. Through this world of Oz, users can do various things such as shopping, socializing with other users from all around the world using automatic translation, and many other things. With its business support and services, companies and even the government set their offices inside Oz. This allows users more versatility to do various tasks in Oz that can directly impact the real world. Since the avatar holds all the personal information of its user, it also has much authority in real life as its user. This world of Oz is protected by its guardian angels called John and Yoko. Basically, this world of Oz is almost like the world of Metaverse that was proposed by Mark Zuckerberg. The scene continues to show two avatars that looked like a monkey and a mouse currently working inside the Oz. The mouse avatar was seen as disappointed with the fact that he failed to represent Japan in the International Math Olympics. Suddenly in real life, a girl named Natsuki came into their room which apparently is inside a school. She was looking for someone that will do a part-time job. At first, the two of them refused because they already have part-time work in Oz, but changed their mind when they know that all they have to do is accompany her back to her hometown. Natsuki then only took the boy who owned the mouse avatar named Kenji because she only need one person. The next scene shows a bunny avatar called King Kazma fighting and winning against all other avatars in the so-called Oz World Championship. Kenji and Natsuki then went together on a train to Ueda which is Natsuki's hometown. Inside the train, Kenji showed his mathematical prowess by calculating the day Natsuki was born from her birthday. On their way to Natsuki's house, they met several of Natsuki's relatives that are also coming home. They then arrived at Natsuki's grandmother's house which is a huge traditional Japanese house Apparently, Natsuki is a descendant of an ancient honored clan that has a long history spanning to the Japanese ancient warring time called the Junoichi clan. All the relatives gather to celebrate their oldest grandmother's birthday. The two of them then met Natsuki's grandmother. Suddenly Natsuki told her grandmother that Kenji is her boyfriend and fiance. This made Natsuki's grandmother and Kenji very shocked. Kenji then had to play along with Natsuki's sudden plan to make her grandmother happy. The next scene shows a dining table full of Natsuki's relatives having dinner while chatting with each other and welcoming Kenji. It beautifully shows the warm dynamics of the very big family with a very long history of having dinner together. At night, Kenji was seen lost in the big house trying to find a toilet. While searching, he met another one of Natsuki's relatives who is a boy playing on a computer alone inside a dark room. The boy then told Kenji the direction to the toilet then continued to play. After that, the whole family was shocked by the appearance of someone called Wabisuke who seemed to be hated by the whole family except Natsuki. Apparently, he is the son of the grandfather's mistress. He went to America after selling the grandmother's certificate to a mountain. After dinner, Wabisuke and Natsuki played a Japanese traditional card game together. Natsuki seemed to really like Wabisuke and act as if Kenji was not there. It seemed so sad to be Kenji at that time. During the night, Kenji that couldn't sleep got a mail on his phone from a mysterious sender The mail is filled with what seemed like a random arrangement of numbers. The curious Kenji who thought that it was a puzzle tried to solve it with his mathematical prowess. He then managed to solve the puzzle in a relatively short time and sent the solution back to the sender. In the morning, two little boys who were Natsuki's relatives woke Kenjiupand dragged him to the tv. The news on the tv said that Oz had been suffered a cyberattack and apparently the culprit was Kenji's avatar and so, Kenji is suspected to be the culprit. All the activities in Oz got messed up which affected all aspects of real-life from shopping to business. The panicked Kenji tried to log into his account but failed. He then tried to find the boy with the computer to borrow his computer so that he can log in. Kenji's friend called Sakuma who is the owner of the monkey avatar previously seen before then called Kenji. He told Kenji that Oz's security which is protected by an encrypted 2056 digit code was deciphered by someone in one night. It was Kenji who deciphered the code and sent it to the mysterious sender. The next scene showed the disordered Oz with Kenji's mouse avatar in the middle of it controlling other peoples' avatars. It was shown that the mouse avatar can steal other people's avatars and control them. Using a borrowed squirrel avatar, Kenji tried to persuade him to stop doing this but was attacked by the mouse's avatar. Suddenly King Kazma came and beat the mouse character up. Apparently, the boy in the room is the owner of the King Kazma avatar and is called Kazuma. But in the middle of the fight, Kazuma is interrupted by the two little boys that suddenly came and caused the mouse avatar to escape King Kazma's grip and steal more avatars. After stealing more avatars, the mouse avatar evolved into a huge god-like avatar that is way stronger than before. He then easily beat King Kazma up due to the power-up. Kenji then saved King Kazma from being stolen by the new god avatar. After that, it was revealed that Kenji's old avatar was hijacked by an AI released by the US military called the Love Machine. In the living room, the whole family was dumbfounded by the news that Kenji was the culprit that caused chaos in Oz. Kenji was then arrested by Shota, one of Natsuki's relatives who is a cop. Shota then takes Kenji to the police station using his car. Inside Oz, Love Machine was seen unlocking the access to the whole of Oz's infrastructure. He messed up the whole system managing Japan such as GPS, Train line, cable line, and so many more, and caused so much trouble in real life. Due to the traffic jam caused by Love Machine messing with the traffic system, Kenji and Shota went back home using a motorcycle. The grandmother who saw this messed up situation then decided to take an action. She took her telephone and a very thick book. She called her grandchildren currently working in important units such as firefighter unit and emergency unit to encourage them. She even called the higher-ups from Japan's important government units such as the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism, The Fire and Disaster Management Agency, etc. She was even directly talking to the Superintendent General. During the phone call, she kept motivating them by telling them to never give up and saying that they can definitely do it. Slowly the order was restored because of the hard work of the people and Kenji managed to solve another encryption which gave him and other avatars in Oz access again. It was then revealed that there are 55 people in the world who also solved the encryption last night but Kenji's not one of them because of a typo in the last word. This cleared Kenji's name from the accusation. Due to the restored order, more family members managed to come home at the night and they all had dinner together. During the dinner, Wabisuke told Kenji and the others that they can't beat Love Machine and revealed that he was one of Love Machine's developer Wabisuke told grandma that he did it to gain money back to that he can repay her. But this enraged grandma who tried to kill him instead. This made Wabisuke leave the house in the middle of the night. After dinner, grandma played the Hanafuda card game with Kenji. Grandma said that if she wins, Kenji must take good care of Natsukieven though grandma already knows that Natsuki asked Kenji to pretend to be her fiance. And in the end, grandma won against Kenji and ended it with a smile. In the morning, everyone rushed around the grandma's room to see her worsened condition. She died surrounded by her family members inside her room. Due to the chaos in the Oz system, grandma's health monitoring system was interrupted and first aid couldn't be given to her. Because of this, Kenji and Natsuki's uncles devised a plan to defeat Love Machine so that this will not happen again to anyone. They spread out preparing for the plan. Uncle Tasuke brought a supercomputer from his electronic store. Uncle Mansuke brought his fishing boat which act as the power source. And the other uncle who works in the military brought a jeep with a military-grade antenna module from Japan's Self Defense Force military base. The preparation ends with the blocks of ice to cool the supercomputer down. After everything is ready, King Kazma then sent an invitation to Love Machine to start a fight. Love Machine who accepted King Kazma's invitation then came and they both have a rematch. King Kazma had the upper hand and beat Love Machine up. Love Machine then tried to escape and use his controlled avatars to attack King Kazma. King Kazma was then saved by uncle Mansuke who used his avatar through a retro gaming console. Thanks to the time he bought, King Kazma was able to escape and tricked the love machine into a trap room that they had prepared before. After Love Machine is trapped, Natsuki's uncles then filled the room with water to make Love Machine drown. But suddenly their trap crumbled little by little due to the supercomputer overheating. The idiot Shota has apparently moved the ice from the computer to grandma's room to cool her room. In the end, Love Machine escaped and took the form of a giant combined form of avatars He then took out King Kazma in just one hit. In real life, the angry Kazuma then hit Shota's face after being ridiculed by Shota the idiot. Upon seeing the monitor back, the clock in Oz suddenly changed into a countdown and showed pictures of nuclear power plants around the world. Love Machine then redirects one of Japan's satellites to hit one of the power plants and that countdown is showing the time before the satellite hit the earth. Seeing that, Kazuma got very angry and tried to attack Love Machine again but was beaten up easily and consumed by Love Machine. Love Machine's form then changed into the form of a god-like bunny. The whole family who was in the living room then know of the real terror of Love Machine. Natsuki then called Wabisuke telling him that grandma is gone. Hearing it, the shocked Wabisuke then rushed immediately back home. Upon hearing grandma's last letter telling them to stay calm, they then all joined together to have lunch with Wabisuke who went home in such a chaotic state. The time shows one more hour before the satellite hit the earth. While having lunch, they discuss the strategy to beat Love Machine. Wabisuke planned to break Love Machine's programming down internally and Kenji proposed to challenge Love Machine to a Hanafuda Card game knowing that Love Machine loves playing games and will accept the challenge. Natsuki then represents the whole family in challenging Love Machine in the game. She bet her family's 20 accounts so that she can take Love Machine's stolen accounts. As Natsuki keep winning the game, she gained more and more accounts and the bet also increases. But, the unfocused Natsuki lost a match against Love Machine and was left with 74 accounts. With the number of accounts available, she cannot continue the match due to the already high bet. Suddenly, all the people around the world who are watching her match approached her and offer her to use their account for the match. Natsuki also received a new skin for her avatar from Oz's guardians. She then bet all of the accounts she have into one final match and finally stripped Love Machine of all the stolen accounts. The countdown finally came to a stop. But while they were celebrating, suddenly the countdown started again and this time the satellite is targeting their home. Love Machine still has control over the satellite. The whole family started to panic and immediately try to evacuate from the house. But Kenji never gave up. In one final fight, Kenji tried to take over the system controlled by Love Machine by solving the 2056 digit encryption. He solved it in a short time but was immediately locked out again by Love Machine. Kenji then tried to solve it again and was locked out again. The third time, Kenji managed to do an incredible thing by doing the calculation inside his head. When Love Machine tried to lock him out again, King Kazma rushed to him to immediately punch him. Upon receiving King Kazma's punch, Love Machine was completely destroyed because Wabisuke had weakened him beforehand. And finally, the satellite's coordinate was changed and redirected from their house. The satellite fell near their house and the impact surfaced a hot spring from inside the ground. In the end, the whole family celebrated grandma's birthday and funeral with a lot of other people attending in front of their ruined house due to the impact of the satellite. The film ends with Wabisuke surrendering to the authorities and Natsuki kissing Kenji while being pushed by the whole family. So that concludes the recap of Summer Wars. What do you guys think? This film is very personal to me as it is one of my very first anime movies and I really liked it. It beautifully presented the warm family dynamic and some geeky sci-fi which is personally very fascinating to me. I can watch it many times and not get bored of it. The film is very pleasing to watch with a very lighthearted story and very interesting sci-fi comedy aspects. It also has amazing animation and a very good fight scene which made it even more enjoyable. At the same time, it also reminds us of the dangerous aspect of the virtual world and how we really need to be more careful with our data and cyber security as it can impact our real-life greatly. Overall, I really recommend you to watch this film and it will remain one of my favorite anime movies of all time. Please tell us what you think through the comment section. If you like this content, please leave us a like and share them with your friends. Thank you for watching, and till we see you again!

text: The movie begins with a child named Sammy Fabelsman standing wearing a blue hat and coat. Sammy soon begins filming regularly, sometimes involving his younger sisters Reggie, Natalie, and Lisa in his shoots. After Burt receives a new job, he and the family, along with his best friend and business partner Bennie Loewy, move to Phoenix, Arizona. Along the way, Sam shoots everyone. Sam also joins them but finds a piece of paper with a hole in the middle of it. The scene then cuts to a room where everyone can be seen sitting and watching Sam’s film. As soon as the action seems comes, a bright light appears when the boys do a shooting. This touch makes the scene extremely realistic, resulting in praise from everyone. On their drive back home, Burt and Sam have a proper conversation about this. When inquired, Sam explains how he did a hole within the reels so when the scene comes, the light passes through it. Hearing this Burt gets stunned and praises him. But still suggest he focus on his studies for a bright future. The family then goes to a forest for a picnic where Sam continues to do the shooting. They all are really happy together as they sat down to sing with each other. In the night, Bennie and Burt argued about how Bennie wants to stay in the same city but Burt wants to move forward. Mitzi who was hearing the conversation come behind Burt and whisper in his ear how she wishes to stay in the same city. As she deeply kiss him, she began dancing with her body being visible from behind, she doesn’t stop. Sam records all of this. A few days later, Mitzi’s mother passes away. She keeps crying on her chest. Seeing this Burt bring Sam a video editing machine asking him to make a movie of all the happy scene of his mother’s life to make her happy once again. Meanwhile, his Uncle Boris visits them and tells them at the dining table how he has worked with numerous film crew members. This sparked Sam's interest and ask he them multiple questions. Even at night, he shows them all his detailed scenes. Boris also admired his creativity and his passion but warns how sometimes a passion of this magnitude can cause him to choose between either his passion or the family. This statement upsets Sam and he becomes upset. After a few days, Boris bids his goodbye leaving Mitzi crying. Sam begins to edit the movie for his mother. He even cut the scenes separately in reels so he can join them properly. By going through them, he sees Bennie and Mitzi extremely close which disturbs him. To confirm his doubt, in one clip, he sees them kissing each other. He gets shocked but still edits the video removing all the scenes. The entire family watches the movie. Especially Mitzi gets happy but as she goes to hug Sam, he leaves silently. Sam now can be seen holding his camera as his friends do the acting of some soldier during the attack. He then directs one soldier to do an emotional impact so he can make his audience go through an emotional breakdown. The actor then walks between the dead soldiers as Sam shoots him. Sam invites the students and their families to see the movie where the emotional ending scene makes everyone cry. Sam ignores Bennie and Mitzi who leave together making him even more upset. The scene then shifts to their home where Mitzi and Sam have an argument resulting in Mitzi hitting Sam on the back. As she follows him to the room inquiring about the reason behind his crudeness. He shows her all the clips. As she watches them, she begins crying slowly. Sam promises not to tell Burt as Mitzi hugs him tightly. Before they can move out again. Sam decides to sell his camera where he met Bennie who insists on gifting him a new camera as his passion makes his mother happy. Bennie gives Sam both a camera and money. He takes departure after hugging him tightly. As they all move to their new home, their face shows their disapproval. When he tries to apologize, Logan threatens him that if he pulls such sort of stunt again, he will kill him. At home, a monkey brought by Mitzi turns the world upside down. This leads them to have an argument where Burt shows his disapproval of Mitzi's lack of interest in the home. The next day, in school Sam saw Logan kissing some red hairy girl.
