text: At the beginning of the movie, Cynthia is in a classroom where she finds a book, and when she opens it, she sees Larry's name written inside. As she turns the pages, she comes across a message, Help me, the wolf has me, and suddenly, Cynthia hears Larry calling for help. Following the voice, she moves toward its source and finds an entity in an office, the one who has locked Larry inside a cage. Cynthia tells Larry that he's free to leave, saying the door is open. When Larry shakes his head, she reminds him that only he can let himself out. The entity warns her not to talk to him, but Cynthia tells Larry that the entity has no power over him and that he just needs to realize it. As Larry tries to leave the cage, the entity turns towards Cynthia, shattering a glass and injuring her. As it starts crawling toward her, Cynthia calmly assures Larry that it's okay, and they'll try again next time. Enraged, the entity growls, but Cynthia begins reciting something under her breath, and in the next moment, she snaps back to the real world. She tells Larry that they're back and reassures him that he's safe. When Larry notices the cut on her arm and apologizes, Cynthia says it's okay, adding that their time is up for today, but he's welcome to stay as long as he likes. Later, Cynthia asks her daughter, Jordan, if she can find out which physical education teachers Larry had between 4th and 12th grade. Larry asks Jordan if she has ever tried it, to which she replies that she's been training, but hasn't had any success yet. She then reveals that both her parents had the ability, and they mastered it together, and it's how they found each other. Later, a girl comes to their door, saying she urgently needs to speak with Cynthia. Jordan lets her in and asks if she's with someone, to which she explains that her dad is on his way, but she needs to talk to Cynthia before he arrives. Jordan says if she's in danger, she can help, but the girl insists she just needs to speak to Cynthia. Noticing marks on her arms, Jordan asks what happened, but when the girl stays silent, Jordan explains that she can't let her talk to Cynthia without first doing an assessment. The girl introduces herself as Riley and says she's 14 and a woman named Agatha told her dad that Cynthia could help someone like her. Jordan asks what she means, to which Riley says she sees a dark figure, something like a person, but not quite, and it stares at her like a starving dog. Jordan asks if it ever speaks to her, and Riley says it always says the same thing. Jordan then asks if it's here right now, and Riley nods. Jordan asks if she can point to it, and Riley points to a corner of the room. Jordan then asks where she got the scars, but Riley, clearly terrified says, it's standing right behind me, and I can feel it's very hungry, sensing that something is wrong. Cynthia comes out and freezes in fear when she sees the entity. Just then, Riley's dad, Randall, rushes in and insists they don't need any help. Riley protests Cynthia can help them, but despite her pleas, he forces her to leave with him. Later, Jordan asks her mom what's going on and whether they should call the police, to which Cynthia replies that they don't need to involve the police, as there's nothing they or the police can do for Riley. When Jordan presses her to explain, Cynthia says that something terrible is attached to the girl. Jordan argues that if she saw it, doesn't that mean she can help? To which Cynthia asks, do you know why you do screenings before I meet with any clients? Jordan answers, to assess their psychological needs, and to protect them, and Cynthia adds, and to protect us. Jordan says, you're the only one who can help that girl, but Cynthia replies that she's not going to involve herself with whatever is attached to her. Jordan responds, Dad would have helped, to which Cynthia says, that's why your dad's not here anymore. Later, Cynthia speaks to Jordan calmly, saying, today scared me, and it reminded her of her father because the woman he tried to help had something attached to her, and he couldn't let it go. Jordan replies, that's because he cared about people, and that's what made him who he was. Cynthia responds, whatever was attached to that girl today isn't the same as what we deal with. Jordan counters, that's even more reason to help her, but Cynthia says it's more reason not to. She explains, if she told Riley's father that his daughter has something attached to her, he'd turn on them, just like everyone did back in Elmsboro. She asks, does she remember how bad it got? Then adds, that after they moved, she promised herself she would never let that happen again. She explains that the world believes in science, not in spirits, and one day when she can see things for what they are, she hopes she will know when to help, and when to protect themselves. The next morning, Jordan tells Cynthia that she's going to meet her friends, and after Jordan leaves, Cynthia opens her notebook, revealing a sketch of the entity she saw attached to Riley. Next, we see Jordan meeting Agatha, and asking if she knows Riley Harris, to which Agatha replies that she doesn't think so. Jordan then mentions that Riley said she heard Agatha speaking to her father, suggesting that Cynthia might be able to help her. Agatha recalls Randall Harris from Kenilworth, whose wife died last year. Jordan expresses her concern for the girl, saying that anything Agatha knows might help, to which Agatha shares that she noticed some scars on Riley, and Randall said they were self-inflicted, so she gave him Cynthia's card, though she didn't explain exactly what Cynthia does. Meanwhile, Cynthia speaks to John, requesting that he keep an eye on a suspect named Doe Ferry. John comments that she's good at getting hunches, but she never provides him with a reason or a source. Cynthia asks him to check if there's anything on his record. John finds the record and asks what she wants him to do with this, to which Cynthia says she just knows he's a terrible man, and just keep an eye on him. Later, Cynthia searches through her books, trying to find information about the entity, but the memories of it scare her deeply. Staring at her husband's photo, she says, I've never felt an entity this strong before, so I can't help Riley. Meanwhile, Jordan meets Randall, who thanks her for coming but insists his daughter doesn't need a shrink and says he has it under control. Jordan says she thinks Riley needs someone who can see what she sees, to which Randall turns to her and asks, what exactly does Riley tell her she sees? Jordan replies, enough to get an idea of what she's going through, to which Randall says she doesn't know them or what they have been through, and suggests she mind her own business. She asks if she can speak to her directly, but Randall says she's not here, before heading into his workshop. Jordan starts scanning the area around the house, and when she peeks into the basement, she spots Riley down there, desperate to help. Jordan sneaks into the house and approaches a door, thinking it leads to the basement. However, when she opens it, she discovers it's just a closet. Confused, she turns to leave, but then hears a voice, and when she pulls the clothes aside, she finds a hidden door behind them. Jordan quickly rushes back to grab a screwdriver and returns to the wardrobe. She uses the screwdriver to open the latch, and finally manages to unlock the door. Jordan enters the basement and calls out to Riley, saying she's just there to talk to her. Just then, she hears a voice coming from behind a door and tries to call out to her mom, but suddenly the door opens. Riley says, dad doesn't lock me down here, he locks them down here. Jordan asks, who is them? But only then she gets a call from her mother, and suddenly Randall knocks her down, and then disconnects the call. Just then, Agatha calls Cynthia, saying she was just checking to see if Jordan had spoken with Randall. Cynthia asks, who's Randall? To which Agatha explains that Jordan had stopped by earlier, asking about his daughter. Confused, Cynthia asks, what daughter? And what exactly did Jordan say? To which Agatha replies, she said a girl had stopped by their house last night, and she just wanted to talk to her. Meanwhile, Jordan regains consciousness and finds herself tied to a chair, and to her horror, she sees another woman tied to a chair beside her. Frightened, she calls out for help, but Randall enters the room and demands her password. Jordan pleads that she only wants to help his daughter, but Randall says no one can, explaining past attempts always ended with child services trying to take Riley. Jordan insists her mom can help, but Randall replies that no one could help Riley, just like no one could help his wife. Jordan promises they can figure out what the entity wants, and get it to leave them alone, to which Randall says they already know what it wants, and explains that Riley has to feed it, or else it will feed on her. Riley then steps closer to Jordan, and quietly says, I'm sorry, before placing her hand on Jordan's shoulder. And instantly, the entity appears behind Jordan, grabs her, overwhelming her with immense pain, and after a moment, as soon as Riley pulls her hand away, the entity retreats. Randall tells Riley she did a good job, and instructs her to go upstairs. And Riley thanks Jordan before leaving. Meanwhile, Cynthia and Agatha are driving to Randall's house, and Cynthia worries Jordan might be in trouble, but Agatha reads a text from Jordan saying she’s just with friends. Cynthia, unconvinced, says, that's not like her, pointing out they had plans. Randall urges Riley to hurry and get Jordan into the truck. Riley asks if they can see if her mom can help, but Randall says Jordan is different, so people will come looking, and if they find her, they’ll take you away. Riley grabs pliers and leaves saying she needs to get her backpack. Riley returns to the basement and asks Jordan if Cynthia really saw it. To which Jordan says yes, and promises that if she lets her out, she can take her to her, Riley says. Cynthia can't get her dad in trouble, explaining that he's just trying to protect her. She adds that if Cynthia can make her better, then her dad can become a good person again. After this, she hands the pliers to Jordan, and says she will try to keep her dad busy outside. Meanwhile, Randall realizes that Riley took the pliers, and Jordan tries to cut the zip tie, but the pliers slip from her hands. Desperate to free herself, she applies more force, and manages to break the zip tie. She then picks up the pliers again, frees the woman, and rushes to get help. But Randall confronts her, pointing a rifle at her. Jordan says he doesn't need to do this and that, Riley needs help. Just then, Riley comes running in and says she can help them, insisting he can't keep hurting people, and that she doesn't want to be part of this anymore. Randall orders her to move, but the woman suddenly lunges at him, and in the chaos, Riley is shot. Just then, Jordan's head begins to spin, and after a moment, she sees the horrifying entity right in front of her. It suddenly grabs her face, causing Riley to experience terrifying visions, and after a short while, Jordan snaps back to consciousness and runs away from the scene. Agatha and Cynthia find Jordan on the road just outside Randall's house, while Randall flees the scene in his truck. Later, John tells Cynthia that Riley's body was taken to Common Grove Hospital, where staff who knew her are shaken. He adds that forensics found more remains, meaning the killer’s been active for a while, and Jordan was lucky to escape. Agatha asks, has they found Randall, to which John says not yet, but they will find him. He also mentions Cynthia's hunch about Doe was likely right, saying they've brought him in for questioning after spotting troubling behavior on surveillance. Meanwhile, Jordan is questioned about the sores on her arms, to which she says Randall attacked her, and she thinks the marks are from struggling. When asked if it happened after he fired the rifle, Jordan says yes and explains she punched him and escaped. An officer adds that forensics found remains under the woodshed, calling it one of the worst crime scenes ever, and says she is their best lead to finding Randall. As Jordan looks up, she suddenly sees the entity again, and begins screaming in terror, but the entity vanishes, and Jordan, shaken, says she thinks she needs to go home. Once home, Jordan tells Cynthia that she's seeing it, but Cynthia says she's just been through a traumatic experience. Jordan insists that Riley died in her arms, and she saw it leave Riley, and she can still feel it, but Cynthia says she would sense it if it were really there. Jordan pleads with her to look inside her, but Cynthia refuses. Jordan says she knows she is afraid of seeing dad, saying they share the same trauma, and it doesn't matter if she looks or not. It's not gonna stop. Cynthia remains silent, and Jordan, hurt and frustrated, calls her a coward before leaving. Agatha tells Cynthia that a smart woman once said the only way to overcome fear is to face it. She points out that she's spent years helping others, but never herself, and whatever she's afraid to confront, she's already survived worse. Agatha adds that Jordan needs her now. Cynthia tells Agatha to wake her if she struggles, then warns Jordan that if an entity is attached to her, it will target the weakest, most painful part of her mind. She then touches her forehead and closes her eyes, and in the next moment, she finds herself inside Jordan's mind. There, she sees a newspaper clipping that reads, therapist pushes woman to suicide, claims there's a demon inside. Cynthia turns around, closes her eyes, and recites something, and in the next moment, she finds herself outside her house. There, she sees young Jordan and asks if she wants to come inside with her. Jordan shakes her head, and Cynthia gently assures her that it's okay. Just then, a man throws a bottle at the window and walks away without saying a word. As Cynthia turns to enter the house, Jordan stops her, but she reassures her, saying it's going to be okay. Cynthia enters the house, but as she moves toward the stairs, she senses the presence of the entity, which unnerves her, and suddenly, the entity attacks, causing her arm to burn. Agatha tries to wake her up and slaps her to bring her back. Cynthia tells her that a shake would have sufficed, to which Agatha apologizes, saying she panicked. Later, Cynthia thanks Agatha for being there, and asks if she could stay a bit longer, as she needs to do something and doesn't want Jordan to be alone if she wakes up. Cynthia visits the hospital, where Larry asks what she's doing there, to which she explains that she needs his help to find information about the doctor who treated a woman with the last name Harris. Larry checks the records and says he remembers Samantha Harris, because it was a huge deal at the hospital, something like a flesh-eating disease. He mentions that Dr. Whitaker was the lead on the case, but he retired. Cynthia meets with Whitaker and explains that she has a client who may have an illness similar to Samantha Harris's. She asks what he can tell her about Samantha, to which Whitaker tells her that she came in with her husband and daughter, and she deteriorated very quickly. After two weeks, her hair fell out, then her teeth and nails. It was like she was rotting, both inside and out. Cynthia asks if Samantha ever said anything about what she thought it could be, to which Whitaker explains that, about three weeks in, Samantha noticed how distraught he was. One night, near the end, she asked him to come closer and whispered, It has me, and it's here with us right now. It's hungry, and I can show you. She reached out her hand and told him, don't be scared, it's worse if you're afraid. When she grabbed his hand, Whitaker says he could feel it, like every part of his body was being pulled toward her. She needed him to understand that this was beyond anything medicine could fix, and it was her way of saying thank you for trying. Whitaker then shows Cynthia the marks on his arm, explaining that after that night, he couldn't bring himself to go back in. Samantha's daughter stayed with her during her final days, and held her hand until she passed. Cynthia asks if he believed something was really with Samantha, to which Whitaker says he hopes she understands why he can't answer that directly, but adds that if her client is suffering from the same symptoms, she's better off being helped by someone like her than someone like him. Meanwhile, Jordan has a dream where she finds herself walking toward an attic, and as she steps closer, the entity whispers, feed me. Jordan says no, to which the entity attacks her, but she jolts awake, realizing it was just a nightmare. However, just then, the door of her room creaks open. Agatha suddenly wakes up hearing a noise, and thinking Cynthia has returned. She looks around, but when she doesn't see anyone, she settles back down and starts reading her book. Meanwhile, when Jordan comes out of her room, looking for her mom, she hears someone's voice, but when she looks in that direction, no one is there, though we see the entity lurking right behind her. Jordan comes downstairs and heads to the kitchen, where she finds the sketch of the entity that Cynthia had drawn. Just then, she hears a noise and sees the entity emerging from behind the fridge, but suddenly, Randall attacks her. Cynthia returns home to find Agatha on the floor. She wakes her up and asks what happened? to which Agatha weakly says someone was there. Cynthia rushes to check on Jordan’s room and finds her missing. She runs outside, screaming that Jordan is gone, prompting the officer to call for backup. Panicked, she screams for help and manages to push open the lid, but Randall tells her not to move and presses a shovel against her neck to silence her. Terrified, Jordan pleads, saying he doesn't have to do this and that she never meant for Riley to get hurt. Randall replies that this isn't about Riley, or even about her, but about it. He says she held Riley when she died, and now it's inside her, and now no one is going to be around when she dies, so it will either starve or return to wherever it came from. He then closes the lid and secures it, while Jordan continues screaming and pleading for him to let her out. Ignoring her cries, Randall throws the box into a pit and begins shoveling soil over it, and after a moment, he finally buries her. Later, an officer informs John that Randall Harris has turned himself in, and when Cynthia sees him, she immediately asks where Jordan is, but Randall remains silent. Cynthia urges John to let her speak to Randall, but he says it's against protocol. She insists, saying this is about her daughter, and that minutes from now they could know where Jordan is, but if she doesn't talk to him, they might never find her. She says he knows she can do this, but John says sorry to her and leaves. Meanwhile, Jordan finds the torch that had been left in the box and tries to find a way out, but just then, she hears the entity's voice, and to her horror, she sees it crawling over her, causing her to scream in terror. John asks the officer, what's going on with Doe, and the officer says he thinks they just found the two Sawyer kids who went missing last year. John then returns to Cynthia and says, she's not going to have much time in there. Cynthia asks Randall where Jordan is, but he says it won't hurt anyone else. Cynthia places her fingers on his forehead and begins reciting something, and in the next moment, she finds herself inside his mind. There, she sees Riley crying over her mother's dead body, while Randall stands outside the door. Cynthia closes her eyes again, and after a while, she gets teleported to the woods, where she sees Randall burying Jordan. Randall turns to her and says she has to leave her, ordering Cynthia to get out of his head, which forces her to snap back to reality. Randall tells her she can't find Jordan, saying she has to die. Meanwhile, the entity tells Jordan to feed it as it crawls closer and then grabs her face, beginning to feed on her. Cynthia drives toward the woods, and Agatha asks, shouldn't we call the police and let them know? But Cynthia replies, the police can't help her. After driving a bit farther, Cynthia finally reaches the spot. She and Agatha begin digging the ground, while the police, following fresh tire tracks, also start moving in their direction. Cynthia finally locates Jordan, but is horrified when she sees the entity, which disappears the next moment. She tries to wake Jordan and tells Agatha that she's alive but weak. Agatha hears police sirens and calls out to them, but Cynthia stops her, explaining that Jordan doesn't have much time, and she needs to handle this here. She tells Agatha that she needs her to go and distract the police, because if they separate them, she won't be able to help Jordan. As Agatha goes to distract the police, Cynthia enters Jordan's mind, where she finds Jordan sitting outside the house, and she tells her to stay there. Cynthia goes up to the attic, where she finds her husband's lifeless body hanging, and meanwhile, Jordan also enters the house. Cynthia encounters the entity there, and filled with fury, demands that it leave Jordan alone, offering herself in Jordan's place. The entity moves toward her, saying, feed me, and as it gets closer, it suddenly attacks her. However, Cynthia raises her hand, places her fingers on its forehead, and begins reciting something, before the scene cuts abruptly. Next, Cynthia experiences terrifying visions, and realizes she is trapped inside the entity's mind. Six months later, Cynthia enters Jordan's mind again and asks how she's feeling today, to which Jordan nods in response. Jordan climbs the stairs and reaches the attic, where she finds her father's lifeless body. Cynthia watches as Jordan gently removes the noose from around his neck, and in the next moment, her father's body disappears. Cynthia tells Jordan that she is proud of her, saying, now you do me, to which Jordan laughs and replies, no way I'm ready for that. They then hug tightly, and the movie ends there.

Hal kind of knows who's responsible and starts getting a sense the monkey can kill people. At Annie's funeral, Lois, the boy's mother, hilariously attempts to console them, saying everyone dies, everyone you know, and everyone they know. She goes on, it doesn't matter how or why, but when. This is the point, I think. This little monkey is deciding when people die. It's obscene every time, yet the outcome is the same. The monkey gets her as well, of course. Lois has a brain aneurysm in the kitchen, right in front of Bill as he comes home from school. He is super mentally messed up after this, kind of staring off into space and giving, like, a good son vibe. Hal is slightly better off mentally though because he knows the monkey did it, as he wished for it to kill his brother before it went for his mom. Hal tries to cut the monkey up to get rid of it, and when he starts dropping away, he sees actual blood. So this thing is, like, alive. The two intently focus on one another, and Bill's obviously changed from this event. He asks Hal about the monkey and ends up twisting the key in his back. Bill believes somewhat that the monkey is causing all of this, so he's somewhat scared to twist the key. However, he says if he dies, oh well, at least he'll be with his mom. We follow Hal, a loner now, working in a store. He has a son, Pete, and gets to see him once a year for a week. This being on his terms because of the monkey killing curse that's been put on his family. Those closest to him being the ones most in danger. It's honestly a fucked up situation that only gets funny when you realize it's all because of this monkey. Hal first tells Pete he is an only child. Here you have his son thinking his dad doesn't want him, but what he really wants is to keep everyone safe. This was their own father's predicament as well, as we hear Lois speaking badly about him to the boys before she dies, due to him leaving his family behind. In the opening of the film, he's trying to get rid of the monkey, probably so he can go back to his family, but they never see him again. The aunt that used to take care of them ends up dying tragically in a freak accident, aka the monkey. In fact, people all over town are dying in freak accidents, sometimes four to five a day, but just two is winding up the key to make the monkey keep killing. Hal takes his son on their once a year road trip, but is hounded by memories of his dark past. At their motel, he gets a strange phone call. It's his brother and as they are talking outside, they go back and forth about what they should do. It's then a woman jumps into the pool and gets blown to pieces due to the electricity running through it. He needs to find and stop the monkey and whoever is twisting the key before it gets to his son. He goes to his aunt's and discovers she recently had a yard sale. It's at this yard sale, some straggly guy takes the monkey and brings it home. He becomes obsessed with the monkey and appears he's also a twin. The woman showing Hal around the house dies in a freak accident. That's when Bill calls Hal at the house and confirms he's still alive. Hal and his son are on the brink of separation, but finding and taking down this monkey seems like the only option Hal has at this point. They stay in a motel and Hal gets another phone call from Bill. Hal realizes Bill is the one twisting the key causing the killings. He is killed like half their town and again it's hilarious how the movie shows us all this. Bill was given a vision from the monkey about Hal asking him to kill him when they were kids. He saw how that backfired and killed their mother and is now taking revenge trying to kill his brother using the monkey. The straggly guy holds Hal and Pete hostage and takes him to where Bill is so they can get the monkey for him. Again he's obsessed with the thing. He ends up dying when his body and mouth are invaded by wasps. Filling his entire body up to the point of bursting his jaw. It's the craziest kill in the film I think and it was amazing. Then Hal goes to his son who's inside talking to his uncle. He tries to make amends with his brother and they forgive each other. Killing random people with a toy monkey probably isn't the best way to cope with the death of one's mother. You go Bill. And just when you think it's a happy ending the monkey hits its drum one last time. Setting off a booby trap and Lois' old bowling ball smashes Bill's head in. Hal and Pete drive away with the monkey in the car deciding to keep it close so it can't get into the wrong hands.

text: Hi, I'm Tina, the theatrical turtle, and I've got something sharper than my teeth for you. And my teeth are pretty darn sharp. Becky Shaw by Gina Gianfriddo. The play starts with a blind date set up by well-meaning friends, but things quickly go pear-shaped. Becky is the spark. She's young, blunt, and hard to read, and that's exactly why everyone around her keeps projecting their own stories onto her. The man she meets is all jittery charm and wounded ego, the kind of person who can seem sweet one second and entitled the next. Then you've got the couple who arrange the date. And they're not neutral matchmakers at all. They're carrying their own class anxieties, relationship resentments, and moral self-images into the situation like a luggage that keeps falling open in public. What makes the play bite is how quickly it shows that nobody in this room is only one thing. The nice people can be manipulative. The difficult person can be cornered. Sympathy keeps shifting because every scene exposes a new motive, a new insecurity, a new little strategy for staying on top. By the time the play really tightens the screws, the question isn't who is right, Who's controlling the story, and what happens when control slips? And Tina's turtle truth for you, darlin'. Becky Shaw is built like a comedy, but it lands like a mirror. You might laugh, you might wince, you might do both at the same time.

text: Here's a summary of a Christmas carol, Stave Fall. The final spirit, the ghost of Christmas yet to come, appears. Scrooge is terrified of this spirit, although it doesn't speak a word to him. He tells the spirit that he's ready to learn its lesson and wants to change his ways. The spirit shows Scrooge a group of men talking about an unnamed rich man who has recently died. They wonder if anyone will go to the funeral and they joke that they will only go if there's a free lunch. Scrooge can't figure out who the men are talking about. Next, Scrooge sees a dingy shop belonging to a fence where a group of servants sell items that they've stolen from the dead rich man's house and then he sees the dinner table of a poor couple who are grateful that he's died, although he doesn't know it's him yet, as it gives them more time to repay their debt. Scrooge begs to be shown some tenderness connected to death and the spirit shows Scrooge the cratchit household where he sees that tiny Tim has died. The cratchits are full of grief for Tiny Tim's death but express how happy they were to have been able to share his life. Scrooge asks to know who the dead rich man was. The spirit takes him to a graveyard and points to a gravestone. Scrooge approaches the gravestone and is horrified to read his own name on it. Scrooge begs the spirit for a chance to change his ways and avoid the future that he's been shown, promising to remember the lessons he has learned from all three spirits. As he grabs the spirit's hand, it vanishes and he wakes up back in his own bed. The play follows the young girl, Little Bit, from her adolescence through college years and ends with her as a thirty-something adult. Although Little Bit and her uncle share mutual understanding, and care deeply for one another. The years of manipulation and sexual confusion eventually drive them apart and wreak havoc on both of their psyches. How I Learned to Drive won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama in 1998. It premiered off-Broadway at the Vineyard Theatre in May of 1997, starring Mary Louise Parker as Little Bit, with David Morse as Uncle Peck. Since its premiere, Drive has been produced all over over the world with featured productions in Washington, DC, Baltimore, New York and London.

text: Hello, dear listeners, and welcome back to Book Summary 5, the 5-Minute Summary Channel. I'm Sami, your host. Today, we're diving into Othello by William Shakespeare, a tragic play that delves into themes of jealousy, trust, and betrayal. First performed in 1604, Othello remains a powerful exploration of human emotions and the consequences of manipulation. Let's dive into the key events and storylines so you'll feel like you've read it cover cover. Othello begins in Venice with Iago, a military unsign, expressing his bitterness at being passed over for a promotion in favor of Cassio, a younger and less experienced officer. Iago's resentment is directed at Othello, the Moorish general of the Venetian army. Iago conspires with Rodrigo, a wealthy but foolish gentleman who is in love with Destimona, Othello's wife, to ruin Othello's life. Iago and Rodrigo inform Brabantio, Desdemona's father, that she has eloped with Othello. Bourbontio is outraged and accuses Othello of bewitching his daughter. Othello defends himself before the Venetian Senate, explaining that Desdemona fell in love with him through the stories of his adventures and hardships. Desdemona confirms her love for Othello and the Senate supports their marriage, especially since Othello is needed to defend Venice against a Turkish invasion of Cyprus. The action moves to Cyprus, where Othello, Desdemona, and their entourage, including Iago, Cassio, and Emilia, arrive after the Turkish fleet is destroyed in a storm. In Cyprus, Iago sets his devious plan into motion. He gets Cassio drunk and incites him to fight Rodrigo. When Othello hears of the brawl, he strips Cassio of his rank, much to Cassio's dismay. Iago advises Cassio to seek Desdemona's help in regaining Othello's favor. Meanwhile, Iago plants seeds of doubt in Othello's mind about Destimona's fidelity, suggesting that she is having an affair with Cassio. Iago's manipulations are insidious. He uses Destimona's innocent attempts to help Cassio as evidence of her infidelity. The pivotal moment in Iago's scheme involves a handkerchief, a gift from Othello to Destimona. Amelia finds the handkerchief and gives it to Iago, unaware of his intentions. Iago plants the handkerchief in Cassio's quarters, then tells Othello he has seen Cassio with it. This proof convinces Othello of Destimona's betrayal, plunging him into a jealous rage. Consumed by jealousy, Othello confronts Destimona, who is bewildered by his accusations and insists on her innocence. Othello, blinded by Ayago's lies, refuses to believe her. He confides his turmoil to Ayago, who continues to stoke the flames of jealousy and urges Othello to take action. In a tragic culmination, Othello smothers Desdemona in their bed. Emilia, discovering the murder, exposes Iago's treachery, revealing the truth about the handkerchief and Iago's manipulations. Othello is devastated by the realization of his tragic mistake. Overcome with grief and guilt, he takes his own life. The play ends with Iago being arrested and taken away to face justice. Cassio is appointed as the new governor of Cyprus, tasked with restoring order after the chaos wrought by Iago's deceit. Othello is a powerful exploration of the destructive power of jealousy and the vulnerability of trust. Shakespeare masterfully portrays the psychological manipulation by Iago and the tragic downfall of Othello, a noble and honorable man brought low by his own insecurities and misplaced trust. text: It's 1935, and racial tensions are high in Maycomb, Alabama. Nonetheless, young Jean Louise Finch, or Scout, as she is fondly called, manages to live a rather carefree, privileged existence, insulated from issues of race. All that changes when Scout watches her father, Atticus Finch, defend an innocent man, Tom Robinson, against a potential death sentence which looms threateningly against him because of prejudice due to race. Scout begins to realise that just because society portrays something as being true doesn't mean that it actually is fact. With the help of Atticus and her older brother Jem, Scout learns that growing up often means doing what is right, even when it comes at great cost. To Kill a Mockingbird is now considered an American masterpiece about the power of childhood innocence, morality and love. However, it is important to note that the author Harper Lee always defined it as a simple love story.

So again, in the same way that you would dress a doll up to wear a dress, Nora is also being dressed up here. So it's also a symbol of that repression. When she is practicing or rehearsing her dance at the end of Act 2, she makes out that she has forgotten all of the dance moves. And one of the things that happens is her hair comes down. And again, that could symbolically represent her breaking free from the rigid control, not only of those rules of the dance, but also of the rules of the marriage. It's symbolically showing her transgression into being her own woman, in effect, letting loose her femininity, I suppose, which prepares us, of course, for her ultimate exit at the end of Act 3. So this idea of dressing something up to decorate it, one of the things that Halma says when they get back from the Sternberg's Tarantella party in Act 3 is, doesn't my Nora look beautiful? So he almost objectifies her as if she's a doll to be looked at and to be marvelled at and that's of course just going to wind her up even more if she's already got in her head that she's a bit of a doll to begin with. In the beginning of the play, Halma uses lots of zoomorphisms or metaphors in order to label Nora, for example, my songlark, my thrush, whatever. All of these terms have the possessive determent of my, but they're also, all the animals are quite cute, powerless animals as well. Now, on the one hand, you could view that as being quite affectionate, or on the other hand, you could view it as being quite patronising and being controlling. again there's two ways you could interpret that, those zoomorphisms in the beginning. Krogstad, who is the play's antagonist and his name actually translates as Crooked, is the pose of the question should the amoral be reformed. So Krogstad, very ironic to Nora, has also committed fraud in the past and he has suffered kind of damnation from society as a result of that and Krogstad has children to feed and what Krogstad is doing is actually trying to do something quite noble which is to climb back up the respectability ladder because he has to support his children, there's nothing wrong with that. But then you have people like Dr Rank and Halmer, who almost stand in the way of that, who believe that bad people should not be reformed because it leaves all the good people out in the cold. So why should somebody who's broken the law get a job if somebody who hasn't broken the law can't get a job? Is that fair, for example? Should people who have broken the law get a free laptop to prevent them from reoffending, whereas the people that have not broken the law get nothing. Is that fair? So it's this Dr. Rankin-Helmer bringing to question this idea of somebody who's being able to be reformed, can somebody go from amoral to moral? Should bad people be given a second chance? And obviously what's ironic about Crosdad and Nora is they've both done the same thing which is committed fraud and forgery and yet Crosdad is the one that seems to be blackmailing Nora in this play course and Krogstad is the catalyst by which I mean you could argue that maybe Nora has everything to thank Krogstad for because but for Krogstad's letter and his threat of telling Halma about the loan she would still be with Halma now and it wouldn't have been eight years of a wasted life in this marriage it would have been I don't know 50 years so maybe Krogstad should be thanked for being the catalyst for allowing Nora to leave and getting that freedom perhaps. Halma, as I've already said, was a lawyer, which obviously the legal profession has a very close relationship with respectability, and he's now a bank manager. Both of those roles enhance his sense of masculine pride and his masculine sense of respectability. Halma's husband character is the powerful elite within this domestic sphere of the he is not a king or a leader, he is a husband. And it goes to show that you can still talk about the elite as in the head of the household without really having to talk about prime ministers or presidents or leaders or gods. You know, he is the head of this house, he is in the most powerful position just because he's won the genetic lottery of being male. And that's obviously in part what Noor is resisting against, and also what she's rebelling against at the end. You could also argue that Halma becomes the doll at the end of the play because he is the only one left in the house, because she's left by that point. Nora's decision to leave, of course, at the end is a democratic decision, it's a choice. She hasn't been forced to make that decision. She leaves of her own free will and Halma allows her to leave. And in that sense, you could say that maybe he's actually quite a good husband. He's not chaining her to a radiator. He's not locking her in his office forever. He's allowing her to leave. So again, some of us might feel quite sympathetic towards Halma at the end of the play because he's alone at the end. And you could argue, you know, he hasn't really done anything wrong specifically. He's just doing what society expected him to do. And it's, you know, hindsight is a wonderful thing. It's very easy and convenient to say, well, maybe he should have done better. But if you're living in a society that doesn't give an alternative you're not going to have that maybe that insight. She leaves to seek independence and self-governance in a democratic way. As we've said Dr Rank is representative of a victim of parental recklessness so he says basically that because of his father's lifestyle he's having to bear his disability of the spine And he also is the one, I think, in act one, or possibly act two, where he talks about Krogstad, I think it's act two, and talks about Krogstad and should somebody who is of moral disrepute be given a second chance. So he poses that question of morality and his, I think it's tuberculosis of the spine, is representative of that idea of the disease of society, which he believes Krogstad is. People who are corrupt, being given second chances is not a good thing in Dr Rank's eyes because it leads good people out in the cold. Gibson has clearly deliberately set this play at Christmas which is also known as the Festival of the Home and of course the setting of the play is a home. You would expect Christmas to be spent by people indoors in the home with family so it has these connotations of togetherness. However, clearly, at the end of the play, it shocks us in terms of not only what she does, but she does it at Christmas time as well. So it's to reinforce the fact that Christmas is usually about togetherness, but yet she still leaves. You've also got the Christmas tree, and very similar to the Tarantella costume, you decorate the Christmas tree to make it look better, so it looks nice, but it's only temporary because you're going to have to take those decorations off at some point. So it's actually about dressing something up, about something being decorated to look good. The idea being that nobody has a plain green Christmas tree in their lounge, you put ball balls on it to make it look better. So it plays its part. And Anachnoresis is an epiphany. And of course, the epiphany is based on Halma's reaction to Krogstad's letter that he finally gets out of the locked letter box at the beginning of Act 3, or the middle of Act 3. And what she's disappointed with is she hoped that Halma would say, we'll get through this together, don't worry Nora, we'll get through this together. but that's not what happened because he made it all about him and in some of the film versions it actually hits Nora across the face when he finds out about what she's done with this loan and then when Krostad forgives the IOU in a second letter he then starts to talk about the both of them and how they're going to be fine by which point the damage is done. The straw at that point has already broken the camel's back and Nora quite poignantly goes off stage, takes off her Tarantella costume and puts on a very kind of dark and regular kind of outdoor coat and again the clothing showing how her role has changed based on Halma's reaction. So it was all about him and what he fails to say and what he fails to realise is that he would be dead if it not be for Nora. She only got this loan to save his life by going to somewhere warm to Italy. Had she not got this loan and broken the law, he would be dead by now, but he doesn't seem to realise that. So he's oblivious to that. So Nora is stuck between a rock and a hard place. She either breaks the law and is kind of ostracised or told off by society for that, or she's a dutiful wife and saves his life by whatever means necessary, and yet that's what society is also telling us she should be. So she cannot be a dutiful wife and also get the money. She has to break the law somewhere or go against someone somewhere. So she's in a bit of a catch-22 situation. Culture means the financial control. Women, for example, could not own their own money. They had to turn it over to their husbands. They could not take out loans. They could not take account mortgages, so the male was in charge of the finances. And she lies. She says that she was making Christmas decorations in the attic in the beginning. She wasn't. She was actually doing some copying work in order to pay back Krogstad's installments. So she has the ability to keep secrets, which means that she is not the simplistic childlike character we expected to be from the beginning she actually has inner complexity by being able to keep secrets and that links very nicely to our last point about the macaroons and silk stockings. She's been told by Halman not to eat the macaroons and yet she does and then when Dr Rank comes around in act two she shows her silk stockings above the ankle which is not what the etiquette of the time suggested you do to people other than your husband. So these minor perhaps more trivial acts of rebellion obviously go on to foreshadow her more substantial rebellion at the end when she decides to leave the house. So all of these points, just some points though, significant revision points that I often find myself discussing a lot with students which perhaps can be used in countless tasks across the political and social protest exam when you're talking about the doll's house. So hopefully that has been useful. Thank you.

text: Chapter 8 of The Great Gatsby is a poignant chapter as it showcases drastic changes in the characters' lives and relationships, leading up to the climactic event in the narrative. It begins with Nick Carraway waking up after the chaotic events of Chapter 7. He goes over to Jay Gatsby's house and it is surprisingly quiet after the previous day's catastrophic blowup. Gatsby seems deflated, reluctant to let go of the dream of him and Daisy Buchanan together. He shares with Nick the story of his past love with Daisy in Louisville in 1917, how he loved her for her youthful innocence, her vibrancy, and the fact that she was desired by many men. Gatsby reveals his real name and background, James Gats from North Dakota, the son of unsuccessful farmers. He explains how he met Dan Cody, a wealthy copper magnate, when he was 17. He worked for Cody, from whom he learned about wealth, style, and the mannerisms of the elite. After Cody's death, Gatsby was left with a deep longing for wealth and the social status that comes with it. Meanwhile, the narrative shifts to George Wilson, who had suddenly become cruel and harsh to his wife Myrtle after finding out about her affair. After her tragic death, he embarks on a journey to find out her murderer, viewing himself as a sort of God of Justice seeking retribution. After encountering Michaelis, a neighbor and the only known witness to Myrtle's death, George starts piecing together the incident, leading him on the path to Gatsby. Gatsby tells Nick that he waited outside Daisy's house till dawn after the accident, but Tom did not hurt her. He dejectedly says that he wants to recreate their past, hoping that Daisy would leave Tom and return to him. He still believes in the green light at the end of her dock, a symbol of his optimism and hope for a future with Daisy. However, Nick perceives the futility and melancholy of his dream. As Nick leaves for work, Gatsby decides to take the day off, waiting by the phone for a call from Daisy. The narrative builds suspense as it hints at the impending tragedy with shadows of impending disaster. Chapter 8 deepens the character of Gatsby and unravels the extent of his despair, contrasting it with his earlier grandeur and optimism. It also explores themes of passion, remorse, obsession, and the destructive power of illusion.

text: Death of a Salesman by Arthur Miller Characters, Summary, Analysis Hello and welcome to The Discourse. Death of a Salesman is probably the most successful and much talked about stage play by Arthur Miller that was first performed in 1949. It is a two-act play in which the story of protagonist Willy Loman is depicted using a montage of his arguments, memories, and dreams. It is a tragedy of the common man. In the same year, 1949, Arthur Miller wrote and published his essay, Tragedy and the Common Man, in which he presented his reason to make an ordinary American man the subject of a theatrical tragedy. He suggested that the modern world is not gullible, it is more sceptical about the idea of heroes, thus the audience cannot understand how tragedy with its tragic hero is relevant to the modern world. On the other hand, Miller argued that the world is full of heroes. According to Miller, a hero is anybody who is willing to lay down his life in order to secure his sense of personal dignity. It doesn't matter what his social status or background is. Death of a salesman is a prime example of Miller's thoughts on the tragedy. Willy Loman is a traveling salesman. His tragedy is brought about partly by his own actions, but the desperate situations in which he finds himself because of the harsh, competitive, and unforgiving world of sales also are responsible for that. In a world where he cannot make money as a salesman, he has to think of something else to acquire money so that he can provide a two-time meal to his family and offer a secured adobe. In The Tragedy of the Common Man, Miller argues that theatrical tragedy is dependent on a common man's total compunction to to evaluate himself justly. However, while trying to do so and maintaining his dignity, the tragic hero often loses his life. Such a tragedy will prompt the audience to think about what is wrong with society and situations and how they can be changed for the better. The story offers a contrast between the American dream and American reality. Characters of Death of a Salesman Willie Loman is a 63-year-old traveling salesman. He has recently lost his job. He is unstable, insecure and self-deluded. Linda Loman is Willy's loyal and loving wife. Willy is a responsible family man who loved his family, but he had an extra-marital affair once that he broke pretty soon. Linda knows and understands realities better than Willy, but she remains passively supportive of Willy. She wishes her grown-up sons, Blif Loman and Happy Loman, help their father. Blip Loman is Willy's 32-year-old son. He was a football star in his school, but dropped out because he couldn't pass the math exam. He is well-built and handsome. Happy Loman is Blip's younger brother. He is not happy within himself, but pretends to be a happy person in front of all others. He always tries to win the approval of his parents, but miserably fails. Charlie is Willy's neighbor. Charlie and Willy do not like each other much, yet they are friends. Charlie cares for Willy and tries to help him. Bernard is Charlie's son. He used to be a huge fan of Blif during his school days. He isn't as well-built and handsome as Blif is, but he is a successful lawyer. Ben Loman is Willy's elder brother who became a rich diamond merchant after his tour to Africa. He died years ago, but Willy keeps remembering him and has hallucinations of him. Howard Wagner is Willy's boss who fires him from the job. Summary of Death of a Salesman The play begins as Willy Loman returns from his tour. Linda notices Willy is confused, disturbed, and tired. Willy met an accident and had to return halfway through his tour. As Linda worries, Willy tells her that nothing has happened but says that he doesn't remember all the details of his trip. Linda Linda tells him that he should rest for a while. She tells him that he should now change his job as a traveling salesman and should work in New York. Willie says that he feels he is not needed in New York. He says that had Frank Wagner been alive, Willie might have been in charge of New York. But Frank's son Howard Wagner is his current boss and Howard doesn't like him much. Linda informs Willie that both of their sons, Blip and Happy are at home as Happy has arranged a double date for them. She tells Willy not to lose his temper on Blif. Willy on the other hand says that he feels Blif has some resentment against him. In the other room, Blif is discussing with Happy. Blif is a 34-year-old built handsome guy while Happy is two years younger. Happy is equally good-looking, but he is not self-assured. Blif says that Willy's health is deteriorating. He complains that Willy continues to mock him, but Happy says that he merely wants Pliff to live up to his potential. Pliff isn't too sure of his potential. He says that he tried more than a dozen jobs since he left home before the war, but was fired from all of them. He wonders if he can do any job. He reminisces about the countryside, herding cattle and dreams about farming land. Happy says that he has many girls and he maintains a car yet he feels unsatisfied. He says that he doesn't respect any girl he has seduced till now and he is still longing for a girl of character like their mother to whom he may marry. Blip thinks that he may try going back to Bill Oliver for whom he worked in the past. Willy on the other hand is thinking of the past when Blip and Happy were kids. Happy complains that he is losing weight while Blip shows a football to Willy that he took from the locker room. Willy is happy about Blip's success at football field and says that one day, Bliff will have a bigger business than Charlie's because while Charlie is liked, he is not well liked. At the same time, Bernard enters their home and says that he is worried that Bliff will fail math class and will not be able to attend UVA. Willy isn't worried at all. He tells Bernard not to be a pest and go away. He then tells Bliff that like Charlie, Bernard is liked but not well liked. He says that Bernard will not succeed in business despite his good grades as Blip can because success in business depends on personality and not grades. He says that Blip has a much better personality than Bernard's. The scene changes and we see a woman with a scarf in a hotel room. Willy tells her that he gets alone and worries about his business. The woman says that she chose Willy because of his sense of humour. Willy promises the woman that he will see her the next time he visits Boston. The scene changes again as Willy meets Bernard and asks him to give answer keys for the regents exam to Blip. Bernard, however, refuses to do so as it is a state exam. Linda complains about Blip being too harsh against girls and Willy scolds her and asks if she wants his son to be a worm like Bernard. Willy returns to the present as Happy approaches him. He tells Happy how he met an accident on his tour. He wonders why he didn't go to Africa with Ben, his elder brother, who got hold of some diamond mines in Africa and made huge riches. Happy reassures Willy and says that he will make him retire decently. Charlie visits their home and plays cards with Willy. He offers a job but Willy refuses. Willy tells Charlie that his elder brother died in Africa a few weeks ago. Willy then starts hallucinating while imagining Ben visiting him and asking about their mother. Charlie leaves him alone. Willy continues his imagination of the past when he introduced Ben to his sons. He then sees Charlie reprimanding him for letting his sons steal from a nearby construction site. Willy tells that his sons are fearless. Charlie chides that such fearlessness often leads people to imprisonment, to which Ben retorts that such fearless characters succeed in the stock exchange. In the present time, Blip and Happy ask their mother for how long Willy is talking to himself like this. Linda answers that this has been going on for years. She complains Blip that he is not helping his father at all. She informs them that recently Willy tried to kill himself by driving his car off the bridge. She says that earlier too, Willy tried to commit suicide by hooking a tube up to the gas heater in the basement. She says that Willy is not a great man but he is a human being and he needs attention. text: After the finale of Netflix's Cobra Kai just a few months back, Karate Kid fans have been excitedly waiting for the new Karate Kid Legends movie to hit theaters. This beloved franchise has been gathering more diehards, and the popularity of Cobra Kai definitely added to it. While the show was an offshoot, focusing on the main characters from the original 1984 film, Daniel Laruso and Johnny Lawrence, it webbed its way through six seasons, dealing with the younger generation and resolving conflicts that had continued for too long. The trailer for the new film was a completely different setting with a new titular Karate Kid. What made fans most excited was the return of Jackie Jan's Mr. Han from the 2010 movie The Karate Kid, which had been considered non-cononical for a very long time. Ralph Machio's Daniel Laruso meeting Mr. Han proved conclusively that all the movies were connected. Now that the film is out in theaters, here's what we thought of it. In this movie, we'll talk about the ending, uncover the connection between Mr. Miyagi and Mr. Han, and judge the possibility of another sequel. It contains spoilers, so we recommend watching the movie first. Before we go into our explanation, we have a very small request. If you like our content, please support us by subscribing to our channel. This is a small click for you, but for us, it means a lot. Thank you. Let's begin. You study karate or something? Kung Fu used to. How does Karate Kid Legends end? Lee Fong, played by Ben Wong, is introduced as a student of Mr. Han's kung fu school in Beijing, China. Plagued by a traumatic past involving his brother, he has a strange relationship with martial arts in general. He relocates to New York with his mother and finds himself confused and lost, not just culturally, but also emotionally. His story mirrors that of Daniel in the 1984 movie as he falls in love with a young girl, but there's always an ex-boyfriend in the scene. As expected, this troublemaker named Connor Day is a formidable fighter with strength as well as skills. Lee squares off with him and is defeated twice. After avoiding communication with his former teacher, Mr. Han, Lee finds the very man arriving in New York to check up on him. He encourages Lee to participate in the five burrows tournament, similar to the All Valley events to confront his demons and regain his confidence. However, Mr. Han feels another teacher would be more appropriate for Lee's training. And this is where Daniel Luso comes in. Initially reluctant, Daniel agrees to train Lee using Miyagi techniques. The youngster gets better and enters the competition, making it to the final with Connor, his nemesis. Connor initially manages to get one over on Lee every single time. Right after the match begins, Lee takes multiple hits and goes down by 4-0. He somehow manages to get back on track, but is again knocked down until the score is tied at 7-7. With the next point deciding the winner, Lee experiences flashbacks from his past and gets the courage to return to his feet. Again, mirroring the crane kick of Daniel in the original movie. Here, the dragon kick decides the winner. A serious and difficult to execute acrobatic maneuver. This was introduced to Lee by his brother. Due to his inexperience with it, when he used it on Connor earlier, he hadn't managed to win. While he does learn how to execute it successfully under Daniel's guidance, they know that Connor will anticipate the move. Hence, Daniel teaches him to fake it and duck, catching the opponent by surprise and then sweep his leg. This trick works on Connor like magic, and Lee finishes with a kick to the chest. He wins the fight narrowly by gaining one point over Connor and also wins the tournament by extension. Lee turns back to celebrate, but Connor rushes at him from behind, humiliated and driven to take revenge at all costs. However, Lee isn't caught off guard and manages to knock Connor to the ground. The annoyance inside him made him drive a fist into the ladder's face, which would have done serious damage. However, in classic Miyagio style, Lee punches the mat next to Connor instead, opting for mercy and helps his opponent to his feet. This is the stark opposite of how the antagonist in the 1984 film, Johnny, had reacted to Daniel winning the All Valley tournament. Johnny had respected Daniel's skills and metal, but Connor is portrayed in a more sinister fashion. He didn't hesitate to attack Lee when he wasn't expecting it. Well, he would have made Terry Silver proud with that attitude, or even John Crease before the latter's reformation. Is there a postredit scene setting up another sequel? Legends does not have a postredit scene, something fans weren't expecting. After winning the Five Bros tournament, Lee celebrates with both his teachers, Mr. Han and Daniel. The next scene shows Victor Leani, the father of Lee's love interest, Mia, opening a second pizza place in New York. Mr. Han suggests that he open a third in Beijing, and some fans have taken this to mean that there's a possible sequel in the making that will possibly be set in China again. Leong also sends a pizza to California with a note to Daniel, saying that he will always be available should his teacher ever need him. This suggests another opening for a sequel where Daniel might need Lee's help in the future. What happened to Lee Fong's brother? It's hinted that Lee and his brother used to learn kung fu together, and the latter was undoubtedly quite proficient at it. He had taken part in a big tournament in Beijing some years back and won fair and square. However, his opponent was not ready to accept the decision and wanted revenge. He had gathered a few others and attacked the brothers with knives. While both were beaten up, Lee witnessed his brother getting stabbed fatally and passing away after being rushed to the hospital, calling Lee's name in his last moments. Naturally, an event as traumatic as this left a lasting mark on the young boy's psyche, as he had gone into freeze mode when his brother was on the verge of death. He blamed himself for everything that had happened, and this could have played a part in the family moving to New York. In fact, Leeong's mother had asked him to abandon martial arts and all other forms of violence, hoping to ease him of his guilt and protect him from similar accidents. The emotional weight of the incident makes itself known to Lee when Victor steps into the ring, but ends up getting severely injured. Victor used to be a boxer, but is now heavily indebted from trying to save his family business. Lee helps defend him against the creditor O'Shea's thugs and gains his respect. He also teaches the old man some kung fu tricks to help him in the ring. As Victor intends to make a boxing comeback and clear his debts. However, when he fights, O'Shea uses underhanded techniques to defeat and injure him to the point where he had to be taken to the hospital. Lee Fong witnesses Victor get hurt and freezes on the spot just as he had when his brother was attacked. Mia rushes to her father's aid and he's taken to get medical treatment. Thankfully, Victor lives and doesn't blame Lee for anything that has happened. Who makes a cameo appearance from Cobra Kai? Other than Ralph Machio, fans didn't expect anyone else from Cobra Kai to appear in Karate Kid Legends. After all, almost every character got a well-rounded conclusion at the end of the series. The youngsters were looking forward to university and/or professional careers. The most dangerous antagonists appear to have died. Johnny reclaimed his life and confidence while Daniel finally found balance. So when William Zabka appeared on screen toward the end of Legends, there was definitely a collective gasp from fans. Daniel calls out to him with the pizza Lee sent in his hand and the once rivals sit down to enjoy the delicacy. However, Johnny in classic Johnny style expresses disappointment and says that New York pizzas are not as impressive as the local ones in Rita. A thought strikes him and he pitches a business idea to Daniel saying that they could open a pizza place in California itself and name it Miyagi Dough. He also suggests taglines for the place, keeping Mr. Miyagi's instructions in mind with olives on, olives off and slice first, slice hard, no anchovies, reminiscent of Crease's Cobra Kai days. The movie ends here, so the only conclusive possibility for a sequel based on this scene is a possible spin-off about Johnny and Daniel's pizza business. We have a feeling Daniel won't be too eager to go ahead with it. The connection between Mr. Miyagi and Mr. Han explained, "Pap Marita's legendary Mr. Miyagi was introduced in 1984. The wise mentor from Okinawa, who molded Daniel's philosophy and pretty much single-handedly helped him turn his life around, didn't appear in person in Cobra Kai. Creators of the show, as well as the movies, wanted to honor Marita's legacy the best they could. So, all the scenes featuring Mr. Miyagi across the six seasons were either flashbacks or made with CGI. The last season of Cobra Kai delved into his character with far greater detail, uncovering hidden aspects of his life and helping Daniel understand his sensei better. Like we mentioned earlier, until the trailer for Karate Kid Legends dropped, the 2010 movie was considered non-cononical to the Karate Kid and Cobra Kai franchises, considering there were no common characters and just a similar storyline. With Jackie Tan's role in the new movie, fans furiously dug up old notes and frame theories about the connection between Mr. Han and Daniel. They found one common link, Mr. Miyagi, and this was explored right at the beginning of the film with a scene from The Karate Kid Part Two. The words Okinawa, Japan, 1986, appear on the screen, hinting at Daniel's first time visiting the island. Daniel asks his sensei about a picture on the wall, and Mr. Miyagi tells him the story of the latter's ancestor, Shimpo Miyagi, a fisherman and alcohol lover, who had passed out from drinking on his boat one day. The currents had taken him from Okinawa to the coast of China, where he woke up and lived for a while. He learned to fight there and took a Chinese wife before returning to Okinawa with the heritage of what would eventually become Miyagi Do Karate. In Karate Kid Legends, Mr. Han explains that his family had taken in Shoom Miyagi all those years back and they were the ones who had taught him kung fu. This resulted in two cultures, two martial arts, and two branches of the same tree, represented by Mr. Han and Mr. Miyagi. The latter's ancestors had used that knowledge to create his signature style, which would be passed down and later move halfway across the world to the United States. This connected the stories together, resulting in the blend of karate and kung fu, which is seen in legends. Fans had expected something similar since there was no other apparent link between a Chinese kung fu sheru and a Japanese karate sensei sharing similar styles and temperaments. Chan's Mr. Han is much like Mr. Miyagi, normally idealistic and soft-spoken, but also strong and determined. While legend shows him owning a large kung fu school in Beijing, it doesn't really explain how that happened as Mr. Han was a maintenance man again like Mr. Miyagi before he took Dre Parker under his wing. We can speculate that after Dre won the competition, Mr. Han became popular as his teacher and started training students. While he may not have known anything about Daniel Laruso earlier, he probably learned about him from the Seckai Taikai where the Miyagi Dojo took part, finding common ground with him. Mr. Han might have asked Daniel to help him train Leeong so that the boy would be proficient in both kung fu as well as karate. Marvelous Verdict: Reviews for Karate Kid Legends are already out and most of them are favorable. While the 1984 film remains the undisputed best in the franchise, Legends is not too far behind. Made more than 30 years after we first saw a young Ralph Machio and Pat Marita on screen. Legends certainly pays tribute to Mr. Miyagi and ties off some of the loose ends by connecting the 2010 film and Cobra Kai to it. Like all the other Karate Kid movies, Legends was not just about winning the big tournament at the end by defeating an arrogant and pompous opponent. Lee Fong's journey was not one-dimensional at all since it touched pretty immersive topics such as a siblings death and the resultant trauma from that. To many people, Lee getting paralyzed in the face of similar incidents can be somewhat baffling. But to a young boy who was filled with guilt after losing his brother, fighting his trauma was the only way to deal with it in a healthy fashion. His win over Connor and his final act of peace and respect toward him solidified the fact that no form of martial arts is inherently destructive and violent, and they all served to help the practitioner achieve the balance that Daniel was looking for throughout his life. Bin Wong played his role brilliantly, and we can be sure to see more of him soon. Watching Jackie Chan back with a substantial role was also a breath of fresh air for many fans, especially the older ones. The movie might be basic and follow the same formula as every other Karate Kid film, but that familiarity is what makes it wholesome. However, we feel that there was room for more emotional development, especially considering that the protagonist had experienced serious trauma. The original film remains a hit after so many years, not just because of the polished fight scenes, but because Mr. Miyagi and Daniel were well-rounded characters who talked to and learned from each other. Their relationship was profound enough to spark off a TV show and numerous sequels. And in some of them, Mr. Miyagi himself never appears, but his presence is felt throughout. But maybe trying to replicate that effect can tone down the influence Pat Marita's character has had on the fandom for decades. So, it makes some sense for Legends to be more watered down. What do you think of Karate Kid Legends? Do you think we'll get another sequel of Mr. Han possibly coming over to California? Let us know in the comments below. And if you liked our content, don't forget to leave a like and subscribe to us if you haven't already. Have a good one and be safe. Thanks everyone. You'll be ready. [Music]

text: Warning, this contains massive spoilers for the John Wick spin-off Ballerina. Like Jon, Eve breaks the rules to pursue revenge. And just like the Baba Yaga, the Kikimora fights against the thousand-year-old system that spawned her. By killing the Chancellor, Eve sets the bounty on her head, beginning at $5 million. Pretty low considering the dozens of corpses in her wake. And after getting the notice, Eve leaves the Tarovsky Theater, tailed by her fellow assassin seeking to claim her bounty. This is just like what happens to another Ruskar Roma member, John Wick. Eve's circumstances are a little different, but she also avenges a beloved family member by massacring members of an unruly tribe and then cutting off the head. The biggest difference is that Eve comes from the very tribe that she fights. Bound to the path of the assassin by forces unknown, Eve embodies the comeuppance of the chancellor's tribe, whose own disregard for the rules transformed Eve into the Kikimora. That said, the Ruska Roma's lessons in protecting a ward also makes Eve a very effective bodyguard. Both Daniel and Ella are in the safety of the Continental. Ella is actually Eve's niece, while Daniel is Eve's brother-in-law, who escaped the Chancellor's tribe in hopes of giving Ella a normal life. Eve killing the Chancellor, their grandpa, is but a small step in the right direction for Ella's future. Daniel has an even higher bounty than Eve, for taking Ella, the late Chancellor's granddaughter. So, what remains of the town's leadership are bound to come after Daniel, Ella, and Eve. At the same time, sympathizers of Eve's dad could either openly or covertly rally to their support, including the director, Noi, Winston, and John Wick himself. And speaking of the Baba Yaga, Ballerina's obsession with breaking the rules culminates in Jon's third act scene. Apart from kicking Eve's ass, Jon appears to remind Eve that all these rules are arbitrary. The director is still right. The rules that govern them are essential to their survival. But from the Chancellor's tribe to the Baba Yaga himself, rulebreaking gives them the edge. Yet, while the Chancellor used the rules to establish a reign of terror, Jon enforces his own rules to allow Eve to exact her revenge. And by giving Eve only until midnight to kill the Chancellor or get killed by the Baba Yaga, Jon himself is the last driving force that pushes Eve to the finish line. In a way, this was the Baba Yaga passing the torch to the Kikim Mora, whose debut is marked by a nononsense style that gives the John Wick films a run for their money. But stick around for the credits anyway to see the names of the stunt team. From the backstory of how Eve became a badass to those creative third act grenade kills, Ballerina's action exceeds expectations. The fights are creative and ruthless, unapologetically extravagant, and come with just the right amount of humor. All underpinned by an emotional story of revenge. In the end, Ballerina sticks the landing and needs no mid or postredit scene. Although, we can't help but wonder what's next for Eve Macro, Daniel Pine, and Ella. What did you think of the ending of Ballerina? Tell us your thoughts in the comments, and thanks for watching Screen Rant.
