text: The movie begins of an island where Vikings live. Every day, dragons come to the island and attack their animals. The Vikings are always ready to fight and protect their home. One day, the dragons attack again. Loud warning sirens go off and all the Vikings rush out to fight. A boy named Hiccup is standing outside watching everything. Just then, a dragon almost attacks him, but their leader, Stoic, saves him. Stoic tells Hiccup to stop getting in the way and go back to his work. Hiccup isn't a fighter like the other Vikings. Instead, he helps make weapons with his partner, Gobber. But deep down, Hiccup really wants to become a real Viking. He shows Gobber a machine he made to trap dragons using a rope. Gobber doesn't think it's very useful. While they talk, the dragons keep attacking. A fire starts spreading on the island. A few kids work together to stop the fire. A smart girl climbs to a high place and cleverly uses only a little water to put out a big fire. Hiccup watches her and is impressed. Her name is Ash, and he has always liked her. Meanwhile, the attack gets worse. Stoic and the Viking fighters are trying their best. Stoic even manages to catch a few dragons. But this time, a powerful dragon called the Night Fury is also attacking. It's so fast that no one can even see it clearly. Gobber has to join the fight, so he leaves. When Hiccup is alone, he decides to try out his machine. He sees the Night Fury flying and shoots his rope weapon at it. He hears a loud cry and thinks he might have hit it. Excited, Hiccup runs out to check. He sees signs that the dragon might have been caught, but before he can celebrate, another dragon shows up to attack. Stoic saves him again, but the dragon's fire burns many homes. Stoic gets very angry at Hiccup. We then find out that Stoic is Hiccup's dad. Hiccup tells him, "I think I hit the night fury. Let's go to the forest and check." But Stoic doesn't listen and tells him to go home. Even though his dad told him not to, Hiccup sneaks off into the forest to find out if he really caught the Night Fury. Meanwhile, Stoic gathers all the Viking kids for a meeting. He says they must find the dragon's home and destroy it once and for all. Gobber talks to Stoic about Hiccup. He says that even though Hiccup isn't strong, he still deserves a chance. But Stoic doesn't agree. He thinks Hiccup is too weak to be a real Viking. In the forest, Hiccup finds the Nightfury dragon trapped in his rope weapon. He takes out a knife, ready to hurt it. But then he sees that the dragon is scared of him. Hiccup feels sorry for it and decides to let it go. He cuts the rope and sets the dragon free. The dragon roars, maybe to say thank you, and tries to fly away, but it can't fly properly because one of its wings is hurt. Meanwhile, Hiccup goes back home. Stoic tells him that he can now start Viking training. Stoic says he's going on a sea journey to find the dragon's nest and wants Hiccup to become a strong Viking while he's gone. He gives Hiccup his own axe before leaving. The next day, training begins. Ash and the other kids are already there. Everyone sees Hiccup as weak. Gobber is their new trainer. He says the best student will get to fight a dragon in front of everyone and join Stoic's army. Gobber releases a chained dragon and teaches the kids how to use their shields and attack a dragon's eyes to blind it. When the dragon comes at Hiccup, he freezes in fear. The dragon almost hits him, but Gobber saves him. He warns Hiccup never to stand still when facing a dragon. Hiccup thinks about Night Fury, who didn't hurt him. He goes back to the mountain and finds the dragon still trying to fly. Hiccup draws a picture and realizes that one of Night Fury's tail fins is missing. That's why it can't fly or hunt. Later in training, no one wants to sit with Hiccup. They think he's a coward. After class, he reads a book about dragons, but there's nothing useful about Night Fury, only a warning that it's very dangerous. Hiccup knows this isn't true. Meanwhile, Stoic and his army search other islands for the dragon nest. But when they get close to one island, many dragons attack their ship. Back in training, a new dragon is brought in. Everyone is scared except Ash, who fights bravely. The dragon attacks Hiccup, but Ash saves him and tells him to be more careful. Hiccup realizes he must improve. He visits Nightfury again and brings fish. He shows he has no weapons. The dragon eats half the fish and gives the other half back to Hiccup, a friendly sign. They bond. Hiccup even touches the dragon and it seems happy. At night, Hiccup goes home for more training. The next day, Gobbber tells a story about how he lost his leg and hand fighting dragons. He says the best way to stop a dragon is to cut off its tail fin. Hiccup remembers Night Fury's tail is broken and gets an idea. He builds a new tail fin in his workshop. The next morning, he brings it to Nightfury and attaches it while the dragon eats. It works. The dragon is so happy that it lets Hiccup ride it. They go flying. Hiccup is scared, but also amazed. Later in training, Gobber introduces a dragon that gives off smoke and electricity. Gobbber tells them to throw water on it. Everyone wastes their water, but Hiccup uses a fish to calm the dragon and quietly puts it back in the cage. Everyone is shocked and impressed. Hiccup hides the fish so no one knows his secret. Days go by. Hiccup keeps training and also spends time with Nightfury. He builds a saddle to ride more easily. They fly together every day and Hiccup learns more and more. One day they find a strange place full of flowers. Nightfury smells them, sneezes, and falls down. Hiccup realizes the flowers can make dragons fall asleep. He collects them. At his next training session, he uses the flowers on a dragon and it faints. Everyone is amazed. They start calling Hiccup a legend. The other kids want to be his friend, but Hiccup still likes spending time with Night Fury the most. While playing, Hiccup learns a new trick. Dragons fall asleep when their necks are rubbed from below. He uses this trick in the next class. He quietly goes under a dragon, rubs its neck, and puts it to sleep. Everyone cheers for him. Now all the kids look up to Hiccup, even more than Ash. Ash feels jealous. She worked very hard to be the best, but now Hiccup is winning every time. She wants to know how Hiccup is doing it. So she follows him one day. But before she can find out where he goes in the forest, Hiccup disappears. The next day, Hiccup's father, Stoic, returns to the village. As he arrives, he hears people praising Hiccup. Gobber and the others tell him how Hiccup defeats dragons quickly and is doing great in training. Stoic is shocked. Meanwhile, Hiccup has learned to fly with the night fury and knows how to talk to it through signals. That night, Stoic hugs Hiccup and says, "I never thought you could fight dragons. I used to think you'd embarrass us, but now I'm proud of you. You're a true Viking." Hiccup feels unsure. He hasn't really learned to fight. He's just using tricks he learned from the night fury. The next day is the final class. The best student will get a chance to kill a dragon in front of the whole village. Ash asks Hiccup to let her prove herself. He agrees, but during the fight, Hiccup suddenly jumps in and uses a trick to knock out the dragon. He wants to make his dad proud. Ash gets very upset. The teacher announces Hiccup as the best student. Everyone cheers and Stoic is proud, but Hiccup isn't happy. He quietly leaves. Ash follows him into the mountains. She knocks him down and demands the truth. Just then, night fury arrives. Ash thinks it's attacking and gets ready to fight, but Hiccup says, "Wait, he's my friend." To stop her from telling everyone, Hiccup asks Nightfury to pick her up. Ash screams as the dragon flies fast through strong winds. Hiccup tells her to say sorry to Nightfury. Ash, scared, apologizes. The dragon then calms down and gives them a smooth, fun ride. While flying, Hiccup explains that dragons are scared of humans, just like humans are scared of dragons. Ash doesn't believe it. She says dragons burn their homes and steal their animals. Night Fury then takes them to a far away island with a volcano. There they see dragons dropping animals into the volcano. Inside lives a huge dragon called the Red Fury. It's so dangerous that it eats other dragons if they don't bring food. That's why dragons attack villages to stay alive. Ash now understands. Dragons are not evil. They're just scared. She wants to tell the villagers, but Hiccup says no. He's afraid Night Fury will be hurt. He promises to tell the truth at the right time. The next day, Hiccup is chosen to kill a dragon in front of the whole village, but he throws away his weapon and calms the dragon instead. He tries to explain that dragons are not dangerous, but before he can finish, the dragon gets angry and attacks. Hiccup tries to protect himself. Suddenly, Night Fury shows up and saves him. Night Fury defeats the dragon, but is caught by the villagers. Stoic gets angry and sends Hiccup away. Night Fury is locked up and becomes sad. At home, Stoic argues with Hiccup. He says, "Dragons are enemies. One even killed Hiccup's mother." Hiccup says they don't eat people. They only feed their leader to survive. Stoic is shocked. He asks if Hiccup has seen the dragon nest. Hiccup says yes, and that night fury showed him. Stoic decides to attack the nest. He tells Hiccup he's not one of them anymore. Then he and the villagers leave, taking Nightfury with them. Hiccup feels broken. Ash comforts him. She says, "You're the first Viking in 200 years to ride a dragon. You're brave." Hiccup says, "I became friends with Nightfury because we were both scared." Ash replies, "Real friends never leave each other during hard times. You need to save him." Her words give Hiccup courage. His classmates join him. They free the other dragons, become friends with them, and fly toward the dragon nest. At the same time, Stoic and the villagers reach the nest and start attacking. Suddenly, a huge red fury dragon comes out, much bigger than any dragon they've seen. This is the real enemy. Hiccup and his team arrive. While Ash frees Night Fury, Hiccup tries to distract the Red Fury. The monster attacks and knocks everyone into the water, including Night Fury. Hiccup almost drowns trying to save him, but Stoic rescues him. They manage to free Night Fury. Stoic finally understands the truth and says sorry to Hiccup. Then Hiccup and Night Fury go to fight Red Fury. They trick it into flying high into the sky. Red Fury breathes fire, but Night Fury dodges and fights back. He blasts fire at its wings. When Red Fury opens its mouth to attack, Night Fury fires a fireball straight into it. The monster explodes, but just before it dies, Red Fury's tail hits Hiccup and knocks him into the volcano. Night Fury dives after him as fire and smoke fill the sky. The smoke clears, and Stoic fears that Hiccup is gone, but then Night Fury flies out of the smoke with Hiccup safely wrapped in its wings. Hiccup is alive, but he's not waking up. After 7 days, Hiccup finally wakes up in his bed. He sees Night Fury beside him at home. His father, Stoic, has accepted the dragon as part of their family. Hiccup feels sad when he finds out he lost one of his legs during the big fight. But Nightfury gently comforts him and takes him outside. There, Hiccup sees something amazing. The villagers and dragons now live together in peace. Stoic smiles and says, "You changed 200 years of our history. You're truly brave." Ash shows up. She's still a little upset that Hiccup scared her during their first dragon ride, but she smiles and gives him a kiss. Then Hiccup, Ash, and all their friends fly happily into the sky on their dragons.

text: [Music] Materialists 2025 tells the story of Lucy, a woman living in New York who works as a matchmaker after once attempting acting. Lucy is good at her job. She's helped bring together nine couples in successful marriages through her firm, Adore. Despite her success connecting others, Lucy holds firm on her own rule. She'll only date or marry a wealthy man, even if it means going without romance for a while. She's a self-declared voluntary celibate with strong ambitions shaped by the tough realities of love and money in New York City. The film unfolds kind of like a diary of Lucy's days full of little victories, harsh disappointments, and the pressure of making it in a city where image and wealth mean almost everything. Things begin at a wedding. Lucy is being celebrated for her successful matchmaking. Friends and co-workers raise their glasses and tell stories about how Lucy has the sharpest sense for chemistry, that she somehow knows how to assemble just the right pieces to produce couples that last. We see snippets of Lucy's interactions with her clients. Very honest, sometimes blunt, always practical. Dating is treated like a market. People are evaluated by income, looks, height, and age. Both the men and women in this world feel like commodities. Each person rating themselves and everyone else wondering if they're valuable enough to win the right partner. There is a running thread that keeps coming up in various forms. Are we just what we appear to be or is there something deeper that makes us worthy of love? After the ceremony, Lucy talks shop with her colleague, brainstorming ways to match a client named Sophie. Sophie is one of the main supporting characters and her journey becomes woven in with Lucy's own. Sophie is realistic and sweet, but the dating market is cruel and keeps rejecting her for not standing out or for being too old. At 39, Lucy tries to encourage her, but the feedback from male clients is clear. They want younger, flashier, more valuable women. Watching Sophie take rejection after rejection, even from men who obviously lack her intellect or kindness, really shines a light on some of the pain beneath the surface of this matchmaking world. At this same wedding, Lucy meets Harry Castillo, a successful financer and the brother of the groom. Harry is charming, direct, and most importantly, wealthy. He's almost the perfect answer to what Lucy has always told herself she needs. But right as she's introduced to Harry, Lucy also bumps into her ex-boyfriend Jon, who is working as a caterer for the event. Jon is an actor still struggling to make his dreams real. The way Lucy and Jon reconnect is full of bittersweet memories. Their breakup was not because they stopped loving each other, but because of constant fights about money and the exhaustion of trying to keep their relationship alive in a city that measures happiness by bank accounts and branches, not feelings. The film cleverly sets up a love triangle where every option for Lucy comes with risk and compromise. Harry represents status, stability, and the fulfillment of Lucy's public ambitions, while Jon symbolizes the powerful but messy emotions Lucy has tried to suppress. As Harry starts courting Lucy, he does all the right things, takes her to nice places, acknowledges her worth, and genuinely seems to respect the drive and independence she radiates. But there's a distance. Money smooths over everything, but it also makes some feelings hard to reach. Lucy agrees to move forward with Harry. Their relationship quickly becomes official in the eyes of their friends and co-workers. Suddenly, Lucy is energized. Her confidence surges at work. She manages to successfully match up Sophie with Mark, a handsome doctor. Instead of just onward and upward, Lucy feels she might be on the right path. That elusive route where everything finally clicks, where the formula works. At the same time, however, she keeps crossing paths with Jon. Her ex Jon is sensitive, creative, and very much aware that Lucy still affects his heart. He's open about his feelings, but also a little ashamed of his financial struggles. There are moments where Lucy almost gets swept away by their history, remembering what it felt like to fight less about bills and to just belong to someone by choice, not by calculation. A big turning point comes when Lucy and Harry go to see Jon perform on stage. The event is charged with unspoken tension. Jon's discomfort at seeing Lucy with someone else is obvious. Afterwards, Jon corners Lucy and confronts her about why she's with Harry. Is she really happy or is she running from something? Lucy is defensive, but the question lingers. The story then pivots around a major conflict at work. Lucy's boss, Violet, informs her that Mark, the man Lucy matched with Sophie, assaulted Sophie, and now Sophie is bringing legal action against the agency. This is the crack in Lucy's confidence. Until this point, her matchmaking formula seemed to promise security and predictability. But here, in failing to see danger behind Mark's resume and clean-cut appearance, Lucy is confronted by her own blind spots. The company's official stance is to sweep things under the rug and let the legal team deal with it. But Lucy feels guilty. Ignoring Violet's advice, she reaches out to Sophie. Sophie, hurt and angry, says Lucy never really took the time to protect her, that she just tried to fill the market demand. The friendship ends. Lucy is left rattled. It's the first time her decisions have had such personal negative consequences. At this low point, Lucy is supposed to be traveling to Iceland with Harry. She has sublet her apartment, but the idea of the trip now fills her with dread. She finally admits to herself that she doesn't love Harry. She breaks things off amicably. Without a place to live, Lucy moves in with Jon. They take a trip upstate with some money Jon earned from his show. This intimacy away from the city and its material pressures feels honest. At a wedding together, Lucy kisses Jon and feels a flicker of hope. But Lucy can't shake her ongoing conflict. Her values are split. She tells Jon she doesn't know if they're getting back together because part of her is still tied up in that old narrative, survival, pride, the desire not to end up struggling. Jon confesses that he never stopped loving her and imagines a future together. While Lucy admits her pursuit for money and status blinded her to what matters. Suddenly, Sophie calls in a panic. Mark, the man who assaulted her, is outside her apartment and the police won't intervene. Lucy and Jon immediately drive to Sophie's place. Mark runs away, but Lucy helps Sophie file a restraining order. This moment is crucial because it refocuses what the stakes in the story actually are. Love and relationships are not just about chemistry and deals. They're about protecting each other, being responsible, and standing up for the vulnerable. For all her past mistakes, Lucy proves herself willing to do the right thing when it matters. As Jon and Lucy prepare to say goodbye, Jon makes a final plea. They should try again as a couple. Lucy, finally breaking through her fears, agrees. The ending unfolds softly. Lucy's boss, Violet, offers her a promotion, the chance to run the New York office of Adore. Lucy, however, now thinks about leaving the company and the marriage market behind, but she hesitates, not yet sure how to rewrite her life. During a simple lunch in Central Park, Jon proposes. Lucy accepts, sealing it with a kiss. In the credits, we see glimpses of various couples, including Lucy and Jon, getting marriage licenses. Life goes on. Love takes many forms, and though not every match is perfect, there's always the possibility of growth and healing. Throughout the film, the world of materialists is one where everyone is always performing, whether for love, money, or acceptance. Each character rides the fine line between genuine desire and what they've been taught to want. The repeated references to value, both as self-worth and literal financial value, echo in nearly every conversation. In Lucy's profession, a person's height can be surgically enhanced. A fuller bank account can almost double social value. and age is a ticking clock for both dreams and love. The film uses very plain, often funny dialogue to let the audience see beneath the glittery surface to the exhaustion and quiet desperation. The film's main message is in its title. Everyone is a materialist to some degree. In New York, even love is a luxury good. The matchmaking firm Adore doesn't just promise love. It sells hope, status, and the feeling of being chosen. This idea plays out most sharply with Lucy. She's not just matching others. She's trying to match herself to a worth that feels difficult to reach. Her cander, humor, and sharp business sense make her likable, but also prone to cruelty when she's too focused on results rather than reality. Sophie's arc acts as a parallel cautionary tale. Despite her kindness and accomplishments, she's passed over for being ordinary in an environment that's obsessed with what sets people apart. Her heartbreak show the limits of treating love like a numbers game. The disastrous match with Mark is the harshest lesson of all, a reminder that relying on stats and resumes while ignoring stories and warnings ends up hurting real people. Sophie's experience forces Lucy to question not only her practices, but also the industry she works in. Jon's character stands for a different approach. He's creative and in almost every measurable way a worse catch than Harry. He doesn't have a stable income. He's awkward with money and he hasn't made it. But Jon brings to the table something the others do not. devotion, vulnerability, and a willingness to start from scratch again and again for love. The movie sprinkles bits of symbolism throughout. Don't look at the moon tonight. You'll never be in the house. Lucy repeats to herself at times, recalling an old belief that yearning after impossible things only leaves you stranded. The moon here hints at longing for love that is too far away or outside one's reach because of practical or material obstacles. Weddings recur as symbols, too, not just as romantic milestones, but as complicated, high-pressure business deals, deeply revealing of what each person in attendance values most. For Charlotte, the bride in the opening wedding, the marriage is about winning, about feeling more valuable than her sister. For her, and maybe at first, for Lucy, love is both personal and competitive, a commodity to be earned and displayed. The ending cementss the idea that love in real life is often imperfect and comes with risk. Lucy doesn't pick the right man by everyone else's standards. She chooses Jon, chooses uncertainty, messy finances, compromise, but also the realness of emotional connection. The way Lucy finally says yes to Jon at a picnic in the park puts away all the theories and formulas. In the end, the head and the heart have to agree. Rather than leaving everything tied up with a neat bow, the story closes with snapshots of other couples, some probably happy, some probably not, but all stepping forward willingly. This choice in the film avoids fairy tale simplicity. Even after the credits roll, it's clear love is less about winning or being chosen than about showing up, forgiving, making mistakes, and sometimes risking comfort for something real. Materialists can be compared to other romantic dramas like The Wedding Planner, How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days, or even shows like Sex in the City. When New York's dating scene is both a playground and a battlefield, but where those stories often lean on snappy banter and inevitable happy endings, materialists lingers on small wounds and doubts. It lays bare how much women especially are made to feel their value drops as age or that happiness is something bought or bartered rather than built. It also shares a kinship with films like Marriage Story through its honest sometimes uncomfortable look at why relationships fall apart. There's also a touch of past lives, another Seline Song film in the way that characters must decide between the life they imagined and the one that's possible right now. The dialogue about money, awkward, brutal, funny, and sad, underscores another message. In our world, everyone, even those who claim otherwise, are shaped by material forces. Lucy's confession to Jon that she hated him for being broke and hated herself more for feeling that way is maybe the film's most honest moment. She says what a lot of people feel, but are too embarrassed to admit. Love does not exist in a vacuum. It's not pure or untouched by rent, parking tickets, or dinner tabs. But admitting that is the first step in figuring out how to move beyond it. In the end, Lucy and J's wedding isn't glamorous or high stakes. It's a quiet ceremony, one story among many. Lucy's willingness to finally put her own rules aside, to trust in forgiveness, and to let love be what it wants to be, not what she thinks she deserves, is the point. It's about learning that value isn't something set by a person's resume or bank balance. It comes from staying, helping, and seeing someone clearly, flaws and all. Materialists leaves the audience with a sense that if there is a secret to love, it's about showing up for each other even after we've been measured and found lacking in someone else's eyes. The film asks viewers to reflect on what they measure in others, what they value in themselves, and what risks they're willing to take if the reward is messy, unpredictable, and honest love. The movie ends not with a grand promise, but with a possibility, one that's shaky, hard one, and all the more hopeful for it. Lucy's story in Materialists is a very modern one. Set in New York City, where love and money often get tangled up, sometimes in ways people can't even see coming. Lucy was once a struggling actress, but now works as a matchmaker at a company called Adore. She finds partners for other people and has already helped form nine marriages, which is a big deal in her job. But even though she works with romance everyday, she is careful with her own love life. She avoids relationships and says she'll only date or marry a rich man. It's not just snobbishness. She knows being poor is hard because she grew up that way. And even her last relationship fell apart because of money problems. The film kicks off with the wedding of one of her successful matches. A clear sign to everyone that Lucy is good at her job. At the fancy party, she gets approached by Harry Castile, a very wealthy financer who is also the brother of the groom. Harry is smooth and direct. He shows that he likes her right away. Lucy, not quite sure about his intentions, brushes him off and suggests he join the company as a client instead. She thinks guys like Harry just want someone young and pretty, so she doesn't really expect anything for herself. Then, out of nowhere, Lucy runs into her ex, John. He's working as a caterer at the wedding and is still chasing an acting career that hasn't taken off. Even though it's awkward seeing him, there's still a kind of comfort there, a reminder of what they had. They chat about their old relationship, which ended mainly because they couldn't pay the bills together. The meeting is friendly, but carries a weight of the things they didn't resolve, mostly about money and dreams. Harry doesn't give up on Lucy, though. He starts pursuing her in ways that are new to Lucy. Nice restaurants, expensive dates, sweet compliments. Lucy is at first confused. She wonders why a rich, handsome guy like Harry would go for her when he could have anyone. She lays out her case. She's older. She has student debt. She's not rich or glamorous. And she's not even as pretty as the much younger women he could be dating. Harry listens, but tells her those things don't matter to him. He appreciates her mind, her self-worth, and her approach to life. He argues that he's not looking for someone just to look good on his arm. He wants a real partner. He likes that Lucy understands how the world works and still tries to do things right. Slowly, Lucy starts seeing Harry differently. She's used to being the person who matches up others, but now she's the one being courted and chosen. Harry isn't only about the money for her, but she can't shake off how money makes every interaction easier, smoother, more comfortable. She feels herself drawn in and not just because of Harry's looks or wealth, but also because of how he makes her feel valued, respected, wanted. Lucy agrees to start dating Harry seriously. And oddly enough, her work begins to improve as well. She seems more energetic, matching up her oldest client, Sophie, with another guy named Mark. Everything feels like it's becoming perfect, but love stories in real life rarely go so smoothly. Lucy and Harry go together to Jon's play, which Jon worked hard to put together. Jon is quietly heartbroken to see Lucy there with another man, especially someone so obviously wealthy and successful. That night, after the show, Jon takes Lucy aside and asks questions about her new romance. For him, it's confusing why she's suddenly attached to the sort of man she always said she disliked. Lucy feels unsettled both by Jon's sadness and by her own feelings towards Harry. Then sudden trouble strikes at work. Lucy's boss, Violet, calls her into the office with bad news. Sophie, the client Lucy had recently matched up, has been assaulted by Mark, her date, and Sophie is suing the company. Violet tells Lucy to stay out of it and let the company's lawyers handle things, but Lucy can't let it go. She contacts Sophie, apologizes deeply, and Sophie, hurt and angry, ends their friendship. Lucy is rattled. Her confidence in her career, which was just growing, drops again, and she wonders if maybe she isn't as good at matchmaking as she thought. Lucy's personal life spirals, too. She had planned a big fancy trip to Iceland with Harry, even subled her apartment to be away, but something feels wrong inside. The more time she spends with Harry, the more she realizes she just doesn't love him. The relationship feels empty, like it's just going through motions because it's right on paper. He's rich, she's successful, they look good on dates, but there's no deep love. Lucy breaks up with Harry gently, explaining she can't force herself to feel something that isn't there. With her apartment gone for the time being, Lucy turns to Jon, her ex, and moves in. There is something about being with Jon. Shared memories, old jokes from when they dated, moments that feel safe. Jon isn't rich or famous, but he cares for her and she can be herself around him. They take a trip upstate together. A small vacation paid for with the money Jon got from his play. During a wedding they attend, nostalgia and feelings run high, and Lucy kisses Jon. Still, when Jon asks her if this is them getting back together for real, Lucy can't say yes. She's not sure yet. Her values are still tangled. Does she want wealth and comfort, or does she want real love, even if it means financial uncertainty? Jon, however, opens up honestly. He tells Lucy he never stopped loving her, and he can still picture a future together. In his eyes, Lucy's past fixation on money and security was just a way of protecting herself, but it doesn't make their love any less real. Lucy confesses she once put the pursuit of wealth above their love. She feels small and guilty about it, but Jon doesn't judge her. After this, the pace of life picks up again. Lucy gets a sudden call from Sophie, who is terrified. Mark, the man who assaulted her, is outside her apartment, and the police won't help. Lucy and Jon rush to save her. And when they arrive, Mark flees, but Lucy helps Sophie file a restraining order. The moment is intense, but it makes Lucy feel needed, responsible, like she's more than just someone who fixes updates. Now, Jon makes one final emotional plea for Lucy to give their relationship another shot. This time, Lucy agrees, seeing that her feelings for Jon are stronger and deeper than anything she had with Harry. Soon after, Lucy gets another curveball. Her boss, Violet, offers her a promotion. Lucy was already considering quitting after everything that happened with Sophie, but now she's not sure. It's a big step up, the kind of stable, successful life she once dreamed about. The story ends in a gentle, quietly hopeful moment. Lucy and Jon are having a casual lunch in Central Park. Jon proposes right then and there. No grand gestures, just an honest, simple question. Lucy says yes, sealing it with a kiss. The credits show scenes of happiness for many of the couples Lucy has put together, especially her and John, as they get their marriage license. It's a humble ending, but it feels right. Love doesn't always come with fireworks, but sometimes it's about choosing the person who feels like home. Looking at the characters, Lucy is someone who always works hard, but feels she can only win in life by changing herself, by becoming the kind of woman you need to be for rich men to notice you. Her own experiences with poverty and failed dreams push her to put up walls. She is smart, funny, a little stubborn, but not cynical. She wants love. She's just scared of making the same mistakes as before. Watching Lucy helps us see how money influences self-worth, especially for women in a society that judges them by looks, income, and background. Harry, on the other hand, is the model of the perfect bachelor. He's rich, confident, respectful, even kind. He represents the kind of security Lucy always thought she wanted. But underneath the charm, what he offers is only material, fancy dates, the promise of stability. His interest in Lucy is genuine, but he thinks value comes from intangible things. Trust, respect, the ability to be a team. It's not Harry's fault that Lucy doesn't love him. The romance between them fails not because he's bad, but because Lucy needs something he can't offer. Emotional messiness, growth, acceptance. With Jon, it's the reverse. He has none of Harry's success. No big job, no penthouse. Still fighting for his acting dream. But Jon offers the one thing Lucy can't buy. Unconditional love, patience, and emotional safety. Their connection feels imperfect because it comes with insecurity about the future, but it's also real, messy, and human. The moments Lucy and Jon share are not showy, but they are honest, giving both of them space to be flawed and to choose each other, not because it's practical, but because it's right for them. Sophie's story, woven in as a subplot, is about the risks of matchmaking and dating in the modern world. Despite all the algorithms and careful interviewing, sometimes people get hurt. Sophie, like many, puts her trust in a system meant to find her love, but instead ends up traumatized. When Lucy apologizes and Sophie can't forgive her, it shows that even with the best intentions, the process of sorting through love as if it's a business can go badly wrong. Throughout the film, there are deep themes about love, money, risk, and what it means to choose a partner. Lucy's job makes her think about dating as a series of checklists: income, age, looks, background. Clients at Adore are shown with their impossible lists of expectations, wanting to customize their ideal partner. But time after time, Lucy has to remind herself and her clients that people aren't luxury products. You can't build the perfect person or predict everything about love. Dating is risky, messy, full of uncertainty. The movie uses New York City wonderfully as a backdrop. skyscrapers, fancy restaurants, apartments that cost more than most people can imagine, but also little streets, small theaters, cramped rooms. There are sharp contrasts between wealth and struggle everywhere. For Lucy, every part of the city reminds her of where she came from and where she could go. Her choices about love always feel tied up in her bank account and her address. There is a lot of symbolism throughout. Lucy is always on the move, never rooted in any one place, which shows how she's unsure of her life. When she sublets her apartment for Iceland, she literally has nowhere to go, mirroring how lost she feels inside. The play Jon acts in and Lucy watching it represents what they once hoped for and maybe what they can still be to each other. Characters trying to make sense of their lives on a stage, waiting to see if someone will clap for them. There's foreshadowing when Lucy talks about clients wanting unicorns and possible partners who are perfect in every way. Harry is that unicorn, but in the end, it's Jon messy and struggling who is really her match. The very title materialists refers to how easily love can be confused with material comfort. Lucy has to work through her beliefs about money to find out what she really wants. Hidden in the story are questions about class and gender. Lucy knows that men and women face different pressures. For men like Harry, money and status are the ticket to almost any life they want. For women like Lucy, money is both a shield and a prison. Other clients at a door, a woman who only wants a young, fit guy, and another who lists 30 different requirements show how modern dating can get stuck on superficial attributes. Lucy tries to manage their expectations, but she's just as lost as they are at times. At the end, the film asks if happiness really comes from finding a partner who ticks every box. Lucy tried that with Harry and realized she wasn't in love. She goes back to Jon, risky as it feels, choosing connection over comfort. The wedding license scene is understated, showing happiness as something small and real, not flashy. Love is about imperfect people making an honest promise, not about achieving some impossible standard. Materialists can be compared to other romance films and shows that look at love among the rich. Think of movies like Crazy Rich Asians or series like Sex and the City. But Materialists is less about showing off money and more about questioning what money does to people on the inside. It's closer in spirit to something like the big sick or eternal sunshine of the spotless mind, where love is about accepting flaws rather than buying perfection. The ending is especially meaningful for Lucy. Being proposed to buy Jon in the middle of Central Park without fanfare is finally getting what she needs. This proposal isn't about money or status. It's a simple question about the future asked by someone who has always seen her real value. For Jon, finally being chosen is a reward for his patience and faith in their messy shared history. By agreeing to marry him, Lucy tells herself and everyone watching that taking a risk for love is worth more than any amount of money in the bank. At the heart of everything is the message that loving someone and being loved is never about earning it through status or wealth. It's about seeing and accepting another person completely, flaws and all. Lucy's journey is really about learning to value herself and then choosing a partner who values her for the right reasons. through all the fancy dinners, awkward dates, and tough work days. That's what makes materialists a story with real heart. Lucy is a young woman who once dreamed of becoming an actress. But after many years of struggle and never really finding success, she found a different path for herself as a matchmaker in New York City. Working at Adore, a high-end matchmaking service, she is proud of the career she has built out of bringing people together in love. Even if her own love life doesn't mirror the happily ever after she arranges for clients, Lucy has a rule for herself. She's voluntarily celibate and will only break her rules for someone who is truly wealthy. Her line of work surrounds her with luxury, ambition, and people who want to buy happiness. But she can't help feeling distanced from real connection. She acts with certainty and efficiency, pairing people together based on dozens of designer checklists, social compatibility interests, but above all status and appearance. Even though methodical in her work, Lucy is lonier than she admits. At one of her successful matches weddings, Lucy is approached by Harry Castillo, the groom's brother, who is a handsome and extremely wealthy financer. Harry is charming, unafraid, and expresses romantic interests right away. Lucy, who keeps her personal and professional boundaries rigid, tries to deflect Harry's advance, instead suggesting that he become a client at a door. Her insistence on keeping love transactional sets an early tone for how Lucy sees herself and others as commodities to be traded for value, affection, or advancement. It isn't just Harry who reappears in her life that night, though. Jon, Lucy's ex-boyfriend, happens to be working the same event as a caterer. He is a tender, struggling actor, her old flame from a simpler time when both were poor but in love. Seeing Jon stirs up old memories and heartache, especially as they recall how their relationship was torn apart by financial struggle and unmet ambitions. Despite her attempts to stay aloof from Harry, he pursues her with persistence. Harry takes Lucy to expensive restaurants and gives her attention that flatters her. But there's an underlying negotiation playing out. Lucy can't help but wonder if his attraction to her is a game if she is another prize to be claimed in his successful life. Harry assures her he respects her principles and sees her as special. Eventually, Lucy lets herself lower her guard and they start officially dating. Their relationship is transactional at its core. She offers him access to her world, wit, and charm. He offers her the luxury and security she claims to crave. Professionally, the upswing in her personal life breathes new confidence into Lucy's work. She manages to make a particularly proud match for her longtime client Sophie with a man named Mark, celebrating what she believes is an excellent pairing. In the midst of these developments, Harry suggests more intimacy and commitment. While Jon, still in Lucy's periphery, tries to process her budding romance with someone so unlike him. Lucy brings Harry to see Jon's play, putting her ex and her new boyfriend in direct contact, and the tension is clear. While Lucy is enjoying new heights at work and in her supposed dream relationship, doubts about her decisions start to surface. The mood changes dramatically when Lucy's boss, Violet, brings her bad news. Sophie, her close client and friend, is actually suing Adore because Mark, the man Lucy matched her with, assaulted her. Violet attempts to console Lucy, saying that burnout is common and that Lucy just needs a break. But Lucy feels crushed by guilt. The successful glossy world she built begins to appear shallow and deceptive. Sophie reviews Adore as a scam. Angry that the expert she relied on matched her, not with love, but with someone who hurt her. Sophie's words pierce Lucy to her very core. I thought we were friends. Sophie points out how algorithmic and impersonal the matchmaking process was. Lucy knew salary, height, job, but not the man, not the person who could harm her. Lucy tries to apologize, desperate to fix what's broken, but Sophie sees her as complicit, treating people as goods to be paired off. Sophie sees herself as worthless merchandise to Lucy, someone she could just spawn off. Sophie's declaration, I am not merchandise. I am a person and I deserve love. It's hard making Lucy reconsider the entire basis for her career and selfworth. Their friendship is over and Lucy's sense of herself is in pieces. Lucy spirals after this event. Without much direction, she calls Jon, the only person with whom she feels she can be brutally honest about her failure and guilt. She's not supposed to talk about the lawsuit, but she confides in him anyway, seeking comfort. Jon listens and reassures her, sharing a kind of quiet understanding that comes from their history. Their conversation is warm, honest, and open in a way that Lucy's life with Harry never quite manages. The bond between Lucy and Jon is about vulnerability, sadness, shared disappointment, and empathy rather than status and perfection. Harry and Lucy plan a trip to Iceland together. But as the date approaches, Lucy can't pretend anymore. A conversation with Harry reveals more hidden truths. Harry and his brother once underwent leg lengthening surgery, something that allowed them to meet the arbitrary minimums. Women often searched for like 6 feet tall. Lucy, who spent her professional life measuring people by such boxes, is confronted with the literal cost people will pay to fit into these categories. Harry asks Lucy if knowing this about him would change things. But Lucy admits her real problem. She doesn't truly love Harry, and he doesn't love her either. She tells him that love, real love, isn't a business deal. And while matching checkboxes can make for a comfortable arrangement, it can't generate actual passion or connection. They break up in a moment of mutual understanding. With her apartment sublet for Iceland and nowhere to go, Lucy shows up at J's apartment. She's vulnerable in a way she hasn't allowed herself to be with Harry. Jon welcomes her, offering his messy, honest life as a safe harbor for Lucy's storm. They decide to drive upstate, funded by the small stipen Jon received from his acting work. Their getaway is emotionally charged but laced with uncertainty. At a wedding they attend together, Lucy kisses Jon and Jon seizes on a glimmer of reconciliation. But Lucy still struggles. Is she only here because comfort and familiarity are easy? or has she finally released her obsession with status? Jon admits he has always loved her, still does, and dreams about a future together. Lucy recognizes that her years of trying to trade up for money and lifestyle have left her emotionally bankrupt. She confesses that in her pursuit of wealth, she lost sight of genuine love. Life interrupts when Lucy gets an urgent call from Sophie. Mark, her assaulter, is outside her apartment. Lucy, with Jon's help, rushes to Sophie's side. Even though they can't confront Mark directly, he flees. Lucy supports Sophie in getting a restraining order. It's here, acting not as a matchmaker, but as a friend, that Lucy finds a sense of purpose and redemption. As they leave, Jon tries again, asking Lucy if she wants to rekindle their relationship. Lucy, for all her uncertainty, says yes. Afterwards, Lucy meets with Violet who announces that the London office has asked for recommendations to promote someone as head of a Dors New York office. To Lucy's surprise, Violet wants her to take over. Lucy confesses she was actually going to quit. Feeling too disillusioned to keep pairing people without heart. Violet, not wanting to lose her best matchmaker, encourages her to think it over, promising a bigger salary and more support. Lucy laughs, torn between the security and structure she's always sought and her new understanding that life and love can't always be measured by titles or paychecks. The movie wraps up with Lucy and Jon meeting for a casual lunch in Central Park. Jon, as simple, hopeful, and unpolished as ever, proposes to Lucy. This time, Lucy doesn't hesitate. She says yes, sharing a kiss. In the background, the credits roll showing Lucy and Jon and other couples celebrating love not in five-star hotels or fancy offices, but at the ordinary marriage license office, capturing quiet, authentic joy. Materialist tries to pull apart the world of luxury matchmaking, showing how people like Lucy, who think they know the rules to love, can be blinded by superficial markers, money, height, style, while missing the crucial factor, real connection. The movie examines every character through this lens. Lucy treats her position at Adora like therapy for the lonely rich, but the movie is honest about the limitations of anyone, promising love as a commodity. The casual conversation with her boss, Violet, hits on some of the film's major themes. Violet says they're better than therapists because clients will tell them anything. Yet the whole operation is built on the fragile hope that love can be delivered like a product customized and transactional. The movie's message is that while people crave the shortcuts to happiness, hire the matchmaker, check the boxes by the lifestyle, there is no algorithm for happiness. The character of Sophie serves as a reflection of Lucy's moral crisis. Their relationship started as professional but grew personal. When Sophie sues Adore after suffering real harm, her words to Lucy expose how Lucy without meaning to treated her like inventory. Sophie's point that she deserves love and not just any match, but the right one breaks to Lucy's professional armor, and the audience understands that even the most sophisticated systems can let people down when they value profile over personhood. Harry, Lucy's ideal, match, illustrates another angle. He is the embodiment of material success. Wealthy, handsome, by design, connected. But even Harry cannot buy Lucy's real affection, just as Lucy can't force herself to feel passion for a resume. Their breakup is almost business-like. They both say the right words, admit it won't work, and move on. Harry's confession about his surgery done to fit a dating app checkbox is quietly tragic. He literally changed his body, which should be intimate and unique, just to fit a marketplace of attraction. This is a blunt metaphor for how people in Lucy's line of work and the modern dating world are trained to change and sell themselves. When Lucy realizes that not even Harry's wealth can fill the absence she feels, she finally accepts that love and security do not always go together. Jon, on the other hand, is everything Lucy tried to leave behind. poor, undermployed, awkward. But Jon never tries to be something he's not. He loves Lucy without calculation, and even in their lowest moments, their conversations are deeply honest. His proposal at the end is almost cliche, yet it feels right because after all the bargaining and status games, it's simple. The dream Lucy describes at the end, wondering what made the first couple of cave people fall in love, is significant. She wonders if it was about status, matching backgrounds, or something more mysterious. Lucy's journey is about rediscovering that love, though sometimes messy and imperfect, is not about measurable compatibility. The movie suggests that something about us, about people, goes deeper than any box you can tick. Materialists is also critical of New York's luxury dating culture where love is treated as the final item to acquire in a life of relentless self-improvement. Several scenes emphasize this, especially the ongoing banter in the adore office. Staff members joke about clients absurd demands and Lucy voices growing disillusionment with how transactional everything has become. The list of client requirements, height, income, profession, attractiveness, resembles shopping more than romance. The industry's success stories, like all the marriages Lucy mentions, are weighed against silent failures and even tragedies like Sophie's. There's a strong sense of foreshadowing when Lucy is told repeatedly that burnout is common in her profession. Matchmaking, especially at the level adore operates, is emotionally draining because trying to manage other people's happiness without real power is a losing game. Underneath the zippy dialogue and beautiful settings, the film's mood turns somber as Lucy confronts the human cost of her success. It asks the audience, "Can you really control love? Or are all our attempts to package and perfect it doomed to fail?" Symbolically, Lucy's job represents not just matchmaking, but all the ways in which modern life turns intimacy into something transactional. Dating apps, personal, brands, the endless negotiation for a better position or partner. The term materialists refers not only to people who want more stuff, but to those who treat relationships like acquisitions. Lucy starts as the perfect materialist, ambitious, logical, searching for status, and ends as someone finally able to choose messiness and love over comfort and security. The ending, where Lucy chooses Jon and accepts his proposal, is deliberately not a fairy tale. Even as Jon proposes, their conversation touches on doubts about growing to hate each other, about infidelity, divorce, about whether doing it differently than their parents matters. The film points out the real risks and anxieties attached to commitment. Many romantic comedies end in marriage, but Materialists invites us to see marriage not as the finish line, but as another uncertain beginning filled with both hope and peril. In its use of dialogue and setting, the film is reminiscent of other modern romance dramas like Noah Bombach's marriage story and Greta Gooig's Francis Ha, but with its own angle. Here, relationships are underscored by commerce. The focus on matchmakers as quasi therapist brings to mind shows like Netflix's Indian matchmaking or Bravo's Millionaire Matchmaker. But instead of celebrating the industry, materialist peels back the glossy veneer to reveal the toll it takes on those inside and outside it. Lucy's story is not just about choosing between two men. It's about learning to value herself and others as more than commodities. Her decision to stay with Jon doesn't guarantee happiness. The movie refuses a strictly happy or tragic ending. Instead, it offers a nuanced hope. Love is hard, imperfect, risky, and can't be calculated. But it's also unpredictable and beautiful when you let go of the algorithms and embrace the unknown. By the epilogue, as we see flashes of couples at the city clerk's office, materialists comes full circle. What started as an operation to steer people's choices for money returns to the simplicity of two people choosing each other in all their imperfection and uncertainty. Lucy's arc from shrewd guarded status chasing matchmaker to someone willing to risk her future on love instead of a sure thing suggests that happiness can't be manufactured or bought and meaning comes from facing life with openness and honesty even when it's scary. The film doesn't offer answers so much as permission to stop chasing perfection and allow life and love to surprise us.
title: Materialists (2025): Recap and Ending Explained

text: If you like Mark Flanigan, the creator of Midnight Mass, you probably enjoy The Life of Chuck as well. Then there's The North Star. Did you just see that? Honestly, I did not know much about the movie before watching it, except that Tom Hiddston stars in it. At one point, I even wondered if Mike Flanigan cast him just because he saw the viral video of him dancing. Just looking at the poster, you'd think it's just a simple drama about life. And in some ways, it is, but in other ways, it is not. I have a few questions about the life of Chuck. What is real and what is not? Did the world really end? Why is Chuck all over the newspapers, billboards, and TV? In this video, I'll explain the movie The Life of Chuck. The Life of Chuck is a story told backward, beginning just before the world ends, even though people don't notice it right away. It takes place in a small town where we follow a teacher named Marty and his ex-girlfriend Felicia, as their world slowly starts to break down. At first, the signs are small and strange, like billboards and ads suddenly showing up to thank a man named Charles Grants, played by Tom Hiddson, for 39 years of service, even though no one knows who he is. After that, things get worse really quickly. Disasters like earthquakes, wildfires, and sinkholes start happening more often, and parts of the country actually break off. People can't reach the outside world anymore and all the technology stops working as everything falls apart. The mysterious man Charles Grants show up more and more like a warning that something big and final is coming. As the town starts to fall apart for real, Marty and Felicia lean on each other knowing the end is near. The stars in the sky begin to disappear one by one like someone blowing out candles. With Charles Crant's face appearing in the background and the couple accepting what's coming, the story shifts to its next part. Next, we meet Charles CR, the mystery man from the posters. Everyone calls him Chuck. And at first, he seemed like a regular guy. He's an accountant, has a wife and kid, and lives the kind of life many people dream about. But there is more to Chuck than meets the eye. Through flashbacks to his childhood, we learn he has a big love for music and dancing. One of the most fun scenes in the movie shows Chuck dancing in the street with a group of musicians full of energy and joy. But even during his happy moment, something doesn't feel right. Chuck starts getting bad headaches and looks like he's in pain, a sign that something is seriously wrong. As we get to the last part of the story, everything begins to come together and we finally understand who Charles CR really is. Chuck is shown as a young boy who faces a heartbreaking tragedy when he loses his parents and onboard sister in a car accident. After that, his grandparents Sarah and Albby CR take care of him. Through Chuck's point of view, we see the ups and downs of growing up, like his first crush, his first embarrassing moment, and his first kiss. Living with his grandparents, Chuck discovers a love for music and dance, which his grandmother supports, encouraging him to be playful and express himself freely. At the same time, his grandfather teaches him the value of math, helping him stay focused and grounded. The story also brings in something strange in otherwise normal town. Sock's grandpa, Albi Crance, keep the room at the top of the stairs locked up tight. Even though Chuck tries to get inside, it's clear that whatever is in there is something Albi is really afraid of. Whoever enters the room is forced to see how they will die. Since the story is told in reverse, we slowly discover the truth. Everything we've seen so far is not just the story of Chuck's life, but also how it ends. Charles CR dies from cancer at the age of 39. What is real and what is not real in the beginning? Did the world really end? The story is told in reverse, which helps reveal its true meaning. The world ending scenes at the beginning aren't about the actual end of the world. Instead, they represent Chuck's mind and body slowly shutting down as he dies from a brain tumor at 39. It means that nothing that takes place in act three is technically real. By the time you finish the life of Chuck, you realize that all the people disappearing in the first part are actually from Chuck's memories. People he knew and cared about during his life. When Chuck dies, they vanish too because they were part of him. As the movie unfolds, something beautiful and unexpected begins to happen. Characters and moments we saw earlier during the apocalyptic chaos of the first act start to appear again, but in a new light. We see their true relationship with Chuck and how their presence in his mind shaped the world that collapsed in the beginning. This realization that the end of the world is really just the end of Chuck's consciousness gives the story emotional weight. It paints the picture of a man whose internal universe is filled with memories of everyone who mattered to him. His mind isn't just shutting down. It's saying goodbye to each person he ever loved or noticed one by one. In the middle act, during the now iconic street dance scene, we saw Chuck in his most alive moment. He dances spontaneously with a busker, not caring about what others think, just soaking in the moment. We catch a glimpse of the shadow hanging over him. The brain tumor that will eventually end his life. That conscious makes us seem more powerful. It reminds us that life is fleeting and we often don't know when the end will end. The message is clear. Live while you can. Savor the ordinary moments and don't hold back joy. One of the deeper layers of the film comes from the memory of Chuck had as a kid in school. He heard Walt Whitman's poem, Song of Myself, where the poet famously says, "I contain multitudes. A whole universe right between my hands." That line clearly stayed with Chuck. It shaped how he saw the world and his place in it. The film takes idea and bring it to life. Chuck really does contain multitudes. His mind is a universe of people, places, memories, regrets, and joys. When he dies, the universe fades, but the beauty of it was real. The film suggests that every person's life made up of their memories and relationships. It's like its own unique universe. So when someone dies, it's not just the end of life. It's like an entire world disappearing. In the final act of the film, young Chuck finally gathers the courage to enter the mysterious copula in his grandparents house, a place he always feared. What he finds there changes everything. A vision of his future, including the moment and matter of death. He doesn't know when will it happen, but he now understands that it will happen one day. His life will end and the certainty stays with him. From then on, he lives with the awareness that time is limited. Instead of letting that realization crush him, it inspires him knowing that his life will someday end gives him a reason to fully live. It pushes him to take risks, to connect with others, and to find joy even in the smallest moments, like dancing in the street with a stranger. That moment of dancing isn't just random. It's a choice, a declaration that even though life will end in tragedy, it is still worth celebrating while it lasts. Chuck's journey reflects a powerful truth to contain multitudes. As Walt Whitman's wrote, it's to live fully and deeply, embracing every part of life. Thank you for watching and see you in my next video. [Music]

text: In a world where dragons rule the skies, a young Viking must choose between war and peace, between what he's told to be and who he truly is. This is Burke, a rugged Viking island, always cold, always dangerous, and always under attack by dragons. Here, dragons aren't fairy tales. They're real. They steal food, burn homes, and leave chaos behind. But the people of Burke, they fight back. They're Vikings, and they don't run from battles. They start them. During one of these terrifying raids, we meet Hiccup, a skinny, awkward teenager desperate to prove himself. Everyone tells him to stay inside, but Hiccup sneaks out, hoping to make a difference. But instead, he causes destruction and almost gets someone killed. Hiccup isn't strong. He's not a fighter like the rest. But he dreams of one thing, killing a dragon. Not just any dragon, the rarest, most feared of them all, the Night Fury. In the middle of the raid, Hiccup spots a shadow in the sky and fires one of his inventions, a ropel loaded cannon. To his shock, he hits something. The night fury crashes far into the forest. No one believes him. Not even his father, Stoke, the vast chief of the tribe. To everyone else, Hiccup is still a mistake. But the next morning, Hiccup follows the trail and finds it. The night fury, wounded, helpless. This is the moment he's waited for. He raises his knife to kill it. But when he looks into its eyes, he can't. Instead of finishing the dragon, he cuts the ropes and sets it free. The night fury pounces, but doesn't hurt him. It spares him just like he did. And in that moment, something changes. Back home, Stok sends Hiccup to dragon training, a brutal test where young Vikings must learn to kill dragons or die trying. Hiccup joins Astrid, Snotlout, Fish Legs, Roughnut, and Toughnut. They're fighters. He's not. But as each lesson goes on, Hiccup starts winning, not by fighting, but by using kindness and clever tricks. The others think it's luck. Astrid grows suspicious. But Hiccup has a secret. He returns to the forest again and again, bringing fish, drawing in the dirt, and slowly earning the dragon's trust. He names it Toothless. Then he notices Toothless can't fly. One of his tail fins is missing. So Hiccup does the unthinkable. He builds a new tail. He builds hope. Together, they learn to fly. Toothless soarses. Hiccup steers. For the first time, he feels alive, but secrets don't stay hidden. Astrid follows him and discovers Toothless. At first, she's terrified. But after a wild ride through the clouds, she begins to see what Hiccup sees. Dragons aren't mindless monsters. They're just misunderstood. During their flight, they follow a pack of dragons to a hidden island, and what they find shakes them both. A mountain full of dragons, all feeding a giant, terrifying queen beast. A dragon so massive it eats its own if they fail. This isn't just a fight for food. It's slavery. The next day is the final trial. Hiccup is named Top Slayer, chosen to kill a dragon in front of the entire village. He steps into the arena. The gate opens. The monstrous nightmare roars, but Hiccup drops his sword. He won't kill. Not today. The crowd is confused. Stoke is furious. The dragon attacks, but Toothless, sensing Hiccup's danger, breaks free and crashes into the arena. He saves Hiccup and fights off the nightmare. But the Vikings don't understand. They capture Toothless and Hiccup is shamed. His father is heartbroken. Angry, he downs Hiccup and uses Toothless to find the dragon nest. Stoke and the warriors set sail to destroy the nest, but they don't know what's waiting. The dragon queen attacks. The battle is hopeless, but just when all seems lost, Hiccup returns, riding other dragons with Astrid and the teens. Together, they join the fight. In the final, most emotional moment of the movie, Hiccup and Toothless fly into battle. They outsmart the queen. They dive through fire, dodge massive jaws, and in a blazing final move, they bring the beast down, but Hiccup falls. He disappears in the fire, and Toothless dives after him. Later, Hiccup wakes up. He's alive, but he's lost a leg. Toothless is beside him. Stoke hugs his son, finally proud. The village sees dragons differently now. No longer enemies, but allies. Irk changes. The skies are filled with dragons. And Hiccup becomes a hero. Not because he killed a dragon, but because he befriended one. How to Train Your Dragon is more than just a fantasy tale. text: A24's warfare devotion to realism in modern combat makes it a true standout in the war film genre. This left many audiences wondering how accurate this story actually is. Ray Mendoza and Alex Garland directed Warfare. You may know Garland for his work on Annihilation, Exmachina, and Civil War. Mendoza, on the other hand, is a firsttime director. The former Navy Seal has worked with Garland before as a military adviser on Civil War. Critics and veterans noted Mendoza's work for its incredible realism, which sparked a deeply personal idea. During his time as a Navy Seal, Mendoza was part of a mission that trapped him and his platoon inside a house. This is the exact mission we see take place in the film, making this one of the most authentic depictions of modern war we have ever seen. Seeing as Mendoza and Garland set out to make this film as realistic as possible with the writing, acting, and direction, every effort was made to show accurate depictions of war without the Hollywood sugar coating. You can hear this in the screenplay as most of the dialogue is ripped straight from the military. The actors even participated in a heavily modified Navy Seal training program. This is where they learned the jargon, movements, and mannerisms. In interviews, the actors revealed that they were all given code names after this training. The directors wanted this cast to feel like a squad as most of the film hinges on their interactions. There is little character development or arc. Most of the characterization you get is based on how someone reacts to a situation. This meant the actors needed to feel like they were plucked out of the seals. This film was incredibly personal to Mendoza. He had been thinking of creating it for over 20 years. And after working on films like Act of Valor, Lone Survivor, and finally Civil War, he was ready to tell this story. He would say about the movie, "I have one opportunity to tell it right, to get it right, and to honor the people that were there." He would also talk about how hard it was for him and other veterans to talk about what they went through. Using this film as a tool for them to explain is another reason Mendoza was so excited about this film. Garland would share this sentiment after working with Mendoza and hearing his story. After Garland finished Civil War, he wanted to make something that felt as real as forensically possible, which aligned perfectly with Mendoza's vision. Warfare is very much a true story, potentially the most accurate form of a war story like this. The film has received nearly universal praise for, in large part, its devotion to realism that Mendoza and Garland were so adamant about. How accurate did you find the film?
