In the eagerly awaited sequel to 2016's The Accountant, we return to the world of Christian Wolf, the highly skilled accountant with autism who uses his extraordinary mathematical abilities and combat training to untangle complex financial crimes while maintaining a strict moral code of his own. This time the stakes are higher as Christian must reunite with his aranged brother Braxton to help Treasury agent Mary Beth Medina solve the murder of her former boss, Treasury Director Ray King. As they delve deeper into the investigation, they uncover a sinister human trafficking operation and face some of the world's most dangerous assassins along the way. The movie opens with an energetic sequence at a bowling alley where we see people enjoying themselves. This light-hearted scene serves as a stark contrast to the darker elements that will soon unfold in the story. Meanwhile, we're introduced to Treasury agent Mary Beth Medina, who has risen through the ranks since we last saw her in the first film. She's now the deputy director of Finen, Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, a position she achieved with help from Ray King, who recognized her potential and mentored her. Tragically, Ray King is found murdered, discovered in a tavern along with several other victims, all former Chilean special forces soldiers. This shocking event serves as the catalyst for the entire plot. Medina, devastated by the loss of her mentor, initially investigates the case through official channels, but quickly realizes there's more to the murder than meets the eye. When she finds a mysterious photograph hidden in the tavern, she begins to suspect a connection to a larger conspiracy. The photo shows a Central American family, Edith Sanchez, her husband, Gina, and their young son, Alberto. According to the information Medina pieces together, this family left El Salvador to come to the United States, but subsequently disappeared. What's most intriguing is that Ray King appears to have been investigating their disappearance before his death, suggesting he had uncovered something significant. With limited options and facing bureaucratic hurdles within her own department, Medina makes the difficult decision to contact Christian Wolf, the enigmatic accountant she encountered years ago during the Living Robotics case. Though Christian operates outside the law, Medina knows his unique skills and moral code make him the perfect person to help solve this increasingly complex case. Finding Christian proves challenging as he's deliberately kept a low profile since their last encounter. Medina eventually tracks him down through his connection to Harbor Neuroscience, a specialized facility where he regularly donates money. This facility cares for individuals with unique neurological conditions, including Justine, a non-verbal autistic woman who works as Christian's handler and information broker. It's through this connection that Medina finally reaches Christian. Christian, living in his customary minimalist fashion in an Airstream trailer and working legitimate accounting jobs when not taking on more dangerous clients, is initially reluctant to get involved. However, when he learns that Ray King has been murdered, he agrees to help. King had spared Christian's life years ago at the rave night, establishing a strange bond of respect between them. Christian also feels a connection to the missing family in the photograph, particularly the young boy who he suspects may be neurodeivergent like himself. To effectively tackle this case, Christian realizes he needs help from his aranged brother, Braxton. The brothers haven't spoken in 8 years, not since their violent confrontation in Chicago during the events related to the living robotics case. Their relationship is complicated by years of resentment and miscommunication. Braxton feels abandoned by Christian, who has kept his distance to protect his brother from the dangerous individuals who might target him because of Christian's work. Despite the tension, Braxton reluctantly agrees to help when Christian calls, though he makes it clear he's doing it for payment, not out of brotherly love. Their reunion is awkward and filled with unspoken grievances. Braxton has built a life as a highlevel mercenary and security specialist. Using the combat skills their military father taught them both as children. Together, this unlikely trio, the methodical accountant with autism, his volatile brother, and the buy the book treasury agent begin their investigation into Ray King's murder and the disappearance of the Sanchez family. Christian's approach is systematic and detail oriented, analyzing tax returns, employment records, and financial transactions to trace the family's movement after entering the United States. Their investigation leads them to discover that Edith Sanchez had been working at a pizza restaurant in Los Angeles. Filing tax returns that showed suspicious inconsistencies. When they visit the restaurant, Christian quickly determines the business's laundering money, using inflated sales figures to hide income from another source. The restaurant owner reacts violently to their questioning, confirming their suspicions that he's involved in illegal activity. Through Christian's meticulous analysis and Braxton's more direct interrogation methods, they learned that the pizza restaurant was part of a human trafficking operation. The Sanchez family, like many others, had been captured after crossing the border and forced into modern slavery. Edith had been working in exploitative conditions until she was involved in a serious car accident. This accident is a crucial turning point in the story. They discover that Edith was critically injured and taken to a hospital with severe trauma, including brain injuries. The hospital records reveal something extraordinary. After the accident, Edith experienced a rare condition called acquired soant syndrome. Her brain trauma rewired her neural pathways, giving her exceptional pattern recognition and problem solving abilities, particularly in areas related to combat strategy and threat assessment. The neurologist who treated Edith explains that while she lost most of her memories of her previous life, she gained these remarkable new abilities. Even more significantly, her personality changed dramatically. She became more isolated, aggressive, and eventually escaped from the hospital after attacking a security guard and stealing his gun. This revelation leads to the movie's major twist. Edith Sanchez transformed into Anaise, a deadly assassin who's been working for various criminal organizations. The evidence suggests that Ray King had discovered this connection and was trying to help her, possibly reunite her with her son before he was killed. Meanwhile, Medina's investigation has drawn unwanted attention. A contract is put out on her life by those connected to the trafficking ring. After narrowly surviving an assassination attempt, she realizes the danger is escalating. Christian, using his contacts in the criminal world, identifies the person behind the contract, a powerful Eastern European crime boss named Batineetsk, played with chilling efficiency by Andrew Howard. The tension builds as Christian, Braxton, and Medina, follow the trail of evidence while evading the assassins sent to stop them. Their search takes them to various locations across Los Angeles, including underground fight clubs, high-end hotels, and abandoned industrial sites that serve as fronts for the trafficking operation. In one of the film's most emotionally resonant scenes, Christian and Braxton attend a country western bar where they briefly let their guard down. After a few drinks, Braxton finally confronts Christian about his feelings of abandonment. Is it because of you or because of me that you don't miss me? He asks, revealing the deep hurt he's carried for years. Christian, typically uncomfortable with emotional conversations, struggles to express himself, but acknowledges that his condition makes it difficult for him to process certain emotions. This heartfelt exchange begins the process of healing between the brothers as they start to understand each other better. The scene is interrupted when a bar patron harasses another customer and the brothers intervene, showcasing their formidable fighting skills in a sequence that balances intense action with moments of dark humor. Their synchronized combat style reveals how similarly they were trained by their father. Despite their different paths in life, as their investigation deepens, they uncover more about the human trafficking ring that had captured the Sanchez family. This criminal enterprise forces migrants into labor in various industries, farms, slaughterous, factories, essentially modern-day slavery. The operation is vast and protected by corrupt officials and dangerous enforcers. Their breakthrough comes when they discover that a convoy of buses is transporting captured migrants, including children, to a remote location. Among these children might be Alberto Sanchez, now a teenager. Despite Medina's insistence on following legal procedures, Christian and Braxton decide they can't wait for official action and plan a rescue operation. What follows is one of the film's most intense action sequences. As Christian and Braxton intercept the convoy in the desert. They methodically take down the armed guards and free the captives. The scene showcases both brothers exceptional combat skills while highlighting their different styles. Christian's precise, efficient movements contrast with Braxton's more aggressive, improvisational approach. During the rescue, they find a teenage boy they believe is Alberto Sanchez. The boy is initially fearful, but responds to Christian's calm, direct manner of speaking. Christian recognizes signs that the boy may be neurode divergent, like himself, and adapts his communication accordingly. This moment reinforces one of the film's key themes. Christian's autism gives him unique insights and abilities that others lack. Meanwhile, Medina has been pursuing her own angle of the investigation through official channels. She's identified connections between the trafficking ring and several legitimate businesses, including construction companies and agricultural operations that employ undocumented workers. However, her efforts are hampered by obstacles within her own department, suggesting possible corruption at high levels. After successfully rescuing the captives, Christian arranges for their safe transport to authorities who can help them. However, he keeps Alberto with them. Believing the boy is still in danger and that he might be the key to finding Anise, his mother. The climax begins to build as Christian reaches out to his mysterious handler, Justine, for help locating Anaise. Using advanced surveillance technology and a network of neurode divergent hackers at Harbor Neuroscience, they identify a woman matching Ana Isa's description entering the tavern where Ray King was killed. This confirms their suspicion that she was present at the murder scene, but her role remains unclear. Was she the killer or another target? Christian, using his understanding of how Savant abilities work, develops a theory about Anaisa's motivations. He believes she's been systematically hunting down members of the trafficking organization that captured her family, using her enhanced cognitive abilities to identify and eliminate them. Ray King wasn't her target, but may have been caught in the crossfire or killed by others trying to stop his investigation. As they close in on Anaise, Batunetsk escalates his efforts to eliminate them. He sends his most skilled assassins, resulting in a tense pursuit through the streets of Los Angeles. During this sequence, Medina is seriously injured and hospitalized, removing her temporarily from the action, but raising the emotional stakes as Christian and Braxton vow to complete the mission and protect her. With Medina in the hospital, Christian decides to take a more direct approach. He contacts Batu Netsk directly, using his knowledge of the crime boss's operations as leverage. In a tense conversation, Christian demonstrates his thorough understanding of Netsk's criminal empire and threatens to dismantle it completely unless he calls off the contract on Medina. Impressed by Christian's audacity and recognizing the genuine threat he poses, Netsk agrees to cancel the hit. The final act brings all the story threads together as Christian and Braxton finally locate Anise. They find her in an abandoned warehouse preparing for her next target. The confrontation is tense as Anise initially sees them as threats and nearly kills Braxton before Christian manages to establish communication with her. In an emotionally charged scene, Christian connects with Anna East through their shared neurode divergence. He explains that he understands her need for patterns, order, and justice. He shows her the photo of her family and brings in Alberto, creating a momentous reunion between mother and son. Though Anaise doesn't fully remember her past life, she recognizes something in Alberto that transcends her memory loss. However, their reunion is interrupted when Netsk's men, defying their boss's orders, attack the warehouse. What follows is the film's most elaborate action sequence with Christian, Braxton, and Anise fighting side by side to protect Alberto. The scene showcases each character's unique fighting style, Christian's precise, almost mathematical approach, Braxton's raw power and adaptability, and Ana Isa's savant-like ability to predict and counter her opponent's moves. During this climactic battle, we see the full evolution of Christian and Braxton's relationship. They protect each other instinctively, their years of estrangement melting away as they fall back into the synchronized combat their father taught them. In a particularly poignant moment, Braxton takes a bullet meant for Christian, demonstrating his renewed brotherly love despite their complicated past. With the immediate threat neutralized, Christian confronts the leader of the trafficking ring who has been revealed to be a seemingly legitimate businessman with connections to powerful political figures. In true accountant fashion, Christian delivers justice in his own way, ensuring the man can never harm another family while also securing evidence that Medina can use to dismantle the entire operation through legal channels. In the aftermath, we see the various characters beginning to heal and move forward. Medina recovers in the hospital and receives a visit from Christian, who provides her with detailed financial records documenting the full extent of the trafficking operation. These records will allow her to build cases against numerous criminals and corrupt officials, advancing her career while doing genuine good. Anise and Alberto begin the process of rebuilding their lives. With Christian arranging safe identities and a secure location for them, though Anaise may never fully recover her memories, she and her son form a new bond based on their present circumstances rather than their past. The most significant resolution comes between Christian and Braxton. As Braxton recovers from his wound, the brothers have a genuine heart-to-he heart conversation. Christian admits that he stayed away to protect Braxton, not because he didn't care. Braxton acknowledges that he's always needed Christian's approval and recognition more than he realized. They reach a new understanding based on acceptance of each other's differences and recognition of their unbreakable bond as brothers. In the film's final scenes, we see Christian and Braxton traveling together in Christian's Airstream trailer, heading toward a state park where Christian has made reservations. This simple act of planning a trip together symbolizes Christian's growth. He's making room in his highly structured life for his brother. When Braxton complains about Christian hogging time with a cat they've apparently adopted, we see a glimpse of normal sibling bickering that suggests their relationship will always have its challenges. But the fundamental connection has been restored. The final shot shows the brothers sitting outside the trailer at sunset. Christian explaining constellations with his characteristic precision while Braxton listens with a mixture of amusement and genuine interest. It's a quiet moment that contrasts with the film's intense action sequences and underscores its central theme, the complex bonds of family that persist despite differences, trauma, and separation throughout The Accountant 2. Director Gavin Okconor balances spectacular action sequences with nuanced character development. Ben Affleck's portrayal of Christian Wolf remains compelling, showing how the character has evolved while staying true to his autistic traits. The film doesn't treat his autism as a superpower, but as an integral part of his identity that comes with both challenges and unique perspectives. John Bernthal brings depth to Braxton, showing both his resentment and his enduring love for his brother. Their relationship forms the emotional core of the film, exploring themes of family, acceptance, and reconciliation. Cynthia Adai Robinson's Medina serves as the moral compass, representing the legal systems limitations while demonstrating that justice can sometimes require working outside established boundaries. The film also explores deeper themes about human trafficking and modern slavery, shining a light on real world issues while avoiding exploitative depictions. The character of Anaise represents the trauma of these experiences, but also the resilience and strength of survivors. Her transformation from victim to powerful agent of her own destiny provides a compelling arc that avoids typical survivor narratives. The Accountant 2 expands on the original film's universe while maintaining its unique blend of action, intricate plotting, and character-driven storytelling. The financial crimes that Christian typically investigates take a backseat to human trafficking in this installment, but his methodical approach to solving problems remain central to the narrative. His ability to see patterns that others miss allows him to connect dots between seemingly unrelated events and ultimately solve the case. The action sequences are brilliantly choreographed, showcasing Christian's unique fighting style that combines his military training with his precise mathematical mind. These scenes aren't just exciting spectacles, but revelations of character, how Christian processes the world, how Braxton channels his emotions, and how Ana Isa's savant abilities manifest in combat situations. Director Gavin Oconor builds on the established world of the first film while exploring new territory. The visual style combines sterile, ordered environments, reflecting Christian's preference for structure with chaotic, dangerous settings where the brothers must exercise their lethal skills. The contrast between Christian's meticulous personal life and the violence he's capable of creates a fascinating tension throughout the film. The script by Bill Deuke maintains the original's balance of complex plotting, character development, and moments of unexpected humor. Christian's literal interpretations of figures of speech and social situations provide both comic relief and insights into how he experiences the world. His relationship with Braxton allows for more emotional expressiveness than we saw in the first film, as Braxton serves as both a foil and a bridge to understanding Christian better. The performances across the board are strong with Ben Affleck continuing to find new dimensions in Christian while maintaining consistency with his established character. John Bernthal brings both intensity and vulnerability to Braxton, making his resentment and longing for connection equally believable. Cynthia Adai Robinson expands on Medina's character, showing her growth in confidence and authority while still wrestling with moral complexities. Daniela Pana's portrayal of Anna East is particularly noteworthy, capturing both the deadly efficiency of an assassin and the underlying trauma of a mother separated from her child. Without relying on extensive dialogue, she conveys the character's internal struggle between her pre-ac identity and the person she became after her transformation. JK Simmons, though his character Ray King appears only in flashbacks, establishes the emotional stakes that drive Medina's quest for justice. His presence looms over the film, representing both the institutional power of law enforcement and the personal connections that transcend official relationships. The film's pacing deserves special mention as it balances complex exposition of financial crimes and trafficking operations with pulse pounding action sequences. Unlike many action thrillers that sacrifice character development for spectacle, The Accountant 2 allows quiet moments of connection between its characters to breathe, making the subsequent action more meaningful because we understand what's at stake personally for each character. The cinematography enhances the storytelling with distinct visual approaches for different settings, the clinical precision of Christian's living space, the gritty underworld of trafficking operations, the sterile government offices where Medina works, and the warm nostalgic atmosphere of the country bar where the brothers begin to reconnect. These visual choices reflect the film's themes of contrast and connection. The score complements the visuals using mathematical patterns in its composition that subtly reflect Christian's way of thinking. During action sequences, the music intensifies while maintaining these patterns, creating a unique auditory experience that puts us in Christian's headspace as he calculates trajectories and identifies threats. The Accountant 2 succeeds as both a standalone thriller and a sequel that deepens our understanding of its central character by expanding Christian's world to include his reconnection with Braxton and his empathy for Alberto. text: What happens when a genius cryptographer turns rogue? From a visionary director James Halls, renowned for his work on Slow Horses and Black Mirror, comes The Amateur, a gripping espionage thriller that redefineses a genre. Oscar winner Rammy Malik delivers a powerful performance as Charlie Heler, a CIA analyst thrust into a perilous quest for justice after his wife's tragic death. CIA cryptographer Charlie Heler is working on restoring an old Cessna plane, a gift from his wife Sarah. Sarah informs Charlie that she must leave for a 5-day business trip to London. At the CIA's decryption and analysis division, Charlie interacts with a field agent known as the bear. While reviewing files as office, he receives a cryptic message from his online friend, Inqualine, revealing classified government information. Hela makes a horrifying discovery. His own government orchestrated drone strikes on allied nations. Key figures, Director Moore and an operative named Caleb are implicated. The next morning, Moore escorts Heler to a meeting with Director O'Brien, who sadly informs him that Sarah has been killed during an attack. Moore shows Heler the news footage, leaving him devastated. As the days pass, Heler questions Moore and Caleb about next steps. They assure him everything is under control. When Sarah's body is flown home, Heler tearfully sorts through her belongings. Driven by grief, Heler investigates the attack independently. He discovers that four attackers were involved. During a confrontation at the airport, one of them killed a security guard, causing chaos. In confusion, they grab hostages, including Sarah. Mishkablasic and Ellis were among the attackers. It was during the chaos that Sarah was killed. Heler shares his findings with Mo and Caleb, but notices their suspicious lack of surprise. Realizing they knew more than they admitted, Heler confronts them. Moore vaguely explains that their larger goal is dismantling a rogue organization. He also pressures Heler into attending a therapy session. In therapy, Heler vents his frustration about the government's inaction. Determined to take matters into his own hands, he hatches a plan. Secretly, he bugs a CIA ID card, sneaks into restrictive files, and prints sensitive documents, exposing more and Caleb's crimes. He hides these files cleverly, including making it seem like he's using an old CD jukebox at a local bar. The next morning, Heler blackmails Moore and Caleb. He threatens to leak the files unless they let him hunt Sarah's killers. Moore, seeing no choice, agrees and assigns a trainer named Henderson to prepare Heler. Training proves tough. Heler is terrible at shooting, but naturally gifted at creating explosives. Henderson notes Heler's hesitation to kill, even up close, and forges fake passports for him. Meanwhile, Caleb grows wary. He digs through Heler's records and home but finds no hidden files. Suspecting the bar connection, they check the juke box only to realize Heler had bluffed. Fearing exposure, they order Henderson to bring Heler back. But when Henderson checks his room, he finds it empty. Heler has fled with the fake passports. In London, Heler tracks down arms dealer Gretchen Frank. He breaks into her home, but can't pull the trigger when faced with her. Instead, he poisons her hospital oxygen tank. Gretchen survives long enough to escape, but is hit by a car and killed. Heler steals her phone and flees to France. While at a bar in France, Heler notices Henderson tailing him. After a quick distraction, Hela confront Henderson, who advises him to let go of the past. During their conversation, Heler escapes. Seeking help, Heler contacts Inqualine and travels to Istanbul. There, they regroup at her safe house, piecing together leads. Meanwhile, Director O'Brien begins suspecting more misconduct, noticing Henderson's unauthorized training of Heler. Back at the safe house, Heler and Inqualine learn that one of the killers is in Madrid. Heler tracks the target, who regularly swims alone in a high-rise sky pool. Crafting a sabotage device, Hela confronts him poolside. When the killer refuses to cooperate, Heler shatters the pool's glass, causing the killer to plunge to his death. Inqualine warns Heler that Henderson is on his trail. As Henderson closes in, another CIA agent loyal to O'Brien intervenes. A brutal fight ensues. Henderson is shot by reinforcements. Heler, though wanting to help Henderson, is pulled away by Inqualine. Meanwhile, O'Brien continues investigating more, catching him in more lies. Surveillance footage from Madrid suggests Inqualine's involvement, leading the CIA to track her to Istanbul. One night, agents raid the safe house. During a chaotic escape, Inquiline is fatally shot. A heartbroken Heler says goodbye to her before fleeing. Later, Heler arranges a weapons deal through Frank's old contacts. Using tech to digitally disguise his whereabouts, he fools the CIA into thinking he's in Berlin while staying hidden. Setting another trap, Heler rigs a bomb to explode if tampered with. He captures another killer, extracting intel that their leader operates from a ship. As Heler leaves, the captive triggers the bomb and dies. If you jump really fast, you might survive the blast. Meanwhile, the CIA realizes they were chasing a decoy and halts their search. Heler travels to the Baltic Sea, staking out shady transactions near ship. Unexpectedly, he reunites with a bear, who reveals he's also gone rogue and offers to help. Soon after, Heler is captured during a bot surveillance attempt and brought aboard the ship to meet Slater, the ring leader. Slater taunt Heler, saying he lacks the will to kill. Handing Heler a gun, he challenges him to pull the trigger. Heler hesitates, but reveals he doesn't need to shoot. He's hacked the ship's controls, steering it into Finnish waters. With Interpol and Finnish authorities alerted, Slater and his crew are arrested. Simultaneously, Moore and Caleb are taken into custody back in the US. In the final scenes, Heler finds closure for Sarah's death. In a surprising twist, Henderson, surviving his earlier shooting, appears once more. In the last moments, Heler takes the skies in the small plane Sarah once gifted him, feeling her presence as he flies into a peaceful future. text: The film begins with Yolina Bova, also known as Black Widow, standing on top of a tall building. She jumps off and crashes into a lab. She knocks out the first guard and keeps moving forward. Inside, she fights more guards and finds the research and artifact she was sent to collect by Valentina for the OXC group. A scientist tries to stop her by pointing a gun and warns her about Valentina's project Sentry, saying it could destroy the world. Yelina replies that it can actually save the world. She throws the gun away and pins him down, but he grabs the gun and shoots at her. They struggle and he ends up shooting himself by accident. Yelina takes what she needs and blows up the lab before reporting back to Valentina that the job is done. In Washington, DC, Bucky Barnes, is now a congressman and takes part in a trial where Valentina is facing impeachment for running secret missions. Her loyal assistant Mel is also present there. The judge blames her for running a unregulated labs in foreign countries and making normal human to superhuman. Valentina defends herself by bringing up the Red Hulk incident and says that since the Avengers are no longer around to save the world in times of crisis, she had to take action to protect the world. She further tells the Congressing Committee to stop this investigation. Meanwhile, Yelina visits Alexe Shastikov at his house where he lives alone. She tells him she's unhappy with the work she's been doing and still feels sad about Natasha's death. After talking with Alexe, Yolina leaves the place and calls Valentina and asks hers to take on a new mission. Valentina agrees and gives Yolina her next mission. She must go to a vault hidden deep inside a mountain where Oexie stores all its important assets. Her target is Ava Star and Yolina is ordered to kill her. When Yelina arrives and starts looking for Ava, she is suddenly attacked by US agent John Walker. Yelina tells him he's not her target, but Walker says she is his and beats her up badly. As he's about to finish her, Antonio Draov shows up and attacks Walker, saying he is her target. Then Ava appears. She has the power to disappear and a fight breaks out between all four. They all start attacking each other's targets until Ava reappears in front of Antonia and shoots her in the head. After Antonia dies, the remaining three, Yolina, Ava, and Walker, find a strange civilian named Robert. He tries to escape, but all the doors in the facility suddenly lock. They point their guns at him and ask who sent him. Robert says no one did. They soon realize they all work for Valentina and that she sent them to kill each other. The artifacts in the building also belong to the OXE group, and Valentina is trying to destroy all the evidence, including the assassins. Ava tries to phase through the doors, but a supersonic machine activates and blocks her powers. Yolina finds the machine's power source and Walker smashes it. Ava is then able to get through and opens the door, letting the others escape just as the incinerator turns on. Yolina finds herself stuck in a memory. She sees herself as a child, luring another girl, Anna, into the woods to be executed as part of her first test in the red room. She snaps out of it and realizes she was holding Robert's hand. She quickly pulls away and asks if he's okay. Walker wakes up and angrily questions Robert how he got there, thinking he's not a normal civilian. Robert says he doesn't know how he got there. He just woke up in the room. He then mocks Walker, telling him he is not a Captain America, he is just an idiot. Angry, Walker tries to confront him, but Yelina stops him. Walker and Ava start looking for a way out. Robert suggests they climb up by locking arms and walking along the walls. They agree and give it a try. During the climb, Walker almost falls when he grabs one of Yolina's batons to pull himself up, but they all make it together. At the top, Walker touches Robert's hand and sees a painful memory of himself, arguing with his wife. She's upset because he cares more about news articles, calling him a failed Captain America than spending time with their son. Meanwhile, Valentina is at a galla with Mel, and Bucky is there, too, working with Congressman Gary to take Valentina down. While they talk, Bucky walks up to Mel and gives her his contact info in case she ever wants to work for someone more honest. Mel leaves with Valentina and later checks the vault surveillance footage. She sees that Yolina, Ava, and Walker have somehow escaped and teamed up. She reports this to Valentina. Later, Mel calls Bucky. He asks her to testify against Valentina, but she refuses and instead tells him to track her phone. Meanwhile, Valentina decides to send a team of mercenaries to the vault to kill Yolina, Walker, and Ava. However, she tells them not to harm Robert since he's the only survivor of the Project Sentry Experiments. The mercenaries surround the facility with guns. While inside, the assassins fight their way through. They kill some of the mercenaries and use their uniforms to disguise themselves and escape. They make it out and Ava brings a van. They hide Robert in the back while the three sit up front. At the main gate, the guards stop them and ask for ID. When they can't answer, the guards grow suspicious. Before things get worse, a gunshot is heard from the back of the van. It's Robert. He steps out and distracts the guards so the others can escape. The guards open fire, shooting him multiple times. Valentina, who wants Robert alive, orders them to stop. To everyone's surprise, Robert isn't hurt at all. Even he gets multiple shots. Suddenly, he begins flying high into the sky, but he passes out midair and crashes back into the vault. Valentina and her team then capture him. Yelina, Walker, and Ava walk through the desert trying to find a way out. Ava talks about Antonia and Yolina says she was just another victim like them. The next morning, Alexe shows up. He's dressed as Valentina's limo driver and came after learning Yolino was being hunted. They all get in and drive off. Soon, a convoy of vans full of mercenaries starts chasing them, shooting as they come closer. Ava tries to use her powers, but they're blocked by another supersonic device. Just in time, Bucky shows up and throws grenades, destroying the vans. But when he tosses a chain to the limo, it ends up flipping over. Meanwhile, Robert wakes up and sees Valentina, who tells him that as Sentry, he has god-like powers. When he asks about Yolina and the others who helped him, Valentina lies, saying they're all criminals and can't be trusted. She manages to convince him to join her side. When she touches his hand, she sees a memory from her childhood where she had let a man into her home who later killed her father. Robert then promises her that he can keep his powers under control. Back with the group, Bucky captures Yolina, Alexe, Walker, and Ava. Later, he gets a call from Mel, who warns him about Valentina's plans with Robert, now known as Sentry. She reveals that Robert's files show he was mentally unstable when he was chosen for the experiment. Hearing this, Bucky decides to team up with Yolina to stop whatever Valentina is planning. Meanwhile, Valentina overhears Mel's talking with Bucky and tells her that in the world there are bad guys and worse guys. She admits she's one of the bad ones, but insists she's trying to stop the worst ones from gaining power. The team goes to stop Valentina, but they're all quickly overpowered and knocked out by Sentry. No matter how hard they fight, they can't match his strength. Feeling defeated, they go outside, frustrated, and thinking they failed because they're not real heroes. As the group splits up, Alexe follows Yolina, who breaks down and admits she feels lost, alone, and relies on drinking to cope. Alexe gives her an uplifting speech, reminding her that she's much stronger than she thinks. Yelina starts to feel better, but then they notice a crowd looking up. Century is in the sky, now fully transformed into the void. He starts using his powers to turn people in New York into shadows. The Thunderbolts regroup and try to help the citizens, but the void spreads complete darkness across the city. Yelina decides to enter the void herself to stop Sentry. Inside, she's pulled into painful memories, including the one with Anna. She pushes through the trauma and finally finds Robert sitting alone in a room looking normal. Robert's memory shows him being abused by his father and blamed by his mother for trying to protect her. Yelina talks to him as she had earlier told him to shove his negative feelings deep down inside instead of properly dealing with them. As the rest of the team joins her inside the void, Robert's darker side. The void starts attacking them and chain them. Robert fights the void, but it only gets stronger the more he resists. Yelina and other breaks free and run and hugs Robert, reminding him he's not alone. The rest of the Thunderbolts join in and their support calms Robert down. He finally breaks free from the void and the city and its people return to normal. Outside the void, Robert has no memory of what just happened. The Thunderbolts move to confront Valentina, but she protects herself by holding a press conference. She claims forming the team was her idea from the start and introduces them as the new Avengers. As the crowd cheers, Yelina leans in and tells Valentina that this now means she works for them. During the mid-credit scene, Alexe is at a supermarket and sees the new Avengers on a Wedi box, just like he once dreamed of. He tries to get a woman nearby to recognize him and buy the cereal, but she just walks away unimpressed. During the postredits, 14 months later, the new Avengers receive mixed reactions from the public. Some see them as heroes, others don't. Sam Wilson is even suing them over the use of the Avengers name. Meanwhile, Bob struggles to control his powers, afraid the void might return. Suddenly, the team is alerted to a space crisis. A strange aircraft is approaching Earth, and from their cameras, they spot a large number of four on its side. The final text states that the new Avengers and Robert will return.

text: As it turns out, the most advanced and logical AI ever developed is no match for Ethan Hunt. And as with any Mission Impossible finale, Ethan's trust in his team proves to be his greatest strength. From Paris performing emergency surgery to Grace having just 100 milliseconds to trap the entity, Ethan's team pull off a string of impossible scenarios to save the world. This includes Ethan surviving his deadliest aerial battle yet to finally kill Gabriel. But while the team prevents the nuclear apocalypse, the final reckoning is not so final. Instead of being destroyed, the entity is trapped in Luther's 5D data drive. Like a mythic evil jin, awaiting the day its bottle falls in the wrong hands. Ethan and his team still need the entity in the event that an even more dangerous AI rears its ugly head. A likely scenario considering how the entity was created. Contained within Luther's Drive, the entity is trapped in a form where it can be controlled. So when a greater threat inevitably appears, Ethan's team won't be behind the technological arms race. Benji is likely already figuring out how to use the entity for this exact purpose. Moreover, while Luther died in the final reckoning, it is his tech that transforms the rogue AI into the IMF team's greatest weapon. And on top of this vital legacy, Luther's final self-destructing message underscores why the IMF team can be trusted with this power. Apart from wrapping up the most crucial emotional beats of the Mission Impossible franchise, Luther's last words are capped off with a reminder of the team's core function. All that is good inside us is measured by the good that we do for others. So, while the governments of the world will never fully trust Ethan Hunt, he and his team will always save them from the next crisis, even if it means living an anonymous, thankless existence in the shadows of history. And the IMF team aren't the only ones driven by this sense of duty. By disarming America's atomic arsenal, President Sloan laid out a viable plan B against the nuclear option, proving to the entity that it still has a lot to learn about humanity. And combined with Briggs and Ethan finally bearing the hatchet, all this lays the groundwork for another intense sequel in the franchise. So, is the final reckoning really the end of the Mission Impossible films? As Cruz told the Hollywood Reporter at the movie's NYC premiere, "It's the final. It's not called final for nothing." So, there you have it. With the world's most powerful AI in Ethan's hands, the team sheds off its underdog status, arguably the perfect way to cap off the long-running eight film franchise. But as the team share knowing looks at Trafalgar Square in the finale, it's clear that containing the entity has only made them not just closer, but more capable of performing their duty than ever before. In short, we're not entirely convinced that The Final Reckoning is actually the last Mission Impossible movie. I need you to trust me. one last time. But what do you think? text: In the end, One Battle After Another refuses to deliver a clean resolution. Bob ultimately reunites with his daughter Willa after a violent showdown, and Willa kills an attacker in self-defense during the intense car chase in the desert. Colonel Lockjaw, the villain who has been seeking to expose and harm Willa (in part because of her mixed heritage), is exposed and eventually eliminated by his own allies who realize the truth of his crimes. And, this is because Willa is found out to be his daughter, following the awkward encounters between him and Perfidia in the past. After they escape the chase, Bob gives Willa a letter from her mother, in which Perfidia apologises for her betrayal and expresses hope for reconnection someday. In the closing scene, Willa hears about protests in Oakland and gets into the car to join them, symbolising that the next generation may take up the mantle of resistance, even under different terms. So in summary, the film ends with father and daughter reunited, the villain defeated, a note of reconciliation from Perfidia, and a passing of the symbolic torch to Willa, suggesting that although this battle is over, the struggle continues in new ways. So the ending of One Battle After Another carries less of a final answer and more of a statement about what it means to live in the shadow of struggle. On the surface, Bob manages to protect his daughter Willa from Lockjaw’s grasp, and the immediate threat of capture or erasure is averted. But the film doesn’t frame this as a neat victory. Instead, it shows that every battle—whether it’s an armed raid, a chase through the desert, or even a father trying to keep his daughter safe—is only one chapter in a much longer and unfinished fight. Lockjaw, as a person, may be dead, but the system he represents remains in place. For Bob, the ending is about reconciling the contradiction he’s carried for years. His desire to shield Willa from the dangers of revolution while knowing that her very existence makes her part of that history. By stepping back into the role of fighter and father, he admits that hiding will never erase the past, and that silence only feeds the power of those like Lockjaw. Willa, in turn, comes of age, recognising that her life is inseparable from the ideals and sacrifices of her parents. The larger meaning is that resistance is not a singular act with a permanent payoff. It is ongoing, cyclical, and often exhausting experience, essentially One battle after another.

In a charming romantic comedy, Love in the Clouds, we're introduced to Brooklyn, a Seattle business reporter who longs to break free from the dry factual reporting of her current position. Brooklyn works at Channel 5 KCT News in Seattle, where she often tries to inject some personality and humor into her segments. We see this early on when she reports on a coffee shop using coffee puns like, "You'll love it a latte." While viewers enjoy her personality, her stern boss, Mary, isn't pleased, warning Brooklyn that she's already received two strikes for her unprofessional approach. One more and she'll be out. Brooklyn confides in her camerawoman and best friend Elise that she dreams of becoming a lifestyle reporter where she can showcase more of her personality and creativity. When the station's regular lifestyle reporter Dwight has a family emergency, Brooklyn unexpectedly gets her chance. Mary assigns Brooklyn to cover the International Balloon Fiesta in Albuquerque, New Mexico, a week-long event featuring hundreds of colorful hot air balloons. Despite being terrified of heights, Brooklyn jumps at this opportunity to prove herself as a lifestyle reporter. With hotel rooms completely booked due to the festival, Mary arranges for Brooklyn and Elise to stay with a local hot air balloon pilot named Jared Troy. Jared runs Love in the Air, a company specializing in romantic balloon rides, particularly for marriage proposals and couples celebrating special occasions. Mary tells Brooklyn that Jared specifically requested his personal life not be part of the story, which immediately makes Mary suspicious. She instructs Brooklyn to dig deeper and find out what Jared is hiding, believing there's a story there. Upon arriving in Albuquerque, Brooklyn and Elise are surprised to meet Jared, who isn't the older man they expected, but rather a handsome, charming pilot in his 30s. Jared welcomes them into a spacious home, and there's an immediate chemistry between him and Brooklyn, though both try to keep things professional. While Brooklyn connects with Jared, Elise hits it off with Carlos. Jared's cousin and ballooning assistant. We soon learn that Jared comes from ballooning family. His parents, Jane and Brad, are both experienced balloon pilots. Brad recently retired from running his taekwondo studio, but seems restless and unfulfilled in retirement. Jane is concerned about her husband's well-being as he seems to have lost his purpose, no longer teaching martial arts or flying balloons. This subplot about Jared's parents enriches the story, showing a mature relationship that's going through a difficult transition. On their first full day at the balloon fiesta, unfavorable winds result in a yellow flag, meaning the balloons can't launch. This gives Jared an opportunity to show Brooklyn around Albuquerque. Though initially hesitant to leave in case the winds change, Jared's father Brad offers to take his place if the green flag is raised, allowing Jared and Brooklyn to spend the day together. Their tour includes riding the Sandia Peak Tramway, terrifying for Brooklyn with her fear of heights, sampling new Mexican cuisine, including the famous green chili, and browsing local art. Throughout their day together, Brooklyn notices that despite owning a business centered around romance, Jared seems cynical about love. When she asks about the couples who've gotten engaged on his balloon rides, Jared dismissively remarks that statistically speaking, many of them probably aren't even together anymore. Brooklyn finds this contradiction intriguing. A man who sells romantic experiences but doesn't believe in love himself. During their conversations, Brooklyn learns that Jared's skepticism stems from personal heartbreak. He reveals that his former best friend Turner and his ex- fiance Amber betrayed him. Jared had proposed to Amber in a hot air balloon, but she later left him for Turner, who was also his business partner. This triple betrayal, losing his fiance, best friend, and business all at once, caused Jared to close himself off to love and relationships. Meanwhile, Mary keeps calling Brooklyn for updates, pressuring her to focus her story on Jared's cynicism about love. Despite selling romantic balloon rides, Brooklyn becomes increasingly uncomfortable with this angle, especially as she develops genuine feelings for Jared. She appreciates how he encourages her to face her fears and admires his passion for ballooning and helping others experience joy. The next day at the balloon fiesta, the winds are again unfavorable. Brooklyn and Elise capture footage of the event and interview Jared about the technical aspects of hot air ballooning. Brooklyn also has meaningful conversations with Jared's mother, Jane, who shares wisdom about relationships based on her long marriage to Brad. Jane explains that she and Brad are working through their own challenges since his retirement, but emphasizes that every relationship has rough patches. She tells Brooklyn that her husband encouraged her to follow her passion for teaching rather than pursue accounting as her parents wanted, illustrating how true love supports personal growth. That evening, Brooklyn, Elise, Jared, and Carlos attend the balloon glow, where pilots light their burners after dark, creating a magical display of glowing balloons against the night sky. The atmosphere is romantic, and Brooklyn and Jared grow closer. Jared gives Brooklyn a beautiful turquoise necklace that had caught her eye earlier, telling her it can remind her of the New Mexico sky and her own strength in facing her fears. At dinner with Jared's parents, Brooklyn observes the loving but strained relationship between Jane and Brad. Brad admits he's lost some purpose since retiring, and Jane expresses that she just wants him to be happy. This leads to a heartfelt conversation where Brad decides to return to ballooning part-time with Jared's company, giving him back a sense of purpose while still enjoying retirement. This subplot beautifully illustrates that love requires both partners to be fulfilled as individuals before they can be happy together. A lesson that parallels Brooklyn and Jared's developing relationship. The climactic moment comes when Brooklyn, inspired by Jared's encouragement and wanting to conquer her greatest fear, decides to go up in a hot air balloon despite her terror of heights. Jared pilots the balloon, talking her through her anxiety with patience and support. As they float above Albuquerque in mass ascension with hundreds of other colorful balloons, Brooklyn is overcome with emotion. She finds herself falling for Jared and impulsively kisses him mid-flight. Rather than pulling away, Jared reciprocates, showing he's developing feelings for her, too. After they land safely, the group celebrates with the traditional champagne toast that follows balloon rides. Jared explains this tradition dates back to 18th century France, when farmers were frightened by the strange flying contraptions landing in their fields. Pilates began offering champagne as a peace offering, beginning a tradition that continues today. This moment symbolizes how traditions and stories enrich our lives and connect us to the past. Just as Brooklyn and Jared's new relationship connects them to a hopeful future, that evening, Jared and Brooklyn have a meaningful conversation by his backyard fire pit. Jared opens up more about his past heartbreak and admits he's afraid of being hurt again. Brooklyn shares that while she's afraid of many things like heights, she's never been afraid to open her heart. She gently suggests that perhaps Jared's fear of emotional vulnerability might lead to regrets later in life. The next morning, their budding romance faces a crisis. While Brooklyn is on the phone with her demanding boss, Mary Jared overhears part of the conversation where Mary mentions focusing the story on the jaded pilot who sells romantic balloon rides. mistakenly believing Brooklyn has been using him just to get a sensational story. Jared feels betrayed and pulls away. Brooklyn tries to explain that she was refusing Mary's direction, not agreeing to it, but Jared, triggered by his past betrayal, won't listen. As Brooklyn and Elise prepare to return to Seattle on their final day, Brooklyn is heartbroken. She doesn't want to leave things unresolved with Jared or return to a job that doesn't fulfill her. Inspired by everything she's learned in New Mexico, Brooklyn decides to create her own story. Not the cynical expose Mary wanted, but a sincere personal reflection on how her experiences with ballooning and meeting Jared helped her overcome her fears and find a new perspective on life and love. With Alisa's help, Brooklyn creates a beautiful segment about the parallels between hot air ballooning and life. how both require you to sometimes surrender control, navigate unexpected winds, and face bumpy landings with courage. She speaks from the heart about finding joy, conquering fears, and being open to love and new experiences. She concludes by encouraging viewers to follow their passion wherever it may lead. After returning to Seattle, Brooklyn is thrilled to discover her segment has gone viral online. When Mary calls, instead of congratulating her, she reprimands Brooklyn for making herself part of the story. Despite the segment's popularity, Mary criticizes Brooklyn's approach and reminds her she's on her final warning. In a moment of clarity and courage, Brooklyn quits her job, choosing to prioritize her happiness and creative freedom over security in a position that doesn't value her talents. Almost immediately after quitting, Brooklyn receives a call from a New Mexico television station offering her a lifestyle reporting position. They loved her balloon fiesta segment and want to bring her creative approach to their team. This opportunity would allow Brooklyn to return to New Mexico, pursue her professional passion, and potentially rekindle her relationship with Jared. Meanwhile, in Albuquerque, Jared's father shows him Brooklyn's viral segment. text: On a stormy night in 1964, two paranormal investigators, Ed Warren and his pregnant wife Lorraine Warren, visit an antique store for their first case. Ed specializes in demonology, while Lorraine possesses strong psychic abilities. Across from them sits a distressed woman named Victoria, who begins to tell her story. Victoria explains that her father often claimed something was following him, and that he heard voices. At first, she assumed it was due to his old age, but then one day she found him dead, hanging from a rope. With tears in her eyes, she continues. "After that," she says, "everything went quiet. But soon, I began to feel it, too. Like someone was always watching me." When Lorraine offers to check the storeroom, Ed hesitates and warns her that it might not be a good idea, but Lorraine reassures him that she'll be fine and steps inside. She carefully observes the antique pieces until she notices a strange, ornate mirror. Immediately, she senses a presence within it. Speaking softly, she says to the spirit, "I'm Lorraine, and I'm here to help you." When there's no response, she gently touches the mirror. Suddenly, it cracks, and a terrifying vision flashes before her eyes, and she immediately goes into labor. Ed rushes in to find Lorraine clutching her stomach and immediately drives her to the hospital. Concerned, he asks her what happened in that room. Lorraine whispers, "There was a mirror in there, Ed. And something evil was inside it." At the hospital, a nurse asks when Lorraine is due. "Next month," Ed replies. As the doctor prepared Lorraine for delivery, the power goes out. In the darkness, she calls out for Ed and sees a creature crawling across the ceiling. At that moment, Ed bursts into the room, and the doctor allow him to stay to help calm Lorraine. The doctor tells her to push, and Lorraine screams as she tries, but he stops her, explaining that the umbilical cord is wrapped around the baby's neck. After a tense moment, they manage to cut it and instruct her to push one final time. She does, and then the room falls eerily silent. The doctor quietly says, "I'm sorry. She's dead." Lorraine breaks down in tears, her cries echoing through the room. But then, almost a minute later, the faint wail of a baby fills the air. Relief washes over Ed and Lorraine, and they name their daughter Judy. Ed and Lorraine raise Judy while continuing their work as paranormal investigators. Over the years, they collect countless cursed objects from their cases, each acting as a conduit for various demons. They store these items safely in an artifact room, with each one sealed through prayers performed by Father Gordon, a priest they met during one of their investigations. As Judy grows older, it becomes clear that she has inherited her mother's gift, the ability to see spirits. Lorraine teaches her a special rhyme, one that helps Judy ground herself and return to reality whenever she encounters these spirits. 22 years pass, and now, in a quiet Pennsylvania neighborhood, we meet another family, the Smurls. The family consist of Jack Smurl and his wife Janet, their four daughters, Heather, Dawn, Kager, and Shannon, and Jack's elderly parents. Today is Heather's confirmation day, and the family is over the moon with excitement. That evening, they gather around the dinner table. Heather's grandfather presents her with a gift, an antique mirror. The moment she unwraps it, their dog Simon starts barking wildly. Heather thanks her grandfather politely, though the mirror fills her with an unsettling feeling. Later, Janet's mother brings out the cake. As Heather leans in to blow out the candle, it goes out on its own. Heather accuses Dawn of blowing it, but Dawn swears she didn't. Suddenly, the dining room light fixture crashes down onto the table, startling everyone. Meanwhile, Ed and Lorraine Warren have retired from active investigations and now lecture at colleges about the entities they've faced. Lorraine talks about one of their most complicated cases, Annabelle, and explains how it preys on vulnerable individuals and manipulates them. Most students aren't interested. One jokingly asks, "So, are you Ghostbusters?" Lorraine chuckles, "No," she replies, "but we did see the movie." Another student asks, "Why'd you stop taking cases?" Ed simply explains that they decided to focus on other parts of their lives. As the students file out laughing, only Judy remains behind. Later, at dinner in a small restaurant, Ed vents his frustration that their life's work is being mocked like an SNL skit. Lorraine gently reminds him, "They're just kids, Ed. They are having fun." Judy looks at her dad and asks, "Dad, why didn't you tell them the truth? That you stopped taking cases because of your heart?" It's revealed that Ed suffered a heart attack during one of their investigations. His doctor warned him that another one could be fatal. Ed waves it off with a chuckle. "Sounds like something an old man would say." Trying to lighten the mood, Judy asks if she can bring her boyfriend Tony to Ed's upcoming birthday party. Lorraine agrees immediately. Ed reluctantly does, too. Lorraine notices Judy quietly humming the rhyme she taught her as a child. Glancing over, Lorraine catches a glimpse of a pale hand retreating behind Judy. She screams, then quickly apologizes. Back at the Smurls' house, Janet receives a call from a friend. As she talks, the phone cord is yanked from her. She shouts at the girls, thinking they are playing a prank, but then sees both of them heading upstairs. Swallowing hard, Janet turns on the light in the closet, only to find that it's empty. Upstairs, Kager and Shannon are playing when Shannon realizes her doll, Susie, is missing. Then she hears its familiar voice saying, "Mommy. Mommy." coming from Heather's room. She follows the sound and freezes as the doll suddenly floats into the air. Behind it stands an old woman with a sinister smile. Shannon screams and bolts. Later, Shannon tells her family what she saw, but no one believes her. After dinner, Heather confides in Dawn that the mirror gives her a strange feeling. Dawn suggests they just throw it out, but Heather hesitates, saying their grandfather would be heartbroken if he found out. Dawn smirks and says, "Tomorrow's trash day." The two girls carry the heavy mirror outside and set it down with the rest of the garbage. The next morning, the trash truck collects the garbage, crushing the mirror in its compactor. At the same time, Dawn suddenly begins to vomit. Panicked, their parents rush her to the hospital. Then Heather goes to check the sink and freezes. Shards of glass glint among the blood. Meanwhile, Lorraine busies herself preparing for Ed's birthday party. Just then, Judy arrives with Tony. Noticing his unease, she reassures him, "My mother already likes you." "What about your father?" Tony asks nervously. Judy only laughs. Ed opens the door, and Judy wishes him a happy birthday, with Tony doing the same. Inside, Judy introduces Tony to Father Gordon. "What do you do, Tony?" the priest asks. Tony admits that he's currently unemployed, but Judy quickly adds that he used to be a cop. Later, Tony notices the artifacts room and asks Judy what's inside. She replies, "All the skeletons." An hour later, Judy goes upstairs to her childhood room, reminiscing about old memories. Suddenly, she hears the creaking of an armchair, and sitting there is the Annabelle doll. Judy freezes. She's had a brush with Annabelle before, once as a child, when her parents had left her alone shortly after acquiring the doll, but luckily her parents came and saved her. And a second time, when her babysitter's friend deliberately touched it, unleashing its power. That time, Judy managed to contain Annabelle by playing an exorcism video. Judy begins chanting the rhyme her mother taught her. The doll vanishes. At that moment, Tony appears in the doorway. Seeing Judy breathless and pale, he asks, "Are you okay?" Tony knows about Judy's abilities and her power to see spirits. Judy reassures him that she's okay. He asks her to explain what she was saying before he came in, and she tells him it's a technique her mother taught her to temporarily shut off her senses. Curious, Tony asks her to recite it again. As she does, he leans in and kisses her. Just then, Lorraine walks in. The two quickly break apart. Lorraine tells Tony that Ed is in the garage playing games with the boys and is looking for an extra player. Tony happily agrees to go. Judy excuses herself, but Lorraine stops her and asks about the incident at the restaurant, questioning whether she's been seeing spirits more often lately. At first, Judy denies it, but she eventually admits that she has. Judy insists that she can handle it, but Lorraine, speaking from her own experience, tells Judy that she can't, and that the only thing she can do is shut them out. Shortly after, both of them go to the garage to watch the game. Ed plays well and beats Tony, but his heart starts pounding hard, and he takes a deep breath to steady himself. Judy leaves to get a drink, while Tony nervously approaches Ed and Lorraine to ask for their blessing to propose to Judy. Even though it has only been 6 months, Tony says that Judy is the one for him. Lorraine tells him that their family isn't like any other, and Tony nods, understanding. She then adds that she and Ed got engaged when they barely knew each other because he was being shipped out, but they just knew they were meant to be together. Lorraine smiles and tells Tony that he has their blessing, though Ed doesn't look entirely convinced. Just then, Judy comes back into the garage and notices the ring box. Tony tries to hide it, but Judy, excited, asks him if it is for her. Tony admits that it is, and Judy, with a big smile, says yes. Seeing his daughter happy finally convinces Ed. Night falls. Father Gordon assures Ed that Judy has good instincts and that he doesn't need to worry. He then tells them that a few families have reached out for help with hauntings and asks if they are willing to take the case, but Lorraine insists that they aren't looking to go back. Meanwhile, Jack Smurl arrives home and informs his family that Father Jensen has submitted their case to the church. In the meantime, Heather suggests going to a motel, but her mother reminds her that there are eight of them and they can't afford it. Don argues that they can't keep living in this haunted house. Jack cuts in and explains that the church has a process where investigators come to document the supernatural activity. And if it's real, the church send exorcists. But Don insists that it's real, but her father doesn't believe her, and she storms off. At midnight, Jack hears a creaking sound in the bedroom and sees an old lady before he begins to levitate. In the living room, Heather inserts her confirmation cassette into the VCR and fast forwards to the part where the candle blew out by itself. After a few tries, she spots the old lady beside her blowing out the candle. Suddenly, a man wielding an axe attacks Heather. Hearing her scream, Janet wakes up and sees her husband floating in midair. She rushes downstairs and finds Heather, who mutters that someone is in the house. The family finally has enough. Jack decides to reach out to the media, hoping someone might help them. Their story quickly becomes the hottest topic, and soon Jack and Janet are invited for an interview, where they recount the terrifying events that have been happening inside their home. A few days later, Lorraine and Judy visit a wedding boutique for some last-minute stitching on Judy's wedding dress. Brenda, the boutique owner, welcomes them warmly before leading Judy into the dressing room. Brenda begins stitching the dress when she hears the phone ringing. She excuses herself to answer it. Judy admires her reflection in the mirror, smiling at how perfect the dress looks. At first, everything appears normal, and she sees herself clearly. But then she realizes that one of her reflections isn't moving with her at all. The dressing room door opens, and thinking it's Brenda, Judy relaxes. But when she looks down, she sees an old lady. Judy screams for her mother and begins reciting the rhyme. The old lady vanishes, but Judy's reflection suddenly reaches out and grabs her by the throat, choking her. Judy gasps and struggles as Lorraine and Brenda burst into the room. Meanwhile, Father Gordon arrives at the Smurl residence. He's immediately met by Janet. Gordon asks about the ambulance outside. Janet tells him that her mother-in-law has fallen down the stairs, pushed by something unseen. "Things have been getting worse, Father," Janet admits, "but I'm really grateful you're here. I honestly thought the church had forgotten about us." Father Gordon quietly explains that the church doesn't know he's here. He reveals that he came on his own from Connecticut, having followed their story in the news. He tells Janet that he has handled similar cases before and believes he might be able to help. He begins reciting verses from the Bible while blessing the rooms with holy water. But as he sprinkles water in the basement, it evaporates instantly. Alarmed, he steps back, clutching his crucifix, and quickly makes his way upstairs. He tells Janet that there's definitely something present in the house and that he's going to the church to get help. A short while later, Father Gordon arrives at the local church. Approaching the front desk, he tells the receptionist that he needs to see Bishop McKenna immediately. She calls into the office and informs Father Gordon that he will be out in a moment. As Father Gordon waits, his nose suddenly starts bleeding. He wipes it away, then looks out the hall after hearing a faint noise. When he turns back, the receptionist is gone. The phone on the desk starts ringing. Hesitantly, he picks it up and hears Judy's soft voice say, "You can go now." Then the door closes. He quickly grabs his cross and begins reciting a verse, but the cross burst into flames, burning his hand. Screaming in pain, he drops it. His expression changes. His eyes glaze over as if something takes control of him. Almost possessed, he picks up a wire and wraps it around his neck. Moments later, Father Gordon hangs himself. Meanwhile, Ed and Tony are in the garage. Tony manages to repair a motorbike, impressing Ed. Ed smiles, then decides to show him the artifact room. He warns Tony not to touch anything, explaining that every item there is either cursed or used in ritualistic practices. Tony, curious, asks why they keep such objects instead of destroying them. Ed explains that sometimes destroying these things only makes matters worse. Trapping them here is the safest way to contain their evil. Tony asks how many cases they've handled. "Maybe a thousand," Ed replies. Tony is stunned. Ed tells him that he and Lorraine started when they were about his age. Then Ed becomes quiet for a moment before sharing something personal. He tells Tony that Judy was stillborn for almost a minute, the longest minute of their lives. "She may be your fiance," he says softly, "but to us, she'll always be that little baby who fought to live." The next day, they attend Father Gordon's funeral. After the service, Judy gently places her hand on his coffin and suddenly feels a vision. Disturbed, she walks off silently. A man approaches Ed and Lorraine, introducing himself as Father Ziegler. He explains that Gordon always spoke highly of them and deeply believed in the work they did together. As he walks away, Judy asks where Father Gordon's body was found. "Pennsylvania," Father Ziegler replies. The next morning, while washing the dishes, Lorraine notices the sink isn't draining. She reaches in to clear it and pulls out her locket. Then the sink fills with blood. Shocked, she screams for Ed. He rushes in as she gasps, "Something's wrong with Judy." Before Ed can ask more, there's a knock at the door. Tony stands outside, pale and breathless. "Judy's gone," he says. "She went to Pennsylvania." They immediately drive out and arrive at the Smurl house. Lorraine, tense and determined, tells Ed that their only goal is to find Judy and take her straight home. Outside, reporters swarm the lawn, shouting questions, but the Warrens push through them and knock on the door. Jack Smurl answers, recognizing them immediately, and invites them inside. They spot Judy. Lorraine rushes to her and pulls her into a hug, asking what she's doing here. Judy explains, "Father Gordon was here. He came before he died. I put two and two together and found them." Lorraine, clearly worried, tells the Smurls that they have to leave, but Judy steps between them and raises her voice. She tells her parents to stop running. "You always taught me that we don't turn our backs on people who need help," she says. "This family needs you, just like the others did. Meanwhile, Judy pulls Tony aside and shares her vision, how she saw Father Gordon die. When Tony asks if she told her mother, Judy shakes her head, saying she didn't want to worry her. She adds quietly that there's something else, something that wants her to be here. Later, Lorraine explores the house and comes across a small music box on a shelf. She turns the crank and listens as the soft, haunting tune fills the room. Outside, Ed is cooking pancakes for breakfast. Tony joins him and asks if this is what a normal case looks like. Ed chuckles and says, "There's never such a thing as a normal case." He tells him that one thing that always remains the same in every case is the fear. "Demons can sense fear," Ed says. "It will try to isolate them and use their fears against them. So, part of the job is to let them know they aren't alone." Then Ed asks Tony why he quit being a police officer. Tony explains that one day, he and his partner responded to a domestic violence call. When they arrived, the suspect opened the door, shoved a gun in his face, and pulled the trigger, but the gun didn't fire. Later, when they arrested him, they discovered the weapon was fully loaded. Tony wistfully says that there is a world where he never got to marry Judy or have children. So, the next day, he quit the force and bought the ring. Suddenly, they hear a noise from upstairs. Lorraine tells Judy to stay downstairs while she goes to investigate. She walks carefully into one of the bedrooms and sees a spirit on the bed. A shadow flickers past the wall, and she follows it into the basement. There, she's struck by a powerful vision. She tells Ed afterward that she saw three people, a husband, his wife, and the wife's mother, who once lived on this land long before the house was built. One day, the husband discovered his wife's affair and killed both women with an axe. Lorraine suspects that a greater entity is at work, using the spirits of the man and his victims as a cover-up. Ed asks what the entity wants and why it's been haunting them for so long, but Lorraine doesn't have an answer. Meanwhile, Judy hears her mother's voice calling her name. She follows the sound up to the attic. There, she discovers a cracked mirror. As she reaches out and touches the cracks, a piece of chalk rolls across the floor. On the dusty wall, Judy reads the words, "Did you miss me?" Judy's blood runs cold. She knows immediately it's Annabelle. She turns to run, but hears Kager's voice calling for help from another room. When she goes to check, she finds the Annabelle doll waiting for her. The doll chases after her, and Judy stumbles back, tumbling down the stairs. Ed and Lorraine hear the crash and rush to her side. Ed and Lorraine share the story of the mirror with the Smurls, explaining how they first encountered it during their very first case. "With these things, it's never that simple," she says. "It wasn't done with you. It wasn't done with us." Don then asks about the woman from the antique store. Lorraine explains that it was their first case. And because of the mirror, they nearly lost their child. The risk was too great, which is why they never went back. They decide to take the mirror back to Connecticut and seal it in the Warrens' artifact room. Inside, Judy has developed a fever. Up in the attic, Ed warns everyone not to look directly into the mirror or touch it. He recites a verse, and they carefully wrap the mirror in a blessed cloth before carrying it down the stairs. Outside, Tony goes to start the car, but the engine sputters and dies. Back inside, Ed and Jack continue to move the mirror, but suddenly the straps securing the mirror loosens. With every step they take, Judy's condition worsens. The cover slips off. Jack glances at the mirror and freezes. The old lady stares back at him, and he screams in terror as he falls from the attic. Ed loses his grip on the mirror, and it crashes down, crushing Jack's foot. Lorraine and Janet rush out at the commotion, but Ed shouts for them to go back to their rooms. Jack groans in pain, but insists he's fine, and asks Ed to free his foot. Outside, Tony finally manages to start the car. But as he's about to drive up, he spots the old lady standing in the middle of the road. He swerves violently to avoid her and crashes into the fence. Inside, the lights flicker, then go out completely. Lorraine shuts the front door as wind howls through the cracks. Then, faintly, she hears a music box playing. Heart pounding, she follows the sound and finds Judy's bed empty. She looks around and sees her daughter crouched in the corner. The entity has completely possessed Judy. A few days later, the cursed mirror is placed in the Warrens' artifact room. Ed tosses the key to Tony. Weeks later, it is finally Judy and Tony's wedding day. After the ceremony, Lorraine tells Ed about the vision she had last night. She says, "I saw our future, Ed. We become grandparents, and we finally write the book. text: Does the dog die at the end of Good Boy? Let's talk about the ending to the new horror film because I think there's something else going on that's far more interesting I'm not seeing anyone else talk about. Obviously spoilers for Good Boy ahead. By the way, the dog lives at the end. Let's just get that out of the way because again, there's something else going on. Good Boy sees Indy the dog and his human Todd move to a farm in the middle of nowhere. It's literally Courage the Cowardly Dog. Todd is very sick. We see this in the opening sequence and later there's a scene where Todd is speaking with the doctor who mentions that whatever he has has progressed to the point where not even experimental treatments can help him. But back to the farm. Indy starts hearing strange noises and notices a kind of humanoid figure always stretching out its hand almost petting Indy but then pulling back at the last second. Not only that but Todd's entire demeanor changes. He starts acting violently toward Indy, pushes him away at one point. Bad bad Todd. At the end Todd and Indy reunite but Todd looks over and finds his dead body lying in the bed. Todd has died from whatever medical issues he was having. We see Todd's spirit get pulled by a train by the humanoid figure from earlier and Indy tries to save him but Todd tells his dog, "You can't save me. You have to keep going." The thing about Good Boy is I don't think the ghosts are actually there. I don't think this is an actual ghost story. The ghosts are a metaphor for how Indy is perceiving these changes to Todd. The entire story of Good Boy is told from the perspective of a dog. We see this with low camera angles, certain stylistic flourishes like how you don't really see people's faces and I think that extends to the ghost. Indy doesn't know that Todd is sick or has cancer whatever whatever he has, Indy can't comprehend that so it's coming up with some kind of explanation for why his human is acting this way. This ties back to something Todd's sister said at the beginning of the film where dogs can sense things that humans can't like medical conditions. Indy can sense that something is wrong with Todd and he's trying to fill in the blanks. Before Good Boy came out everyone was concerned about whether the dog would die. It makes sense. Indy is the hero of this film. He's the main character and the main character of horror films often die by the end.
