text: Hey, everyone! Today we're diving into Flow, a visually stunning animated fantasy that's beautifully crafted and guaranteed to make you cry. It's loaded with meaning, and if you've seen it, you know it leaves you with some pretty big questions. So, in this video, I'm breaking down the mysteries of Flow, unraveling its deeper layers, and offering up some intriguing theories about what's really going on beneath the surface. Let's get into it! For those who haven't seen it, Flow is a 2024 animated fantasy adventure directed by Gints Zilbalodis. It's been making waves globally and it's even Latvia's official entry for Best International Feature Film at the 97th Academy Awards. The story follows a cat forced to leave its home after a devastating flood. Afraid of water and hesitant to connect, the cat ends up joining a boat with a quirky group of travelers: a dog, a capybara, a bird, and a lemur. Together, they journey through a dreamlike, post-apocalyptic world, facing danger and self discovery along the way. Let's break it down, starting with one of the film's biggest mysteries. The flood is almost like a character in the film— a force that drives a story while staying shrouded in mystery. It's also never explained outright. So, we're left to speculate. Here are three theories floating around: First up, let's talk science. On Earth, tides are driven by the moon's gravitational pull. Now, imagine what could happen if this balance was disrupted—say, a larger moon, a closer orbit, or even one that's unstable. These changes could intensify tidal forces, leading to massive global flooding. This isn't just sci-fi; it's grounded in real astrophysics. Billions of years ago, when the moon was closer to Earth, tides were significantly stronger. Plus, in our solar system, moons like Io and Europa experience extreme gravitational effects, causing volcanic eruptions and underground oceans. What if Flow's world is facing something similar, caused by a rogue celestial body or tectonic shifts? Apocalyptic flooding could absolutely happen. Think of Miller's planet in Christopher Nolan's Interstellar. Those towering tidal waves were caused by Gargantua's immense gravitational pull. It's a similar concept—both explore how gravitational forces can dramatically reshape a planet. Extreme tides wouldn't just sink coastlines. Strong tidal forces might trigger seismic activity, causing land to sink in some areas and rise in others. If land sinks rapidly enough, even normal tides could suddenly submerge vast regions, drastically altering the planet's surface. Combined with persistent flooding, this would create a world in constant flux. That image of a boat stuck high up in a tree serves as a clue— these floods keep coming back, looping in cycles. Following that: What if the flood wasn't natural, but man-made? Consider the Three Gorges Dam in China, which holds back a massive basin over 600 kilometers long. Now imagine humanity building a mega-dam on an even larger scale, with ambitions far beyond what's realistic today. It could be part of a larger geoengineering project to counteract climate change or redirect entire oceans. If this dam failed, for example, due to a natural disaster like an earthquake, the resulting flood would be on an unthinkable scale, drowning everything in its path. However, this wouldn't explain the recurring tides. Dams control water but don't alter the gravitational mechanics behind tides. The recurring flooding seen in the movie remains unexplained, unless humanity repeatedly rebuilt the dam. The third theory is more metaphysical: The flood represents a kind of limbo, where the animals are stand-ins for souls on a spiritual journey. Floods have always been powerful symbols in myths and religions. Take Noah's Ark from the Bible, for example: a divine flood cleanses the Earth, paving the way for a fresh start. The animals aboard symbolize survival, hope, and renewal. While Director Gints Zilbalodis mentioned in an interview on The Upcoming's YouTube channel that the Noah's Ark comparisons were unintentional, this doesn't mean the Afterlife Theory isn't worth considering. Still, it's fascinating to consider the movie from this perspective. In Flow, the recurring flood hints that these animals— and maybe the world itself— are stuck in a loop, where each cycle offers the chance for spiritual growth. This aligns with the Buddhist concept of samsara, a continuous cycle of rebirth driven by karma that continues until one reaches enlightenment, or nirvana. Interestingly, it also mirrors real-world phenomena like planetary feedback loops, where ecosystems regulate themselves through recurring natural patterns over time. The cosmic imagery reinforces this interpretation. Stars, auroras, and glowing lights evoke a celestial journey, with the stars possibly symbolizing other departed souls or fragments of consciousness waiting to reunite with the universe. The yellow light represents a destination accessible only to the spiritually prepared— like the bird with the broken wing. The bird's ascension and union with the cosmos suggest it has completed its journey, transcending to a higher realm of existence. The mystery of the flood is a big part of what makes Flow so compelling— it really gets you thinking and questioning what's going on. These theories are great food for thought, especially if you're the type who loves diving into deeper world-building. Here's another big mystery: Where did all the people go? It's clear they were once part of this world, but by the time the story begins, they've completely vanished, leaving only traces behind. Let's start with abandoned house where the cat's journey begins. It feels oddly lived-in yet frozen in time, like the humans just up and left one day. The details in the house are fascinating: glass spheres wrapped in netted rope, hanging from ceiling. At first, they look like decorations, but when the cat uses one to survive the flood, it's clear they were meant to be functional. They might have been designed as flotation devices, suggesting that humans were either living with flooding or actively trying to adapt to it. At the same time, they also remind me of planets, with the netted ropes representing their orbits. That feeling is reinforced by the placement of the telescope in the room, almost as if it's looking at the glass spheres like they're celestial bodies. Even so, I still lean toward idea that their primary purpose was as flotation devices. And then there's the telescope itself, a small but significant detail. It hints that the humans might have been trying to make connections between the floods and celestial events. Perhaps they were searching for answers, studying patterns, or even attempting to predict when the next flood might hit. Then there's all the cat stuff: a woodcarving and a drawing, statues scattered outside the house, and most strikingly, a massive cat statue carved into a mountain. This wasn't just a home, but possibly a place of reverence. The sheer scale of a mountain- carved cat statue implies that it wasn't the work of a single person but an entire society, meaning cats must have held a deep cultural or spiritual significance for them. It makes you wonder: why cats? In many ancient cultures, cats were symbols of resilience, protection, and even divinity. Maybe the cat statue reflects those same ideas— a believe that cats were guardians, spiritual guides, or even beings that could help humans reconnect with the natural world. That's statue could be a way to honor nature in a final, desperate plea for help as the floods became unavoidable. So, what caused the humans to disappear? According to the Moon-Tide Theory, they were wiped out by a massive tidal event. If the floods came suddenly and with overwhelming force, humans wouldn't have had enough time to fully adapt. Even with the best planning, people have a pretty bad track record when it comes to responding to massive disasters— especially when they don't all agree on the threat or the solution. Some probably tried to prepare; others might have been in denial until it was too late. We've seen this play out in real-world events like tsunamis, climate change, or volcanic eruptions. These natural disasters are frequently well-studied but there's often a gap between knowing the danger and actually taking action. That giant cat statue offers a clue. Its unfinished state might suggest the people were caught mid-preparation when disaster struck, leaving behind a partially realized monument to their faith or resilience. When the flood finally hit, it must have been devastating— drowning cities, submerging farmland, and wiping out infrastructure. A sudden and dramatic rise in water levels would have destroyed supply chains, scattered populations, and made coordinated survival nearly impossible. Without the resources to rebuild, societal collapse seems inevitable. One intriguing detail is the question of how advanced these humans were. On the one hand, there's a telescope, which implies some level of scientific knowledge. But on the other, we don't see evidence of other advanced tech. At least, not that I can remember. Were they a primitive society or something more like us? The relics they left behind leave this open to interpretation. At the end of the day, Flow really drives home one unforgiving truth: nature doesn't care about human plans. This is just the harsh reality of nature's overwhelming power. One of Flow's most striking scenes comes when the cat follows the bird up a colossal staircase stretching into the clouds, resembling an otherwardly Himalayan peak. The atmosphere shifts dramatically. Water droplets that once fell now rise, defying gravity, signaling a break from the natural order of things. The scene transitions into something cosmic: the cat and the bird are surrounded by stars and an expansive, swirling universe. At the center of it all, a radiant yellow light glows, drawing everything toward it. The bird flies toward the light without hesitation. The cat tries to follow but cannot. It meows desperately, as if pleading for the bird to stay. But the bird is drawn into the yellow light and vanishes completely. The cosmos dissolves as suddenly as it appeared, leaving the cat alone. The camera pulls back to reveal the cat at the center of a giant, labyrinth-like structure carved into the ground. The complex circular designs surrounds the cat as it stands still, staring upward at the empty sky. If we look at it through the lens of the Moon- Tide Theory, the stars and swirling universe might represent auroras. The proximity or size of the moon could stretch or deform the planet's magnetic field, potentially allowing auroras to form in non-polar regions. The yellow light and rising water droplets seem to be strange gravitational anomalies that defy physics. From the Afterlife perspective, this is a moment of spiritual revelation. The cat's journey reflects personal growth. Initially independent and self-reliant, the flood forces it to confront its vulnerabilities and rely on others, particularly the bird. The cat's climb toward the bird symbolizes its newfound reliance and admiration. The bird, with its broken wings, represents longing and a sense of being lost, yearning for a place in the world. This contrasts sharply with the capybara, who stands out as a calm and peaceful figure, seemingly unchanged throughout the story. The capybara embodies wisdom and stability, a mentor-like presence who has "figured it out" from the beginning. Despite its own struggles, the bird serves as the guide and a beacon of hope for the cat. By helping the cat survive, it teaches the value of connection and growth through companionship. When the bird ascends to the yellow light, it signifies the end of its role— having guided the cat as far as it could. Its departure leaves the cat to continue its journey alone. The cat's inability to follow the bird highlights its lingering struggle. Its fall and meowing convey its sadness and longing for the bond it had with the bird and the comfort it provided. The labyrinth-like structure emphasizes the cat's current state. It is caught in a loop, reflecting on its journey and trying to process what has happened. The labyrinth suggests that while the cat is grown, it still has much to figure out. Perhaps the cycles of the flood and the constant loops in the story hint at an internal process of learning, adapting, and finding purpose. The whale in Flow is indeed a fascinating creature, and its unusual appearance could reflect a number of environmental, evolutionary, or symbolic factors. If the world of Flow has been dominated by rising water levels for generations or trapped in endless loops, the whale could represent an evolutionary response to a planet transformed by floods. On Earth, we see something similar: the buoyancy of water allows marine species to grow to enormous sizes, free from the constraints of gravity. In the film, the whale's massive size serves practical purposes, like conserving energy and traveling long distances in a flooded world where food is scarce or widely dispersed. This mirrors how real-world whales have adapted to thrive in vast aquatic ecosystems. The whale's bizarre features—like extra limbs— could also point to unique ecological pressures, such as navigating shallow or debris-filled waters or surviving in an environment drastically re- shaped by climate change. Or the bizarre features could be mutations that mirror real-world phenomena, like how pollution has caused deformities in some animals. If the flood was caused by extreme gravitational shifts, it might have introduced radiation or other environmental stressors. Over generations or loops, these conditions might have triggered dramatic mutations in the whale's genome, leading to exaggerated physical traits over time. In this way, the whale becomes a reflection of its environment's history and trauma. Beyond biology, the whale also carries a deeper, symbolic meaning. In many stories, whales represent ancient wisdom, the unknown depths of the ocean, or the power of nature. But in Flow, this whale, I think, symbolizes transformation— nature's response to a cataclysm, a living reminder of how the forces that reshaped the world also reshaped its creatures. And then there's the possibility of something more abstract. If Flow is a story about transition— if its world exists somewhere between life and death— the whale could be a creature of that liminal space. It's massive, alien appearance might represent the vast, unknowable forces shaping this world. Maybe it's a guardian. Maybe it's a witness. Either way, its presence evokes awe, perfectly capturing the otherworldly nature of Flow's universe. Alright, that's my take on the mysteries of Flow. It's a lot to unpack, and honestly, the story leaves plenty of room for interpretation. What do you think? Did I miss something, or do you have your own theories? Let me know in the comments— I'd love to hear your thoughts. If you enjoyed this, feel free to like the video and subscribe for more. Thanks for hanging out with me, and I'll catch you next time.

text: After the Hunt is a 2025 psychological drama directed by Luca Guadinino, who also directed Challengers and Call Me By Your Name. It stars Julia Roberts, IO Ediri, and Andrew Garfield in a tense academic drama about truth, power, and moral ambiguity inside a university setting. The movie explores how one accusation can unravel multiple lives, and how the truth is never as simple as it seems. We open on Yale University presented not as a place of learning but as a beautiful prison of intellect and reputation. Dr. Alma Mhof, Julia Roberts is the epitome of the polished academic, elegant, articulate, unshakably rational. She's preparing for a lecture on moral philosophy, arguing that truth is not a feeling. It's a construct we fight to preserve. That line, truth is not a feeling, becomes the spine of the entire film. She returns home to her husband, Frederick, a fellow intellectual who treats their marriage like a quiet academic partnership. Their dialogue is distant, rehearsed. Alma pours herself a glass of wine and stares into the empty yard, a ritual that hints at loneliness beneath her perfect facade. Enter Maggie Resnik. Young, brilliant, magnetic. Maggie is Alma's brightest student and emotional mirror. Passionate where Alma is repressed. Instinctive where Alma is cerebral. Alma begins mentoring her intensely. She sees Maggie as a second chance. Maybe even the version of herself she lost to age, marriage, and tenure politics. Then there's Hank Gibson, a fellow professor, charismatic, boyish, popular with students. There's history between Hem and Alma. Subtle, unspoken sexual tension that lingers in their exchanges. They share drinks after faculty meetings. They understand each other's cynicism about the system. The first act ends at a department party. Dim lighting, too much wine, academic laughter, masking competition. Maggie leaves early. Hank follows. We don't see what happens. All we hear is the faint echo of her voice saying, "No, I should go." Then cut to black. The next morning, Maggie arrives at Alma's office, trembling. She confesses that Hank assaulted her. The way the scene is written is brilliant. Maggie doesn't describe events chronologically, but emotionally. She says, "It felt like I wasn't there anymore." Almo listens in silence and for the first time her face cracks not just from empathy but from recognition. Something about Maggie's story resonates too closely with her own past. Alma's moral universe collapses. She reports the incident to the dean. An investigation begins. The university becomes a battlefield of whispers. Hank denies everything, saying they kissed, but that Maggie initiated it. Maggie insists it was non-consensual. The story fractures into competing truths, each plausible, each incomplete. Meanwhile, the camera follows Alma's descent. Sleepless nights, staring at empty lecture halls, drowning in self-doubt. Guadanino shoots her apartment like a museum of guilt. All glass reflections and half-seen shadows. Alma is not just reacting to Maggie's trauma. She's reliving her own, a past relationship with a student that blurred ethical lines. It wasn't an assault, but it violated boundaries, and she's buried that shame for decades. Now, Maggie's pain reawakens Alma's own complicity. The title now takes shape. The hunt is not for the truth. It's the hunt for moral clarity in a world that refuses to give it. Hank's career disintegrates. He's asked to take a leave of absence. He confronts Alma in a quiet corridor. No music, just silence. Hank, you know I didn't hurt her. Alma, you know that doesn't matter anymore. That line encapsulates the modern tragedy of After the Hunt. In a moral landscape shaped by trauma and perception, truth has become irrelevant. What matters is how people feel about the truth. Maggie becomes a symbol, a voice for survivors. She's interviewed, applauded, but she's uneasy. Her eyes flicker with doubt when she reads her own words quoted back to her. Alma begins to see her mentorship as manipulation, not out of malice, but vanity. She tried to mold Maggie into an idea of herself. The more Maggie asserts her independence, the more Alma loses control and identity. By this point, every character is both hunter and hunted. Maggie hunts justice, but becomes consumed by vengeance. Hank hunts redemption but becomes a symbol of guilt. Alma hunts truth but ends up facing her own lie. The university clears the case with no conclusive evidence. Hank resigns, vanishes. Alma faces an ethics inquiry herself after a student files a complaint about her biased handling of the situation. The institution turns cold on her. The system she served now devours her. One evening, Maggie visits Alma's office. It's after hours. The lighting mirrors the opening lecture. Warm, academic, deceptive. The script gives them a long, minimalist scene. No score, just dialogue that feels like chess. Maggie, I remember pieces. Some nights I think maybe I invited it. Alma, you didn't invite anything. Maggie, but it felt like that. And feelings are real. Alma, facts aren't feelings, Maggie. Maybe facts don't matter anymore. That exchange is the philosophical climax of the movie. A collision between reason and emotion, intellect and instinct. The very gap that defines generational feminism. The two women sit in silence. Then Maggie reaches out, touches Alma's hand. For a moment, it feels like forgiveness, but it's not. It's exhaustion. It's the human need to rest. Even in moral fog, Alma breaks down crying for the first time. Not for Hank, not for Maggie, but for herself. For all the years she's lived pretending clarity was possible. The next morning, Alma walks across campus. The students she once taught don't look at her. She's become a ghost in her own temple of reason. We see Maggie again leading a seminar. She repeats one of Alma's old lines. Truth is not a feeling. It's what survives feeling. Her students nod, but Maggie's expression says she no longer believes it. Alma watches her from a distance, unseen. There's no music, only ambient sound. Then fade to black. The ending is not about forgiveness or guilt. It's about coexistence with ambiguity. Alma's arc is about dismantling intellectual arrogance, realizing that logic can't clean emotional truth. Maggie's arc is about realizing that emotional truth without accountability can become manipulation. Their false reconciliation is the meeting point of these ideas, a quiet recognition that no one can live in absolute moral purity. The title After the Hunt refers to what happens after moral pursuit ends when you've caught nothing but the cost of chasing. It's about living after the search for clarity when all you have left is yourself. Every character remembers selectively. The film uses memory fragments to show how perception creates its own truth. Alma's tragedy is her certainty. The moment she believes she's doing the right thing, she becomes dangerous to herself and others. Alma watching Maggie from afar isn't just closure, it's succession. The cycle repeats. The mentor gives way to the student who will one day face her own reckoning. The hunt never really ends. Only the hunters

text: The movie opens on Prison Island in Japan, where security guards are keeping an eye on Shadow the Hedgehog, who has been kept in stasis for 50 years. Shadow experiences flashbacks of a girl named Maria. Suddenly, a heavy heartbeat registers on the monitor. Guards check it and find out that their system has been hacked, and soon Shadow wakes up. The gunmen prepare themselves and storm the place. Just then, Shadow wakes up and bursts through his containment pod. He uses teleportation powers to attack the agents, knocking all of them out before making his escape in nearby town, Tokyo. In Green Hills, Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles are ready to see who is the fastest out of all of them. Tom and Maddie start the countdown, and the race begins. Sonic ends up being tricked by holograms and goes back to find that Tails, Knuckles, along with Tom and Maddie, have prepared a celebration for Sonic's anniversary of his arrival on Earth. A party for me? The day you came to this planet is the day all our lives changed forever. Let's party! Yeah, do it. Later, Sonic and Tom come upon Sonic's old cave that he lived in before meeting Tom. They see a drawing that Sonic made of Longclaw, and he admits that he still misses her. Meanwhile, Shadow is walking through the town when he notices the year 2024 on the screen. He realizes he has been trapped for 50 years. Suddenly, a group of mercenaries surrounds him with guns, and Shadow asks why they won't leave him alone. Leave me alone. Commander Walters is requesting Team Sonic's immediate assistance. Sonic is off to save the day. Director Rockwell takes the three into the helicopter, and they fly to Tokyo, Japan. Look out! One million Suddenly, Shadow appears, and Tails and Knuckles comment that he is just like Sonic. Sonic jokingly asks why he looks like him. Sonic also goes to fight him, but is also knocked out, proving that Shadow is FAST AND POWERFUL. OKAY, HE TOOK US ALL AT ONCE. Shadow gets on a bike and speeds off while Sonic gives chase. Shadow fires his gun at him, but Sonic manages to evade the bullets. Shadow eventually flees from Sonic's view. The trio goes to Chao Garden and meets Commander Walters. He explains to them that Shadow was discovered in a meteor that came to Earth. He possesses chaos energy and was deemed too dangerous. The lab where he was experimented on exploded, and the professor who tested him was arrested and incarcerated. Moments later, Egg Drones arrive and attack, fatally injuring Walters, but not before he gives Team Sonic a key card to a secret gun weapon. A mysterious biker bursts in and disables the drones before riding away. The trio flees before Rockwell and other agents arrive, and she assumes that they stole the card. Team Sonic goes after the biker and catches up to him. He pulls off his helmet, which turns out to be Agent Stone. He tells them he is not there to fight, but claims that he and Dr. Ivo Robotnik are not responsible for Shadow's escape. Stone brings the three into a giant mechanical crab and takes them to Ivo, who has fallen into a junk food depression since his last defeat. Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles reluctantly agree to an alliance with Ivo and Stone after Sonic gives Eggman one of his quills. Meanwhile, Shadow goes to the old GUN facility. He finds a skate boot that Maria used to ride with and remembers his time with Maria, with whom he developed a friendship. While he is glancing at the mirror, Professor Gerald arrives, the one who created Shadow. Shadow expresses sadness about his friend Maria, saying he still remembers her. The professor tells him that they have to punish those who are responsible for Maria's death. Soon after, Sonic and the others arrive at the facility, where they meet Gerald. While they are searching the facility, Shadow captures them except for Ivo. He then brings them to Professor Gerald, his grandfather, for the first time. Ivo is elated to have a member of his family alive. The Robotniks and Shadow tie up Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles. Sonic then finds out that Professor Gerald is the one responsible for Walter's death and Shadow's breakout. Gerald explains that he needs a second key card to activate the Eclipse Cannon, a super weapon hidden underneath GUN headquarters that is powered by Chaos energy and is capable of global destruction. The villains leave Team Sonic as they activate a black hole that sucks up the whole facility after Shadow takes the key card they already had. The trio manages to grab a ring and open a portal to escape. OH, YES! SOMEBODY BETTER CALL GOOGLE MAPS. MEANWHILE, Ivo takes Gerald to his facility, and they start spending quality time together in a virtual simulation to catch up on lost time. Seeing their bond, Stone feels left out and neglected by the man he has always been loyal to. Tom and Maddie are at home when Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles arrive. Sonic asks them for their help on his mission, to which they agree because they are bored without him. Sonic says they need to go to London GUN headquarters to plant a USB drive and shut down the Eclipse Cannon, which is capable of global destruction. They need to stop it. They travel to London to GUN headquarters since that is Gerald and Shadow's primary target for the Eclipse Cannon. Tom and Maddie use suits to disguise themselves as Rachel and Randall to make their way inside. They insert a drive that allows Tails to hack into the system and disable an energy shield so Sonic can enter. When they find the room with the key card, they find that Ivo and Gerald have already made their way inside with their own super suits. Before they can get to the key card, Rockwell finds them and manipulates the gravity in the room before other agents storm the place. Knuckles bursts in to save them, but he smashes the gravity keypad and causes everyone to either float or get stuck to the ground. Rockwell eventually gets the key card and gets away, but Tom disguises himself as Commander Walters to trick Rockwell into giving him the key card. Just as Tom informs the group that he got the key, Shadow arrives. Shadow sees Tom in disguise and punches him, thinking he is Walters in retaliation. Tom is knocked out and Shadow takes the key card. Sonic runs to Tom's side in a panic, triggering Shadow's memory of his final moments with Maria. Shadow gets away and gives the key card to Ivo and Gerald just as Maddie rushes to Tom's side. Tom is taken to the hospital and Sonic becomes enraged, determined to seek revenge against Shadow. Sonic asks Knuckles where the Master Emerald is so he can become Super Sonic again, but Knuckles refuses, explaining he is sworn to guard it because it is too powerful. Tails tries to calm them down, but Knuckles relents and reveals that Wade is keeping the emerald. Sonic goes to Wade and takes the emerald. The villains raise the Eclipse Cannon from the River Thames and take it high into space. However, Ivo is horrified to learn that Gerald doesn't plan to dominate the Earth, but to destroy it. Another flashback reveals that GUN agents storm the facility to kill Shadow, but a stray bullet caused the explosion that killed Maria. This drove Gerald and Shadow to seek revenge against all of humanity. Super Sonic then flies at high speeds, crashing through the facility and fighting Shadow. The two hedgehogs fight after crashing into a field, but Shadow taunts Sonic about abandoning his friends and family for revenge. Sonic responds by uppercutting Shadow all the way to the moon. Before Sonic can deliver the fatal blow, he holds back and realizes this is not who he is. He and Shadow express their pain over the ones they lost, Maria and Longclaw. But, Sonic tells him that revenge will not fix things. They resolve to work together and save the world. Meanwhile, Ivo turns on Gerald after he admits that he never viewed Ivo the same way he did Maria. Gerald responds by trying to drop Ivo to his death. But, Ivo rises from a ring portal with Tails and Knuckles. Ivo uses Sonic's super charged quill to poke Gerald in the butt, sending him flying into the chaos energy field and vaporizing him. Ivo, Tails, and Knuckles then try to redirect the Eclipse Cannon's trajectory while Sonic and Shadow, both powered by the Chaos Emeralds, hold off the blast. They succeed in diverting it away from Earth, but end up hitting the moon. Sonic starts to fall back to Earth unconscious, and when Tails tries to save him, he loses consciousness, too. But, Knuckles saves them both. Sonic apologizes to his friends for abandoning them the way he did, but Tails and Knuckles forgive him. The Eclipse Cannon's core is about to overload. Ivo resolves to use his final moments with Shadow to get the cannon away from Earth. Ivo sends out one last stream to Earth to reach Stone, who sees it from London. Ivo thanks him for remaining loyal and being his only friend. Shadow pushes the cannon away from Earth before it is obliterated. Stone bids Eggman farewell. The heroes return to Green Hills with Tom recovering from his injuries. Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles then proceed to race again to see which of them is truly the fastest. In this way, movie ends here. text: [Music] A Real Pain has an ambiguous ending after its equally hilarious and sobering story. Jesse Eisenberg directs, writes, and stars in the comedy drama film. He plays the reserved and anxious David Kaplan, who travels to Poland with his charismatic and troubled cousin Benji Kaplan, Kieran Culkin. They join a Holocaust tour group and also intend the home where their grandmother lived during her time in Poland. A Real Pain's reviews have been overwhelmingly positive since the movie first debuted at the 2024 Sundance Film Festival. Eisenberg has received acclaim for his direction, writing, and for his portrayal of David, with the film proving to be one of the many high points in Eisenberg's career. A Real Pain has also proven to be one of Kieran Culkin's best movies, which led to him winning a Golden Globe Award for his performance. David and Benji's relationship, which was already strained, is put to the test throughout their travels and builds to a largely open-ended conclusion. Why Benji is still at the airport in A Real Pain's ending. There are several interpretations. Benji, Kieran Culkin, smiling in the airport in A Real Pain. After returning from Poland, David suggests that Benji come home with him or that they at least share a taxi together. Benji declines these offers and tells David that he will stay at the airport for now. A Real Pain's final shot sees Benji still sitting at the airport and glancing around at various strangers. While the ending is intentionally ambiguous, Benji still being in the airport indicates that he still feels displaced, unsure of how to move forward with his life, and needs more time to work through his emotions before taking the next step forward. It is possible that Benji is also still at the airport because he is homeless. At the beginning of the movie, he has already been at the airport long before David arrives, and whenever David tries to call Benji's phone, he is always unreachable. Culkin has another interpretation of the ending that he shared at the 2024 SCAD Film Festival via Blavity, which is that the final shot is what David imagines happening to Benji after leaving him, as he is afraid of imagining what Benji may do next after leaving the airport. What David and Benji find at their grandmother's home in Poland. It does not go as planned. Kieran Culkin and Jesse Eisenberg stare up at a statue in Poland in A Real Pain. After spending the majority of their movie with their tour group, David and Benji part ways with them to visit the home where their grandmother grew up. Neither cousin is sure about what they expected to find, but the house proves to be unremarkable. However, it does elicit a memory from Benji of their grandmother slapping him once, which he claims is the best thing that ever happened to him. David suggests that they put a rock on the home stoop to commemorate that they were here. He gets this idea from the Jewish tradition of putting rocks on graves. Putting rocks in front of the home grabs the attention of a neighbor who does not speak English, requiring his son to translate. The cousins clarify that they put the rocks there as a sentimental gesture while the son explains that, regardless, they need to move the rocks as they are a hazard, and the elderly woman living in the home now may trip over them. Like much of the movie, the trip to the grandmother's home does not go as planned and does not provide the closure that is expected. Why David stopped visiting Benji before A Real Pain. Responsibilities and tragedy caused them to drift apart. Jesse Eisenberg and Kieran Culkin in A Real Pain. When David and Benji were younger, they were quite close and used to do everything together, a fact that Benji mentions to the other tour group members early on. As they grew older, their relationship changed as David focused on his wife, child, and his career, and Benji struggled to find his way. David stopped visiting Benji, and they began drifting further apart 6 months before their trip to Poland when Benji tried to take his own life via sleeping pills. David could never stop picturing the sight of Benji passed out on the couch after his overdose. He is haunted by this image, is consumed by fear of what Benji will do, and cannot bring himself to be around his cousin for months. From expressing these feelings to offering Benji to come home with him, David tries to make amends. The cousins have an emotional hug in their final scene together, and the trip has brought them closer together again, but there is still a great deal they both need to work through. How Benji changes future Holocaust tours. James applies Benji's feedback. During their tour of Poland, the tour guide, James Will Sharp, and fellow tour member Alois Kurt Egger, spend a great deal of time sharing the extensive facts that they know about the Holocaust, Poland, and the history of the Jewish people. Benji's frustration with this reaches a breaking point when the group is at a Jewish cemetery. He criticizes James for having the tour treat the devastation of the Holocaust as if it is little more than a list of facts and statistics, and that there should be more emphasis on authentic connection and emotion to the history when the group later goes to the Nazi concentration camp of Majdanek. James takes Benji's words to heart by choosing to only offer minimal information and to allow the group to more silently and authentically walk through the camp where countless horrors once happened. Before David and Benji leave the group to visit their grandmother's home, James expresses to Benji that he is grateful for the honest feedback that has changed his perspective and how he will lead Holocaust tours in the future. The real meaning of A Real Pain's ending. The human condition is complex. Kieran Culkin looking sad in A Real Pain. A Real Pain's characters navigate a story that asks difficult questions without providing easy answers. Some of these questions are specific to the Holocaust, with Benji's criticism highlighting the dangers of Holocaust tourism that has the dangerous potential of dehumanizing the real suffering and history of what really happened. Studying and revisiting this history is intertwined with a personal and collective grief, which is further amplified by the grief that David and Benji are experiencing from their grandmother's passing, and that they are trying to process in their own ways. In addition to asking difficult questions about the Holocaust and about grief, the film asks about questions of identity and pain. David tries to bury his pain and focus on his responsibilities because he believes his pain is unremarkable, while Benji deals with his pain in often self-destructive ways. They try to connect with their roots as they reconcile with their identities, but as seen with the scene at their grandmother's home, it is not as straightforward as they thought it would be. A Real Pain asks challenging questions about the human condition that can never be completely answered.

text: What if you were one of the most powerful beings in the universe, but no matter how far you traveled, you could never escape your past? What if every star in the sky reminded you of everything you had lost? This is the story of Kara Zor-El, the story of Supergirl, a hero born from tragedy, a survivor haunted by memories, and a warrior searching for meaning in a galaxy that often feels cold and unforgiving. Unlike her famous cousin Superman, Kara remembers Krypton. She remembers the cities, she remembers the people, she remembers the day everything ended, and those memories have shaped every decision she has ever made. This is not a simple superhero adventure. This is a cosmic journey across the stars, a tale of revenge, justice, loss, and redemption. And by the end of this story, Supergirl will discover that being a hero is not about strength. It's about choosing hope when darkness seems inevitable. Long before Earth ever knew the name Supergirl, Kara Zor-El lived on Krypton, a magnificent world filled with towering crystal cities and advanced technology. Krypton was a civilization unlike any other. For generations, its people believed their world would last forever, but they were wrong. Scientists [clears throat] warned that Krypton's core was becoming unstable. The planet was dying, yet many leaders refused to listen. They dismissed the warnings, ignored the evidence, and continued living as though nothing was wrong. Among those who understood the danger were Kara's parents. They knew disaster was coming, and they knew they had little time left. As tremors shook the planet and chaos spread across cities, preparations began. A desperate plan, a final chance for survival. Kara would be sent away, away from Krypton, away from everything she had ever known. Her mission was simple, protect her younger cousin, Kal-El, the child who would one day become Superman, but fate had other plans. As Krypton collapsed, Kara's journey became far more complicated than anyone could have imagined. Years passed. The destruction of Krypton remained a wound that never healed. Unlike Kal-El, who grew up surrounded by love on Earth, Kara remembered everything. Every face, every voice, every moment. She remembered friends who never escaped, family members who vanished in the catastrophe, entire cities erased forever. No amount of distance could silence those memories. Every night she dreamed of Krypton. Every morning she woke to the same painful reality. She was one of the last survivors, and surviving came with a terrible burden. >> [clears throat] >> Guilt. Why had she lived when so many others had died? Why was she given powers while her people were gone? The questions haunted her. There were no answers, only endless stars and endless loneliness. Instead of settling down, Kara chose to travel. She wandered from world to world, planet to planet, system to system, always moving, always searching, searching for purpose, searching for peace, searching for something that could fill the emptiness inside her. Her only constant companion was Krypto, the loyal super dog. Together they crossed distant galaxies. They visited thriving civilizations, dangerous frontiers, forgotten worlds, and places where hope seemed impossible. Yet no matter where Kara went, she never truly felt at home, because home was gone, destroyed long ago. One day everything changed. On a remote world, Kara encountered a young girl named Ruthie. At first glance, Ruthie seemed ordinary, but behind her eyes burned a fire, a determination stronger than steel, a desire for revenge. Ruthie's father had been murdered. The killer was a ruthless criminal known throughout the stars, Krem of the Yellow Hills, a man feared by countless worlds, a predator who left suffering wherever he went. Most people were too afraid to pursue him, but not Ruthie. She wanted justice, or perhaps something darker, revenge. And she would stop at nothing to get it. Kara understood pain. She understood loss, perhaps better than anyone. That's why she couldn't simply walk away. Against her better judgment, she agreed to help Ruthie. What began as a simple act of compassion soon became a dangerous mission. Together they followed clues across the galaxy. Each lead brought them closer to Krem, but every step also brought new dangers, mercenaries, pirates, alien warlords, and criminals eager to eliminate anyone who stood in their way. The hunt had begun. Krem was more than a murderer. He was a symbol of everything wrong with the galaxy, cruel, greedy, merciless. He exploited the weak, destroyed families, and escaped justice time after time. The deeper Kara investigated, the more horrifying stories she uncovered. Entire communities had suffered because of him. Countless victims had never received justice. For Ruthie, the mission became personal. For Kara, it became a responsibility. If someone possessed the power to stop evil, didn't they have an obligation to act? The answer seemed obvious, but reality was never simple. As the journey continued, Ruthie became increasingly obsessed. Every setback fueled her anger. Every delay strengthened her desire for vengeance. Kara began to worry, because she recognized the signs. She had felt those same emotions herself. The temptation to let rage take control. The temptation to answer violence with violence. The temptation to believe revenge could heal pain. But revenge never truly heals anything. It only creates more suffering. And Kara feared Ruthie was heading toward a dangerous path. The hunt eventually attracted unwanted attention. Powerful enemies began closing in. Bounty hunters tracked their movements. Criminal syndicates wanted them dead. Entire armies stood between them and their goal. For the first time in years, Kara was forced to unleash the full extent of her powers. Battles erupted across alien landscapes. For the first time, Kara allowed herself to mourn. Not as a hero. Not as a survivor. Simply as Kara. A daughter. A friend. A refugee from a world that no longer existed. And in accepting her pain, she discovered something unexpected. Strength. The hunt finally came to an end. Krem stood before them. The man responsible for so much suffering. And perhaps most importantly, it's about the fear that your best years may already be behind [music] you. One of the reasons this story feels so authentic comes directly from John Carney himself. Unlike many directors who simply use music as a backdrop, Carney was once a musician. Before becoming a filmmaker, he played bass guitar in the Irish band The Frames. That personal experience allows him to understand the emotional highs and lows that artists experience throughout their careers. For Carney, Power Ballad became an opportunity to explore a question that fascinated him. What happens to a musician after youth ends? Hollywood usually focuses on dreamers chasing success. Power Ballad focuses on someone who stopped chasing, someone who chose family over fame, someone who thought he had made peace with that decision until fate suddenly forced him to reconsider everything. And that's what makes Rick Power such a compelling protagonist. He's not trying to become someone new. He's trying to figure out whether the person he already became is enough. What makes Power Ballad especially fascinating is that the casting feels almost too perfect to be accidental. When John Carney began putting together the film, he wasn't simply looking for recognizable names. He needed actors who could bring genuine emotional truth to characters whose lives revolve around music. That challenge was particularly important for Danny Wilson. The role required someone who understood what it feels like to experience enormous fame, lose momentum, and then attempt to reinvent themselves under the glare of public scrutiny. As it turns out, Nick Jonas had already lived much of that story. During early conversations with Carney, Jonas reportedly told the filmmaker something incredibly revealing. He believed he was one of the few people who had actually experienced what Danny was going through. And when you look at his career, it's easy to understand why. Nick Jonas rose to international fame as 1/3 of the Jonas Brothers, one of the defining pop acts of the late 2000s. Alongside his brothers Kevin and Joe, he experienced the type of success most aspiring musicians only dream about: massive tours, chart-topping albums, television stardom, worldwide recognition. But then came a difficult transition. The group disbanded in 2013, and each brother was forced to discover who they were outside the band that had defined their lives. For Nick, that meant navigating a solo career while trying to establish his own artistic identity. Those experiences became invaluable when building Danny Wilson. Jonas understood the emotional complexity of being famous. He understood the pressure to stay relevant. He understood how seductive success can become. And perhaps most importantly, he understood the loneliness that sometimes accompanies celebrity. According to Jonas, Danny sees songwriting as his true passion while his boy band years almost feel like a detour. That's a fascinating detail because it adds another layer to the character. Danny isn't simply chasing fame. He's chasing legitimacy. He wants people to see him as an artist, not merely a celebrity. That distinction drives much of his behavior throughout the film. John Carney recognized immediately how important Jonas's real-world experience would be. In fact, Carney emphasized that they needed someone who wasn't just pretending to be a singer. They needed someone who had actually lived the lifestyle. Someone who understood the realities of touring, recording, fame, and public expectations. Jonas brought all of that naturally. Producer Anthony Bregman described his performance as balancing humanity and celebrity simultaneously. That's a difficult combination to pull off. Many performers lean too heavily toward one side or the other, but Danny needed to feel both larger than life and deeply vulnerable. Based on the production notes, Jonas appears to have delivered exactly that. Then there's Paul Rudd. At first glance, Rudd might seem like an unexpected choice for a musical drama. Most audiences know him as Ant-Man, or from Anchorman, or Knocked Up, or countless comedy classics. But that's precisely what made the casting so interesting. John Carney wasn't looking for a conventional movie star performance. He was looking for someone who could embody disappointment without becoming cynical. Someone who could make audiences laugh while simultaneously breaking their hearts. Someone who could portray a man whose dreams never fully disappeared. According to Carney, he simply sent the script to Rudd and asked a straightforward question. Do you know this guy? Rudd's response was immediate. He loved the character. He understood him. And perhaps most importantly, he wanted to be him. That emotional connection became the foundation for Rick Power. One of the most surprising revelations from the production notes is how nervous Rudd was about taking the role. Despite decades of acting success, he openly admitted that singing and performing music at this level pushed him outside his comfort zone. In fact, he described being scared. But rather than viewing that fear as a weakness, he embraced it. Because fear often means you're reaching for something genuine, something vulnerable, something human. And vulnerability became one of Rick's defining characteristics. Unlike many cinematic musicians, Rick isn't portrayed as effortlessly cool. He doubts himself. He second-guesses himself. He carries regrets. He wonders whether life could have been different. Those insecurities make him relatable. Nick Jonas observed that Rudd brings a melancholy quality to the character. Rick can be cynical. He can be jaded. Yet there's still a spark inside him, a spark waiting to be reignited. That spark becomes the engine driving the entire story. Interestingly, many people involved in the production discovered that Rudd's musical knowledge was far deeper than expected. John Carney described him as a walking encyclopedia of music. The two bonded over classic artists, obscure music trivia, and shared appreciation for decades of rock history. Producer Anthony Bregman even suggested that playing Rick Power felt like Rudd was living a personal dream. Watching him perform on stage reportedly felt completely natural. And perhaps that's because performance itself is part of Rudd's DNA. Whether he's delivering comedy, drama, or music, he understands how to connect with an audience. That connection becomes crucial because Rick needs viewers to root for him. Even when he makes mistakes. Even when he spirals. Even when his obsession with the song begins damaging relationships. Audiences have to believe he's worth following. Rudd's natural likeability helps make that possible. Another fascinating aspect of the production is the relationship between Rudd and Jonas themselves. Rather than creating distance between the characters, the filmmakers encouraged genuine collaboration. The two actors spent significant time working together musically. Rudd even joked that performing alongside Jonas felt similar to throwing a football with elite NFL players. You're standing next to someone operating at the highest level of their craft, and you hope some of that talent rubs off on you. That dynamic mirrors the relationship between Rick and Danny perfectly. Rick admires Danny's success. Danny admires Rick's authenticity. Each sees something valuable in the other. That mutual admiration becomes the foundation for their friendship, which makes the eventual betrayal hurt even more. But Power Ballad isn't only about its two leads. One of the production's biggest strengths appears to be the supporting cast. Peter McDonald, who co-wrote the screenplay alongside John Carney, also plays Sandy, Rick's loyal bandmate and closest friend. That dual role gave him a unique understanding of the character. Producer Rob Walpole even suggested there may not be another actor who could have played Sandy as effectively. After all, McDonald helped create him. Sandy serves as both comic relief and emotional support throughout the story. When Rick eventually travels to Los Angeles seeking answers, Sandi accompanies him. Together, they become fish out of water navigating a world of celebrity excess far removed from Dublin wedding gigs. The friendship between Rick and Sandi adds warmth to the film and reinforces one of its recurring themes. Success matters, but relationships matter more. The rest of The Bride and Groom also received careful attention during casting. The filmmakers wanted the band to feel authentic, not simply like actors pretending to be musicians. According to McDonald, there was a delicate balance involved. The band members needed enough swagger to believe they're stars while simultaneously looking like ordinary guys playing weddings. That tension creates much of the film's humor. They're dreamers, they're performers, they're entertainers, but they're also just regular people trying to make a living. Carney believed their chemistry came partly from shared musical tastes. Many cast and crew members loved the same music. They spoke the same language creatively, and that connection helped create the feeling of a real band rather than a manufactured one. Then there's Rick's family. Marcella Plunkett plays Rachel, Rick's wife, and Beth Fallon portrays their daughter Asia. Together, they provide the emotional anchor of the story. Without them, Rick's struggle would simply be about fame. With them, it becomes about choices. Rachel represents the life Rick built, the family he chose, the stability he created. Plunkett explained that she approached the marriage realistically. Rick and Rachel aren't a fantasy couple. They're a long-term couple. They've weathered years together. They've made sacrifices. They've adapted. They've built a life. That authenticity gives their relationship emotional weight. Perhaps even more significant is Asia, because while Rick initially appears obsessed with proving ownership of the song, the deeper truth is far more emotional. How to write a song was originally written for her. Every fight, every argument, every sacrifice, every regret ultimately traces back to that connection. Beth Fallon described Asia as someone who deeply loves her father while also navigating her own teenage life. She recognizes similarities between herself and Rick. They're alike enough to clash and alike enough to understand each other without words. That dynamic becomes especially important because music serves as the emotional language connecting the family. Characters often struggle to express their deepest feelings directly. The songs do it for them. In many ways, that's one of John Carney's greatest strengths as a filmmaker. Music isn't decoration. It's communication. It's the language his characters use when ordinary conversation isn't enough. And nowhere is that more evident than in Power Ballad. By the time production fully came together, Carney had assembled a cast capable of delivering comedy, drama, heartbreak, and music with equal conviction. But assembling the cast was only the beginning. Because next came the challenge of creating two completely different worlds. One grounded in working-class Dublin wedding culture, the other immersed in the wealth, glamour, and excess of Los Angeles celebrity life. If the story of Power Ballad explores the collision between two very different lives, the production itself was built around that same idea. From the beginning, John Carney envisioned a film that would move between two worlds that seemed completely disconnected on the surface. One world belongs to Rick Power. It's grounded, modest, comfortable. It's wedding receptions, local pubs, family dinners, and small stages filled with familiar faces. The other world belongs to Danny Wilson. It's massive arenas, luxury homes, private parties, managers, publicists, industry executives, millions of fans, constant pressure. The challenge facing the filmmakers was making both environments feel equally authentic. And according to producer Anthony Bregman, that responsibility largely fell to production designer Anna Carina and costume designer Triona Lillis. Anna Carina had the enormous task of visually creating two completely separate realities. Rick's Dublin is a world of ordinary people trying to build meaningful lives. The homes are modest, the clubs are small, the environments feel lived in. Nothing is flashy, nothing is overly glamorous. Everything reflects the reality of someone who once dreamed of superstardom, but ultimately chose a different path. What ultimately makes Power Ballad stand out from other music-centered films is that it isn't really about a stolen song. That's the hook, that's the conflict, that's the premise. But underneath all of that, John Carney is telling a much more personal story. It's a story about identity, about regret, about gratitude, and about the complicated relationship people have with the lives they chose versus the lives they imagined. As the conflict between Rick and Danny intensifies, both men begin realizing something uncomfortable. The song isn't actually the thing they're fighting over. Not really. The song is a symbol. For Rick, it represents every opportunity he thinks he lost, every stage he never stood on, every audience he never reached, every dream that slipped through his fingers. The success of How to Write a Song forces him to confront questions he had spent years avoiding. What if he had never settled down? What if he had stayed in America? What if he had kept chasing fame? What if he had bet on himself instead of choosing family? Those questions slowly eat away at him, and that's what makes Rick such a compelling character, because most people have their own version of those questions. Maybe it isn't music. Maybe it's a career, a relationship, a business idea, a life-changing opportunity. Almost everyone has wondered at some point whether a different choice would have led to a better life. Power ballad taps directly into that universal feeling. Producer Anthony Bregman believes that idea is actually the heart of the entire movie. He points out that Rick eventually discovers something many people spend their entire lives trying to learn. Sometimes the life you're searching for is the life you already have. That's a powerful message, especially in a culture that constantly tells people they're supposed to want more. More money, more fame, more success, more recognition, more followers. >> More achievements. >> Power ballad asks a different question. What if enough is already sitting right in front of you? That realization becomes Rick's true journey. Not reclaiming a song, reclaiming perspective. Learning to appreciate the things he spent years taking for granted. His wife, his daughter, his friendships, his music, his community, his life. John Carney described this evolution beautifully when discussing the origins of the story. He became fascinated by the idea of revisiting the traditional musical love story later in life. What does a love story look like when the characters aren't teenagers chasing dreams? What does it look like after marriage? After children? After responsibility? After disappointment? After real life happens? Those questions led him toward Rick Power. And the answer surprised him. The love story wasn't necessarily between Rick and Rachel. It wasn't even between Rick and music. In some ways, it was between Rick and the younger version of himself. The version that still believed anything was possible. The version Danny reminds him of. That's why Carney jokingly refers to part of the film as a bromance. Rick becomes emotionally invested in Danny because Danny represents something deeply personal, a reflection of who Rick once was. At the same time, Danny is experiencing his own crisis. From the outside, Danny appears to have everything: money, success, recognition, celebrity. Yet as his career begins soaring once again, his personal life starts becoming increasingly isolated. The film cleverly contrasts Rick's frustrations with Danny's loneliness. Rick wants what Danny has. Danny wants some of what Rick has. One has fame but lacks connection. The other has connection but feels overlooked. Both men are convinced the other possesses the missing piece. And both eventually discover reality is more complicated. Nick Jonas connected strongly with that aspect of the story. He described Power Ballad as two people asking to be told they're enough. Not successful enough, not talented enough, not famous enough, just enough as human beings. That simple emotional truth is what elevates the film beyond its premise. It's not about winning, it's about self-worth. One of the most interesting things revealed in the production notes is that Carney deliberately avoided creating a traditional hero versus villain dynamic. Danny isn't a monster. Rick isn't perfect. Both make mistakes. Both behave selfishly at times. Both hurt people. Both struggle with their decisions. The film trusts audiences to wrestle with those complexities. And that's becoming increasingly rare. Modern storytelling often prefers clear heroes and clear villains. Power Ballad lives in the uncomfortable gray area between with everyone, even when they disagree with their choices. That's a risky approach, but it often creates the most memorable stories because real life rarely offers simple answers. The film's emotional depth also extends into Rick's family relationships. One of the most touching details from the production notes involves the true meaning of how to write a song. For much of the story, people assume it's a romantic ballad. Even Danny believes it was written for a partner. But the truth is much more emotional. Rick wrote it for Asia, his daughter. Suddenly the conflict changes. This isn't merely an artist losing credit. It's a father losing ownership of something profoundly personal. A musical expression of love. A piece of himself. A piece of his relationship with his child. That revelation adds enormous emotional weight to everything that follows. Beth Fallon, who plays Asia, described music in the film as the expression of feelings characters struggle to say directly. That's exactly what How to Write a Song Becomes. It's all the things Rick can't easily put into words. His pride, his love, his hopes, his fears, his regrets. The song becomes his emotional voice. And watching someone else take ownership of that voice is devastating. Yet despite all the pain, all the conflict, and all the difficult questions, Power Ballad never loses sight of hope. In fact, nearly everyone involved with the film highlighted its warmth, its humanity, its humor, its heart. Producer Rebecca O'Flanagan perhaps summed it up best when she said that John Carney's films always come out on the side of humanity. That's a wonderful description. Because no matter how complicated the situations become, Carney remains interested in people. Not plot mechanics, not twists, not spectacle. People. Their flaws, their dreams, their contradictions, their capacity for growth. Power Ballad appears to continue that tradition beautifully. The production notes also reveal how much the theatrical experience mattered to the filmmakers. This wasn't designed as background entertainment. It was designed as an event, something audiences experience together. Marcella Plunkett encouraged viewers to watch the film with a crowd, to feel the laughter, the tension, the emotion, the music together. Paul Rudd echoed those sentiments, describing music as a universal language that bypasses intellectual barriers and goes directly to the gut. Anyone who has ever attended a concert understands exactly what he means. Music can unite complete strangers. It can trigger memories. It can transport you back to specific moments in your life. It can make you laugh, cry, celebrate, reflect. And John Carney wanted Power Ballad to capture that same feeling. In fact, he repeatedly compared the experience of watching the movie to listening to an album, not simply hearing songs, experiencing them, living with them, allowing them to unfold emotionally over time. That philosophy shaped every aspect of the production. The writing, the performances, the music, the cinematography. Everything works together toward that goal. Looking at the finished project as a whole, it's easy to see why so many talented people were eager to join it. Paul Rudd stepping far outside his comfort zone. Nick Jonas bringing personal experiences to the role. Peter McDonald helping write and perform a deeply personal story. John Carney returning to the themes that have defined much of his career. Even the production itself feels like a collaboration built on passion. A group of artists coming together to explore creativity, ambition, friendship, and identity. And perhaps that's the ultimate takeaway from Power Ballad. Not who deserves credit, not who wins, not who loses, but the reminder that success means different things to different people. For some, success is fame. For others, it's family. For others, it's simply knowing that what they created mattered. Power Ballad seems determined to remind audiences that life's greatest achievements are not always the ones the world applauds. Sometimes, they're the relationships we build, the people we love, the moments we share, the songs we leave behind. And maybe that's why this story feels so relatable. Because beneath the music industry setting, beneath the celebrity culture, beneath the comedy and drama, lies a question almost everyone has asked themselves at some point. Did my choices matter? If Power Ballad succeeds the way its creators clearly hope it will, audiences may leave theaters with a surprising answer. Yes, they did. And that may be the most powerful ballad of all. We'd love to hear your thoughts. Thanks for watching, and we'll see you in the next one.

text: I saw Ben McKenzie's new documentary, Everyone Is Lying to You for Money. The documentary follows him as he learns about cryptocurrencies and how he advocates that they are a scam. Have you seen this documentary? What did you think? Drop a comment down below. Ben is an actor with an economics degree. He wrote, directed, and produced the film. As someone who is interested in how finance films use filmmaking techniques to explain financial concepts, I was curious to see how an actor would approach this topic and how it might compare with other finance films. So, let's recap the movie and discuss if it worked as an explanation of cryptocurrency. The film opens with Ben saying that money is trust. Then there is a title sequence where the word scam is emphasized. Ben talks about how he's still known as the guy from The O.C. Now, I never saw The O.C. I just know that The O.C. took Adam Brody away from Gilmore Girls, but that's a discussion for another day. Early in his career, Ben's friend Dave told him to invest in a medical company. Ben ended up losing money on the investment and it taught him this lesson, never invest in what you don't understand. Fast forward to Dave talking to Ben about crypto. Ben doesn't understand crypto, but with his economics degree, he thinks he can figure it out. Ben hires a film crew to follow his journey to learn about crypto. He goes to a Bitcoin conference where, surprise, Bitcoin stops working as a form of payment to vendors at the conference. El Salvador is the first country to declare Bitcoin as a legal currency. Yet Ben cannot find anyone at the market who uses it. Ben is convinced that regular people are losing money to crypto. Ben learns about Celsius, a cryptocurrency claiming to give money back to its users instead of to shareholders. Ben visits with the founder at South by Southwest 2022, pretending to be a gullible actor interested in crypto. He gets several non-answers to his questions. In Florida, a crypto skeptic explains how crypto scams work. Insiders control both buying and selling, which raises the price of a coin. Other users join this bandwagon, but then the insiders cash out, crashing the value of a coin. After Celsius crashes, Ben talks with regular people who invested in it. With the crash, they lost significant money. Several cryptocurrencies fail. Enter Sam Bankman-Fried, who says he can save crypto. He opens FTX, an exchange with multiple cryptocurrencies. He starts pouring money into political donations. Ben sets up an interview with Sam. Now, I saw in interviews about the documentary that this was one of the highlights of the film, and how awkward the interview was as Ben asked difficult questions. To me, it didn't seem that awkward. Sam didn't seem flustered or annoyed by the questions. Sam says that a good use case for crypto is cleaner payments, but Ben says that people don't use it for payments right now. Sam agrees that people are holding crypto as an asset. Ben says that crypto is gambling. Later, FTX crashes. In December 2022, Ben testified on a panel in Congress along with pro-crypto businessman of Shark Tank fame, Kevin O'Leary. Ben emphasizes that regular people have lost money and how crypto is built on a story about the American dream. It's a story with enormous power. Sam Bankman-Fried goes on trial and Ben explains how two lines of code allowed Sam to borrow from users' accounts. Oh, and many of Sam's political donations were illegal. Ben writes a book about what he's learned. As the movie draws to a close, he says that he's learned so much yet had less of an impact than he would have hoped. What filmmaking techniques did Everyone Is Lying use to teach about financial concepts and were they effective? Ben structured the film as a story about his journey to learn about crypto and it was easy to follow. We learned about crypto as he learned about crypto. It was effective and I'll talk more about that in the next section. While Ben does have moments where he explains or narrates, it's juxtaposed with interviews. Whenever Ben explains aspects of how crypto's code works, it's illustrated by an arcade game similar to Donkey Kong. This emphasizes the gamification aspect of crypto. People think they can win this game. I like the connection between crypto's code and video game code. However, there was one aspect where I felt the documentary failed. It does not spend a lot of time explaining the underlying technology of crypto. At the beginning, he talks about how Satoshi wrote the code for Bitcoin and how he created a limit on the number of Bitcoin. And that's pretty much it. There are other references to code and how people trust in the code of cryptocurrency, but never a thorough explanation of how it works. I can see why it may have been left out though. Perhaps it's in the book and perhaps the runtime didn't allow for it. Perhaps other documentaries cover it whereas crypto as a scam might not be as well covered. Perhaps Ben felt it was more important to focus on crypto as a scam than to focus on the technology. Because if it is a scam, then it might not matter exactly how the technology works. And when Ben interviewed people in the industry, they kept talking about the promise of crypto and the future uses of crypto instead of how it works or how it's beneficial right now. It does a great job with the scam part, not so much with the explanation of crypto part. So how does everyone is lying to you compare with other finance films? To be fair, this is a documentary and not a fictionalized film. Ben says early in the documentary that cryptocurrency was created as a response to the 2008 financial crisis. So we'll compare it with films about the subprime mortgage crisis. This documentary reminded me of The Big Short in several ways. We follow Ben as he is learning about the concepts just as The Big Short follows its characters as they learn about the impending 2008 financial crash. Ben talks with people in the industry who are fully invested in crypto despite the warning signs. Just like The Big Short characters talk with people in the banking industry who can't see the impending crisis. It's not just similar to The Big Short in structure, it's also similar in style. Both films feature frenetic editing, irrelevant TV interviews, newsreels, and more. The lack of explanation of crypto's code very much reminded me of Margin Call and the 2008 financial crisis where Margin Call does not explain the exact formula for mortgage-backed securities or the exact math of how it was flawed. But rather relies on the impact of the information. How does Everyone is Lying compare with one of the biggest finance documentaries, Inside Job?
