text: On the way to the biggest race of his life, a hotshot rookie race car gets stranded in a rundown town and learns that winning isn't everything in life… Today we will recap the story of the 2006 movie: Cars. The film starts with two commentators, Bob Cutlass and Darrell Cartrip getting ready for the Dinoco 400, which is the last race in the Piston Cup Series, a highly renowned and distinguished race in America. At this point in the racing season, three drivers are in contention for the Piston Cup Championship, all of whom are tied for the season point's lead. One of the contenders is Strip Weathers, who is popularly known as "The King." He is a seasoned racing veteran and has already won seven Piston Cups to his name. It's widely rumored that he may retire after the current season. Chick Hicks is another experienced racer who has always been a runner-up to The King throughout his career. Lightning McQueen, on the other hand, is a rookie in his first year of racing, and he has been performing exceptionally well. Many believe that he has a chance of winning the Piston Cup, Rookie of the Year, and a Dinoco sponsorship, which would be a remarkable achievement. The time has come for the final race of the season, which will determine the winner of the coveted Piston Cup. During the race, Chick Hicks, who is desperate to win, deliberately collides with another car, causing a massive pileup involving multiple vehicles. Lightning manages to navigate his way through the wreckage and stays in close pursuit of the leading cars. In a bid to maintain his position at the front, McQueen chooses to stay on the track while all the other racers head to the pit. The commentators reveal that Lightning has recently fired his third crew chief and speculate that he prefers to work alone. Throughout the race, Lightning adopts a risky strategy of making brief pit stops each lap to refuel, rather than complete pit stops. However, this plan backfires on the last lap when his tires blow out. Despite this setback, McQueen puts up a brave fight to cross the finish line first, resulting in an absolute dead heat. After the race, reporters approach Lightning for an interview, while the judges argue over the result. During the interview, McQueen reiterates his stance as a "one-man show," and his pit crew, who have grown tired of his disrespectful behavior, quit on the spot. Chick and Lightning exchange insults until The King intervenes and advises McQueen that his attitude is hindering his remarkable talent, and that he cannot win without a good team supporting him. Lightning's idea of a good team is Dinoco, the most prestigious sponsor in the racing circuit and The King's current sponsor. McQueen is convinced that if he wins the Piston Cup, he will be offered a Dinoco sponsorship. A broadcast over the loudspeakers informs everyone that the race has ended in a tie, and a tiebreaker race will be held in California the following week to determine the ultimate winner of the championship. After the announcement, Lightning meets with his transporter, Mack, a 1980 Mack Super-Liner truck. Mack reminds McQueen that he has a personal appearance to make for his sponsor, Rust-Eze. Lightning grudgingly films a commercial for Rust-Eze and interacts with a group of rundown vehicles brought to the event by Rusty and Dusty, the heads of the company. McQueen puts on a show for the crowd, but his dissatisfaction with working for a small-time sponsor is evident. While on the road with Mack, Lightning is determined to arrive in California before any of his competitors. He forbids Mack from stopping to rest and pushes him to drive through the night. However, Mack becomes drowsy on Interstate 40 and is accosted by a group of street racers, causing him to veer onto the shoulder. The rumble strips cause a Lightning figurine to land on the button that opens the back door of the truck, resulting in Lightning falling out while he was asleep. Panicked about being lost, Lightning frantically tries to locate Mack, but he mistakenly follows a Peterbilt truck, believing it to be Mack. The Peterbilt driver rebuffs Lightning, telling him to turn on his headlights. As Lightning McQueen is driving in the countryside, he loses his way and finds himself on a dark road. He speeds past a police car, and the officer begins to pursue him. Thinking he's being shot at when the police car backfires, Lightning speeds up even more, losing control of his vehicle and getting caught in some power lines. His car spins out of control and crashes through a small town, creating a huge tear in the street before finally stopping in front of the local sheriff. The following day, Mack arrives at the racetrack without Lightning and a search team sets out to locate him. Meanwhile, Lightning regains consciousness to find himself immobilized by a parking clamp in an impound lot, where he meets a rusty tow truck named Mater. Mater informs him that he's in a small town called Radiator Springs, located near the old U.S. Route 66. Soon after, the local Sheriff arrives to take Lightning to court for causing damage to the town's main street. Lightning finds himself facing the wrath of the other residents of Radiator Springs, including Fillmore, who sells organic fuel, Luigi and Guido, who run a tire shop, Ramone, who specializes in car paint and body work, Flo, who runs a gas station and cafe, Sarge, a Humvee that sells surplus parts, Lizzie, an antiques dealer, and Red, the town's fire truck. All of them are furious with Lightning for his reckless driving, which caused a significant amount of damage to the town. In Radiator Springs, Doc Hudson is both the town's judge and physician. When he arrives to try Lightning's case, he is initially prepared to give the racer a harsh sentence. However, after a closer look, Doc orders Lightning to be thrown out of town. A new arrival, Sally Carrera, interrupts the proceedings, and Lightning is immediately taken with her. Sally is actually the town's attorney, and she convinces Doc to sentence Lightning to community service to repair the damage he caused to the road. Doc ultimately agrees and tells Lightning he can leave once the road is fixed, which he estimates will take about five days. Mater brings out Bessie, a large machine used for asphalt paving. After Lightning's parking boot is removed, he tries to escape but only manages to travel a short distance before breaking down. Sally and the Sheriff catch up with him and mock his failed attempt, revealing that they had drained his gas tank. The townsfolk observe as Lightning starts repairing the road. Lightning tries to impress them with his celebrity status, hoping to be released from his sentence. He manages to grab Luigi's attention by mentioning his career as a racecar, but Luigi quickly loses interest when he realizes that Lightning is not a real Formula One racecar. Lightning remembering the agreement that he will be released once the road is finished, Lightning pushes the paving machine to the limit, resulting in a rough and uneven surface. The people of Radiator Springs are offended by his behavior and shoddy work. Doc proposes a race to settle the matter: if Lightning wins, he will be set free; if Doc wins, Lightning must remove the current layer of pavement and start over. Although Lightning underestimates Doc's ability, he agrees to the challenge. At a nearby dirt track, Lightning takes off at top speed, while Doc stays still. However, when Lightning hits the dirt on the first turn, his tires give out and he crashes, allowing Doc to win by default. Reluctantly, Lightning goes back to work, scraping up the pavement as he grumbles. Despite offers of help from the townspeople, such as Luigi's tire sales, Fillmore's organic fuel, and Ramone's custom paint jobs, Lightning is too frustrated to accept their assistance. The next day, Doc inspects the progress of the road and finds that only one-third of it is completed. He discusses this with the Sheriff, who tells him that Lightning had run out of asphalt while working and had spent the entire night trying to navigate the troublesome turn that caused him to crash earlier. Doc advises Lightning to "turn right to go left," but he is initially doubtful. After trying it out, Lightning loses control and ends up falling off the cliff. As Lightning resumes paving the road, one of his tires develops a slow leak. Guido, who dreams of working in a real racetrack pit stop, comes to fix it. Sally is impressed by Lightning's hard work and how he has positively impacted the town, so she offers him a room at the Cozy Cone motel instead of spending another night in the impound. Lightning can't resist the offer and decides to stay there. The Sheriff assigns Mater to keep an eye on Lightning for the night. Mater takes Lightning to a remote field and introduces him to tractor-tipping, which involves sneaking up on a sleeping tractor and startling it, causing it to rear up on its back wheels. Mater demonstrates it but is only able to tip one tractor at a time. Lightning takes it up a notch and tips over every single tractor. They almost get caught by Frank, the large threshing machine in charge of the tractors, and must make a quick escape. On their way back to town, Mater shows off his remarkable skill of driving in reverse, which impresses Lightning. Mater considers Lightning to be his "best friend," and Lightning appears to be touched by his affection. The following day, Lightning is waiting at Doc's garage for his daily gas allowance when he stumbles upon Doc's dusty workshop. Inside, he discovers that Doc is actually the legendary Hudson Hornet, a racecar with a record-breaking 27 wins in a single season in 1952. Lightning is amazed by the trophies and racing memorabilia on display, but Doc dismisses them as mere "empty cups" and refuses to talk about his racing career. Later, Sally takes Lightning on a tour of Radiator Springs, explaining its history and significance as a famous stop along U.S. Route 66. However, when Interstate 40 was built, the town was bypassed, causing it to fall into decline as almost no one travels through it anymore. The next day, the town is thrown into chaos as the tractors run amok through the streets. While helping to corral them, Lightning catches a glimpse of Doc racing around a dirt track outside of town. Curious, he confronts Doc and questions why he never pursued a racing career with his obvious talent. After some prodding, Doc reveals the truth: he was actually forced into retirement by the racing organization after a horrific crash left him sidelined for an entire season. When he finally recovered and attempted to return, the sponsors passed him over for a hotshot rookie, just like they did with Lightning. Doc had given up on racing altogether until he met Lightning, who reminded him of his own younger self. The following day, the townsfolk wake up to discover that the road is now complete. Although he finally has the opportunity to leave, Lightning chooses to stay and accept the services of the locals, including new fuel from Fillmore, tires from Luigi, and a new paint job from Ramone. As the town celebrates late into the night over their new road, a swarm of reporters and media vehicles descend upon Radiator Springs to take McQueen back. Lightning doesn't have the chance to explain anything or speak to any of the townsfolk before he's loaded onto Mack and sent back to California. Sally discovers that Doc tipped off the media to Lightning's whereabouts and is angry with him. After arriving in California, Lightning prepares for the big race with Mack serving as his pit crew. The King and Chick Hicks get off to a decent start, but Lightning's memories of Sally and his time in Radiator Springs interfere with his performance and cause him to lose time. When McQueen attempts to compose himself, he hears Doc's voice over the radio. Doc, along with the majority of the Radiator Springs locals, has arrived to provide support and assist Lightning as his pit crew. Doc is now the crew chief and is adorned in his former paint job. The audience's cameras spot Doc in the midst of the crowd and acknowledge the return of the renowned Hudson Hornet. In a desperate attempt to catch up with the others, Lightning accelerates out of the pit area. As the race approaches its end, Chick collides with Lightning, causing him to spin out of control. However, Chick is caught off guard when Lightning unexpectedly zooms past him, driving in reverse. Later on, Hicks tries to push McQueen off the track, causing Lightning to experience a tire blowout. Guido, who is prepared for Lightning's arrival, executes the quickest pit stop in Piston Cup history by single-handedly changing all four tires in less than four seconds. The forklifts on Chick's pit crew are amazed and drop their mustache-shaped grilles in surprise. Guido proudly taunts Chick's crew, exclaiming "Peet stop!" As the three racers approach the last lap, Lightning secures the top position. However, Chick strikes Lightning once again, causing him to veer off the track. Lightning regains the lead by turning his wheels hard to the right while sliding to the left, regaining the top position. In a final attempt to win, Chick intentionally collides with The King, causing him to flip multiple times through the air and land heavily damaged on the infield. Upon witnessing the state of The King, Lightning abruptly stops in his tracks, recalling Doc's fate. As a result, Chick Hicks is able to cross the finish line first, taking the top spot. Lightning goes back to help The King, pushing him the remainder of the way to the finish line, allowing the well-known competitor to finish his last race with dignity. Parroting Doc's words, Lightning tells The King that the Piston Cup is merely "an empty cup." Chick Hicks is awarded the Piston Cup, but the crowd boos and ridicules him for his unethical behavior, rendering his victory meaningless. In contrast, Lightning is applauded and praised for his sportsmanlike conduct. Tex, the head of Dinoco, offers Lightning a sponsorship due to his exceptional performance. Although Lightning contemplates the offer, he ultimately decides to remain with Rust-Eze, the company that gave him his big break. Guido and Luigi are amazed when a real Ferrari arrives at their store, as Lightning McQueen had previously recommended it as the best place in the world to get tires. McQueen returns to Radiator Springs and chooses to establish his headquarters in the town, restoring its fame and leading to the maps being redrawn as "Historic Route 66." Thank you for tuning in to our Alpha Recaps channel where we discussed the beloved animated film, Cars. We hope that our recap has reminded you of the heartwarming message of friendship, hard work, and perseverance that this movie portrays. From Lightning McQueen's journey from a self-centered racer to a humble friend, to the quaint and charming town of Radiator Springs, Cars has captured the hearts of both children and adults alike. We hope that our recap has reignited your love for this timeless classic and that you will continue to join us for future movie discussions. Thank you for your support, and we'll see you in the next one!

text: On July 16, 1988, a singularity struck the city of Tokyo in Japan, destroying the entire region and initiating World War III. After the war ended, the city was rebuilt on a large artificial island in Tokyo Bay and renamed as Neo-Tokyo. Thirty-one years after the calamity in 2019, Neo-Tokyo is still recovering. However, the place is now plagued by corruption, anti-government groups, terrorism, and gang violence. The industrializing city has the atmosphere of a city in collapse. Amidst the chaos of Neo-Tokyo, there is a biker gang called "The Capsules" led by Shotaro Kaneda, with members Tetsuo Shima, Yamagata, Kaisuke, and three others who are not important. This group engages in various criminal activities, mainly vandalism and fighting with other gangs. One day, Kaneda and his group face off against some members of a gang called "The Clowns." The chase between them extends through the streets of Neo-Tokyo. Despite being teenagers, Kaneda and his group are not afraid to confront the authorities. During the clash with the other gang, the police are called, but this does not scare Kaneda and his gang. Meanwhile, not far from there, a severely injured man is carrying what appears to be a child to another location, but he is being pursued by the police. The man and the child pass near a police blockade due to protests. Because he was armed, the police did not hesitate to fire warning shots. Among the protesters, another man and a woman watch everything, trying to get closer. The man hit by the warning shots, in his last breaths, tells the child to find Ryu. This child has a different appearance because he is an Esper. Espers, also known as Numbers, are government test subjects for a project called ESP that started a few decades ago. These test subjects are children with psychic powers. Currently, there are three known Espers: Numbers 25, 26, and 27. When Number 26, Takashi, sees the man dead in front of him, his abilities temporarily go out of control, causing great destruction in the area. Because of this, chaos ensues, and soon after, Takashi disappears, and a general fight breaks out. The man who was watching from afar is called Ryu, and the woman is Kei. They were there to meet Takashi, but because of all this chaos, they lost sight of their target. Elsewhere, another Esper, this time Number 27, Masaru, senses Takashi's powers, indicating to Colonel Shikishima where to find the lost test subject. Meanwhile, Kaneda and his gang continue pursuing the rival gang. While crossing a bridge, Tetsuo ends up going ahead. Tetsuo and Kaneda are best friends. Since childhood, Kaneda has always protected Tetsuo, but Tetsuo himself did not like it very much. He wanted to prove that he could take care of himself. Tetsuo manages to get rid of the other gang members but suffers a severe accident when Takashi suddenly appears in front of him and blows up the bike Tetsuo was riding. A few minutes later, Kaneda and the others arrive at the scene where Tetsuo is. They find their friend badly injured but still alive. Kaneda sees the strange boy walking away from the scene, but before he can confront him, the army arrives. Masaru convinces Takashi to go with them as they would not survive long without the army's help. At the same time, Kaneda's group is surrounded. Since they are just teenagers, the soldiers only detain them, except for Tetsuo, who is taken along. Kaneda and the other gang members are taken for interrogation, but the only charge they face is public disturbance. Besides, they are all still teenagers, so they end up getting released. After the chaos caused by Takashi's attack, several people were arrested by the police, and one of them was Kei. While waiting to be released, Kaneda became interested in her. Suddenly, in the interrogation room, a terrorist attacks the guards and tries to blow up the place, but luckily, the grenade he was using didn't work, and he ended up being subdued. With the confusion over, Kaneda and his friends are released. Before leaving, Kaneda claims there is another member of their group. Since the guard didn't know any of them, Kaneda managed to get Kei released, but this was only because he was interested in her. As they leave, Kei has more important things to do than pay attention to a teenager, so she abandons Kaneda as soon as she meets her partner, who had also been arrested. Meanwhile, due to the current state of public calamity in Neo-Tokyo, Colonel Shikishima is under increasing pressure from the government since he is supposed to be responsible for keeping the city under control. However, the Colonel is currently focused on a more important project. After Tetsuo was taken by the army, he underwent some tests. Doctor Onishi discovered that Tetsuo has an energy pattern similar to Akira's and might be the key to understanding Akira's growth process. Since the data they have is old, they will need to conduct more tests. The problem is that Tetsuo could become violent, so they will need to control him to prevent the events of 31 years ago from happening again. Despite this, the Colonel is unsure if they are capable of handling such immense power—the power of God. If the situation gets out of control, they will have to kill the boy. Back to Kaneda and the others, after receiving punishment at school, the group decides to take a ride. They still don't know what happened to Tetsuo; they were only informed that he was taken to a hospital, but no one said which hospital. Meanwhile, at some hospital, Tetsuo managed to escape. Not knowing where to go, he went to find his girlfriend, Kaori. Tetsuo is still a bit dazed from the tests, but he doesn't want to go back to the hospital, so he decides to flee with Kaori. The next morning, they steal Kaneda's bike. Tetsuo always wanted to have his friend's bike, but Kaneda never let anyone else ride it since no one but him knew how to handle it. Unfortunately, as they flee, members of the Clowns gang are nearby, and to make matters worse, Kaneda was right about using his bike; Tetsuo can't make it work properly. This gives the Clowns an opportunity to get close and violently attack them. Luckily, Kaneda wouldn't let anyone take his bike, even his best friend, and it doesn't take long for Kaneda and the others to find Tetsuo. Even as a teenager, Kaneda commands respect from any gang. After being saved, Tetsuo vents his anger on one of the rival gang members, showing signs of losing control. Kaneda tries to stop him, but this only makes Tetsuo angrier because he is tired of Kaneda trying to boss him around. Tetsuo's mind begins to suffer from the effects of his latent power, and he has visions he can't understand. He feels a severe headache followed by hallucinations. Due to the psychic waves Tetsuo is emitting, Doctor Onishi is able to locate him, and once again, he is taken away by the army, with his friends unable to do anything to stop it. Later that day, Kaneda, Yamagata, and Kaisuke are still frustrated about losing their friend again. While thinking about what to do, they notice a nearby attack by revolutionary members. Yamagata and Kaisuke decide to leave to avoid getting caught up in another problem, but Kaneda realizes that the girl he helped at the police station is part of the incident, so he decides to get involved too. Ryu and Kei escape to an abandoned building where they decide to split up to evade the soldiers. Kei goes through the sewer system but is soon surprised by some guards and ends up cornered. Luckily for her, Kaneda was following all along and managed to surprise one of the guards but found himself in another guard's sights. This made Kei react instinctively, shooting the guard. As more guards approached, Kaneda grabbed Kei and fled. Despite being a member of the revolutionary group, Kei had never taken a life before. Meanwhile, Tetsuo was having memories of his past, from when he lived in an orphanage. However, his memories began to be affected as if his mind was shattering, a reflection of his growing power. Elsewhere, Doctor Onishi and Colonel Shikishima are with another Esper, Kiyoko, Number 25. She had a dream where she saw Neo-Tokyo being destroyed and the Espers meeting Akira again. Before falling asleep, Kiyoko warned them not to let the fourth boy continue. Onishi suspects that Kiyoko had a premonition, suggesting that a new singularity might occur. If this is indeed true, the government needs to be alerted. The colonel, the doctor, and a few scientists go to a secret underground laboratory to verify if Kiyoko's premonition is related to past events. This is the place where Akira is sealed. Far away, Kei and Kaneda arrive at one of the revolutionary hideouts. When they meet the other members, Ryu and the others are not pleased with Kaneda's presence, fearing he might be a spy. Despite this, Kaneda only got involved in the whole mess because he was interested in Kei. The rebels are devising a new plan to try to invade the government laboratory. The man who died trying to protect Takashi was part of the rebel group. At that time, the rebels believed Takashi was Akira and tried to rescue him from the military but failed. Now, the objective is to collect data on the new specimen. According to Ryu, during the escape of Subject 26, a boy was injured and taken as a new human test subject. They are talking about Tetsuo. While they were discussing, they heard a noise coming from the ventilation ducts and found Kaneda eavesdropping on the conversation. Kaneda explains the situation to everyone; he knows the person Ryu is talking about and wants to help. Thus, Kaneda inadvertently ends up joining the rebels. Later, Ryu meets with a government parliament member, Mr. Nezu, who is also the leader of the terrorist resistance movement against the government, a group that Ryu, Kei, and now Kaneda are part of. Nezu is responsible for passing information to the rebels. Ryu informs him about Kaneda's entry into the group. They still don't know if the boy can be trusted, but Kaneda knows too much to be discarded. Even though they are fighting against the corrupt government and trying to save Neo-Tokyo, they know they won't be the ones to see the city saved. They are fighting for future generations. Besides the terrorist groups, there are also those who believe that Akira is the world's salvation and are waiting for his return. This quasi-religious group rejects science and is led by Lady Miyako. The city of Neo-Tokyo is in a state of calamity. Terrorist activities led by anti-government groups have increased, the public security budget is overstretched, and there is also the problem of information leaks about the test subjects. All this has fallen on the shoulders of Colonel Shikishima. To make matters worse, due to the premonitions of Number 25, he wants an even larger budget for military experiments. Adding to the fact that the colonel's influence within the army is very high, his presence has become a problem for government parliamentarians. Taking advantage of this situation, the parliamentarians decided to oppose the Colonel, using the excuse that he is spending all the funds that should be used for the reconstruction of Neo-Tokyo and accusing him of being responsible for leaking information about Akira to the public since this project was supposed to be secret. In truth, they are just a bunch of corrupt officials trying to seize control of the city. With his hands tied, the Colonel can do nothing, so the parliamentarians decide to remove him by placing him on an inquiry committee. Meanwhile, in a hospital, the rebels begin their plan entering the government facilities in disguise. In the same place, Tetsuo is being held and is beginning to awaken his powers. While in his room, Tetsuo starts having new visions. He is initially dazed, not knowing if what he sees is real, but these visions gradually become more terrifying and seem to attack him. Not understanding what is happening, Tetsuo tries to escape while his entire room transforms into toys. Scared, Tetsuo releases his power and accidentally injures himself by stepping on a glass. The blood frightens the monsters, revealing them to be the Espers, who were trying to attack Tetsuo but soon disappear. However, this failed attempt to stop Tetsuo only makes him angrier. Using his power, Tetsuo locates the room where the other children are and takes his fury out on his enemies, starting a violent rampage against everyone in his path. Elsewhere in the building, the rebels continue trying to find a way to the test subjects, but they are discovered. Due to the chaos Tetsuo is causing, the number of guards has increased, causing the rebels to fail in their plans once again. During the fight, Kaneda manages to recover one of the bikes being used by the guards and saves Kei from the attack. The problem is that he left the rest of the group behind. At that moment, inside the hospital, Kiyoko sensed Kei's presence in the building. While trying to pilot the flying bike, Kaneda and Kei hear about Tetsuo's rampage on the radio, so they decide to try to find him. Inside the building, soldiers are trying to stop Tetsuo, but his powers are evolving at a frighteningly rapid pace, leaving destruction and death in his wake. No weapon can stop him, and he reaches the children's room. The place looks like a large kindergarten with various toys scattered around. The Espers try to scare Tetsuo again, but this time he is prepared; the illusions no longer work. Now that he knows he can use powers, the small Espers stand no chance and can only escape. To seek help, Kiyoko uses her powers to control Kei's mind and guide Kaneda to where they are. The three Espers gather, and Takashi and Masaru use their powers to protect Kiyoko. Of the three, Kiyoko is the most physically fragile, which is why she spends so much time in bed. But even with the combined efforts of the two Espers, Tetsuo proves superior. Despite his power having only recently awakened, he already has better control. At this moment, Shikishima and Onishi also arrive in the room with other guards, Tetsuo is still adapting to so much power, and his mind can't handle the energy for long. The pain and confusion only make Tetsuo even more angry with everyone. Kiyoko tries to warn Tetsuo that bad things can happen if he continues to use his power this way, but Tetsuo no longer listens to anyone. Kiyoko continues to say that if Tetsuo doesn't stop, someone stronger might appear. If he keeps pushing his power, Akira might return, and no one will be able to prevent the singularity. The energy that Tetsuo feels trying to invade his mind, he believes to be Akira, and because of this, he wants to find him. Tetsuo begins his attack against everyone. Kaneda and Kei manage to reach the floor where the chaos is happening, and without wasting time, they head to the room. The place is already a complete mess, but Kaneda arrives to save Tetsuo once again. However, now with so much power, Tetsuo can finally take care of himself and no longer needs to depend on anyone, just as he always wanted. But the power has gone to his head; Tetsuo is completely out of control, even attacking his own friend. Kiyoko tries to stop Tetsuo, but he uses his power to read her mind, discovering that Akira is hidden beneath the Olympic stadium. After this, Tetsuo flies out of the building, leaving everything behind. Kiyoko warns the Colonel that Tetsuo is heading towards Akira, and they cannot let the two meet. Kei recognizes Kiyoko as the child who was invading her mind. After this, Kei and Kaneda are arrested. Outside, Colonel Shikishima is gathering his soldiers to attack Tetsuo, but he is stopped by a government representative. According to the inquiry, Colonel Shikishima has been accused of military conspiracy and must leave his post immediately. However, Shikishima is a man of few words and orders one of his soldiers to shoot the representative. Before a military war can start, Shikishima tells all the soldiers that they must stop acting under the orders of a corrupt government and should fight for the city. With his strong influence, Shikishima declares a state of emergency and stages a military coup, ordering the arrest of all government members. Elsewhere, Yamagata and Kaisuke are worried about their friends since they haven't heard from Kaneda and Tetsuo for a while. They go to a bar they used to frequent together, but when they arrive, they find the place completely destroyed and the bartender dead. They soon realize that Tetsuo was nearby. Tetsuo is now clearly unstable and highly drugged. Yamagata tries to confront him, but things get out of control again. Meanwhile, in prison, Kei tells Kaneda about Akira. She says that Akira is like an absolute energy, a power that exists within all things. This power gives humans energy and knowledge, allowing the evolution of everything from a tiny cell to the universe itself. It is the power of creation and destruction. However, if this power, which exceeds universal capacities, were generated by something with the sole purpose of destruction, it could mean the end of everything. This is what Tetsuo has become, and this was the power the government wanted to control, which led to Tokyo's destruction 31 years ago. Kaneda thought he was talking to Kei, but it was actually Kiyoko controlling her again. Suddenly, the cell door opens, and the two can escape. In the city, the army mobilizes. The primary objective is to capture Subject 41, but the problem is that he is leaving a trail of destruction wherever he goes. Kaisuke finds Kaneda near the bar and tells him that Yamagata was killed by Tetsuo. Now Kaneda knows there's no other way—he needs to put an end to his childhood friend because, at that time, the "talk no jutsu" hadn't been invented yet. Before heading to the confrontation, Kaneda pays tribute to Yamagata by taking his friend's bike for one last ride. At this moment, Takashi appears and takes Kei away, and they disappear in front of Kaneda. Kaneda thinks all of this is Takashi's fault, but Kiyoko's voice resonates in his mind, saying that Akira's power has been within everyone since the beginning. Once this power awakens, it is up to each person to choose wisely how to use it. Some people may not be ready for it, as in Tetsuo's case. Kiyoko considers Tetsuo a friend and feels partly responsible for everything that is happening. That's why they took Kei; she can help fight Tetsuo. Although Kaneda isn't too happy about this, Tetsuo is his best friend, and if anyone is going to kill him, it should be him. Meanwhile, the city of Neo-Tokyo couldn't be in a worse situation. Due to the coup d'état, Nezu attempts to flee the country. Despite his facade of wanting to help the rebels overthrow the corrupt government, Nezu was just as corrupt as all the other politicians. The difference was that he was using the rebels to take control of the city. When the parliament was overthrown, Nezu planned to rule Neo-Tokyo. However, his plans were thwarted by Colonel Shikishima's actions. While Nezu was packing to flee, Ryu appears in front of him. Believing he was betrayed by Ryu, Nezu shoots him fatally, although Ryu had done nothing and was already severely injured. He took the shot for nothing. On the streets of the city, which is already in complete chaos due to Tetsuo's actions, Nezu suffers a heart attack. He tries to take his medication but ends up dying in an alley. Ryu, even mortally wounded, manages to follow Nezu almost like a ghost haunting him, but Ryu also doesn't survive for long and dies shortly after. The city is in a state of destruction, violence, and disorder. When the population sees Tetsuo's actions, they believe him to be Akira. Some begin to follow him as his devotees, while others flee, and the police attack. A true war is unfolding. Not far away, Kaori watches her boyfriend's actions on TV and goes to meet him. Although Tetsuo can fly, he makes a point of walking to the stadium just to destroy more things along the way. Lady Miyako's group follows Tetsuo, believing he is Akira, at least until partway there. When they reach a bridge protected by soldiers, Tetsuo destroys everything, killing both his followers, including Lady Miyako, and the soldiers. In another part of the city, Dr. Onishi monitors Tetsuo's energy. He realizes that the test subject's energy is synchronizing with the data they have on Akira's energy, proving they were right about Tetsuo's potential. After brutally making his way through the city, Tetsuo finally reaches his destination, although the excess energy he is using is starting to affect him. But now nothing will stop him from meeting Akira. Upon entering the underground laboratory, Tetsuo finds Kei being controlled by the Espers, and they engage in battle. Since Tetsuo refuses to listen to anyone, the only option is to defeat him. At the same time, Kaneda arrives at the scene. He takes the opportunity to equip himself with one of the laser weapons the soldiers were using. His goal now is no longer to talk. Back to the battle, Tetsuo manages to remove Akira's container from the underground. But the Espers haven't given up yet. Kei's latent power is strong enough to keep her in the battle for a while. The fight between the two destroys the containment capsule, but in the end, Tetsuo emerges victorious. Now that no one is around, he can finally release Akira. When Tetsuo opens the last layer of the capsule, the only things he finds are test tubes containing frozen human remains. Shikishima approaches and says that this is Akira, or at least what remains of him after his awakening. While trying to convince Tetsuo that Akira no longer exists, Shikishima tells his soldiers to prepare the SOL, the Satellite Orbital Laser. But Tetsuo is still not satisfied. If Akira no longer exists, then no one can stop him. Kaneda approaches his old friend, ready to do whatever it takes to stop this madness. Using the rifle, Kaneda begins his attack. The laser is strong enough to wound Tetsuo's body, but his psychic powers protect him and make it difficult for Kaneda to land a precise shot. During the confrontation, Kaneda takes advantage of a distraction to try a shoot, but unfortunately, the weapon runs out of charge at the critical moment. Now without a weapon, Kaneda doesn't have many options. However, they are not the only ones fighting. From space, a burst of energy begins to concentrate and a powerful shot hits directly, tearing off Tetsuo's arm. Kaneda, seizing the opportunity, tries to crush his friend with a rock, but another shot from the satellite nearly hits them both. Kaneda is saved only because Tetsuo creates a protective barrier that, luckily, covers Kaneda too. Tetsuo then flies into space and begins pulling the satellite back into orbit. On Earth, Kaisuke arrives to help Kaneda and Kei, who were almost caught in the satellite's blasts. The Colonel has lost his main weapon and there isn't much they can do now. In the satellite's debris, Tetsuo uses metal parts to create a new artificial arm. The Espers prepare for the moment when Tetsuo's power reaches its peak. In the 1960s, years before the events that led to Tokyo's destruction, the government initiated a project called the ESP Project. This military project aimed to develop psychic abilities in humans. Forty subjects were used in this project. The Espers, or Numbers, were children who demonstrated extraordinary psychic abilities. They underwent a series of tests and training to develop this power. Among the known subjects were Numbers 25, 26, and 27: Kiyoko, Takashi, and Masaru. But there were others, such as Subject 19, also known as Lady Miyako, and Subject 28. The majority of the subjects died due to brain injuries or failed to develop their psychic potential. Those who survived suffered side effects from the excessive use of inhibitory drugs to try to control their powers. The drugs stunted the children's physical growth but not their biological aging, which is why Kiyoko and the others have their appearance. Additionally, some developed certain diseases, such as Masaru, who has polio, and Kiyoko, who is bedridden. The drug also limited brain development to prevent the children's powers from going out of control. This is why, despite so much time passing, they still have a childlike mentality. This was how the scientists attempted to control the powers, but one subject exceeded the predicted limits. On July 16, 1988, the power of Subject 28 grew unimaginably, causing the singularity that destroyed Tokyo. This subject was named Akira. Since the ESP Project was a secret, the world believed this energy was the detonation of a bomb, which led to a new world war. After the city's destruction, scientists managed to recover Akira's body and dissected it to try to understand the pattern of sudden growth, but they couldn't find an answer. Fearing that something like this could happen again, the scientists placed Akira's remains in containers and cryogenically froze them in an underground container. Soon after, the project was shut down, the remaining children were isolated, and all information about the project was erased, making Akira's existence a controversial issue among the upper echelons of Japanese politics, with many even questioning if Akira really existed. Five years before the current events, the project was reactivated under Colonel Shikishima's command, who sought to obtain this power to restore order in Neo-Tokyo. During this time, various pieces of information about the project and Akira began leaking to the public, giving rise to the rebel group that Kei and Ryu are part of. When the rebels managed to kidnap Takashi, leading to Tetsuo's accident, the scientists noticed a similarity between Tetsuo's power and Akira's, so they made him Subject 41. The scientists believed they could control Tetsuo's power with the technology they currently had. Since most of the data on Akira was erased, they didn't have much information about the events of 1988. However, Tetsuo has been unstable from the beginning, leading to this wave of destruction. Before preparing for the next attack on Tetsuo, Colonel Shikishima goes to Dr. Onishi and discovers that the doctor has been hiding the analysis results showing Tetsuo's energy in sync with Akira's, meaning Tetsuo poses a real threat to the world. Despite this, Onishi still wants to use him in his experiments. Kaneda also prepares for the attack, ensuring that the laser rifle won't fail again. Later, Kaori goes to the stadium where Tetsuo is. She wants to know what is happening to him, but at this moment, Tetsuo is suffering from the side effects of his own power. Not only his mind but now his body is being affected. The Colonel also arrives, this time to talk. He knows Tetsuo needs inhibitors and tries to convince him to return to the hospital, but Tetsuo refuses. However, his powers are reaching a critical state, and his body is undergoing an irreversible transformation. Tetsuo attacks the Colonel as his arm begins to deform. Luckily, Kaneda appears and saves Shikishima, and the two former best friends begin their final battle. Tetsuo continues to overuse his power, pushing his body to the limit. His energy is reaching its maximum point, so the Espers decide it's time to intervene. Takashi protects Kaneda from Tetsuo's attack while Kiyoko and Masaru go to the remains of Akira that Tetsuo had kept. Kaneda takes this chance to attack again, which triggers Tetsuo's energy to go completely out of control. His body starts to transform into a giant mass of flesh, as if a new form of life is being born. During the transformation, Tetsuo absorbs Kaori and then Kaneda into his body. Meanwhile, the Espers gather near Akira's capsules. Inside the mass of flesh, Tetsuo's mutant body begins to form and destroy itself simultaneously, which unfortunately causes Kaori's death due to the pressure. Kaneda, luckily, still has the rifle and uses it to cut through the flesh and free himself. Despite losing control of his powers, Tetsuo is still conscious and desperately asks his friend for help, but no one understands what's happening to him. Tetsuo's body continues to grow and transform into something never seen before. The Colonel tries to protect the Espers who were almost devoured by Tetsuo's body until Akira finally appears before them. Despite his appearance, Akira's body is spiritual, as he had transcended to a higher form beyond human limitations. Akira's energy starts to repel Tetsuo's body, and then the Singularity occurs. Kiyoko protects the Colonel by sending him to a place far from the explosion. At this moment, the energy begins to absorb everything in its path. Kaneda tries to help his friend and is caught in the power. Takashi decides to help; Kaneda is the least culpable in this mess. He was dragged into it by chance to save a friend. Masaru warns that they might not be able to escape, but Takashi enters the energy, followed by Masaru and Kiyoko. Even if they are not strong enough to escape, they still can save Kaneda. Just like 31 years ago, a massive energy explosion consumes the city, devastating everything in its path. While inside the energy, Kaneda experiences Tetsuo's memories from when they were in the orphanage during childhood and also the memories of the Espers from when they were part of the government project. The Espers tell Kaneda that they called Akira and that Tetsuo will now be taken to another place, a safe place. Additionally, Kiyoko says that Kei is also starting to awaken. Kaneda is sent to one last memory, from when he and Tetsuo became friends, and finally, Kaneda wakes up outside the explosion. Akira's energy spread over a large part of Neo-Tokyo, destroying the city again. The rapidly expanding energy reverses into a black hole, contracting and pulling everything around it. Dr. Onishi remained analyzing the energy data, but this prevented him from escaping, and he ended up caught in the impact. However, in his final analysis, he concluded that the generated energy is similar to the birth of the universe. With the disappearance of the energy, all that remained was a large crater, and Neo-Tokyo, located in Tokyo Bay, was flooded due to the explosion. When Tetsuo was attacking a rival gang member and began to awaken his abilities, the visions he had were precisely of these events. At that time, he felt the moment when the Espers called for Akira and the transformations his body would undergo. When Akira awoke, Tetsuo's energy was already greater than Akira's, so he used his power to neutralize Tetsuo's energy, completely absorbing his body and taking Tetsuo to an empty place in space-time, where Tetsuo now has full control of his powers to create a new universe. Like Akira, Tetsuo also transcended, becoming a god. The Espers were also taken with Akira, and they were the ones who brought Kaneda back with the help of Kei's latent powers, allowing Kaneda to be 'pulled' out of the Singularity, showing that now there will be people who will develop these powers naturally and gradually. Thus ends the events of Neo-Tokyo's destruction, exactly as Kiyoko's premonition showed her. Kaneda, Kei, and Kaisuke survived, as did the Colonel. Kaneda doesn't exactly know what happened—Tetsuo, Akira, and the children disappeared—but he believes they are still out there somewhere, as an energy present in all things, from a tiny cell to the universe itself. The power of creation and destruction— if this power, which exceeds universal capacities, were generated by something with the sole purpose of creating, it could mean the beginning of everything.

text: Spa weekend begins with four childhood friends who have reached very different points in their adult lives. Jane, Sophie, Coco, and Mel have known each other for years, but growing responsibilities, relationships, and personal problems have slowly pushed them apart. Jane has perhaps the most overwhelming life of all. She is a lawyer, a single mother of two children, and also responsible for caring for her elderly father. Her schedule is so packed that even making plans with friends requires arranging dates months in advance. She has become so focused on taking care of everyone else that there is almost no space left for herself. Sophie is dealing with a completely different kind of pressure. She works as a personal assistant for a wealthy billionaire named Toby, but the job has taken over her life. Toby constantly demands her attention and treats her as though she has no personal life outside of serving his needs. Coco is recently divorced and carrying plenty of unresolved anger. Her relationship with her former husband Roger ended badly, and she is not fully moved on from either the marriage or the emotions surrounding its collapse. Then there is Mel. Unlike the others, Mel has plenty of money and appears to be living a carefree life in Europe. She made her fortune through an online business that she insists is completely legitimate, despite the fact that everyone else seems slightly suspicious of it. Mel is loud, chaotic, and completely incapable of filtering her thoughts, which is exactly why her friends sometimes love her and sometimes desperately need a break from her. Coco decides that the group needs to reconnect and suggests a luxury spa weekend in Palm Springs for Jane's upcoming birthday. >> [music] >> The idea is simple. Relax, enjoy massages, eat healthy food, and spend some peaceful time together. But there is one important detail. Jane, Sophie, and Coco intentionally do not invite Mel. They know exactly what will happen if Mel arrives. Their peaceful weekend will probably turn into a disaster. Sophie eventually feels guilty and invites her at the last minute, secretly hoping that Mel will not actually be able to come. Of course, Mel arrives. From the moment she appears at Solaris Eden Beach, it becomes obvious that the weekend is not going to follow the original plan. The spa is built around calm energy, meditation, healthy living, and peaceful self-reflection. Mel immediately clashes with all of it. She mocks the spiritual atmosphere, makes fun of the yoga sessions, and has absolutely no interest in quietly following the rules. Instead of adapting to the spa, Mel slowly forces the entire spa experience to adapt around her chaos. But underneath all the destruction, Mel also begins interfering in her friends' lives in ways that unexpectedly expose what each of them has been avoiding. For Jane, Mel creates an opportunity for romance with Kai, the attractive Australian yoga instructor. Jane is initially captivated by him during a sensual tantric hand massage, and their connection eventually develops into something much more physical. However, the relationship also creates an emotional conflict for Jane. Kai appears interested in more than just a temporary encounter, but Jane struggles with the idea of allowing someone new into her life. She has spent so long organizing her entire existence around work, parenting, and family responsibilities that romance feels almost impossible to fit into her carefully controlled world. Mel's interference forces Jane to confront an important question. Has she become so busy taking care of everyone else that she has forgotten she is allowed to want something for herself? Coco's situation becomes equally complicated when Mel arranges for Roger to arrive at the spa. Roger is Coco's ex-husband and his presence immediately brings all of her unresolved feelings back to the surface. The two reconnect despite the complicated history between them and despite Roger now being involved with someone else. Their relationship is not magically repaired by one weekend. Instead, their reunion forces Coco to confront the anger, attraction, and pain that she has been carrying since the divorce. For someone who has been emotionally stuck, even the chaotic reconnection becomes a form of release. Sophie receives perhaps the most unexpected transformation of the entire trip. Mel's interference eventually contributes to Sophie losing her job. >> [music] >> At first, being fired seems like another disaster caused by the weekend's chaos. But Sophie's job was already making her miserable. Toby controlled her time, constantly demanded her attention, and treated her personal life as though it did not matter. So, losing the job becomes less of a tragedy and more of an escape. The peaceful spa weekend then becomes increasingly less peaceful. Mel brings cocaine into the situation. >> [music] >> Drinking and partying take over. Male strippers appear. The women steal a golf cart, which eventually goes over a cliff after they jump out. A goat yoga session turns into complete mayhem when the goats get loose and begin attacking people. The destruction becomes so extreme that the spa's general manager, Shanti, completely loses patience with the group. What was supposed to be a luxury retreat has become a nightmare for everyone working there. Mel's behavior also pushes the friendship itself to its breaking point. >> [music] >> Her jokes, reckless decisions, and constant interference may occasionally lead to something useful, but she has also caused genuine damage and frustration. Eventually, Jane, Sophie, and Coco can no longer ignore the problem. The climax of Spa Weekend comes when the four women finally confront everything that has been building between them. They have not only been separated by busy lives. They have also been avoiding honest conversations with each other. The confrontation with Mel makes them acknowledge that she is exhausting, destructive, and often completely out of control. But the movie also makes an important point about why Mel remains part of their friendship. Mel may have ruined the weekend they planned, but she also forced them to stop pretending that everything in their lives was fine. Jane needed to remember that she could have desires and a life outside of responsibility. Sophie needed to escape a job that was consuming her identity. Coco needed to confront the emotions she still had about Roger and her failed marriage. Mel did not carefully solve these problems. In fact, she mostly created bigger problems while crashing directly into everyone else's lives. But sometimes chaos exposes what comfort allows people to ignore. That is the real meaning behind the ending. The women originally wanted a relaxing weekend where nothing would go wrong. Instead, they got the exact opposite. Their trip was filled with arguments, drugs, damaged property, stolen vehicles, escaped goats, and enough chaos to make Shanti regret ever allowing them inside the spa. Yet, by the end, they realize that the peaceful weekend they wanted was not necessarily what they needed. Their friendship survives because they finally talk honestly about their frustrations and recognize how much their bond still means to them. Despite everything that happened, none of them truly wanted to lose the others. The ending therefore brings Jane, Sophie, Coco, and Mel back together. text: Buddy starts from a premise that on paper could easily be reduced to a macabre parody of Barney. A seemingly harmless children's mascot begins murdering the kids who live inside his show. But Casper Kelly uses that idea as an entry point into something broader. The film turns the rules of children's television into physical laws, traps its characters inside a fiction, and builds its central conflict around a simple question. What happens when someone stops playing the role that world has written for them? That is why many of Buddy's most important ideas are not only found in its plot, but in the way its songs, credits, sets, resets, the relationship between Freddy and Grace, and the suggestion that Buddy may not represent the limits of this universe all function. From there, the film can be read as a story about authority, denial, free will, and childhood nostalgia transformed from a refuge into a mechanism of control. What is really happening inside It's Buddy? At the beginning, Buddy presents a children's television show modeled directly on American kids programming from the 1990s. It's Buddy has songs, artificial sets, saturated colors, talking objects, and a group of children who live alongside Buddy, a giant orange unicorn whose role is to teach small lessons about friendship, coexistence, and happiness. The first rupture appears when one of those children, Josh, stops behaving the way the program expects him to. The important point is that It's Buddy is not simply a television show performed by actors. The children actually live inside that world. They have been taken from reality, lost the memories of their families, and remain trapped inside an episodic existence that operates according to the conventions of a children's TV show. For them, cardboard houses, spontaneous songs, and objects capable of speaking are not pieces of production design. They are the natural laws of reality. Casper Kelly explained in an interview that one of the ideas behind the film came from his own childhood. When he watched children's shows, he imagined that the kids really lived inside them. What particularly unsettled him was the way everyone would suddenly start singing at the same time. And he wondered how they all knew exactly when to do it. That childhood question, whether they were being controlled, ultimately became one of the foundations of the film. Buddy then does not simply ask what would happen if Barney became a killer. It takes the conventions of that kind of television literally. If the characters actually live there, then someone has to decide when they sing, when an episode ends, what story they're telling, and what happens when one of them refuses to participate. That someone is Buddy. Why does Josh's disappearance break the rules of the show? Josh commits what initially seems like a minor transgression. He does not want to dance. That gesture matters because it introduces something Buddy's world does not know how to process. In a conventional children's show, a child may face a problem, learn a lesson, and ultimately join in. The structure always leads toward a positive resolution. But Josh does not have a problem that needs to be solved. He simply does not want to do what Buddy wants him to do. Buddy first tries to absorb that resistance into the logic of the program. If Josh does not want to dance, then there must be some device or lesson that will make him change his mind. But Josh keeps resisting. At that point, he is no longer questioning one activity. He is questioning Buddy's authority to decide what every child should want. His disappearance becomes the first proof that the happiness of It's Buddy only exists for as long as no one contradicts the character controlling that world. Buddy kills Josh off screen and then tries to transform his absence into a new official version of events. Violence and cover-up appear almost simultaneously. That is what begins to wake the others up. Josh's absence creates a gap between what the children remember and what Buddy insists they should believe. What does Buddy need from the children to keep his world running? Buddy needs obedience, but obedience alone is not enough. He also needs affection. The show is built around him. The children must participate in his games, listen to his lessons, and above all, love him. That is why rejection has a deeper meaning for him than simple disobedience. Buddy believes the children's affection belongs to him. In an interview, Keegan-Michael Key explained that he partially based Buddy's voice on Dwight, the abusive stepfather played by Robert De Niro in This Boy's Life. The reference helps explain Buddy's psychology. >> [music] >> He does not see himself as a monster. He can convince himself that his victims force him to react in certain ways and frame his own violence as a consequence of other people's behavior. >> [music] >> Casper Kelly also compared Buddy in another interview to Jack Torrance from The Shining, particularly because of that combination of pathetic vulnerability, humor, and danger. He also mentioned Annie Wilkes from Misery as a reference, someone desperately needy, capable of maintaining a mask of friendliness, and fundamentally incapable of accepting responsibility for her own outbursts. That is why Buddy is more interesting while he is still trying to behave like the cheerful host of the show. His violence does not contradict his need to be loved. It comes directly from it. Why is Freddy the only one able to break the logic of the show? Freddy does not possess a special ability that the other children lack. Her difference is that she begins to trust the contradictions she notices. The film builds her arc around doubt. >> [music] >> First, she realizes something does not fit. Then she sees that Buddy's explanation does not match what she remembers. That small distance between perception and the official version of reality eventually becomes enough to break the conditioning of the program. Freddy starts behaving in ways its Buddy cannot easily absorb. She investigates, asks questions, distrusts what she is told, and accepts that reality may be far worse than what she has been taught. In that sense, her process mirrors Grace's in the outside world. Both feel that something is missing and refuse to accept the most comfortable explanation. Freddy does not defeat Buddy because she is physically stronger. She defeats him because she stops accepting his authority to define what is real. Why does Buddy become obsessed with Grace? Grace represents a threat because she belongs to the world Buddy tried to erase. For much of the film, she lives with Ben and their sons while feeling that someone is missing from her family. She cannot identify exactly what that absence is, but there is an empty space that no explanation manages to resolve. That absence is Freddy. Buddy did not merely kidnap the girl. He also altered the memories of everyone who knew her so that her disappearance would never trigger a search. Grace, however, begins to resist that erasure. Her memories do not return immediately, but her intuition remains. When Buddy draws her into his world and turns her into Nurse Grace, he tries to integrate her into the same system he uses to neutralize the children. Instead of confronting a mother searching for her daughter, the program turns her into another character. That neatly summarizes Buddy's method. Whenever something threatens the fiction, he tries to assign it a role inside the fiction. What does the relationship between Freddy and Grace reveal about the children's true origins? The revelation that Freddy is Grace's daughter confirms that the children were not born inside the show and are not simply characters created by Buddy. They come from the real world. Memory loss therefore serves a practical purpose. In order for a child to live indefinitely inside its Buddy, they have to stop asking about their parents, their home, or their previous life. The show needs to erase every reference to an outside world. The relationship between Freddy and Grace also proves that this erasure is not perfect. Memories may disappear, but the film suggests that certain emotional connections remain as an absence that is difficult to explain. Grace does not initially remember Freddy, but she knows that her family is incomplete. When she finally recognizes her, the revelation does more than deliver a plot twist. It confirms that beneath the bright children show aesthetic is a system that kidnaps people and then erases even the grief their disappearance should cause. Why can Buddy erase the children from their families' memories? The film does not explain the mechanism scientifically or establish exactly what power allows Buddy to do this. And that appears to be deliberate. Casper Kelly has said in interviews that he developed more rules and mythology for the universe than what ultimately appears on screen. His intention was to know how the world worked without necessarily explaining all of it to the audience. What is clear is the narrative function of the memory erasure. Buddy does not only need to remove the children from reality. He needs to prevent reality from demanding their return. If their families no longer remember that they existed, the disappearances stop producing consequences. >> [music] >> It is an extreme form of impunity. The victim does not simply disappear physically. They also disappear from the memories of the people who might have searched for them. What function do the songs, hugs, and happy endings serve inside It's Buddy? In children's television, the final song often works as a mechanism of closure. The conflict is resolved, everyone has learned something, and the episode can end. In Buddy, that same device becomes a tool of control. Buddy needs the children to return to the correct structure. Reconciliation, song, hug, closure. Happiness stops being an emotion and becomes a formal requirement. It does not matter what happened before. The episode has to end like an episode of It's Buddy. That is where one of the film's darkest ideas emerges. The system does not process trauma. It replaces trauma with a happy conclusion. Something terrible happens, but the structure demands that everyone keep smiling. The comparison works because in Buddy, that denial is not merely psychological. It has physical consequences for the world. When Buddy successfully completes an episode, the credits appear and a new one begins. With that transition comes a reset. Injuries disappear, sets return to their previous state, and Buddy can recover from damage that should have incapacitated him. The film, therefore, turns episodic television structure into an actual supernatural law. It is a particularly coherent variation on one of the classic mechanisms of the slasher film. The killer who always manages to come back. Buddy does not survive because he is inexplicably durable. He survives because the show starts over. The consequence becomes essential in the ending. Killing him permanently requires more than injuring him. Freddy has to prevent the story from reaching the ending that would allow him to be restored. How does the film use television form as a mechanism of horror? This is probably one of Buddy's strongest ideas. The film does not use children's television merely as an aesthetic. It turns its language into a structure of power. Songs determine when a character is supposed to feel something. Sets establish the limits of where they can go. The moral lesson simplifies every conflict. The star of the show functions as an authority figure. The credits erase consequences, and the next episode returns everything to a false sense of normality. In an interview, Kelly described Buddy as an expansion of certain ideas he had already explored in Too Many Cooks, especially weaponized nostalgia and the feeling of being trapped inside a television form. The connection is clear. Too Many Cooks began by imitating the credits of a sitcom before turning that structure into a nightmare. Buddy does something similar with children's television, but develops the consequences on a feature-length scale. The form itself is part of the monster. Buddy has power because he controls the narrative logic in which everyone else is forced to exist. What does Diamond City really represent? Diamond City appears as the promise that something exists beyond Buddy's small world. The possibility of reaching it allows the children to imagine an escape. But when they finally arrive, they discover that the shining city on the horizon was not a real place in the way they expected. It is another construction. It's most obvious function is to destroy their trust in the boundaries of the world. Every time the characters believe they have found a more authentic layer of reality, they discover another artificial one. Diamond City also reveals how Buddy uses storytelling itself to control a crisis. When the children begin questioning the show, the response once again takes the form of an adventure. Instead of giving them information, the system gives them another story to follow. That is why the model matters. The promise of escaping the set was itself another set. What do Willy and George reveal about the existence of other shows? Willy and George expand the scale of the universe. Until that point, It's Buddy could be understood as an isolated phenomenon. But both characters appear to come from a different form of television entertainment and have learned how to survive outside Buddy's controlled spaces. Their presence implies that there is more than one program, more than one aesthetic, and possibly more than one narrative system turned into physical reality. We do not know exactly how those worlds relate to one another. We also do not know who created them. But Willy and George prove that the film's universe does not end with the show we have been watching. That prepares the final revelation. Buddy may be extremely powerful inside his own space, >> [music] >> but he may not be the origin of everything. What exists behind the sets of It's Buddy? When the characters begin physically crossing the boundaries of It's Buddy, the film leaves the visible surface of the program and begins showing something closer to its infrastructure. [music] The Worrywell functions as one of those transition points. Beneath the scenery are spaces that no longer belong to the children's show world. There are tunnels, technical areas, and elements that bring the characters closer to a kind of metaphysical backstage. The decision fits Kelly's original question. If the children really live inside a television program, what exists behind what the audience sees on screen? The answer is not a clean explanation. The film prefers to reveal layers. First, the set, then the woods, then Diamond City, then spaces behind the program itself. Finally, the network of televisions. Each new layer makes the previous one look more artificial. Is Buddy truly responsible for everything, or is he part of a larger structure? The film makes it clear that Buddy is directly responsible for the disappearances, the control, and much of the violence. What it does not establish is whether he created the system that makes all of this possible. The final sequence suggests a larger infrastructure. There are multiple televisions connected to homes in the real world, along with elements suggesting other shows or similar creatures. That opens up a disturbing possibility. Buddy may simply be one figure operating within a machine that existed before him. It is important not to treat that possibility as a confirmed fact. The film never reveals a higher entity or identifies a creator. Kelly himself has spoken about broader rules and lore that he deliberately chose not to explain completely. That is why the ending works better if the uncertainty remains intact. Freddy discovers how to escape her prison, but she never discovers who built the prison. Why does Buddy become more monstrous as he loses control? Buddy's physical transformation accompanies the collapse of his facade. As long as he controls the situation, he can preserve the gentle voice, the songs, and the paternalistic personality of a children's presenter. Once the children stop obeying him, that performance becomes increasingly difficult to maintain. The violence then reveals something that was always there. His kindness depended on no one ever refusing him. One of the most explicit moments comes when he tries to follow the children through a space too narrow for his body and decides to cut pieces of himself away so that he can fit. The scene pushes his need for control to a grotesque conclusion. Buddy is willing to destroy even the friendly image represented by his own body if that is what it takes to prevent someone from escaping him. How does Freddy finally break Buddy's cycle? The first step is to stop behaving like a character. Freddy and the others gradually abandon the rules that guarantee the continuity of It's Buddy. They stop accepting the adventures Buddy gives them, stop trying to complete a moral lesson, and eventually prevent the episode from reaching its conventional ending. During the final pursuit, Freddy becomes the only child left alive. Grace has sacrificed herself to make the escape possible. Wade is dead. Hannah and Oliver also fail to survive. Buddy continues pursuing Freddy through spaces that already exist outside the visible logic of the show. Freddy ultimately manages to make Buddy crash violently into the metal mailbox after Strappy intervenes during the chase. The difference from Buddy's earlier injuries is that this time there is no completed episode capable of restoring him. There is no hug, no song, no internal credits. Buddy dies inside a story that can no longer reset itself. What does the room full of televisions reveal at the end? After defeating Buddy, Freddy still has not reached the real world. She arrives in a space filled with screens that appear to be connected to different homes. The revelation changes the scale of everything we have just seen. The televisions do not function only as devices broadcasting It's Buddy toward an audience. They also work in the opposite direction. They are access points. That explains how people from the real world can end up inside the show, and why television has occupied such a strange role throughout Grace's storyline. But the number of screens raises a much larger question. If there is a network capable of connecting multiple homes to these television spaces, how many children have been taken this way? The film chooses to end before answering. It is an important decision because it transforms what seemed to be a story about one individual monster into the possibility of a systemic problem. Why is Freddy's ending an incomplete victory? Freddy survives and achieves what seemed impossible. She crosses through one of the screens and returns to the real world, but she appears in the wrong house. There is no reunion with Ben or her brothers. We do not know whether her family will recover the memories that were erased. Grace is dead and so are the other children. Even Strappy and the mailbox pay a price for escaping. Once outside the television universe, they stop behaving like living beings. Strappy becomes an ordinary backpack again, and the mailbox becomes an object. That detail confirms that the life of those characters depended on the rules of the show. Freddy, by contrast, continues to exist because she never truly belonged to that world. Her victory is therefore very specific. She recovers her status as a person, but the film refuses to turn that freedom into restoration. She cannot return to the previous state because that state has already been destroyed. Why does Buddy use childhood nostalgia as a form of horror? Kelly has used the phrase weaponized nostalgia when discussing the film. The concept summarizes his strategy well. Buddy needs the audience to first recognize the comfort associated with this kind of television. The colors, [music] songs, artificial sets, and friendly mascot belong to a cultural memory associated with childhood safety. If those elements were disturbing from the beginning, the film would lose much of its effect. The horror emerges when the same structure that once promised to protect children is revealed to be capable of imprisoning them. Kelly explained in an interview that even his own children already knew the old anti-Barney songs, versions that transformed "I love you, you love me" into expressions of rejection toward the character. That made him wonder why a figure designed entirely around love could generate such a persistent culture of hostility. Buddy pushes that contradiction to its extreme. What would happen if a mascot designed to receive affection could hear that rejection? And what would happen if he had enough power to punish those who refuse to participate? That is where the film moves beyond simple mascot horror. Kelly has said that he initially hesitated about the project because the subgenre was already heavily established, and because the idea of something cute with an axe did not feel substantial enough on its own. The film tries to go further by turning the mascot into a narrative authority. The conflict is not simply that Buddy is evil. The conflict is that Buddy controls a reality in which everyone is forced to accept that he is good. The ending of Buddy does not completely resolve the mythology it introduces, but it does complete Freddy's central arc. At the beginning, she lives inside a story written by someone else. Her activities, emotions, memories, and even the moment when she is supposed to sing are conditioned by the show. In order to escape, she first has to accept that the world is false, then stop obeying its rules, and finally prevent the narrative itself from beginning again. That is why defeating Buddy is not simply a matter of killing him. It means preventing the reset. Freddy destroys the mechanism that allowed each episode to erase the consequences of the previous one. The cost is high. Grace dies. The other children do not survive. Her family remains beyond her reach, and the real world offers her no immediate explanation for what happened. The film also never confirms that Buddy was the origin of the problem. The network of televisions suggests a larger system and leaves open the possibility that its Buddy is only one part of something much bigger. But that ambiguity does not weaken the ending. What Buddy needs to resolve is not who built the entire universe, but whether Freddy can stop being a character inside it. And when she finally appears in a stranger's house, covered in blood, with no idea what she is supposed to do next, the film deliberately denies her the kind of ending her old program would have imposed. There is no moral, no song, no hug, no next episode. For the first time, the story no longer belongs to Buddy. Thank you very much for watching this video.
