text: Motor City is not a typical revenge movie. Most action thrillers build toward one explosive showdown where the hero defeats the villain, gets justice, and finally finds peace. Motor City deliberately rejects that formula. Instead, it tells a haunting story about what happens when revenge becomes the only purpose left in someone's life. By the end of the film, John Miller finally kills the man who destroyed everything he loved. But instead of satisfaction, he is left with nothing. To understand why the ending feels so powerful, we first need to look at what started John's journey. The story begins in Detroit during the nineteen seventies. John Miller is a Vietnam War veteran who has finally managed to leave his violent past behind. He works in a factory and has built a quiet life with the woman he loves, Sophia. For the first time in years, his future looks hopeful. That future is destroyed because of one man. Reynolds. A ruthless crime boss who cannot accept losing Sophia. Rather than confronting John fairly, Reynolds uses his criminal connections to frame him. Illegal drugs are planted inside John's vehicle, leading to his arrest and a lengthy prison sentence. Everything John has built disappears overnight. Even while John is serving time, Reynolds refuses to leave him alone. He visits him in prison and openly admits that he orchestrated the entire setup. He even shows John photographs proving that he has taken over every part of his former life, including Sophia. Instead of breaking John's spirit, those visits create something far more dangerous. They give him a single purpose. Revenge. John spends years preparing for the day he can escape. Unlike many revenge heroes, he does not rush. He patiently plans every move, builds his own weapons, and waits until the perfect opportunity finally arrives. When he escapes prison with help from trusted allies Youngblood and Singh, his mission officially begins. From that point onward, Motor City tells much of its story without relying on dialogue. Violence, music, and visual storytelling replace long conversations. The movie trusts viewers to understand John's emotions through his actions rather than his words. One of the film's most unforgettable sequences is the brutal fight inside a cramped elevator against Reynolds' deadly enforcer, Savick. The choreography is raw, relentless, and incredibly creative. At the same time, classic songs from the nineteen seventies continue playing in the background. Rather than simply entertaining the audience, the soundtrack becomes another storyteller, expressing emotions John himself rarely puts into words. Eventually, John's search leads him back to Sophia. For a brief moment, it seems his nightmare might finally be over. Instead, he discovers another tragedy. Sophia has been heavily drugged and barely understands what is happening around her. John rescues her and attempts to escape. Then everything falls apart. Reynolds opens fire. Instead of killing John, he accidentally shoots Sophia. She dies during the escape. Because police have already surrounded the area, John has no choice but to leave her behind. This is the true emotional ending of the story. Up until this moment, John believed revenge might allow him to reclaim the life that had been stolen from him. Sophia's death proves that dream was always impossible. There is nothing left to save. Only revenge remains. The film then delivers another violent confrontation between John and Reynolds. During the fight, John finally uses one of the movie's most important symbols. A bullet made from Sophia's wedding ring. The idea is both heartbreaking and deeply symbolic. The object that once represented love, commitment, and a shared future has literally been transformed into a weapon. John has taken the happiest memory of his life and converted it into an instrument of revenge. He shoots Reynolds with the bullet. However, Reynolds survives the encounter. After their vehicle crashes, he escapes. At first, it seems as though John's entire journey has failed. Then Motor City surprises the audience with a massive time jump. Twenty years pass. The story now takes place during the nineteen nineties. Everything has changed. Reynolds has grown older. He has a family. He appears to have left much of his violent past behind. Meanwhile, John has continued carrying the same burden for two decades. Unlike Reynolds, he has never truly moved forward. The revenge that once gave him purpose has also trapped him. Before their final meeting, Reynolds receives a letter from John. It serves as a warning that the past has finally caught up with him. John quietly enters Reynolds' home. There is no elaborate action sequence. No massive gun battle. Instead, the confrontation feels surprisingly calm. For the first time in years, the two men simply face each other. Reynolds admits that he loved Sophia. John quietly replies that he loved her too. That brief exchange reveals something important. Despite everything they have done, both men are still haunted by the same woman. Sophia remains the emotional center of the story even though she has been gone for twenty years. John then shoots Reynolds. His revenge is finally complete. Yet the movie refuses to celebrate the moment. There is no triumphant music. No emotional release. No feeling that justice has finally been achieved. Instead, the ending feels strangely empty. That emptiness is entirely intentional. Motor City argues that revenge cannot restore what has already been lost. John succeeds in killing the man responsible for destroying his life. But Sophia does not come back. The years he spent in prison cannot be recovered. The twenty years he devoted to revenge cannot be reclaimed. Everything he sacrificed is still gone. The wedding ring bullet perfectly captures this message. At the beginning of the story, the ring represented hope. Marriage. Love. A future together. By turning it into a bullet, John transforms love into violence. The very thing that should have symbolized life instead becomes the tool that delivers death. It is one of the film's strongest visual metaphors. Even after Reynolds dies, Sophia has been gone for two decades. Nothing John accomplishes changes that reality. Ultimately, the ending of Motor City is less interested in revenge than in its consequences. The film asks a difficult question. What happens when someone spends an entire lifetime chasing justice, only to discover that justice cannot heal grief? For John Miller, revenge was never truly about killing Reynolds. text: The ending of the Odyssey goes in a completely different direction than the source material. And it delivers a plot twist that changes the entire movie. Throughout the film, we keep hearing about the terrifying people of the sea that leave entire civilizations in ruin. But during Odysseus's conversation with Penelope disguised as a beggar, we learn the truth. That Odysseus and his men were the people of the sea all along. And the movie wasn't hiding it. Circe literally turns them into pigs. Villages set themselves on fire the moment their ships appear. But because we're following Odysseus's journey home, the film convinces us to see him as a hero. Except he isn't. He and his men are the villains in everybody else's story. The very people the movie warned us about way back in the beginning. They preach Zeus's law, yet violated Troy's hospitality with the Trojan Horse. Unleashing 10 years of rage that decimated an entire civilization. And it all culminates with Odysseus watching a priestess of Athena get beheaded. The moment where he realizes the true horror of what he's helped create. And personally, I believe Athena takes that form throughout the rest of the film to serve as a constant reminder of he and his men's sins. But that's why Nolan changes the ending. In Homer's version, Odysseus reclaims the throne and rules Ithaca with Penelope. But Nolan's Odysseus, crushed by guilt, crowns Telemachus instead. Placing his hope in a generation that might finally break the cycle of violence. Then he keeps his promise to Sinon, sailing west with Penelope into a self-imposed exile to honor the men who never made it home. It's a powerful reminder that war isn't something to celebrate. It destroys civilizations, scars everyone it touches, and leaves the next generation to pick up the pieces. text: On a deserted highway, a heist crew driving three modified black 5th-generation Honda Civic coupes assault a truck carrying electronic goods, steal its cargo, and escape into the night. The following day, a joint Los Angeles Police Department and FBI task force sends LAPD officer Brian O'Conner undercover to locate the crew. He begins his investigation at Toretto's Market, ordering his regular tuna on white, no crust, and flirting with its owner Mia, sister of the infamous street racer Dominic Toretto, while Dominic sits in the back office reading a newspaper. Dominic's crew, Vince, in a 1999 Nissan Maxima; Leon, in a 1995 Nissan Skyline GT-R R33; Jesse, in a 1995 Volkswagen Jetta GLS; and his girlfriend Letty, arrives. Vince, who has a crush on Mia, starts a fight with Brian until Dominic intervenes. That night, Brian brings a modified 1995 Mitsubishi Eclipse to an illegal street race, hoping to find a lead on the heist crew. Dominic arrives in his 1993 Mazda RX-7 and initiates a drag race between himself, Brian and two other drivers. Lacking money, Brian is forced to wager his car. Dominic wins the race after Brian's car malfunctions, but the LAPD arrive before he can hand over his vehicle. Brian, in his car, helps Dominic escape, but they accidentally venture into the territory of Dominic's old racing rival, gang leader Johnny Tran and his cousin Lance, who destroy Brian's vehicle. Later, Dominic reiterates that Brian still owes him a "10-second car". The two then walk back to Dominic's house together, where an altercation between Vince, who is upset that Brian is at the house, and Dominic breaks out. Brian brings a damaged 1994 Toyota Supra to Dominic's garage as a replacement. Dominic and his crew begin the long process of restoring the vehicle, and Brian starts dating Mia. He also begins investigating Tran, convinced that he is the mastermind behind the truck hijackings. While investigating one of the garages at night, having driven a 1999 Ford F150 SVT Lightning Brian is discovered by Dominic and Vince who demand an explanation. Brian convinces them that he is researching his opponents vehicles' for the upcoming desert Race Wars. Together, the trio investigate Tran's garage, discovering a large quantity of electronic goods. Brian reports the discovery to his superiors and Tran and Lance are arrested while the Toyota Supra is restored and built. The raid fails, however, when the electronics are proved to have been purchased legally. Brian is forced to confront his suspicion that Dominic is the true mastermind. Brian is given 36 hours to find the heist crew, as the truckers are now arming themselves to defend against the hijackings. The following day, Dominic and Brian attend Race Wars after test driving the newly built Supra, off U.S. Route 101. At Race Wars, Jesse wagers his father's MK3 Volkswagen Jetta GLS against Tran in his Honda S2000, but flees with the car after he loses. Tran demands Dominic recover the vehicle, and accuses him of reporting him to the police. Enraged, Dominic beats up Tran. Later that night, Brian witnesses Dominic and his crew leaving and realizes that they are the hijackers. He reveals his true identity to Mia and convinces her to help him find the crew. Dominic, Letty, Vince, and Leon attack a semi-trailer truck, intending it to be their final heist. The armed driver shoots Vince and runs Letty off the road. Brian arrives with Mia and rescues Vince. He is forced to reveal his identity to call in emergency medical care to save Vince. Dominic, Mia and the rest of the crew leave before the authorities can arrive. Some time later, Brian arrives at Dominic's house to apprehend him as he is getting his father's 1970 Dodge Charger R/T out of the garage. He demands Brian leave, since he is not running, but is going to rescue Jesse who has no one else to look after him. Instead, Jesse arrives at his house and pleads for protection. Tran and Lance ride by on motorbikes and shoot Jesse dead for reneging on their bet, hitting the Volkswagen in the process. Brian and Dominic give chase in their separate vehicles, finding and killing Tran and injuring Lance. Brian then pursues Dominic, with them both eventually acquiescing to a quarter-mile drag race. The pair barely cross a railroad before an oncoming freight train passes, which ends the race in a draw, but Dominic crashes his car into a truck, injuring him. Instead of arresting him, Brian gives the keys to his own car to Dominic, asserting that he still owes him a 10-second car from their first race. Dominic escapes in the Supra as Brian walks away. In a post-credits scene, Dominic is seen driving through Baja California, Mexico, in a 1970 Chevrolet Chevelle SS.

text: Have you ever watched Barney and Friends and thought, "This isn't real, man. Life is more than a series of lessons neatly wrapped in sing-along. Life is a nightmare, death, and suffering, the inescapable void." We've all thought that, and we've all screamed it at random children on the street. Now, all we have to do is show them Buddy, a movie about a show called It's Buddy, modeled after children's programming of the '90s. It asks questions like, "What if Timmy doesn't feel like dancing today? And what are these kids up to between episodes?" It is a surreal trip from the mind of Casper Kelly, the same mind that cooked up Too Many Cooks, the viral Adult Swim short from 2014, where a TV opening just keeps going and going and going, getting more absurd, surreal, and nightmarish as it goes. Kind of a precursor to Buddy. More recently, he wrote and directed one of my favorite segments from VHS Halloween, Funsize, where he once again employed his unique blend of surreal horror comedy, twisting the familiar and seemingly innocent into something sinister. Now, let's talk about Buddy, full spoilers ahead. The movie begins in the world of It's Buddy, as though we're simply watching episodes of a forgotten children's show from 1999, a show starring the magical unicorn Buddy teaching the cast of children lessons with help from Betty Bunny and some talking objects like Mr. Mailbox, Clocky the Clock, and Strappy the Backpack. Except in today's episode, Josh doesn't feel like dancing. He just wants to be left alone. Buddy asks nicely and even conjures him some magical dancing shoes, but Josh refuses. So, Buddy takes him off camera, we hear sounds of a struggle, and no more Josh. Buddy assures the other kids Josh loved dancing after all, so much so he decided to go on a dancing tour in Diamond City. Except Freddy sees something weird in the trash. Josh was reading a book earlier, and now that book has been thrown out, stained with Josh's blood. At the end of the episode, they all hug Buddy, sing the closing credits song about how they love him and Buddy loves them. The credits roll, and a new episode begins. The cut to black and wooshing sound effect gives a sense that this is more than just putting on the next episode. It's more like reality has reset. And we'll later find out that It's Buddy is not a TV show airing anywhere. It's more like a pocket dimension, an alternate reality that resembles quintessential '90s children's shows, a reality Buddy oversees like that kid in the Twilight Zone episode, It's a Good Life. The answer to those questions, what do the kids do between episodes, where do they sleep, where do they go to the bathroom? The answer is there is no between episodes. Every time the credits roll, things reset. The kids have a vague idea they've done this before, but don't know how many times and don't recall any life before Buddy's world. On the next episode, where Josh has been replaced by the new kid, Hannah, Freddy talks to the nurse about Josh's bloodied book. So, the nurse talks to Buddy, and Buddy chokes her to death. Freddy, Wade, and Stripy the backpack see it all happen. So, on the next episode, they convince Hannah and Oliver that Buddy is dangerous, and they've got to escape the park. Their escape attempt does not go well. Buddy kills Charlie the train and almost kills Wade until he and Freddy light Buddy on fire, which doesn't kill him, but does horribly disfigure him and make him mad. He kills Mailman Miles and Wade while Freddy, Hannah, and Oliver climb over the fence and run into the forest. Then, we cut to the real world, and having not watched any of the trailers for this movie before release, I I didn't actually know if we were ever going to do that, or if this movie was going to take place entirely within the confines of the fake show. The cut doesn't happen until close to the 30-minute mark, which is an impressive commitment to the bit, and exactly what makes this movie so good. Barney, but what if he was a jerk, or what if Sesame Street had to deal with more mature themes, is an old bit, and it's easy to mine for a throw away gag or sketch. But, Buddy makes it fresh and funny all over again by spending enough time to let you buy into the world first. Casper Kelly told Bloody Disgusting, "Don't make it satirical. Play it as straight as humanly possible." There was an earlier incarnation of Buddy where his eyes looked crazy, like he looked like a crazy person. I'm like, "No, he needs to look comforting, just like a real show." Playing it all with a straight face is what makes it so hilarious when Buddy first loses it, when Josh refuses to dance, and he's like, "Just stick your leg out, Josh. Would you just dance?" Or the little touches, like after he kills the nurse, Buddy notices a witness, Clocky the Clock, and has to kill him, too. It's so funny to have to deal with the actual consequences of the familiar, yet bizarre realities crafted by these kids shows. Yeah, if you commit murder, suddenly sentient household objects become a real problem. All of this only works if the craft and performances are up to the challenge, and they definitely are here. Keegan-Michael Key is awesome as the voice of Buddy. I didn't even recognize him at first. I just accepted it as the voice of a Barney-like character. He's physically brought to life by Sergey Garashevsky wearing the suit, surrounded by real physical sets believable as a '90s children's show. And same for the puppetry on all the anthropomorphic objects around them, not to mention the children, they straddle that line of giving the fake sort of performances you expect for the over-the-top happiness demanded in this kind of show, swapping for something more genuine as they wake up to the sinister truth. Especially Delaney Quinn as Freddy, who becomes the main character. At around the 30-minute mark, we cut away from the show and see the real world, where we meet Grace, Ben, and their children Timothy and Derek. A picture-perfect family until one night Grace looks around the dinner table, looks at the extra empty chair, and screams, overcome by a sense of loss. What the hell was that all about? When therapy doesn't offer an answer, Grace turns to parapsychology. A psychic, she calls out to the spirits and the TV turns on to an episode of It's Buddy. Grace researches the show and there's no trace of it. It doesn't exist. She starts piecing things together. There's a gap in the years between when Timothy and Derek were born. They are supposed to have another kid in between them, but it's like reality has been altered. Like their daughter has been erased from this world and planted instead in Buddy's. Soon Buddy shows up on Grace's TV and pulls her into it. The moment she's gone, reality blinks. Furniture and pictures on the wall are replaced and the room gets a little messier. This sequence teaches us the mechanics of how Buddy pulls children into his world without anyone catching on. Because when he does, reality changes to make it seem like the person never existed. This family does not remember having a third child. And now, with Grace gone, things have changed again. The furnishings look more like those of Ben as a single father. In place of a dresser and mirror, a TV stand and flat screen. Because in this new reality, Grace doesn't exist, and she isn't there to ruin his good time anymore. I just want to watch TV in bed. I love how in this whole sequence, it takes a while for Grace to acknowledge out loud that she believes she used to have another kid. It gives the audience a chance to realize that for themselves first. Something strongly hinted at by lingering shots on those stickers you put on your car to represent the members of your family. The focus on that empty chair, the feeling of realization is always more satisfying than when the characters spell things out for you. This sequence also adds stakes. Yes, in the preceding 30 minutes, children were in peril and dying, but the context was so surreal and over the top, it's hard to take too seriously. Probably a good thing, otherwise that would get in the way of the humor. But now, for at least a bit, absurdity takes a backseat, and Cristin Milioti's performance takes the forefront. Things get real, because in her performance, we see a mother's grief and longing for a lost child. But the humor is never gone entirely. Tofer Grace as the dad who just doesn't want to deal with any of this is hilarious with how obvious he doesn't know he's being. Like when she tells him that the empty chair made her feel worse than she's ever felt, and he's like, "But you're better now, right?" And she's like, "No, I'm not." Or when he suggests, "Oh, then we'll get rid of the chair. We barely use it anyway." Problem solved. Back in Buddy's world, Grace is cast as the nurse, and as she bandages Buddy's burns, he licks her and and gets inappropriate until she pushes him away. Freddy, Hanna, and Oliver make their way through the forest toward Diamond City, where they hope salvation awaits. Along the way, they make camp and run into a couple of fellow survivors, Willy and George, an old man dressed as a cowboy and a talking marionette. They escaped Buddy years ago, back when the place was Western-themed, like a '50s kids show, before it was updated for the '90s. And they tell the kids what happened back in their day, when the credits rolled, instead of the usual happy song, "I love Buddy, yes I do. I'm so glad he loves me, too." one kid sang a mean version, "Stab your heart and kick your knee. Buddy, you're my enemy." Buddy got mad and changed. He hurt the kid real bad. George and Willie barely escaped. The next day, Buddy kills George and Willie, while the kids escape to Diamond City, which doesn't exist. Turns out, it's just a small model, something that looks nice in the backdrop of the show. They wallow in heartbreak for a few seconds, long enough for Buddy to catch up, grab Freddy, and sing the song, finally ending the episode. It's always great seeing Clint Howard show up, and he's fun as part of the cowboy marionette duo. I was hoping once the kids got out of the park, there'd be more to see in the surrounding areas, but I also kept expectations in check, considering the movie's presumably low budget. The sets can only get so varied and elaborate. That's why I kind of knew Diamond City would be a bust from the start. So, the fun of the outside world doesn't come from new sets and locations, but new people. George does appear to be a child predator, but he gets what's coming to him, so you know, everything works out in Buddy's world. With Buddy's song and end credits, a new episode begins. This time, Freddy visits the nurse, and slowly, the two start to remember their old lives. It turns out, Grace's missing child is Freddy. They are mother and daughter, finally reunited. And finally, Freddy has had enough. She leads Hannah and Oliver in a song that starts, "I hate Buddy, yes I do and ends with get an axe, chop off your head, I wish you were dead. I love how the sky darkens and the movie revels in their anger. So satisfying after more than an hour of them at Buddy's mercy, mostly helpless. It really pisses Buddy off and he transforms into a demonic form, perhaps his true form. Grace stabs him in the eye giving her and the kids a chance to run, but where to? Mr. Meow Meow Box points at the worry well. Magic things come out of that well, maybe going through it is a way out. Except demon Buddy is still out there. He kills the new mailman, kills Betty Bunny and Couchy. While he's distracted, they make a break for it and get down the well thanks to Grace's sacrifice. She buys them time by attacking Buddy with a bat and getting herself killed. Admittedly a disappointing end for the character. It didn't feel like she had to die because earlier when she stabbed demon Buddy in the eye, it bought them a lot of time. I remember feeling like where did he go? She stabs him and then runs to Freddy and they start talking and I'm like isn't he like 5 ft away? Get out of there. After he seemed so easily avoidable in that scene, it felt like the movie just wanted Grace's sacrifice in the next. So suddenly Buddy is too powerful to get around. While Freddy, Hannah and Oliver go down the well, demon Buddy hugs Tyler, the kid who replaced Wade, to reset the episode and revert back to normal Buddy form. He kills Tyler, tries to go down the well, but he's too large. So he cuts off enough flesh to make himself small enough. And here is where we get into true ending explained territory. At the bottom of the well, the kids find a workshop where an older unicorn who looks like a faded Buddy is at work. It appears to be where characters for the show are made. We see mouths on the table all yapping away, presumably mouths that are meant to be sewn onto things like a couch or a backpack. Buddy breaks in, kills Hannah, and then Oliver who gives himself up. He just doesn't want to run anymore. Now all that's left is Freddy and a couple of her inanimate object friends, Strappy the backpack and Mr. Mailbox who she's been carrying around. Freddy carries her two friends and keeps running through another door that leads to a school hallway filled with locked doors. Looking through the window of one door, she sees an empty classroom with a TV in front playing It's Buddy. Above each empty desk there are helmets with wires sticking out of them. You can imagine that typically the room would be filled with kids wearing those helmets and watching the show. Either the helmets are measuring their brains' reactions to that show or perhaps it's reading their imaginations to create that show. More on that soon. In another room she sees three mailboxes marked step one, step two, and step three. Perhaps a room where the living mailboxes are created or studied. This is starting to feel very backrooms. Buddy chases her until Strappy extends his straps to trip Buddy who falls onto the sharp end of Mr. Mailbox's wooden post wielded by Freddy like a weapon. Freddy walks away from Buddy's corpse and enters the gymnasium where she finds a big TV playing It's Buddy. Across from it wall of smaller TVs each showing a child watching from somewhere in the real world. It seems to be a nexus between realities. Buddy calls to the children through the big screen and the smaller TVs act like portals connecting his world to theirs. So Freddy finds an empty one and crawls through it into some stranger's living room. She brings Mr. Mailbox and Strappy the backpack with her, but sadly in the real world they lose their sentience and simply become the inanimate objects they represent. The father of this household sees the strange girl in his living room and asks who she is. The end. So, how do we interpret this ending? Casper Kelly told Nerdtropolis, >> I love world building and it's fun to set up things and to set up questions that I don't answer, but I I I think it's important to have the answers myself, but I don't always give them to the audience. >> Meaning there are answers to be found here if we can just piece the clues together. We actually get a clue early on. The book Josh reads, the one that gets stained in his blood, is titled A Wrinkle in Reality, a fake book Casper Kelly based on the real book A Wrinkle in Time, a story about children traveling across the universe by folding space-time. Buddy parallels that story in a few ways. The book involves the children visiting different planets, each representing vastly different worlds. Just like its Buddy takes place in its own world, the book's antagonist turns out to be an evil entity called It. Not the killer clown, but a force that removes people's uniqueness to enforce order and conformity. Kind of like Buddy who wants everyone to be happy, dance, and learn lessons. Not wanting to dance even one time is reason enough to die, and the book touches on strange cosmology, higher dimensions, bending time, something Buddy clearly does as well. He appears to live in another dimension, and we see reality bend in real time, changing the past and present to explain a missing child or mother. Freddy wasn't just kidnapped from the real world, her past was erased as though she never existed. That's all simple enough. An evil entity exists in a dimension that happens to resemble children's programming. To amuse himself, he kidnaps children and people from our world to play roles in his cast of characters, but there's clearly more to it. The school at the end with that nexus in reality, helmets with wires. So, what is really going on? Did scientists discover an alternate reality and now they're studying it? But, why are they seemingly complicit in feeding children to the entity which lives there? They have that set up in their gymnasium with the big TV across from the small TVs. Why would they do that? And why is their research apparently being conducted in a school? The thing my mind goes to is that perhaps they have to do this to appease the monster. Maybe these scientists were doing some crazy cosmological research and stumbled upon a wrinkle in reality. They found another world, and how awesome is that? Except that other world contained an evil entity with vast power, and now that they found it, it found them, putting their world in danger. Maybe the being is so powerful it cannot be destroyed, but in their studies, they found ways to alter reality. So, they attempted to alter the monster's world. And how should they alter it? Well, what is the most wholesome, innocent, and harmless thing imaginable? A children's television show. So, the scientist trapped him in one, turning him from the demonic thing we see at the end of the movie into a magical unicorn. There are signs that Buddy is not all powerful in this world and doesn't even fully comprehend it. For example, he doesn't refer to the end credits as credits. Instead, he says, "I hug the kids and sing the song, and the words come up." Like he himself has had to learn the rules of this world. And why do the scientists work out of a school? Perhaps altering reality is achieved through imagination. >> Imagination. >> Something more powerful in the minds of children. That's why Freddy spotted that classroom with those wired helmets. The scientists hook children up to the helmets and use the power of their imagination to craft Buddy's world. Maybe it's a process that has to be repeated again and again. Every time they bring in a new generation of children, it's refreshed based on the shows they watch in their era. That's how the world transformed from a Howdy Doody 50s style show, the one George and Willie escaped from, to a Barney 90s style show. Ultimately, this traps the entity in his Buddy persona, but it still requires sacrifice. He needs children to occupy him so he can teach them lessons every week and play his role as the Barney-like figure. But at least it's done in a controlled manner, rather than an all-you-can-eat buffet of the entity reaching into reality and wreaking havoc. So, the scientists set up that system, the big TV across from the wall of small TVs, each a portal to another child. It's not a perfect system. If the kids do not play along or anything breaks the reality too much, the system falls apart. Buddy can revert to his demonic form, like we saw. To be fair, he is ultimately killed and it didn't seem that hard to kill him, but I have my doubts about that. If the Buddy persona is simply a containment system for a greater evil, I bet his essence is still alive. Maybe killing the Buddy character was actually a mistake, freeing him from that form. And a sequel could reveal he's a bigger threat than ever. Now he can invade our world, like Insidious out of the further, never mind. And that's my theory. There is another lingering question about Freddy's fate specifically. She's back in the real world. Does that mean reality reverts to a version where she does in fact exist? Does her father now remember having a daughter? Or is Freddy now a stranger in this world with no past? Those questions are left open. We also don't know how this reality accounts for Grace missing. Like what does Ben remember about how he had his children? All left ambiguous. Anyway, that was a lot of speculation and more than I usually do, but I think Kelly invites it with that ending. He provides so many little clues. It just begs for theorizing. I would love to see a sequel that expands on the idea and delves into more twisted horrors. Kelly even hints at it with a mural painted on one of the walls in that school. It shows Buddy along with two other unicorns, Bobby and Benny. Maybe personas belonging to two other trapped entities. Like I said, I also have my doubts about the permanence of Buddy's death. Overall, Buddy is a great time. It has so many lines to straddle, but after so much absurd surrealism in his career, it's like this is the moment Casper Kelly has been training for. He has to kill a bunch of kids without being too much of a buzz kill. He has to craft a surreal world but hold on to a grounded narrative about a mother and daughter attempting to reunite across dimensions. And somehow wrap it all in hints of a mythology that doesn't spell everything out, but gives you just enough to buy there are rules to this even if we don't know them. It isn't just a fever dream Kelly is making up as he The real world story and Buddy story meld shockingly well. From a pacing standpoint, I like the movie's choice to not intercut between reality and the Buddy show too much. Rather than constantly going back and forth, each world gets its own segment and complete story. We only see the real world once in that extended sequence and then again briefly at the end. That helps us get immersed in each world separately and experience them fully. especially on the buddy side. In the first half hour of the movie, you feel the claustrophobia of lives forced to exist within the confines of 10-minute episodes, all prescripted around particular lessons. Though with the real world segment sandwiched between the first and final act, which take place in Buddy's world, it felt a tad unfinished and unsatisfying to me. I got really bought into Grace's story, especially thanks to Kristin Milioti's performance. But once she's in Buddy's world, she's pacified by having to play the nurse character. Once she wakes up, it's only briefly before that contrived sacrifice. It had to happen so Freddy is forced to do this on her own without a grown-up stepping in to solve her problems, but I wonder if there was a way to satisfy both Freddy and Grace's arcs. But that does little to change my overall view. I had a great time with this movie. I never found it particularly scary or unsettling, but I was honestly having too much fun to care. Buddy does a better job than most at delivering on the old bit of finding the darkness in the colorful sets and painted-on smiles. The places and things that appear so bright and happy, you just know they're hiding something. Except Gil explains, "I'm not hiding anything at all. Why would you even suggest that? Now, why don't you press your hand against the TV and join me?" Wait, you're watching on a phone? You're You're not even watching, you're just listening. How does Buddy make this look so easy?

text: What if the love of your life disappeared because of one missing digit? Not because they ghosted you, not because they rejected you, but because of one tiny mistake that completely changed the course of your life. That simple idea becomes the foundation of Finding Emily, a romantic comedy that looks familiar on the surface, but quietly explores how modern relationships are shaped by social media, assumptions, and the stories we tell ourselves. Today, we're diving into what makes Finding Emily work, where it stumbles, and why this film has sparked so much conversation among rom-com fans. So, whenever another rom-com arrives, the biggest question isn't whether it'll use those familiar ingredients, it's whether it can make them feel fresh. Finding Emily starts with an incredibly simple premise. A young musician named Owen meets someone during one unforgettable night. They instantly connect, conversation flows naturally, there's chemistry. For one evening, everything feels effortless. Then she gives him her phone number, except she's missing one digit. That's it. How do people fall in love today? In previous generations, relationships often depended on chance meetings. Now, every interaction continues online. You meet someone, then you search their Instagram. You look at their photos, their friends, their interests. Within minutes, you feel like you know someone you actually barely know. The movie cleverly plays with this reality. Owen's search doesn't stay private. Instead, it snowballs. Suddenly, other people become involved. Opinions form, strangers judge him. Social media begins shaping the narrative. Some people see him as hopelessly romantic. Others think he's crossing boundaries. And that's one of the film's most interesting ideas. Online, the same action can be interpreted in completely opposite ways. The internet rarely waits for context. It decides first, then asks questions later. The film never turns into a lecture. Instead, it quietly asks viewers to think about how easily people become characters inside stories written by complete strangers. While Owen searches for one Emily, another Emily enters his life. And that's where the emotional core of the movie really begins. This Emily is practical, analytical. She's studying psychology. Unlike Owen, who believes feelings should lead the way, she believes feelings can often fool us. Their personalities couldn't be more different. Yet, that's exactly why watching them together becomes so enjoyable. They challenge each other. Owen teaches Emily to embrace uncertainty. Emily forces Owen to question whether he's in love with a real person or simply an idealized version he's created in his own mind. The movie also explores an uncomfortable truth. Sometimes we're so focused on chasing the fantasy we've imagined that we completely overlook what's already right in front of us. That's a timeless rom-com idea, but Finding Emily presents it through the lens of today's generation, one shaped by viral moments, constant comparison, and digital identities. One reason critics have been divided is because the movie balances several different ideas at once. It's funny, it's romantic, it's awkward, sometimes surprisingly emotional. It also explores grief through Owen's family situation. That storyline reminds us that his search isn't only about romance. It's also about trying to reconnect with hope after loss. Meanwhile, Emily's academic project raises another fascinating question. Can love actually be studied? Can you reduce emotions to research? Or does love refuse to fit inside neat psychological theories? The movie doesn't offer easy answers. Instead, it suggests something much simpler. Real relationships aren't sustained by magical first meetings. They're built through time, shared experiences, honesty, trust. The butterflies eventually disappear. What remains afterwards matters much more. That idea quietly becomes the heart of the film. Without focusing on every plot detail, the ending reinforces the film's central message. Both main characters have to let go of the stories they've been telling themselves. Owen learns that idealizing someone from one perfect evening isn't enough to build a future. Emily realizes that keeping emotional distance doesn't protect her from vulnerability. In different ways, both characters stop chasing theories and start embracing reality. That's ultimately what Finding Emily argues. Love isn't something you discover through algorithms, or research papers, or viral internet fame. It's something that grows slowly between two people willing to truly know each other. Is Finding Emily revolutionary? Probably not. It still embraces many classic romantic comedy traditions. You'll recognize familiar story beats, predict where certain moments are heading, and some subplots may not land equally well for everyone. But the movie succeeds because it understands something important. Sometimes audiences don't need a completely new formula. They simply need familiar stories told with sincerity, strong performances, warm humor, and characters worth rooting for. That's where Finding Emily shines. Keep in mind that what I am telling you here is the filmmakers ' perspective, and I am not giving my own opinion. Let's first talk about what the core theme of this entire film is. Because if you understand that, then everything else will start to become clear on its own. This film is basically a reflection of director Jane Schoenbrun's own journey of discovering their gender and sexuality. Jane is a trans filmmaker herself, and they have openly said in interviews that their three films—meaning two before this, such as one being We're All Going to the World's Fair—Then the second movie, I Saw the TV Glow, and now this third movie, Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. These three are a kind of spiritual trilogy that shows different phases of their own life. Keep in mind that the stories of the three films are not connected at all. These films are only connected spiritually. In the first film, we see a confused, isolated teenager searching for their identity in the world of the internet. In the second film, we see the journey of dysphoria and finding one's true self. And the third film, this one, means finally fully accepting and enjoying one's own body, identity, and sexuality . Jane herself has said that she wrote this film a year or two after her transition, when she first felt comfortable in her own body and was finally learning how to be intimate in a healthy and satisfying way. That is why the film's entire tone is quite different from the first two. It is more fun, campy, and hopeful. Whereas the first two films had a lot more dread and loneliness. Now, if we look at this in context, Chris's character feels exactly like a fictional version of Jane. Chris is also a young, acclaimed indie filmmaker whose first film gained a lot of fame, and now studios are asking her to apply her intellectual artistic sensibility to a big franchise. In real life, too, Jane must have faced many such meetings after World’s Fair and TV Glow, where studios wanted to put her into their mainstream projects. And that is why the meltdown scene on the Zoom call was shown in the film. Where Chris crosses all her personal and professional lines . Because this scene is directly a satire of Jane’s own industry experience. Now let’s talk about the impact Camp Massacre had on young Chris . In the film, we are shown a flashback where an 8-year-old Chris is watching the original Camp Massacre on VHS for the first time, and that very moment sets the trajectory for her entire life . This wasn't just nostalgia for a movie-loving kid; rather, it was an awakening of her, well, her feelings. The look in Billie's eyes when she was being intimate with Alex and Little Death stabbed her—that look awakened something inside Chris that she kept chasing her whole life. This is the reason why Chris is so obsessively attached to this franchise and why she wants Billie to be the lead in her reboot. Because somewhere, Chris feels that if she could recreate that exact look and that exact feeling of Billie’s, perhaps she herself would be able to experience that feeling in her own life. In a way, the entire film is Chris’s attempt to relive that first awakening moment from her childhood. Now, what does Little Death represent? Understanding this is the most important thing about this film. The character's name, Little Death, actually comes from the French phrase " la petite mort." Which literally means exactly that: a little death. But this phrase is traditionally used to describe that moment where you completely lose yourself for a short while. Just as usually happens while watching the climax of a movie. So, Little Death isn't just a slasher villain; it's an eternal, primal embodiment of desire. And it represents the most raw, unfiltered, and deeply buried feeling within everyone—the one we often suppress, feel ashamed of, or intellectualize until we lose its true meaning. That’s why, when Little Death begins its work in the film, the entire mood of the scene shifts. I mean , the grainy 80s look disappears, replaced by modern, saturated visuals, and the music turns uplifting instead of eerie. This stylistic shift is intentional, helping us understand that when someone accepts their deepest desire, the experience feels liberating and cathartic rather than frightening. At this point, Billy's famous "flesh and fluids" dialogue also starts to make sense. When Chris explains the film using heavy academic theories, Billy stops her and says the real thing isn't that complicated. According to her, the original Campias was only about two things. It was about the body and that pure physical sensation, not about any discourse or theory. That is why the line "flesh and fluids" was used there. At first, it seems like Billy is just an out-of-touch, old-school, simple woman who doesn't understand the queer community's modern terminology. But slowly, it’s revealed that Billy actually understands how desire feels far more deeply than Chris does because she has lived it in her own body. She hasn't just read or thought about it. This is the central tension of the entire film. It's overthinking versus feeling, mind versus body, and Chris's entire journey is about bridging this gap. Now, let's talk about the franchise's transphobic origins, which is actually the film's cleverest reclamation move. If you look closely, Camp Miasma's backstory literally seems inspired by the 1983 real-life film*Sleepaway Camp*. Where a similar type of gender twist is revealed. The legend of the original Little Death was that they were a gender-fluid child who presented as both a boy and a girl on different days , and for this reason, bullies drowned them in the lake. In older films, characters like this were depicted through horror and shame. Like Norman Bates in*Psycho*or Buffalo Bill in*The Silence of the Lambs*. Where gender non-conformity was literally linked to monstrosity. In the film, Chris herself points this out when she is watching the original movie with Billy and bluntly says that this part is transphobic. But Billie silences him and tells him to keep watching. There are many such small moments in this film that I didn't tell you about during the explanation. Otherwise, I would have to explain the entire movie line by line. But the point here is that this small moment speaks volumes. The film doesn't just say that old things are wrong; it shows how reclaiming a problematic, hurtful trope can turn it into a source of pride and power. The same Little Death who was once a victim of shame and bullying. That same character has now become eternal, unstoppable, and celebrated, which is also a metaphor for trans and queer resilience. Now friends, the sexual symbolism in the film's visuals is also placed quite intentionally. If you watch the film, you will understand many things. I cannot tell you everything openly. I will just tell you that the motif of holes appears repeatedly in the film. Like the hole under the lake, the hole in the center of Little Death's air-vent-like mask, and the hole in the wall of the secret video room from where the VHS tapes emerge. If you look at all these things , they clearly create imagery of the female space. Whereas Little Death's spear and his entire tall, rigid figure carry symbolism like a male space. In fact, in one scene where Chris is excitedly telling her agent that she wants to cast Billie, you will see a tree on the side, and it also resonates with the male part—meaning it looks like it. So, these imageries and combinations are kept deliberately so that every visual element of the film, whether it's Billie's sketch where she repeatedly darkens the hole or that video room from where the tapes come out. These all point towards one thing: that desire, creation, and creativity all emerge from the same place, from the same raw, physical earth. There is another very interesting angle connected to this. There is literally a concept of a movie within a movie, and we are told what it means. It is revealed in the film that Little Death himself makes all the Camp Miasma films . Meaning he makes real campers the actors and victims of his own fictional world. When Chris pitches this to her producers on a Zoom call, she says that we didn't create Little Death, but rather he created us. This line is a meta-commentary on the entire film about how fiction and reality shape each other. Just as Chris had her own awakening from watching this film, the film itself was crafted from someone else’s reality. Everything we consume , whether it’s horror movies or any media, shapes us, and we then express those same ideas back into our lives, our art, and our identities. It’s an endless loop where the line between fiction and reality blurs, creating that dreamlike, Mulholland Drive-esque quality. Now, the most discussed part is: what does the ending actually mean? Her partner Mari, Mari’s partner Thor, her agent, and all the producers or filmmakers, and Little Death kills them one by one. Now, this wasn't just random killing, friends; it was the symbolic elimination of all those distractions, pressures, and stresses in Chris's mind that were stopping her from fully feeling. Then, when Chris and Billy finally become intimate inside Bunker Number Five, where the original film was shot, Little Death pierces both of them with a single spear. This moment signifies feeling intimacy to the very end—you know what I mean—and simultaneously, it’s their death. Meaning two things are shown in a single frame, which is the very title of this film,' Sex and Death, 'which literally cannot be separated, at least in the language of this film. But the question is, once those people were killed, why were only Chris and Billy the ones who seemed to come back to life later? Why didn't we see the others come back to life? Well, the most convincing explanation is that of all those killed by Little Death, only Chris and Billy actually complete their journey. Meaning they both fully accept their desires, their shame, and their vulnerability, and reach that final moment. The other characters like Mari, Thor, the agent, and the producers were just external forces distracting Chris from her true self. Meaning they never got the chance to complete their own journey. That is why they are permanently wiped out. What Billy experiences is a metaphorical Little Death. text: [bell and music] Eternity forces Joan to choose between her first love and her lifelong husband, setting up the film's ultimate moral. Eternity introduces a unique perspective on the afterlife, where people choose where their afterlife is and with whom. This complicates Joan's situation, however, as her two deceased husbands compete for her affections. The film is largely rooted in the choice Joan has to make, whether she'll reunite with her long-dead first husband, Luke, or if she'll remain with her lifelong spouse, Larry. It's a film that doesn't paint either side as villainous or perfect, which plays into the film's themes about romance and passion. Does Joan choose Larry or Luke in Eternity? Eternity is rooted in the decision that Joan has to make over which husband to spend her afterlife with. And although she initially chooses Luke, she eventually decides on Larry. After dying peacefully not long after her husband passed away, Joan reunites with Larry and quickly tries to adjust to the afterlife. This is complicated by the presence of her first husband, Luke, who died during the Korean War. Luke has waited for decades to be reunited with her, setting up both men to compete for her affections in hopes that they can convince her to join them in their respective eternities. However, when a frustrated Joan almost chooses to ignore them both, Larry realizes that Joan's form in the afterlife is based on her happiest moments and that she looks like she did when she was with Luke. This prompts Larry to back out of the competition, allowing Joan to go into an afterlife with Luke. Eternity is about the question of whether the heights of first love are more valuable than a more enduring one. While Luke and Joan are initially happy together, Joan grows increasingly distant from her first love and begins to miss Larry. Eventually, Luke reluctantly comes to terms with this and helps her escape. While Luke and Joan do love each other on some deep level that will never go away, it's clear by Eternity's third act that her true love is with Larry. She'll always wonder what could have happened if Luke hadn't died in the Korean War. But she can't deny that she and Luke have found true happiness together. How eternity's afterlife works. A24, a courtesy Everett collection. The afterlife in Eternity is rooted in choosing specific paths forward. Every person who dies is greeted with a choice on where they want to spend the remainder of their existence. A floor show and salesmen frequently try to pitch new arrivals on their own afterles, but with no clear hierarchy at play. This is jokingly referenced multiple times in the film with no clear deity identified. Instead, the afterlife is treated as a bureaucracy where people have to follow specific rules. As the film progresses, it turns out that even the employees of the afterlife are regular souls instead of angels or demons. Because they have not chosen their own eternity or have found a new purpose in helping others on their own path, they remain in the limbo space between forevers. This turns out to be Anna's backstory as she quietly reveals to Larry that she came from a hard life but has found meaning in her position as an afterlife coordinator. If someone wants to remain in that space, they have to find a position in the afterlife. This is what happens to Larry after he believes Joan has chosen Luke, electing to take Luke's now open position as bartender. Deciding he doesn't want an eternity without Joan, Larry simply remains behind to lend an ear to other wandering souls. Choosing an eternity is meant to be a oneanddone decision. As Joan and Larry eventually discover attempting to escape an eternity can get someone dropped into an empty void, which is described as the closest thing to hell in this world. That Joan is willing to risk this to reunite with Larry speaks to her love for him. The true meaning of eternity. At the core of eternity is the difference between young passion and enduring love. While Joan is quickly lost in Luke's eyes and overjoyed to see him again, they have little actual chemistry in the long run. Luke is active in a way Joan isn't, and their differences only grow more pronounced as the film progresses. Although they'll always love one another on some level, Luke and Joan both acknowledge that their relationship was built up in their heads precisely because it ended prematurely. They never got the chance to grow and change and be new people together. This gives their romance a wistful quality and a bittersweet edge. By contrast, Joan is quick to bicker with Larry, but is also more comfortable with him than anyone else. Larry and Joan laugh together and have fun with their situation. Larry knows Joan's favorite music, notices the changes in her hair, and is blunt with her in a way no one else is. He's her partner in every way. All of this is presented as Larry being frustrating and even annoying at times, but he also makes Joan happier than anyone else in the film. Their love has endured tragedy, happiness, and complacency. It's not just passion that drives them together. It's a relationship that keeps them together. This is the ultimate moral of eternity with Larry happily risking his own existence for a chance to spend a quiet eternity with Joan. Notably, they don't choose a mountain, a beach, or any vacation destination. Instead, they just want to be in a suburb that resembles the one where they raised a family and grew old together. It's a sweet conclusion to the film and one that highlights why Joan chooses Larry. While Luke may be young love personified, he's become an idea to Joan instead of a person. By contrast, for all his faults, Larry is the person she knows and cares about. It's a sweet emotional core that helps Eternity stick a potentially tricky ending.

text: Today we're diving into Eternity, A24's charming, surprising, and sometimes heartbreaking afterlife romcom directed by David Fry. It's a story that blends romance, metaphysics, comedy, and a love triangle that literally spans lifetimes. At its core, Eternity asks one impossible question. If you could choose who to spend forever with, what would you do when your heart belongs to two different lives? We start with Larry and Joan Cutler, an ordinary couple who have spent 65 years together. Their life has been long, imperfect, but filled with love. They've raised children, watched their grandchildren grow, and live through enough arguments and reconciliations to fill several novels. Their story begins at a gender reveal party for their granddaughter. The family buzzes with excitement. Larry, older now, wanders over to a bowl of pretzels for a snack. And then, in the most brutally mundane A24 way possible, Larry starts choking. A few coughs, a stumble, and then silence. With shocking abruptness, Larry dies. But death is not the end. Larry awakens gasping. Suddenly decades younger, now played by Miles Teller, standing at what looks like a giant retrofuturistic train station. Think Grand Central Terminal meets Disneyland's Tomorrowland. A large glowing sign reads, "Welcome to the station. Your eternity awaits. This is where everyone arrives after death. And in this world, you don't go straight to heaven or hell. Instead, you arrive at the station, return to the age you are happiest, choose an eternity package, board a train to your final destination. Some eternities look like vacations, some look like fantasies, some are deeply weird, but each is forever. Larry meets two afterlife coordinators. Anna, played by Divine Joy Randolph, and Ryan, played by the hilarious John Early. They act like cruise guides crossed with DMV employees. Charming, chaotic, and sarcastically overworked. They explain Larry has one week to choose his eternity. Once he boards a train, the choice is permanent. And yes, he can wait at the station for someone else to arrive, but people don't come in order. Larry thinks immediately of Joan. She's been battling cancer, so she might arrive soon. He decides to wait. The station is huge with hundreds of people waiting for loved ones. One of them is a bartender, handsome, confident, old-fashioned. His name is Luke. He's been waiting behind that bar for 67 years. He died young in the Korean War. He was Joan's first husband, her first love, the one she married at 20, but lost almost instantly. Luke is played by Callum Turner, and the moment he hears Larry mention Joan's name, he freezes. He's been waiting not months, not years, but decades, hoping Joan would one day walk into the station. Two men, one lifetime shared, one lifetime stolen, and both claimed the same woman. After days of waiting, the station doors open, and there she is, Joan. now young again, played by Elizabeth Olsen, walks inside confused and emotional. She sees Larry first, runs to him, laughs, and cries at the same time. But then she turns and sees Luke, the man she loved first, the man she lost too soon, the man she never got to say goodbye to. Her face freezes, her soul fractures, and the real story begins. Joan now has to choose between Larry, the man she built a life with. Kids, grandkids, messy years, joyful years, and Luke, the man she barely got to start with. The what if, the unfinished love, the dream. Both options are beautiful. Both are tragic. Both are forever. While Joan struggles, the film takes us deeper into the station. We see Studio 54, Eternity, Disco Lights Forever, No Men, Eternity, immediately popular. Smoking eternity, cigarettes can't kill you twice. Quiet eternity. Just endless peace. Chaotic eternity for people who apparently liked stress. There are brochures, sales pitches, holograms, long lines. It's a hilarious bureaucratic mess wrapped around cosmic existentialism. But Joan can't even think about eternity. She hasn't even processed dying. Her entire emotional system has just been rebooted. And the two men circling her aren't making it easier. Larry tries to be patient. He had Joan for 65 years. He knows her like no one else ever could. Meanwhile, Luke is overflowing with longing and frustration. He's waited nearly 70 decades for a chance to live the life he was robbed of. And Joan sees truth in both of them. With Luke, she feels the rush of being young, fearless, idealistic, newly married. With Larry, she feels safety, memory, family, history. This isn't a triangle. It's two different versions of her own heart. As the deadline approaches, staff members Anna and Ryan check in constantly. Your eternity window is closing. If you don't choose, you'll be assigned. Please don't make a mess in the lobby. They try to help Joan, but even they admit no one can tell you what eternity should look like. Joan finally cracks under the pressure. She confesses to both men. I don't know what I want. You're both my life. Just different pieces of it. Larry breaks. Luke breaks. Joan breaks. The station feels smaller. The clock feels louder. Every eternity starts looking wrong. For the first time, Joan feels truly dead. Cut off from everything that wants to find her. The three of them sit together, quiet, defeated, and Joan finally makes her decision. The film doesn't treat it like a twist. It treats it like a truth. She chooses the person who reflects who she became, not who she used to be. She chooses the love that grew with her, aged with her, frustrated her, comforted her, challenged her, raised a family with her. Joan chooses Larry. But in the afterlife, love doesn't erase pain. Luke is devastated. Not angry, just heartbroken in the way only seven decades of hope can produce. He hugs her goodbye softly with acceptance. Then he walks toward his train, toward an eternity he must now face alone, a world he never wanted without her. It is one of the film's most quietly crushing moments. Larry and Joan board their train together at last. The station shrinks behind them. The sky screen dims and the train glides forward into whatever eternity they have chosen. Something simple, peaceful, and shared. But before the doors close, Joan looks back one last time. Not with regret, but with gratitude. Luke watches from a distance. He smiles. a small, broken, beautiful smile just before his own train departs. Eternity ends on a warm, bittersweet note. Love is complicated. Timing is cruel. Life isn't fair. But choice gives us meaning even after death. And Joan choice reflects a deep truth. Forever isn't about excitement. It's about the person who walks with you through every season of your life, even the last one. Eternity mixes humor, metaphysics, and romance to deliver one of A24's sweetest films in years. It's simple, whimsical, and emotionally grounded, even when it doesn't explore its afterlife concept as far as it could. But in the end, it gives us something surprisingly rare. A love story big enough to last beyond life itself.

text: Whenever I hear a new zombie survival thriller film on the block, I waste absolutely no time in checking it out. I mean, yes, it often ends in disappointment, but my recent outing in this Australian horror flick called We Bury the Dead was rather fruitful. I love the unique take on the genre, far from the stereotypical approach, and I have to appreciate the director, Zach Hilditch, for the vision. It tells the story of a woman who seeks out her missing husband in the aftermath of an accidental experimental weapon detonation gone wrong, where, you know, some of these affected are turned into violent zombie-like beings. In this video, I will break down the movie for you and also elaborate on the emotional ending and the unique type of undead that you see in this film. There will be some major spoilers going ahead, so you have been warned. The movie starts off with a catastrophic event that is the root cause of all the trouble that starts brewing. An experimental weapon is accidentally triggered in Tasmania, and this affects all animal and human life on the island. Those who were affected by the impact of the weapon end up in a comatose state, completely unconscious. Most of the victims are usually dead following this, but some who regain consciousness end up in a situation that I can only describe as worse than death. The disaster relief crew in Tasmania reports about some of these instances, where the victims awaken from their coma and start behaving violent. Their appearance and mannerisms are just like the undead, but it would be wrong to view them as the kind of undead we see in horror fiction in general. I will come back to this later, but let me first take you to the protagonist, Ava Newman, who is caught up in the middle of this tragedy. She was not in an ideal marriage, but things go terribly wrong for her when she realizes that her husband, Mitch, was on a business trip on the west coast of Tasmania, rendering him vulnerable to all that has transpired. Ava is determined to get to her husband at any cost, and she comes up with a smart plan for that. She signs up as a volunteer as a part of an effort to retrieve and dispose the bodies of the population assisted by the US military. To make matters worse and far more concerning for her, she finds out on the first day of her unit's efforts that the soldiers accompanying them murder any of the victims who wake up. I mean, that would be a typical military response to a potentially threatening undead uprising, but you know, it puts her husband at a great risk, and the odds are worse for Ava. By now, I'm totally smitten by the performance of Daisy Ridley as the protagonist as the Star Wars veteran steps into a challenging role effortlessly. And finally, the driver allows himself to be killed with a shovel who finishes burying them all. So, are the corpses more than mindless beasts and do they have some kind of intelligence that tells them when attacking someone would be futile? Well, I will come back to this in a jiffy, but let me finish up with the story first. Finally, after all her gruesome adventures, Ava makes it to the hotel where her husband, Mitch, is stationed. But, there's no good news awaiting for her here because she finds out that Mitch never woke up from death and she also comes to her startling realization that her husband had cheated on her with a co-worker. Also, she reunites with Clay at the hotel and they both place the lifeless body of Mitch on a motorboat and they set the boat on fire before sending it out to the sea. Quite an aesthetic funeral, if you ask me. It's somewhat of a grim ending to the movie and I surely expected more drama and action than the emotional climate. As Clay and Ava make their way back to Hobart, they encounter Riley's wife and she has now given birth. She dies shortly, but Ava and Clay find the newborn in a nearby ruin. Now, the best part of this tragedy is that the baby is alive and looks completely healthy with no features of the undead. Did she not pick up on the impact of the deadly weapon? Well, presumably not and it's a bittersweet moment in Ava's painful journey. She picks up the baby and cries tears of joy and the movie ends on this note. Not with a promise of a better tomorrow or a happy ending for Ava, but with hope for her and something for her to hang on to in these desperate times. So, there you go with the story and the dramatic climax, but the real deal with the film is actually the nature of the undead. I don't know about you, but I have never come across such a unique form of zombie, if I can even call these zombies in the traditional sense of the term. Firstly, the zombies are not caused by an infection or bite, but they're the side effect of a military super weapon. A US experimental weapon is accidentally detonated in Tasmania. It wipes out all human and animal life in the blast radius by shutting down their nervous systems, which is essentially total brain death. Most state dead, but a subset of the dead bodies later reboot and regain motor function and some consciousness. These are the film's undead. Crucially, this is not classic Romero virus lore. There's no spread, no contagion, no turning from bites. If you didn't die in the blast, you don't become one. And if you did die there, you might later get up. Director Kiah Roache-Turner has even said that the zombies were added to serve the themes, not to deliver hard sci-fi rule. They stay very recognizably corpse-like rather than mutating into monster. They look like victims of a devastating blast and subsequent rot, not fresh amp. The undead have missing limbs, exposed bone, partially decomposed torsos dragging themselves. And the makeup leans into classic corpse horror. The nashing teeth grinding is a signature marker of the undead, including one type that makes a disturbing clicking sound teeth. I also find their lifeless eyes to be rather disturbing. Some are heavily decayed like the RV driver and Riley's chained test subjects. And you know, others are partially decomposed like Riley's wife, the pregnant woman at the end. But the through line is that they're visibly dead walking and not infected living host. Some of them are extremely dangerous as we find out during the gas station attack scene. There are aggressive attacking zombies that are straight out of a classic zombie scene with a sudden lunge, relentless pursuit, and dangerous close quarter struggle. But more importantly, many zombies are not in pure predator. A major point of the film is that each reanimated corpse [music] seems driven by a specific piece of unfinished business, rather than random hunger. The RV zombie driver wakes up and calmly begins digging a grave for himself and his family's corpses. He notices Ava, right? But, doesn't attack and allows himself to be killed and buried after the job is done. Riley's wife's body decays in bed while he obsesses over her. When she finally wakes, she doesn't ambush Ava, but just stands and watches. Then later is found walking with a hugely pregnant belly, clearly focused on the fate of her unborn child rather than random violence. Finally, she's aware enough to seek help for her newborn, then walks away once Ava moves toward the crying baby. So, technically, we have two types of zombie. The aggressive hunter zombies, if these are not destroyed quickly, they get more agitated and dangerous over time. Then there are the task-driven undead whose actions are organized around one lingering compulsion that is more than feeding. Some critics have called the zombies an embodiment of grief and the weight of unfinished conversation rather than predators alone. As for their intelligence, the military insists the undead are mindless and executes any that move. However, the film steadily proves this wrong as many zombies retain fragments of memory, identity, and purpose. I have noticed that several corpses in the background do hesitate hide or cower instead of charge. The director and cast have discussed in an interview how part of the challenge was playing zombies whose struggle mirrors the grief of the living, not as creatures to be mowed down. Lastly, the undead are not invulnerable, and there are methods to kill them off quite comfortably. The headshot kills are surely straight from the zombie mythos in general, and we see the military doing the same here. Ava even kills one with a shovel to the head, even though it wasn't even aggressive towards her. The most comforting thing for me was that the undead weren't exactly super fast. Yes, some were faster than the others, but none were sprinters really posed a serious threat. Also, another striking moment for me was the normal human baby born from a zombie mother, which suggests that she was pregnant before being affected by the weapon and it did not affect the fetus. I'm guessing the baby already had developed a nervous system by the time that, you know, the impact hit the mother and changed her. All in all, this was one memorable undead type that I hope gets explored further if we ever get a seek. As far as the movies concerned, I will certainly rate this well above average for the generic flicks that we find in the genre. It has its share of gnarly moments as you can tell from the story and the horrifying details of the undead, but at the same time, the film cares to give a more human side of the outbreak as well. I mean, even the undead or the zombie-like entities are not just the average flesh-eating monster that we see in such films and I was quite impressed by the fast-paced narrative that doesn't keep you waiting for action. In short, this is an effort that deserves your attention and I will strongly recommend checking out this unique zombie drama with a tinge of tragedy and some serious thought-provoking moments. Let me know in the comments below what you think of the story and also share your thoughts in the nature of the undead shown in the film.

text: Art has always imitated life. At any given point, cinema has always reflected the circumstances surrounding it. Dead Man's Wire stars Bill Scarsgard as Tony Curitus, a man living in Indianapolis who falls behind on the mortgage payments for a real estate property that he intends to develop into a shopping center. When his mortgage broker, Hall, refuses to give him more time to pay, Curitus becomes convinced that Hall and his son, Richard Dick Hall, intend to take the property. If Dick tries to escape, or if someone takes Tony out from a distance, the wire will pull the trigger, killing Dick. Using this crude but effective mechanism, Tony forces Dick out of his office and back to his apartment. Law enforcement, led by Detective Michael Greybel, attempts to negotiate with Tony, whose demands are simple. He wants Meridian Mortgage to pay him $5 million for allegedly sabotaging his plans concerning the property. No charges pressed against him for the kidnapping.
