Hill stars as Tony's brother, Jimmy, while Kelly Lynch appears as Dick's wife, Mabel. The screenplay is by Austin Coladney, who began writing it in 2020 and enlisted the help of documentarians Alan Barry and Mark Enox, who were behind the 2018 documentary Dead Man's Line. Dead Man's Wire is a showcase for Bill Scarsgard. First and foremost, Dead Man's Wire is meant as a showcase for Bill Scarsgard, and the actor more than delivers. Those familiar with his work beyond the mainstream horror projects he's most famous for won't be surprised. But for anyone who's best acquainted with him for playing Pennywise, Dead Man's Wire will be a revelation. Tony is a singular character, too deluded to take seriously, yet too unpredictable to ignore. Scarsgard plays him with tremendous empathy, which Nan Sant very much shares. However, they don't bother themselves by excusing Tony. In fact, they don't seem particularly interested in making you understand him either. Instead, they aim for something far simpler. They just want you to see Tony and in the process perhaps discover something about yourself and the way you see the world. Scarsgard's greatest asset as an actor has always been his physicality, which he puts to excellent use here. His long limbs tremble with anxiety, too desperate to act without actually knowing what to do. His wide, manic eyes go from one place to another, not really noticing anything. His hunched back making him seem pitiful, but never outright pathetic. Yet, Scarsgard remains a commanding presence, perhaps not menacing, but still undeniably discomforting. Kuritis was described as psychotic and paranoid during his trial, and Scarsgard perfectly captures that. He also embraces the absurdity inherent in the situation, adding a much appreciated comedic edge to his work. As the plot progresses, whatever feeble grasp Tony has on the situation slips, allowing Scarsgard to go into full diluted mode. It's a striking performance that very clearly wants to echo Pacino's legendary work in Dog Day Afternoon. And while it doesn't reach those heights, it comes remarkably close. If Scarsgard is the chaos of the storm, then Daker Montgomery is the stillness before and after it. The actor, best known for his villainous work on Stranger Things, has the tough task of remaining subdued throughout the picture, both emotionally and physically. Any outburst risks pulling the trigger. Montgomery isn't flashy, but there's a remarkable aspect to his meek, defeated approach, without which Dead Man's Wire wouldn't work. In the supporting roles, neither Domingo nor Pacino gets much to do, but they both make the most out of their limited roles. Pacino is particularly effective in his brief antagonistic role, embodying the monolithic nature of the very same institutions that Tony blames for his predicament. Pacino delights in playing this wicked, cynical, unforgiving man. Capitalism embodied, hiding behind a facade of fair play while a devout acolyte of the mighty dollar. As for Elwez and Mihala, they have a couple of standout scenes, but their roles don't really amount to much. Indeed, this is Bill Scarsgard's show, and he makes the most out of it. Dead Man's Wire is topical and ultimately impactful. Ever the observer of human nature, Vans film feels like an extension of Tony Kuratis himself as the Oscar nominated director adopts an urgent approach behind the camera, as if operating under a ticking clock. Considering Tony and Dick's ordeal lasts only a few days, and perhaps because the film shooting took only 20 days, Dead Man's Wire feels as distressed and short of breath as its protagonist. Somewhat confusingly, Vans never lets the story fly off the rails despite a central performance that's barely keeping it together. If there's one major flaw here, it's The Dead Man's Wire never allows itself to let its freak flag fly. The production design is minimal, but it faithfully recreates 1977 through the type of muted yellowish visuals we've come to expect from 70s movies. The settings are few. Dick's office, Tony's apartment, ML's hotel room, the room where the FBI, and the officers plot to contain the situation, making the characters feel trapped not only in the situation, but more importantly, in a perpetual cycle of misguided choices that lead to inescapable mistakes. Perhaps that's Dead Man's Wire's biggest statement. Life is a trap and to escape it, we have to lead ourselves somehow. In interviews, Van Sand has discussed the story similarity to Luigi Mangon's case. At its core, Dead Man's Wire is a story about rebellion. It's not so much that it has a profound sympathy for Tony Kuratis or antipathy for ML and Dick so much as it has an unequivocal and moral opposition to the institutions that create men like them. The film sees these people as players in a game that's rigged and everyone is using someone. Tony is using Dick. The media is using Tony. The cops are using Jimmy. And in the end, pretty much no one wins but the system that profits off Tony's desperation, Dick's suffering, ML's ambition, and the world's willingness to turn a blind eye. Ultimately, Dead Man's Wire doesn't reach the same heights as Gus Vans's Greatest, largely because it operates on a small-scale approach that limits the impact that such an offbeat, unbelievable story could and should have. However, it's a worthwhile addition to his filmography and his best movie in ages, probably since 2008's Milk. Perhaps more importantly, it's also an effective condemnation of capitalism without ever falling into the typical eat the rich trappings that too often lessen the impact of these narratives. And with a delightfully gono performance from Bill Scarsgard that should have received some attention this awards season, Dead Man's Wire is a successful throwback to the classic crime stories that once dominated cinema. They also bring in a new chorus master: the driven and uncompromising Dr. Henry Guthrie, played by Ralph Fiennes. The community discovers that in the midst of chaos, loss, and repressed emotions, singing becomes their way to cope, connect, and find resilience. Nicholas Hytner, who's collaborated with Bennett before on things like The History Boys and The Lady in the Van, directs with a gentle, unsentimental touch – letting the wit, poignancy, and humanity shine through. It's got Bennett's signature sharp dialogue and common sense, subcontracting the big emotions to the soaring choral music, especially Elgar's piece which bookends the film beautifully. Ralph Fiennes is fantastic as Guthrie – prickly, demanding, but with a sensitive heart underneath. He plays it grounded and subtle, reminding us why he's one of the best, grounding the ensemble with gravitas while allowing others to sparkle. The supporting cast is a treasure trove of British talent: Roger Allam, Simon Russell Beale, Mark Addy, Alun Armstrong bringing warmth and humor to the committee members, and the young actors like Taylor Uttley, Oliver Briscombe, and Amara Okereke feeling fresh and authentic as the teens discovering their voices – literally and figuratively. The film touches on themes like repressed passion, community in crisis, the role of art in dark times, and subtle hints at Guthrie's sexuality and grief, all handled with candor and care without overwhelming the story. Visually, it's classic period elegance – rainy Yorkshire streets, cozy rehearsal halls, with the music swelling to give those emotional lifts. At 1 hour 53 minutes and rated R for some language and thematic elements, it's mature but accessible, blending quiet drama with moments of dark humor and heartfelt uplift. It premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival back in September 2025, hit UK theaters in November, had a limited US release over Christmas, and now it's going wider on January 16, 2026 – great for some thoughtful winter viewing. Critics are mixed but appreciative – it's at 64% on Rotten Tomatoes, with many praising Fiennes' stellar turn, the sharp script, ensemble warmth, and how it captures music's power to unite. Some call it stirring, funny, and impressively unsentimental, a quiet pleasure with a heartbeat of wit. Others note it can feel scattered with too many characters or low-key to the point of slightness, but the performances and final emotional punch win out for most. If you enjoy period pieces that explore humanity through art – think The King's Speech or even Bennett's own works – or just love great British acting and choral music that tugs at the heart, definitely seek out The Choral. text: The movie opens in a quiet suburban neighborhood. Sunlight streaming through kitchen windows, laughter echoing in the background. We meet Morgan Grant, played by Allison Williams. She's a woman who's learned to play it safe. A responsible mother, loyal wife, and steady friend. But beneath that perfect surface is a woman who wonders what might have been. She became a mother at 18, giving up college dreams for her daughter, Clara, played by the brilliant McKenna Greece. Now Clara's 17, confident, artistic, stubborn, and full of that restless energy that reminds Morgan a little too much of herself. At the start, their relationship feels distant. Not hostile, but tense. Clara rolls her eyes when Morgan talks. Morgan worries too much, trying to protect her from every possible mistake. And then there's Chris, Morgan's husband. A good man, everyone says, reliable, hardwork, the kind of dad who always remembers birthdays. The Grant family looks perfect from the outside, a model of stability. But like all Hoover stories, appearances lie. Morgan's sister, Jenny, her best friend since childhood, is cheerful and impulsive, the opposite of Morgan's steady calm. She's married to Jonah, played by Dave Franco, and the four of them share a close, almost too close friendship. Barbecues, coffee mornings, family dinners, a small circle of trust until it all shatters. One quiet afternoon, Morgan is making dinner when the phone rings. A voice on the other end tells her there's been a car crash, a fatal one. Two people dead. Morgan drops everything and rushes to the hospital. And when the doctor says the names, time stops. Her husband Chris and her sister Jenny, both gone. The movie sound design fades. We hear only her breathing, broken sobs, and silence. It's not just death. It's confusion. Why were they together? They'd said they were each somewhere else. At the funeral, Clara sits pale and motionless beside her mother. The grief is raw, but their reactions couldn't be more different. Clara idolized her father. She's angry at the world, angry at fate. Morgan, meanwhile, is numb because deep down something doesn't add up. Later, police reports confirm what Morgan already suspected. Chris's car was found miles away near a motel. Jenny's things were inside. That moment, when realization hits, is the true breaking point. Morgan doesn't scream. She doesn't throw things. She just sits there broken as tears slide silently down her face because she hasn't just lost a husband. She's lost her sister, her best friend, and her entire sense of truth. After the funerals, grief settles in like fog. Morgan barely speaks. She hides away the photos, packs Chris's things, and tells herself it's better this way. Clara doesn't need to know the truth. But Clara sees this as betrayal. To her, her mom's silence feels cold, like she's trying to erase her father from their lives. She doesn't understand that Morgan is trying to protect her. She only feels the distance growing wider every day. Clara starts sneaking out, skipping school, trying to escape the suffocating sadness of her home. And that's when she meets Miller Adams, played by Mason Thes, a boy from her school with a reputation for trouble. But Miller isn't what he seems. He's not a cliche bad boy. He's lost, too. He understands pain. At her father's funeral, he shows up quietly, stands in the back, and when Clara runs outside in tears, he follows. That moment marks the beginning of something new. They talk. They share silence. They laugh again. Something Clara hasn't done since the accident. And for a brief moment, she feels alive. Miller buys her weed. A small rebellion that gives her a taste of freedom. But it also marks a turning point. Morgan finds out, and she's furious. To Morgan, Miller represents everything she fears. the loss of control, the mistakes she once made. To Clara, Miller represents everything she's craving. Connection, comfort, and escape. One night, while searching through Chris's old toolbox, Morgan finds something that freezes her in place. A stack of letters. At first, she thinks they're from work. Then, she sees the handwriting. It's Jenny's. As she reads, her face falls apart. Every letter a confession of love. Every page proof of betrayal. Her husband and her sister. All those late work nights. All the excuses. It all makes sense now. She breaks down completely, curling up on the floor, sobbing into her hands. This scene, played with devastating restraint by Allison Williams, is the emotional heart of the movie. The moment Morgan's pain transforms from grief into anger. But she doesn't tell Clara. She locks the letters away. And this silence, this decision to protect her daughter only makes Clara hate her more. As Morgan sinks into quiet despair, Clara runs toward anything that feels alive. She throws herself into Miller's arms. Their chemistry is undeniable. Innocent yet charged with raw emotion. He becomes her safe place. But even Miller isn't perfect. He's dating someone else, a college girl he doesn't really love. Stuck in a relationship he can't escape. Still with Clara, he feels real. They start sneaking around. Late night drives, secret texts, soft kisses in the dark. But secrets always come out. When Morgan catches them together, it's explosive. She sees her daughter making the same mistakes she once did. Falling too young too fast, trying to fill the emptiness with someone else. Their argument is brutal. Clara screams that Morgan doesn't understand. Morgan yells that Clara is throwing away her future. And for the first time, Clara says it. You're just mad because you regret your own life. The words land like daggers. Morgan walks away, heart shattered, because deep down she knows her daughter isn't entirely wrong. Meanwhile, Jonah, Jenny's widowerower, returns to town with his infant son. He's broken, haunted by doubts about whether the baby is even his. Jonah and Morgan's friendship becomes a strange mirror. They're both grieving the same betrayal. Both raising children who've lost their parents. They lean on each other quietly, painfully. But unlike Chris and Jenny, they never cross the line. In one scene, Jonah admits that despite everything, he still loves Jenny. And Morgan whispers, "I wish I didn't. It's a powerful reflection on how love and betrayal can coexist. How sometimes you can hate someone for what they did but still ache for them. After learning the truth, finally discovering that her father was having an affair, Clara runs away. She finds herself at the old theater, a place she and her dad used to visit together. It's dark, empty, echoing with memories. She sits on the stage, tears falling, as she replays everything she's learned. Then Morgan finds her, and for the first time, there are no lies, no defenses, just two people, mother and daughter, facing the truth together. Clara admits that she's been lost, that she hates her father for lying, but hates herself for still loving him. She says she feels like him, broken, selfish, unfaithful because she kissed Miller knowing he had someone else. Morgan takes her hand and says softly, "We are not our parents. We don't have to make their mistakes." She admits that she's been tempted too, that Jonah was there and that she cared for him, but she chose not to act on it because love is about choice. The tears flow. The years of resentment melt away. Mother and daughter collapse into each other's arms, sobbing. This theater scene is the emotional climax, the point where regret transforms into forgiveness. In the film's final act, we see life slowly returning. Morgan smiles again. She forgives, not for the dead, but for herself. Clara and Miller continue their relationship, this time honestly with Morgan's cautious approval. Jonah becomes a devoted father, deciding that love, not blood, defines family. In the closing scene, Morgan and Clara walk by the lake near their home. The sun sets behind them. A new day on the horizon. Clara takes her mother's hand. No words are spoken. They don't need them because sometimes healing isn't about forgetting. It's about remembering without the pain. Regretting you is not just a story about infidelity or grief. It's a meditation on motherhood, forgiveness, and the fragile line between love and regret. It reminds us that even the strongest families can break, but they can also rebuild piece by piece if they're brave enough to tell the truth. It's messy. It's human. It's heartbreakingly real. And that's why Colleen Hoover's stories connect with millions because she writes not about perfect people, but about people who are learning how to live with their imperfections. So, what would you do if you discovered your partner's secret after they were gone? Would you tell your child the truth, or would you protect them, even if it meant losing their trust? His men help him put on his armor. Then he goes to the chapel. The Christians are currently at war with the Muslims, but Vlad asks, "Are you sure God wills this?" Sounding like he has some doubts about having to kill so many people. Before leaving for battle, he says, "I will fight in his name, but I ask for one favor. I want him to spare my wife. Vlad's armor looks really cool here, and the helmet resembles a dragon. It is implied in the Bram Stoker novel that Vlad the Impaler and Count Dracula are one and the same. The real life Vlad was known for being a member of the Order of the Dragon, aka Dracul. So, Dracula has often been associated with dragons. One thing I have to say about this helmet is how does he see anything? Is he seeing through the two nose holes? Imagine trying to fight a battle and this is all you can see. At the same time the battle began, the princess was ambushed and forced to try and escape on her own. Right after Vlad's battle is concluded, he is informed that she was ambushed and goes after her. The princess is riding her horse through this bear trap minefield. All the traps are just under the snow, so you can't see them. Eventually, the princess's horse goes down and it's not looking good. The men begin tapping the ground as to not step on a trap. Elizabetha probably should have done the same thing because she steps right into one. As the men are walking her down, about to finish the job, Vlad arrives. He races towards her as fast as he can, but his horse inevitably goes down and he has to run the rest of the way. He easily dispatches two men and throws his sword at the third, impaling him in the back. However, it was too late. The enemy had already stabbed her. Vlad runs to her and only gets a few short fleeting moments with her before she dies. Vlad returns to the priest angry. The one thing he asked for, for his wife to be spared, and yet she is dead and he didn't even get to say goodbye. He demands the priest tell God to send her back. But the priest says that's not possible. Vlad is absolutely furious at this point. He says, "My soul is stained with the blood of our enemies whom I have killed in his name." The priest simply says in a scared voice, "I don't have the answers, my prince. I'm only his humble messenger." Vlad responds in a strange calmness, "Good. I have a message that I want you to deliver to him." He then grabs the staff that the priest was holding, snaps it in half, and runs him through with it, then picking him up off the ground. His men back up in fear and Vlad says, "Tell your God until he brings back my wife. My life no longer belongs to him." He slams the priest onto the table, then looks up and sees the crucifix. He sticks out his arms as if he's mocking the crucifixion. Thunder and lightning erupt, and the eyes of Jesus on the cross begin to cry blood, and a strange, unnatural wind swirls around the room. His men then grab him and carry him out of the chapel. We now skip to 400 years later, but I want to talk a little more about what happened here. First of all, this film takes a lot of the love story aspects from Francis Ford Copala's film, as the original novel was not all that focused on the love story. Also, we never know how Dracula became a vampire in the novel, whereas this event was obviously the catalyst. Something different about this film and the 1992 version is Dracula's reason for anger. In the 1992 version, he's extra angry because his wife took her own life, meaning she will be damned to hell. However, in this version, she was killed, meaning she still went to heaven. When did you arrive? Uh, I have 10 minutes to go. Okay. It's now 400 years later, and this seems to be some kind of hospital or medical center. A doctor is walking with a colleague, and they quickly make their way to the chapel. Waiting for them is a priest. We are never actually given his name, just priest or father. Dr. Demont finds the priest and assumes he's praying, but he's actually enjoying some food and wine. The doctor explains that the hospital's administration is not happy about a priest being here. The medical establishment and the church don't always go so well together. Science verse religion. The doctor leads the priest through the building into a dungeon-like room that's very dark. In the middle of the room is a woman chained to the floor. The doctor reads her file. 25 years old from Bologona, Italy. The husband of this woman is the nephew of the queen, which is why this is being kept very secret. She was brought here because during her wedding, a clergyman arrived and has drove her into a frenzy, which is how he captured and brought her here. The priest then picks up her file and reads this. Born on the 18th of March, 1775. The doctor thinks it must be a clerical error, but the priest isn't so sure. If this is her actual birthday, it would make her 130 years old. The priest is going to conduct a few experiments to see if this is truly a creature of the devil. The first symptoms are longer than average life and an allergy to symbols of our Lord. He takes a closer look at the murder weapon, her teeth. The father says his order has been studying this phenomenon for more than 400 years and himself for more than 30. According to the priest, the doctor here is the first person to ever capture one of these creatures alive. The doctor wonders what exactly is it that he captured and the priest says a vampire. The vampire tries to use her charm on the doctor, but the priest quickly interferes and wants a closer look at her fangs. Two oversized canines. He says, "Contrary to popular belief, vampires adapt very well to light in general. It's direct rays they cannot take." The priest then opens up the window and the direct sunlight burns her skin, causing it to smolder. The doctor is blown away by this. He can't believe what he's seeing. I feel like at this point the priest is being sarcastic and says, "This could be just another anomaly of nature, so we have to continue until we have irrefutable proof." He then pulls a cross from his things and presents it to the vampire. She hisses at it, and it bursts into flames. The priest says, "Well, I think we have all the proof we need, doctor. Don't you?" He wants to ask the vampire, Maria, a few questions and promises to give her something she wants if she cooperates. Blood. He cuts the doctor's assistant and gives her a few drops of blood. He then asks Maria to show her neck. He sees a bite mark and states she is not a first generation vampire. They have been searching for the source for 400 years. Maria then says, "My master." The priest wants to know who this master is and where to find him, but she says, "He will find you. He comes to find his princess." So now the priest knows they need to find this mysterious princess and they might finally find the source. Something interesting to note about this rendition is there is no Renfield type character. Nobody that went to see the count prior to Jonathan. Instead, Maria kind of functions as one of Dracula's brides as well as the Renfield in this film. We now meet Jonathan Harker as he makes his way to Count Vlad's castle at the foot of the Carpathian Mountains. The carriage drops him off far away from the castle and he asks if the driver will help him with his luggage, but the driver refuses and also gives him a cross to take with him. Jonathan says he doesn't believe in God and the driver says, "Well, pray he believes in you." This kind of reminded me of the line from Constantine, but with a twist. Angela says, "I don't believe in the devil." And Constantine says, "You should. He believes in you." Jonathan is being stalked by some wolves on the way to the castle. And I wonder if this wolf is Dracula. He's been known to shapeshift into creatures of the night, including wolves. Jonathan arrives at the castle and is startled by the count, who has a look reminiscent of Gary Oldman from Bram Stoker's Dracula. He welcomes Jonathan and snuffs out his torch with his bare hand. And then suddenly, all the candles in the castle light. Jonathan is led to the dining room where a large dinner has been prepared. Jonathan comments that for such a large castle, he has not seen any staff and Dracula says they stay hidden. Jonathan is there on behalf of his legal firm because they want to purchase a property that belongs to the count, the opposite of what happens in BM Stoker's Dracula. In the original novel and the 1992 film, it's Dracula who wants to buy the property. Anyway, Dracula sees the cross that was given to Jonathan and asks if he believes in God. Jonathan sees the cross as well and nervously replies, "Oh, well, not really. It's just something the driver gave me." When Jonathan looks away, Dracula uses some kind of telekinesis to make the cross slide into the fire. And when it ignites, he gets a feeling of pleasure. He also grabs a rat and crushes it, draining its blood into a cup and drinking it. The count says, "Enough talking for tonight." And Jonathan retires to his room. Dracula goes into another room and plays a gramophone that Jonathan had been fascinated by. The song being played is the same one that came from the music box at the beginning of the film. He then tells a statue to keep an eye on Jonathan. Yes. My apologies for disturbing at such a late hour. The priest goes to meet with the vampire Maria's husband. Of course, he doesn't know that she's a vampire. He wants to know about her condition, and the priest is purposely vague. He wants to see Maria's room to see if he can find any clues about her master or this princess. In the middle of a book, he finds a page that's been ripped from another book, and it says, "Princess Elizabetha." At the castle, Jonathan is reading a book, and there's a page missing, the same one found by the priest. So, Dracula must have given this page to Maria. In the middle of the night, Jonathan's curiosity gets the better of him, and he goes searching around the castle, stumbling upon Dracula's coffin. He finds him there sleeping and without even opening his eyes, Dracula says, "You should not have left your room." He is then knocked unconscious by a gargoyle. When Jonathan awakes, he is tied up and surrounded by Dracula and his stone gargoyle minions. He must have used some kind of sorcery to bring them to life. Dracula says he sustains himself on fresh blood. Human is preferred. So, this sounds like he needs to feed on at least a little bit of blood in order to survive. He also says human is preferred. We seen earlier he fed on rat blood, so it doesn't hurt vampires, but it probably doesn't taste or sustain them in the same way as human blood. He explains that life is difficult and death is the ultimate peace, something God denies him. Jonathan asks why God would do that. He's nothing but love and mercy. Dracula says, "I thought you were not a believer." And Jonathan replies, "I am." Now, this makes the count laugh, but he is so old and starved for blood, his laugh is strained and harsh sounding. Dracula wants to know what his final wish is, and Jonathan wants to hear his story. At first, Dracula is reluctant, but decides to indulge him. He seems to really enjoy Jonathan's humor. He's then painfully lowered to the floor and put in a chair. Vlad begins by saying this. He is denied death by God even though he was one of his most faithful servants. Then his wife was taken. We see Vlad putting roses on his wife's grave. For 400 years he has awaited her return. Jonathan is curious how Vlad knows she will come back. Vlad says sometimes pure souls can be reincarnated and my beloved was the purest of them all. The problem is Dracula does not know when, where, or how she will be reincarnated. The search was difficult. The Black Death spread all over Europe for centuries. Nearly 200 million souls were decimated, half of them women. This made his search very difficult because all the remaining women were gathered in holy places where he is not welcome. So, it sounds like Dracula cannot enter a church or a holy place. And it seems ordinary vampires cannot either. The doctor earlier stated that Maria specifically requested that her marriage not take place in a church, most likely because she can't go in one. Even just the sight of a clergy man was enough to drive her into a frenzy. Dracula was so lonely he became jealous of those that death claimed. Defeated from his search, he returns to his wife's grave and lays on top of it. He did this many times until he lost all faith. One day he went up into his room, broke the window, and threw himself from the castle. Except he did not die. So he did it again and again. As he said, death is a privilege that God denies him. We also see at this time the gargoyless on the castle are already alive. Dracula says after a while all desire disappears, even the desire to die. He still had the hope of finding his love, but he couldn't search everywhere. He had to find a way to make her come to him. He holds up a fancy looking vial, and Jonathan asks if it's poison. Vlad corrects him saying it's a fragrance he developed for over a century. He traveled to the city of Baghdad known for their magical gardens of a thousand and1 flowers. He then continued to Kage in India where he learned to capture the souls of the most sensitive flowers. But it was only back in Europe where his research came to fruition. First in the colorful fields of grass in France, then in the heart of Italy, Florence is where it was created. The man in the shop hands Vlad a bottle of fragrance and says, "I think this is the one." He tries it out right there in the shop, and as soon as he does, all the women begin to turn around and fawn over him, even some coming in from outside. Vlad says it was more powerful than he ever could have imagined. This perfume must be some kind of alchemy or combination of fragrance and magic. We then see Vlad using this fragrance to charm courts all over Europe through the years while looking for Elizabetha. This is a very interesting sequence set to music with everyone dancing. The costumes are very cool. Vlad jokingly says, "I have to admit this period was not the most unpleasant. Finally, his journey ended at the great French court of Versailles." He says, "King Louie, whose number I forget, was having all of his nobles and artists come together so he could keep a closer eye on them. There was no doubt in Vlad's mind that if Elizabetha had returned, this is where she would be. He says, "I had never been so close to finding her." The woman looked similar to Elizabetha, but it was not her. Elizabetha, no, I'm not. Now Vlad's mission was seemingly impossible, and he was becoming enraged. He now felt it necessary to entrust his search for Elizabetha to others. He bears his fangs, then begins biting people at the party. When he bites one woman, her wig falls off, revealing her long red hair. So, this is where he turned Maria. We see him bite at least half a dozen people, but they were all women. He does not turn any men. I guess this would be considered Dracula's brides. Jonathan asks him how many he turned that night, but Vlad says it doesn't matter because they were all as unlucky as him, meaning they could not find her either. After another defeat, he returns to his wife's grave again, looking somewhat aged now, and he becomes enraged, and pushes the lid off of her grave, jumps inside, and breaks the top of the coffin open, finding nothing but dust. Since then, he has rarely left the castle in hopes that one day his disciples will find his Elizabetha. We see that over time, he accumulated a massive amount of wealth. Presumably, he still owned land and he was still a prince of Leakia after all. Jonathan says, "It seems that you know what you're talking about when it comes to love, and so you must spare me." He is in love himself and about to be married as soon as he returns. Dracula asks what she looks like, and Jonathan tells him to look inside the locket he has. Vlad takes a locket from around Jonathan's neck and opens it. When he sees the image inside, he is at a loss for words and he hears Elizabeth's voice. He begins making strange noises and seems overcome with emotion. It's her. Vlad grabs Jonathan and says, "This woman is mine, young man. But I will spare your life for finding her for me." What are the odds he would spend four centuries searching the world and the key to finding Elizabetha walked right into his castle? He leaves Jonathan prisoner and begins shouting at his gargoyle servants. He wants them to refill his vial of fragrance, fetch his horses. He needs to be clean to be beautiful. He needs lots of blood. Something else this film leaves out is the voyage of the demeter. The ship is never mentioned and Dracula just kind of shows up in Paris. Also, there's no mention of him needing to be on Transian soil and he doesn't bring coffins full of dirt with him. So, I guess that's not a thing in this version. As we've seen before in his life, he traveled all over the world. So, he's clearly not confined to the castle like other versions of Dracula. Another difference in this story is that it takes place in France instead of England. Back in Paris, the priest presents the page he found to the doctor and explains more about what's going on. They know he has been searching for his first love for 400 years. He has a book that carries all the findings of his congregation. The book says this. It is likely those created are the way they are as a result of a divine curse. If God can give life, then consequently, he can also give death. But he can refuse in cases of great offense or blasphemy, such as spearing a priest and renouncing God. The offender will be condemned to wander the earth for all time. But even more interesting, God can forgive the offender. In the event of full repentance, death will be granted and the curse lifted. So somehow his congregation figured out that the vampire curse can be reversed by repenting his sins. This also means if they destroy the source, then all infected by him will be cured as well. This all sounds great, but the doctor wants to know how they kill such a creature. You drive a snake through his heart with a hammer and cut off his head. I like how the priest says this like it's totally obvious while the doctor's clearly shocked. Apparently, his book also mentions that garlic can drive vampires away, but the priest does not believe it. So, it's not clear if garlic would actually work against vampires or not. There's also no mention of silver harming them in this story. The most important thing for the priest and the doctor is finding this woman that Dracula is looking for. Then they can find him. Just then, the doctor's assistant says, "That's weird." The woman in that picture looks just like the woman in the waiting room. They all go out immediately to check and sure enough, it's Mina, who looks exactly like Elizabetha. Turns out by chance that Mina had come to see her friend Maria, the one who is a vampire. They want to ask her a few questions about Maria. She had only just met Maria a few days before the wedding where she went crazy. Mina said she seemed very excited, probably because she knew she had finally found what her master was searching for. She becomes more candid and says that she is unsure of her wedding to Jonathan. He's a wonderful man, but she feels as if she doesn't belong in this time. She thinks this sounds insane, but the priest says quite the contrary. They have her write down her address so they can follow up with any questions and she leaves. Next, we see Dracula all covered up wearing a disguise and he is invited into a convent or church with nuns. Before he said he could not enter holy places. But I guess something changed. He uncovers himself and when the woman returns with food for him, she is terrified. She says he has no power in the house of God. But that's not true. Using some kind of magic, he is able to make every nun in the building unable to move, and he begins controlling them like puppets on a string. He makes them all lift him up in this odd but strangely creepy mass of people, and he begins feeding on them. Back at the castle, Jonathan tries to escape by making a makeshift rope and climbing down the wall. Unfortunately, the gargoyless spot him, try to stop him, which leads to him falling off the wall. He doesn't die, though. He's just knocked unconscious and slides onto the ice. The gargoyles try to follow, but they are too heavy and break through the ice, which allows Jonathan to get away. Like I said before, we skip the voyage of the demeanor and Dracula has now arrived in Paris. This is also the first time we get to see Dracula in his young form again. So, by drinking enough blood, he is able to appear as his younger self again. At one point, he says that he actually doesn't like drinking blood despite it tasting good. This is most likely how he ended up looking the way he did. When he arrived at the convent, he had said that he hadn't eaten in centuries. So, it's been a very long time since Dracula has drank a large amount of blood. We did see him drink blood from a rat, and he said that human blood is preferred. So, possibly the animal or rat blood might have had an effect on his appearance as well. When Dracula arrives, he sets Maria free and rewards her for finding Mina, and they immediately go to get her. Maria arrives at Mina and says she's all better now. So they go out on the town together with Maria's friend, the count. When the count first sees Mina, there is no doubt in his mind that it's her. She doesn't take to him right away, but as they go to a fair and the night rolls on, she begins to warm up to him. The three of them end up in the count's hotel room watching the fireworks from the balcony. Maria leaves to get her some hot chocolate and finally Dracula gets some alone time with Mina and he pulls out the music box. He says many people believe it was invented by the Swiss in the 1800s, but he found this one at a merchants's table in Constantinople that dates from the 15th century. No doubt he bought this himself while he was on his travels. She asks if it still works, and he says, "Of course," and winds it up, letting it play that familiar tune. Seems so familiar. When Mina hears the song, she says it sounds so familiar, like from a memory, but she doesn't know where or when. It also seems that she is getting flashbacks of her time with the count centuries ago. He explains that when his wife wanted him to come to her, she would play that tune and it would echo through the castle. Mina is reluctant to accept these memories, so she states that she is Mina and she is getting married in a few weeks. The count apologizes and says, "It's just that she looks so much like his wife. It has brought back painful memories." He then gives her the music box and says, "A gift can never be refused." Just then, Maria comes back and sweeps Mina away to watch the fireworks. After, the count walks Mina home, and when she enters the house, she is greeted by the doctor, the priest, and Jonathan, who has finally returned. He's not in good shape at all. And the priest reveals that the castle he barely escaped from was owned by none other than the count. And Maria was not released from the hospital, but rather escaped, knocking out three guards in the process and almost draining his clerk, completely dry of blood. They also reveal that he uses a special perfume that puts his victims in a trance, and this was most likely used on her. This is all very shocking for Mina to hear because he came off so charming. She wants to see Jonathan, but he's too weak right now. So, she goes to her room. While in there, she uses the music box and begins having more flashbacks of her old life. As she is remembering, the count appears in the room right behind her. Maybe he heard the music box. She's obviously startled, but he assures her he means no harm. She tells him to leave and is very flustered, but eventually calms down. She accuses the count of lying and using his magical perfume, but he reveals that he never used it on her, meaning her feelings for him were genuine. He says he will tell her who he is if she does the same. He asks if she remembers the last thing she said to him. Take care of yourself, my prince, my king. And then suddenly, she finishes the last part, my life, because I cannot survive without you. Just then, it's like she finally remembers everything at once and embraces him. text: What if the person you love the most was the one keeping you here? Keeper isn't your typical cabin in the woods horror. It's a slow descent into madness and intimacy. Liz and Malcolm head to a remote cabin to celebrate their anniversary, but when he suddenly leaves, she's left alone in a house that breathes, listens, and remembers. Director Ozgood Perkins, the mind behind Longlegs, filmed Keeper almost entirely in one location on a shoestring budget, but with suffocating precision. No cheap jump scares, just silence, dread, and that awful sense that the evil isn't outside, it's inside you. Perkins calls the film a story about disgusting maleness, a reflection on control, patriarchy, and the quiet violence hiding in relationships. That's why Keeper doesn't mean someone who protects love, it means someone who pause. Every image, the bloodied finger over the lips, the women from different times, the faceless watchers under the moon, is a riddle about guilt and captivity. The film releases November 14th, 2025, distributed by Neon. Keeper isn't made to make you scream, it's made to make you listen to the silence before it all breaks.

text: The third Now You See Me film rolls in with the swagger of a seasoned magician who knows the crowd is ready for something wild and plans to deliver exactly that. It has that familiar blend of showmanship, chaos, and flashy confidence that makes you wonder if any of these people have ever heard of a normal workday. The franchise has always danced on the line between clever illusion and full-on theatrical mayhem. And this time, it steps right over that line with a grin, a flourish, and a silent promise that whatever is about to happen will definitely not be subtle. Now you see me has always lived in that sweet spot where crime, magic, and general chaos hold hands and jump off a building together, somehow landing unharmed because someone remembered to bring a deck of cards and a dramatic flourish. And in this new chapter, the team returns older, wiser, and still completely committed to baffling law enforcement while maintaining suspiciously good hair at all times. And somewhere between all the card tricks and questionable life choices. Let me slip in a gentle reminder to subscribe to our channel because even magicians need validation. And it turns out so do we. The gang is back and they are not alone. There is a new younger crew of illusionists who appear to have been recruited straight from a talent pool of people who can somehow solve a Rubik's cube while riding a unicycle. These newcomers add a new layer of energy to the mix, which is helpful because the original horsemen have already pulled off so many bizarre heists that topping themselves at this point requires either divine intervention or increasingly creative card manipulation physics. Thankfully, the writers opted for both. The story centers on a diamond heist because, of course, it does. Diamonds are shiny, valuable, and extremely easy to justify in any crime movie. You say there is a priceless gemstone involved, and audiences instantly know someone will either steal it, protect it, or dramatically monologue about it, while sunlight glints off its facets in a very cinematic way. Here, the horsemen and the new crew must team up. Though naturally, they do not begin as best friends. There is a bit of rivalry. Think of it as the magical version of family members arguing over who gets the last slice of pizza. Except the pizza is a high stakes jewel, and the arguments are happening while people vanish behind curtains. Mark Ruffalo returns as the long-suffering authority figure who tries very hard to maintain a sense of control, even though he knowingly surrounds himself with people who think teleporting across continents is a reasonable solution to most problems. Morgan Freeman appears again, dispensing wisdom with the calmness of a man who has absolutely seen enough nonsense to last several lifetimes. His character faces a major emotional turn in this film, reminding viewers that even in a series full of trickery and misdirection, stakes remain real, and not every twist comes wrapped in a safety net. Isa Fischer re-enters the series like she never left, complete with the energy of someone who is absolutely ready to set off fireworks indoors if the moment demands it. Dave Franco brings back his understated charm and quick-handed skills that frankly would make daily household tasks much easier. And Woody Harlson, well, he continues to prove that any movie is improved when he appears looking slightly amused by everything around him. Director Ruben Flesher aims for the tone of a grand stage performance with global stakes. Locations span several countries, each one chosen for its scenic beauty and ability to accommodate at least one chase scene that ends in a dramatic reveal. And of course, The Eye Returns, that mysterious secret society that seems to operate on rules known only to magicians, retired magicians, and people who own suspiciously ornate rings. The film leans into its identity. It is flashy, unpredictable, and confident in its refusal to obey laws of physics, unless those laws are convenient at the time. That is part of the fun. It is entertainment that knows exactly what it wants to be. It gives fans the familiar banter, fresh faces, bold illusions, and the kind of twist of fate that leads audiences to whisper something like, "How did they pull?" That off, even though deep down they know the answer is probably a combination of editing magic and a very patient visual effects department. By the end, the two generations of illusionists share the stage in a way that sets up a clear future. The door remains open for more adventures, more heists, and more scenes where everyone just barely escapes because a carefully timed gust of smoke appears at the exact right second. If you like theatrical chaos, charming thieves, and a storyline that treats reality like loose guidelines, this film delivers the kind of ride you expect, and maybe even one or two surprises you do not.

text: It all begins with a young girl named Mabel, an individual whose intense and boundless passion for all living creatures borders on the extreme, leading her to perform a radical act where she essentially kidnaps every single animal from her classroom with a naive but noble intention of liberating them and setting them free into the wild. She rushes straight to talk to her university professor to discuss why all the animals have suddenly disappeared. text: It all begins in Indiana in the mid-60s. We see Michael Jackson when he was just a child accompanied by his brothers. He assures that they are not tired enough and that their performance has not been satisfactory. Michael tries to intervene, but Joseph takes a belt and hits him, demanding absolute obedience. Then he addresses the rest and orders them to continue rehearsing until they reach perfection. Repeating once more that in this life you either win or lose. Unable to bear it, Michael retreats to his room and breaks into tears. Later, in the solitude of the night, he takes refuge in reading stories, seeking to escape, even if just for a moment, from the pressure that surrounds him. The next day, rehearsals resume with the same intensity. The Jackson 5 continue perfecting their talent and performing on new stages. The days become a relentless routine of practice and performances. They rehearse, sing, dance, and eventually begin to appear on television, always under their father's strict supervision. Whenever Michael doubts or resists, Joseph forces him to continue through punishment, reinforcing a discipline as harsh as it is constant. Over time, that relentless effort begins to bear fruit. Finally, the group reaches a more prestigious stage like the Regal Theater. There, under their father's watchful eye, the brothers go on stage. text: Mother Mary feels like the kind of movie that wants to haunt me before it ever explains itself it does not move like a typical pop star drama it moves like an emotional wound that never fully closed the deeper I got into it the more obvious it became that this story is not about fame or spectacle it is about what happens when two people carry the remains of a broken bond for so long that pain starts to feel permanent David Lawry builds the film around that ache at the center is in Hathaway's Mary a major pop star preparing for her next performance after a shocking incident at her last show nearly killed her looking for the perfect costume Mary turns back to Sam played by Michaela Coel her former designer former creative partner and if I am honest about what the movie is implying great lost love of her life that is what makes Mother Mary emotionally charged from the beginning the movie never needs to say everything directly because it bleeds the truth through pauses looks and bitter cuts in conversation Mary and Sam are framed like two people who did not just end a working relationship they feel like the people who broke each other and kept going anyway the film strongly suggests that what they shared was deeper than collaboration it may never say love out loud but it gives them the language of lovers who split apart and never truly recovered most of the story stays locked around their dynamic usually inside Sam's workshop where they circle each other through conversations about art ambition betrayal memory and the damage that still lives between them that intimacy is the film's strength it is not trying to bury me in plot it is trying to trap me in a room with unfinished feelings and that is where the strangest element enters the red presents Mother Mary introduces a mysterious red spirit like force that hangs over both women and seems tied to their emotional state on the surface it is the clearest supernatural element in the movie but the longer it goes on the more it feels less like a monster and more like emotional pain made visible Sam describes her love for Mary like a broken tooth the kind of pain that keeps throbbing under everything else she also explains that the red presence left her the night she saw Mary performing without her which is also the moment she fully cut herself off from Mary emotionally that detail turns the Red Force into something bigger than a ghost story it becomes grief heartbreak shame longing and everything both women buried instead of facing Mary sees it too more than that the film suggests that she may be consumed by it or at least by what it represents the Red Force comes to her and becomes part of her world transforming heartbreak into exhaustion numbness and depression the smart choice here is that the film never locks down a single explanation I can read the Red Presence as a literal supernatural force but I can also read it as a poetic manifestation of emotional devastation either way it feels more like pain that was never processed and finally became physical that is why the relationship between Sam and Mary matters so much to understanding the ending Mother Mary is not building toward a romantic reunion it is building toward emotional release the film keeps returning to the idea that these two women cannot move forward until they face what they still mean to each other their separation is treated with the weight of a breakup Sam takes Mary replacing her with another designer like a betrayal that cut into her sense of self Mary turns her own pain into cold distance one of the movie's biggest unanswered questions is what really happened when Mary nearly died as details slowly come into focus the film reveals that Mary saw the red spirit during a recent performance while standing on an elevated platform above the crowd she pulls back from it but layer admits to Sam that she is not even sure whether she realized how close she was to the edge then she falls and ends up hanging above the audience after her red costume catches around her neck that sequence opens the darkest reading in the film did Mary try to kill herself was it intentional or was the red presence pushing her toward the edge amplifying feelings she was already too exhausted and isolated to control the movie refuses to simplify that moment and I think that is exactly right earlier scenes show Mary emotionally disconnected from her work and the world around her later she quietly admits to Sam that she still thinks about suicide that confession is devastating because it confirms the darkness is real whether the Red spirit exists literally or symbolically by the end Mother Mary does not offer easy healing and it definitely does not force Mary and Sam into a neat reconciliation they do not ride off into a romantic future in fact the film almost suggests they may never see each other again after this encounter what they do achieve is more mature and more affecting they reach a place of recognition by finally facing the emotional force between them by naming it and surviving it together they create a moment of catharsis that neither could have reached alone that is the real function of the Red Spirit it externalizes what they have been avoiding it drags the truth into the room and once they confront it the film can finally allow Mary to do the one thing she may have needed all along apologize Mary's apology and Sam's willingness to meet her in that moment turn their pain into something they can carry without letting it control them the final meaning feels rooted in that idea Mother Mary is about how unresolved love can linger inside people long after the relationship itself has ended it is about how grief does not disappear just because life keeps moving Sam and Mary have both moved on in a practical sense but neither had truly processed the emotional collapse that shaped them by confronting each other they finally confront themselves that is why the film feels like the ultimate breakup story but not in the obvious way it is not interested in revenge perfect closure or getting the couple back together it is interested in emotional survival after the rupture Sam has built walls sarcasm and distance Mary has buried herself inside performance image and withdrawal both are visionaries in their own fields yet both seem unable to connect honestly with other people I also think that is why the film keeps the red presents from becoming purely malicious even at its darkest it feels like an extension of what is already inside them the enemy is not some outside evil it is the unresolved pain they carried into every room after they fell apart so when Mother Mary ends I do not see two women getting everything they wanted I see two women finally saying what they were supposed to say years ago I see them facing the ghost they made together accepting that some relationships do not return and realizing that peace is not the same thing as reunion that is what stayed with me the most Mother Mary is not asking whether love survives the breakup it is asking whether the people inside that breakup can survive it learn from it and still become whole afterward by the end the answer seems to be yes but only after pain is dragged into the light beneath the pop star imagery and supernatural ambiguity this is a story about two women who were once everything to each other and now have one last chance to tell the truth not to restart not to rewrite the past just to finally face it if this kind of emotionally haunted storytelling is what you want more of this movie is going to leave a Mark and if you have your own reading of that red presence I have a feeling a lot of people are going to see something different in it until the next one stay close to the stories that do not give up their meaning all at once

text: What if the person you trusted most was quietly planning your death? And what if you were doing the exact same thing? No confession. No warning. Just two people smiling at each other while imagining murder. This is Over Your Dead Body, 2026, a dark, twisted thriller where marriage doesn't end in divorce. It ends in survival. We meet Dan, played by Jason Segel. Once a rising film director, now completely washed out. His dream career is gone. He's stuck directing low-budget pop-up commercials. Every day feels like failure. And worse, he knows it. Dan isn't dangerous in the beginning. He's just defeated. But inside that defeat, something darker is growing. A thought he can't escape. My life would be easier if she wasn't in it. Then we meet Lisa, played by Samara Weaving. An actress who never broke through. She isn't just frustrated. She's angry. Not loud anger, but quiet, constant resentment. She once believed Dan was her future. Now, she sees him as the reason she has no future. Dan proposes a getaway. A remote cabin in the woods. No phones, no distractions. Just them. A chance to reconnect. But this isn't romance. It's strategy. Because both Dan and Lisa are thinking the same thing. This is the perfect place to end the marriage. Permanently. Dan's plan is simple. Make Lisa's death look like a hunting accident. Push the narrative that she got lost in the wilderness. Lisa's plan is different. Stage Dan's death as a hiking accident. Use isolation as cover. Both of them even casually tell outsiders these lies. She's going hiking alone. He's going hunting. Every detail is a setup. Every sentence is a lie. But, neither realizes the other is doing the exact same thing. The cabin is quiet. Too quiet. And underneath all that silence, something is already wrong. Dan makes the first move. He tries to act normal. Too normal. But, his plan is already falling apart. Because Lisa is not asleep. She knows something is off. And just as Dan attempts to strike, she turns around and hits him with a taser. Dan wakes tied to a chair. Breathing heavily. Confused. Terrified. Lisa is standing in front of him. And she's not surprised. That's the worst part. She knew. Now the truth spills out. Not just about the murder plans, but about everything before it. Dan admits he failed his career. He feels worthless. He stopped trying long ago. Lisa admits she cheated. She felt abandoned. She never respected him anymore. But then comes the real explosion. They both admit they thought about killing each other for money. Life insurance money. A clean reset. A fresh start without the other. This isn't just hatred. It's grief. Grief for what they used to be and anger for what they became. They scream. They insult. They expose everything ugly. And yet neither leaves because they are trapped in more than a cabin. They are trapped in their history. Then something strange happens. They stop trying to kill A gunshot echoes. Then footsteps. Then chaos. Three strangers enter the cabin. Pete, calm, calculating killer. Todd, violent, unpredictable brute. Allegra, unstable, sadistic wildcard. They are escaped convicts and they are not lost. They are hiding. At first, Pete doesn't kill them. He studies them because Dan and Lisa are useful. Money, power, control. Now the couple's murder plans don't matter anymore. They are no longer predators. They are prey. Dan and Lisa are tied up again. But this time, not by each other. By something worse. A group that enjoys pain. What follows is not just violence. It's domination. Psychological and physical torture. The trio doesn't just want money. They want control. And slowly, Dan and Lisa realize something terrifying. They were never in control of anything. Not their marriage, not the cabin, not even their own plans. Now comes the turning point. To survive, they must work together. Dan and Lisa side by side. The same people who wanted each other dead now depend on each other to stay alive. Something changes in Dan. For the first time, he acts not as a victim, not as a failure, but as someone who refuses to disappear. He fights. He resists. He protects Lisa. Lisa sees it. Not the weak man she hated, but someone trying. Finally trying. And in return, she chooses him. Not as a strategy, but as a decision. Dan is dragged toward death, literally sinking. He tells Lisa, "Let me go." And in the beginning of the film, she would have, without hesitation. But now, she grabs him and pulls him back, struggling, fighting, refusing to let him die. The cabin turns into a battlefield. One by one, the trio falls. Violence peaks. Chaos explodes. And somehow, Dan and Lisa survive. But survival is not clean. People die. Blood is everywhere. The cabin is destroyed. Nothing about this is normal. Dan and Lisa walk out alive, together. Not as enemies, not as lovers, but something new. Something rebuilt from destruction. They even reframe everything. Their trauma becomes content. Their survival becomes a story. Their failure becomes success. A new beginning is born. Not everything fits neatly into happiness because along the way innocent people died. Choices were ignored. Violence was justified. Even Dan's father becomes collateral damage in the chaos. And it's treated almost casually in the aftermath. That's the unsettling layer. At its core Over Your Dead Body is not about murder. It's about transformation. About two people who lost themselves lost each other and almost destroyed everything. But through extreme survival they rediscover connection. Not because violence saved them but because honesty finally did. Love didn't survive because it was perfect. It survived because everything else burned away. And sometimes that's what it takes to see someone clearly again. If you enjoyed this deep breakdown of Over Your Dead Body 2026 make sure to subscribe for more cinematic explanations like this. Because some stories aren't just about what happens. They're about what it costs to survive them. And the next one might be even darker.

The reality is the movie changed the genre from a tragedy to a time loop thriller where James finally broke the cycle.

text: Why Linda makes that lethal decision in Send Help. To understand why Linda finally executes Bradley, you have to realize that the movie is lying to you for the first 40 minutes. We are led to believe this is a survival story where a meek bullied woman uses her skills to keep her toxic boss alive on a deserted island. But the first red flag that Linda isn't the victim appears when she confesses about her husband. She admits she didn't mourn him. She let him drive drunk and die just to escape his abuse. This proves that Linda is patient. She waits for his enemies to destroy themselves. But the reason she escalates from passive observer to active killer with Bradley is far darker than revenge. It's about the secret she was hiding the entire time. The massive twist reveals that Linda was never surviving. She had discovered a fully stocked luxury mansion on the other side of the island on day one. While Bradley was eating bugs and begging for water, she was sleeping in a king-sized bed and eating gourmet meals. She makes the lethal decision to kill Bradley not because he was mean, but because he was the only witness to her fraud. When rescuers arrived, she realized she couldn't go back to being a victim. So she murders the rescue party, tricks Bradley with an unloaded gun, and beats him to death with a golf club, the symbol of his privilege, to steal his life and become the ultimate winner.

text: Iron Long is the indie mega hit that's leaving audiences terrified, impressed, and confused. The film gives you more questions than it answers. A lot of people think that this is a flaw with the film, but they're all dumb, stupid, and wrong. The confusion and the lack of information is intentional. We are purposefully locked in Simon's narrow point of view. The only time we ever see outside the submarine is through a tiny blurry window. >> Wait, you wanted to see out the window? Weird. >> Iron long is fundamentally based on this lack of context. [music] The only way to even see outside the sub is to take a static X-ray of whatever is in front of you. The only way you know where to go is to use trigonometry to plot your course and to pray as you press forward. Simon doesn't know what he's doing or what's happening. Simon's been lied to and put in a place he doesn't understand. And we're in the same sub as him. Experiencing the same dismay and confusion that he does. The blindness we have to the outside world makes every little hint feel groundbreaking. Every unexplored inch of the sub feels important. But what if, like Simon, you hunger to understand a world that isn't made for you to understand it? What if you want to know what Iron Lung is really all about? The world of Iron Lung is an oxymoron because there are no worlds. There are no stars. They all vanish quietly in the night. All that remains of these things are illusions. Light from centuries ago that hasn't caught up with reality. The blood-filled moons and the few ships and space stations that avoided the quiet rapture is all that's left. We know from flashbacks Simon grew up in this world. He was born in a generation where all this had already happened. This lonely, hopeless reality is all he's ever known. forced to obey leaders put in power by a system that no longer exists. He never had a choice in any of this. Not in his life before and not when they set him into a death trap. The few decisions he was able to make for himself are the reasons he's in the Iron Lung. Simon was involved with a terrorist attack that killed dozens of people. While he didn't support the attack and he wasn't the one who pulled the trigger, he didn't really try to stop it either. He was taking the easy way out. He was trying to avoid conflict. But ironically, this backfired by knowing about the terrorist attack and not helping either side, he was seen as a traitor by both. It's unclear what the terrorist attack was specifically about, but if I were to guess, it was for freedom. Freedom to live their last days unrestrained. Freedom from the responsibility of humanity's future. Freedom from building a false hope. Throughout the film, Simon has various visions. He hears voices that aren't there and sees things that aren't real. But how much of this is real and how much of this is entirely imagined is left intentionally vague. There's clues that it isn't real. The high heat, the depleting oxygen, the rising CO2 level. But there's also the clues that it's more real than it seems. The voices having knowledge that seems impossible. The oxygen level slowly rising and him surviving far longer than he should be able to. I think these visions are half real. I don't think the voice he hears is really there, and I don't think what he sees is really there, but there's definitely something making him see it. This could all be from the giant sea creature we catch glimpses of, but personally, I think this sea creature is just a small part of something much larger, like a white blood cell in a body. The blood seems to be some kind of super organism, one living being made from the collection of billions. We see how consuming the blood has strange mindaltering effects. It makes the victims happy to join in to kill themselves to become a part of the super organism. We already know the blood is human blood and my guess is that it's the blood from the quiet rapture. All of the victims are now that ocean. We see the blood mutate and partially absorb Simon. It's stripping him for parts, digesting him like a giant living being. So far, I've talked about the lore of this world, but the fictional story is only one half of the coin. What is the meaning of Iron Lung? What is it as a movie trying to say? At its core, Iron Lung is about the battle between two ideas, hope and acceptance. Simon and the previous prisoners represent acceptance. While Ava and the people outside conducting the Iron Lung mission represent hope, Ava belongs to a group of survivors called the consolidation of iron. And their ultimate goal is for humanity to live on. The Iron Lung is part of a project to try and use the moon's resources to save humanity. It's a long shot at best, but they know it. Simon belongs to a group of survivors from Eden. They think trying to survive is pointless, that it's all already over. Instead, they should focus on making their limited time meaningful. This is best summed up by Simon's line. >> I just want to live. Is that so wrong? >> Why doesn't anybody else want that? >> And maybe the people from Eden are right. If our last hope is unreliable submarines built from spare parts operated by disobedient inmates, maybe it is over. Maybe we should just accept it. live our last days in friendship and meditation, free from the hassle of trying to survive and failing over and over. Or maybe the consolidation of iron is right. Maybe that thin sliver of a chance to make it is worth it. Maybe you'd rather go down swinging. Maybe we have to try even if we know it's almost impossible. Maybe hope is a good enough reason to push forward. The people of Eden look to a new religion for salvation, using the quiet rapture as the basis for their beliefs. The consolidation of iron thinks that this is just a delusion built from no evidence and wishful thinking. And they're right. There is no evidence. But is it any more delusional than believing we'll somehow find a way with no stars, no planets, just hostile living moons that dwarf our abilities? Maybe in this situation, a higher power has the same probability of saving us as we do ourselves. Simon alternates between hope and acceptance constantly. He gets ready to accept his fate and then he sees a shimmer of hope and runs towards it only for that hope to be crushed over and over. Maybe it's not worth it. Maybe if he gave up earlier and accepted his fate, he could have been spared false hope. He would have only had to accept his death once instead of multiple times. But if he never had hope, if he never pushed forward, he wouldn't have gone as far as he did, he never would have discovered the secrets of the blood ocean. He never would have gotten the information that might be critical for humanity's survival. The movie ultimately chooses hope and acceptance. Simon and Ava exchanging names and apologizing to each other is the point where hope and acceptance overcome their differences and come together. Simon accepts that there is no saving him, that it's already over. But he clings on to his actions, giving humanity hope and the hope that it wasn't for nothing and that he'll be remembered. His actions giving humanity one last gasp of hope is ultimately what leads to him dying with acceptance. If you enjoyed this video, I think you'll enjoy this other video I made about Minecraft ARGs. In fact, I think this video about Minecraft ARGs is honestly way better than the video you just watched. If anything, I think you might have wasted your time watching this video. Sorry about that.
