text: Emerald Fennell's Wuthering Heights, 2026, isn't just another adaptation of Emily Bronte's 1847 classic. It's a bold, chaotic, and at times bewildering reimagining. And yes, it comes with quotation marks because Fennell herself insists, "This is not your grandmother's adaptation." It's a film that thrives on extremes, passion, desire, cruelty, and opulent visual indulgence. But here's the thing, if you think of Wuthering Heights as a straightforward love story, well, you're about to have your assumptions shattered. Because in Bronte's story, love isn't just romantic, it's obsessive, destructive, and entirely unforgiving. And Fennell takes all of that and turns it up to 11. Let's start at the beginning. In this version, we meet young Catherine Earnshaw, played by Charlotte Millington, as a spirited, mischievous girl. And her father, the vain, abusive, and alcoholic Mr. Earnshaw, brought to life by Martin Clunes. Catherine's only true companion is the loyal servant Lady Nelly, portrayed by V Newyen. The story kicks off when Mr. Earnshaw, in a moment of charity, rescues a nameless, starving boy off the streets of Liverpool. He becomes Catherine's pet, and she names him Heathcliff, Owen Cooper in his youth. This boy is poor, dirty, and illiterate, but he forms an unbreakable bond with young Cathy, a bond that will shape both their lives forever. From the start, Fennell frames their relationship with tension and intensity, highlighting attraction, friction, and the emotional codependency that grows between them. As children, Cathy and Heathcliff's bond is almost innocent, but not for long. Mr. Earnshaw's cruelty leaves scars both literal and emotional. Heathcliff takes the brunt of physical punishment, reinforcing a dynamic of sacrifice and loyalty that borders on obsession. By the time Cathy reaches adolescence, things shift. Desire enters the picture. Fennell doesn't shy away from this. She's unflinching in showing how Cathy's awakening sexuality complicates everything. Enter social hierarchy. Cathy is torn between Heathcliff, who represents raw, untamed passion, and Edgar Linton, Shazad Latif, a wealthy, socially acceptable suitor. Linton's sister, Isabella, Alison Oliver, also arrives at the Moors, creating further tension. Here, Nelly, played by Hong Chau, acts as both observer and instigator, guiding the trajectory of Cathy and Heathcliff's connection, while also becoming caught up in the swirling emotions herself. When Heathcliff departs, heartbroken, humiliated, and seeking fortune, Cathy chooses to marry Edgar. It's pragmatic, socially conditioned, and emotionally devastating. This is where Fennell's visual storytelling truly shines. Heathcliff is framed in silhouette against a crimson sky, shattered, defiant, larger than life, a visual metaphor for his obsession and simmering rage. Five years later, Heathcliff returns. No longer a poor stable boy, he is wealthy, refined, and strategically dangerous. His goal, to reclaim Cathy and in the process manipulate and dominate everyone around him. This is where the film fully leans into Wuthering Heights themes of desire, vengeance, and psychological destruction. The adult Cathy, Margot Robbie, and Heathcliff, Jacob Elordi, relationship is electric. Every glance, every touch, every encounter drips with longing, jealousy, and fury. Their passion is amplified by Fennell's maximalist approach, slow-motion close-ups of hands, lips, hair, and fleeting gestures that communicate desire without needing explicit nudity. Charli XCX's songs overlay these scenes, bridging 19th century intensity with a modern rebellious energy. Yet, their love is toxic. Cathy's selfishness and social ambitions, combined with Heathcliff's obsessive need for revenge, create a cycle of torment. This isn't a healthy romance. It's about the consequences of desire left unchecked, class tensions unaddressed, and personal trauma magnified. The visual contrasts in Fennell's film are deliberate. Wuthering Heights, the Earnshaw estate, is dark, jagged, almost Tim Burton-esque, a prison of obsession and cruelty. Thrushcross Grange, Edgar's home, is vibrant, theatrical, and decadent, almost cartoonish in its opulence. One is a morgue, the other a bordello. Fennell uses these spaces to externalize the characters' inner lives, confinement versus indulgence, austerity versus excess. The supporting characters amplify the tragedy. Isabella's infatuation with Heathcliff is painful to watch, her humiliation and desperation palpable. Nelly, supposedly an ally, becomes increasingly entangled in the chaos, manipulating, observing, and sometimes enabling the dysfunction. Even Edgar, meant to be a voice of reason, is marginalized, highlighting the story's focus on the destructive central relationship. As the story escalates, Heathcliff's vengeance unfolds. He abuses Edgar's family, manipulates Isabella, and consolidates control over the estates, all while remaining fixated on Cathy. The film's approach is operatic. Extreme emotions, shocking imagery, and heightened sensuality dominate. Fennell doesn't aim for subtlety. She wants audiences to feel the emotional extremity of Brontë's novel. As the film barrels toward its conclusion, Fennell fully embraces the dark destructive heart of Brontë's story. Heathcliff's obsession reaches its fever pitch. He returns to the Heights a wealthy, self-made man, but also a man consumed by vengeance, jealousy, and desire. His single-minded fixation on Cathy dominates everything. Her affection, her life, even the people around her. Cathy, now married to Edgar Linton, finds herself trapped between social convention and her unyielding passion for Heathcliff. The film depicts her inner conflict with heightened sensuality and psychological intensity. Every glance from Heathcliff, every touch, every whispered conversation pulls her deeper into the storm of forbidden desire. Fennell doesn't sugarcoat it. This is love as an addictive, destructive force. The ending is as tumultuous as the rest of the film. Heathcliff, unable to reconcile Cathy's choice to marry Edgar, spirals into obsession. He exerts power over everyone around him, tricking Isabella Linton into marriage, abusing Hindley Earnshaw's heir, manipulating property, and asserting dominance over the Linton estate. His actions are cruel, calculated, and terrifying, yet the film still frames them through a lens of twisted romanticism. Cathy, meanwhile, is both complicit and victim. Her choices, driven by pride, fear of poverty, and societal expectations, have consequences. Fennell emphasizes that their love is toxic, a bond that consumes both of them and harms those around them. It's not a story of reconciliation or redemption. It's a story of obsession, desire, and the cost of unrestrained emotion. The film's climax mirrors one of the most haunting parts of the novel. Heathcliff, in the grip of grief and desire, digs up Cathy's grave, not to desecrate, but in a macabre attempt to be reunited with her. He imagines dissolving into the earth with her, a vision that blurs the line between eroticism, mourning, and madness. Fennell stages these scenes with her signature maximalist style, stormy skies, extreme close-ups, and heightened sound design to evoke an almost operatic intensity. Yet, just as the narrative could tip into full horror, Heathcliff stops. He cannot fully claim her even in death. This moment is symbolic. Their love, no matter how all-consuming, can never be reconciled in life or death. Fennell leaves the audience suspended between awe, desire, and horror, a reminder that Wuthering Heights is not a conventional romance. The final moments of the film offer a rare glimpse of resolution, but not for the main pair. Fennell honors Brontë's subtle denouement. Cathy's daughter, the next generation, quietly teaches Hindley's son to read. It's intimate, gentle, and quietly hopeful. A stark contrast to the chaos, lust, and revenge that dominated the adult Heathcliff and Cathy. Here, Fennell hints at the possibility of growth, learning, and stability in the next generation. The destructive patterns of obsession and class tension don't repeat in the same extreme way. This ending reminds us that Wuthering Heights isn't just a story of romantic passion. It's also a cautionary tale about the consequences of unchecked desire, pride, and vengeance. So, to sum up the ending, Heathcliff remains obsessed and tragic. His love for Cathy unresolved. His vengeance largely complete, but hollow. Cathy's life is defined by her choices and compromises, ultimately leaving her trapped by society and herself. And the final delicate scene with the next generation offers a glimmer of hope, showing that life, and perhaps love, can continue beyond the destructive cycle of the original lovers. It's a bitter, intoxicating conclusion that cements Fennell's Wuthering Heights as a dark, sensual, and emotionally extreme cinematic experience. Love here isn't redemptive. It's dangerous, consuming, and unforgettable. And if you leave the theater thinking about Cathy, Heathcliff, and the Moors, well, Fennell has done her job.

text: With the tree, kill target on sight. >> They're all gone. >> This story begins in a remote corner of the world, on a small island where the only thing that stands out is a watchtower rising solitary against the sea. There lives our protagonist, a man named Mike Mason, who leads an extremely quiet life far from civilization. His routine is defined by the arrival of a supply boat that brings him the essentials for survival each week. During one of these deliveries, the man in charge of the boat decides to send his young niece, Jessie, a girl of barely 10 years old, to carry the boxes to the entrance. Jessie, with the innocence of her age, does not just leave the food. She also leaves a small gift, attempting to break the ice with the mysterious inhabitant of the tower. However, Mike prefers absolute solitude. He remains hidden inside his home and avoids all eye contact. This dynamic repeats for a long time, as we see Mike sharing his days only with his faithful dog. In that isolation, chess is the only hobby that seems to bring him any spark of enthusiasm. As the months pass, the situation changes slightly during one afternoon delivery. Mike happens to be outside his refuge when Jessie arrives, and she takes the opportunity to call out to him. He approaches to see what is happening, and the girl, with some frustration, complains that she has been bringing him gifts for months without receiving a single word of thanks or recognition. Mike, maintaining his distant and somewhat gruff demeanor, responds curtly that it is not necessary for her to return anymore. Faced with such coldness, Jessie does not stay silent and asks him directly why he behaves so unpleasantly, but the man simply slams the door in her face, ending the conversation. Shortly after this encounter, while Jesse tries to return to the boat with her uncle, the weather changes abruptly and a storm of terrifying proportions breaks loose. The sea turns wild and amidst the violent waves, the small boat capsizes, leaving the girl adrift and sinking into the depths. From his window, Mike witnesses the disaster. Without a second thought, his protective instinct kicks in. He runs to his own boat and launches a rescue, defying the force of the water. After a desperate struggle against the waves, he manages to reach Jesse, but he discovers with sorrow that the girl's uncle did not share the same fate and has passed away. Mike pulls the girl into his boat and with emergency maneuvers, manages to get her to expel the water from her lungs and catch her breath. Once safe in the tower, Mike realizes that Jesse has a fairly serious wound on one of her legs. With great gentleness, he breaks the sad news about her uncle's death, leaving the girl submerged in deep grief. The next morning, he examines the injury, which turns out to be quite deep and takes care of cleaning and bandaging it as best as he can. In the midst of her sadness, Jesse asks him why he doesn't try to locate her other relatives. Mike explains honestly that he knows she has no one else, as her parents had already passed away and she only had her uncle. The girl is astonished that he knows so many details about her life, to which Mike reveals that Jesse's uncle was an old friend of his from the days they both served in the Navy. A growing bond and a hidden past. While Mike goes out to perform his usual chores, Jesse is left alone. Feeling vulnerable, she finds a knife in the house and decides to hide it among her belongings to feel protected. That same night, the trauma of the shipwreck manifests as nightmares for the little girl. Hearing her screams, Mike approaches her bed to try to calm her down. But she, in a fearful reflex, pulls out the blade to defend herself. Far from getting angry or frightened, Mike remains calm and speaks to her in a soothing voice to make her feel safe. He even takes the moment to give her a practical lesson on how to hold the knife correctly and how to truly use it if she ever finds herself in real danger. As the weeks pass, the bond between them strengthens naturally. Mike adopts a protective role, almost as if he were the father she no longer has, worrying about her meals and general well-being. Jesse, for her part, develops a special affection for Mike's dog and spends long hours playing with the animal in the garden, something that brings a spark back to the home. One day, the girl learns that the dog has never had a name of its own, so she decides to christen him Tommy. Additionally, Mike is surprised to discover that Jesse knows how to play chess, allowing them to share moments of strategy and fun over the board. However, Jesse's health becomes a concern once again when Mike notices that the wound on her leg is not healing as it should and the swelling persists. Aware that she needs medical supplies he doesn't have on hand, he decides to travel to the nearest coastal town. Once there, Mike acts with extreme caution. He walks with his face hidden under a cap and avoids passing in front of any security cameras, conscious that he must maintain a low profile to avoid being detected by anyone from his past. Meanwhile, the story shifts far from the island to the city of London. In a government hearing room, a man named Sam, the former head of the secret service MI6, faces interrogation for creating a clandestine surveillance system known as Project Eve Adams. This software has the capability to intercept telephone conversations across the entire planet to gather valuable intelligence, representing a severe breach of personal privacy. Sam attempts to justify his actions, claiming that thanks to this system, multiple terrorist tragedies have been averted. Despite his arguments, the authorities demand that the program be deactivated immediately. Sam seeks the support of the Prime Minister, who admits the project's utility but refuses to back it publicly due to the upcoming elections. Ultimately, he suggests that Sam keep the system operating in the shadows and that he himself withdraw from public view for a while. Back at the coastal area, Mike takes advantage of his trip to buy some new clothes for Jesse. As he walks down the street carrying the bags, he unintentionally passes behind some young people who are recording a video for social media. That minor oversight has grave consequences. His face is captured and processed by MI6's EVA system. The information quickly reaches Rose, the new head of the intelligence agency. Upon reviewing the data, Rose discovers that Mike's face is linked to a false identity, marking him as a dangerous terrorist wanted for international attacks. Without wasting a second, she gives the order to dispatch a special forces team to the island to capture him. The following day, in the tranquility of the island, Mike finishes treating Jesse's leg, and she is overjoyed to wear her new clothes. But that peace is shattered during dinner when Mike hears strange noises coming from outside. Looking out, he sees several boats with armed agents approaching his dock. Mike, ever the cautious man, had already installed hidden defenses in the sand. As soon as the officers disembark, he detonates the explosives, causing immediate casualties among the attackers. The surviving agents try to advance, but are quickly decimated by a series of traps. One officer manages to fire at Mike, wounding him. Yet, the protagonist continues to fight with astonishing ferocity, using his bare hands and speed to neutralize his opponents. In the heat of the battle, Tommy the dog tries to defend Jesse, but an agent shoots and kills him. Filled with rage, Jesse tries to attack the man, but he grabs her forcefully and begins to drag her away. Despite his injury, Mike eliminates the remaining soldiers and finally guns down the girl's captor, bringing her to safety. Heartbroken at the sight of his lifeless dog, Mike knows there is no time to mourn and forces Jesse into the boat to flee the island as quickly as possible. From the operations base, Rose watches in disbelief as her men are defeated by a single individual. She realizes she is not facing a common criminal, so she decides to turn to her deadliest agent, an operative known as James. While at sea, Jesse tries to help Mike with his bleeding and asks who these people attacking them are. He confesses that they are mistakes from his past life that have caught up with him. To prepare her, he hands her a firearm and gives her basic instructions on how to use it. They head toward a house on the coast as Mike desperately needs medicine and bandages to keep from bleeding out. As they enter the stranger's home to find a medical kit, a young boy discovers them and shortly after the father appears aiming a shotgun at Mike. The tension is at its peak, but Jesse quickly intervenes by aiming her own weapon at the father leveling the field. Seeing that Mike is truly injured, the girl begs the man to help them. Seeing the stranger's condition, the man agrees to treat him. Meanwhile, at MI6 offices, an analyst discovers something disturbing. The terrorist profile associated with Mike was manually manipulated to frame him. Upon further investigation, they find that Mike Mason's real records were erased and replaced with a fake death certificate. Rose then realizes that Mike is actually a former elite agent of the agency itself. Seeking the truth, Rose confronts Sam, who has also learned that his former protege is still alive. Sam, acting on his own, sends a direct order to James. He must eliminate both Mike and the girl without a trace, identifying Mike by his old code name, Black Kite. At the house where they are sheltering, the father finishes tending to Mike. However, just as they prepare to leave, Mike realizes that the man's son has alerted the authorities. He orders everyone to hide as police surround the premises. Rose monitors everything via cameras and satellites. In a moment of confusion, the father and son attempt to run away, but James, who is positioned in the distance with a precision rifle, fires and kills the father. Mike manages to get the boy to safety and escapes with Jesse through the back of the property. There they face more police officers, but Mike disarms them, steals a patrol car, and they flee at high speed. James pursues them closely in another car, firing constantly. In a risky maneuver, Mike rams James's vehicle, running it off the road, and gaining enough distance to vanish from sight. Rose calls Sam again to demand a full explanation of who Mike Mason is. Sam tells her that years ago he created a black ops unit called Black Kite, and that Mike was his best agent, a killing machine who completed any mission. Everything changed when Sam ordered him to assassinate a foreign official who was allegedly a public threat. Mike refused to carry out the order and disappeared, leading Sam to believe he had turned traitor. Sam warns Rose that Mike is the most dangerous person alive, and that she will need the full power of the state to stop him. However, Rose does not trust Sam's version of events and orders a secret investigation. She discovers that the supposed foreign official was actually a scientist named Chad, who was close to finding an affordable cure for cancer. Sam wanted to eliminate him to protect the financial interests of big pharmaceutical companies. Upon learning of this betrayal, Mike decided to rebel. Sam, realizing that Rose has uncovered his crimes, prepares for the worst. In the car, Jesse asks Mike if she will ever have a normal family. He replies sadly that in his world, family is a weakness that enemies can use against you, and that his priority is to keep her away from that danger. They arrive at a small church to meet an old acquaintance of Mike's, Father Dick. It turns out that Dick is not just a priest, but a former MI6 computer expert who worked with Mike. Dick is shocked to see his friend alive and with a young girl. Together they managed to hack into the EVA system to understand why they are being hunted and discover that Sam has orchestrated the entire manhunt using the false terrorist identity. Mike decides that the only way to end this is to go after Sam and he asks Dick to look after Jesse. Dick hesitates to accept but Jesse notices that the man is ill. Dick confesses that he has had cancer for a few months. Jesse moved tells him that she lost her mother to the same disease creating an immediate bond of empathy between them. To ensure Jesse's escape, Mike decides to contact a high-ranking organized crime boss named Chen. While Dick prepares the getaway vehicle, Mike detects an intruder. It is James who has finally tracked them down. An extremely violent hand-to-hand fight breaks out between the two agents. Both possess identical training and skills but Mike manages to wound his opponent and uses the distraction to flee with Jesse and Dick. During the journey, Jesse asks who that terrifying man was. Dick explains that James is Mike's replacement at the agency. Someone younger who does exactly what Mike used to do before he went off the grid. Eventually, Mike and Jesse part ways with Dick to enter the city and meet with Chen. Jesse questions why they cannot stay together and he explains that as long as Sam is alive, she will never be safe by his side. He promises her he will do whatever it takes to survive though deep down he knows it is a promise he may not be able to keep. Upon arriving at a nightclub owned by Chen, their faces are captured by surveillance cameras and both Roses and Sam's teams mobilize toward the location. Inside the club, Mike speaks with Chen who is shocked to see the legendary agent alive. Mike asks him to use his contacts to send Jesse to Spain providing her with a new identity and money. Chen initially refuses but Mike blackmails him revealing that he knows everything about Chen's illegal human trafficking operations at the docks. If he doesn't help, Dick will send all that information to the police. Left with no choice, Chen agrees and hands over a passport and cash, instructing them to go to the docks to meet the transport. As they attempt to leave the club, chaos erupts. Dozens of agents from both factions storm the building. Mike becomes a whirlwind of violence, taking down enemies while trying to shield the girl. However, in the middle of the shootout, an officer manages to grab Jessie and forces her into a van. Mike radios Dick for help, who uses the city's traffic cameras to track the vehicle. Mike pursues the kidnappers, eliminates them, and recovers Jessie, who now fully understands the nightmare world her protector inhabits. They manage to reach the docks, but James reappears for the final showdown. Mike tells Jessie that she will be safe in Spain and that she can start over there. With tears in her eyes, she confesses that he is the only real family she has ever known. After an emotional goodbye, Mike helps her onto the boat belonging to Chen's men. At that moment, James arrives, and Mike challenges him to a final fight. No weapons, just fists. The battle is fierce, pitting the veteran's experience against the youth's strength. After a brutal exchange of blows, Mike uses a metal object to end James's life. Exhausted but victorious, he vanishes into the shadows of the harbor. A month later, Sam is resting peacefully at his residence when he notices a strange silence. All of his bodyguards have been silently eliminated. Mike appears before him. Sam attempts one last manipulation, telling him that together they could control MI6 and make a fortune. Mike, with unshakable integrity, responds that if his interest had been money, he would have been a mercenary from the very beginning. Without another word, he fires and ends the life of the corrupt former director. The final scene takes us to a sunny restaurant in Spain, where Jessie is trying to lead a normal life. Back in London, Rose watches her through the EVA cameras, knowing that Mike must be nearby. In that instant, a waiter hands Jessie a small package from a stranger. Upon opening it, she finds a chess piece, the white queen. Jessie looks up and smiles, knowing that her friend is alive and watching over her from a distance. Mike, walking through the crowd, flashes a peaceful smile before disappearing from sight, bringing the story to a close.

text: Set in an indeterminate year of the 1820s, the opening scene shows Hugh Glass (Leonardo DiCaprio) speaking to his son Hawk (Forrest Goodluck) in an Indian language (Pawnee), telling him that even though he is scared and wants his trouble to be over, he must fight as long as he can grab a breath. As we hear Glass' voice, we see images of Glass with his Pawnee wife and son, his home being set on fire, and him holding his wife in his arms. Glass and Hawk are walking through a river with other men from their hunting party as they stalk elk. They are camped by a river in rural Missouri with other fur-trappers. They are led by their captain, Andrew Henry (Domhnall Gleeson). A naked missing man from their party walks into the settlement and collapses forward with an arrow in his back. Another man is shot in the neck with an arrow and falls into the campfire. The hunting party is attacked by a tribe of local natives who are Arikara Indians, also known as 'Ree'. The men fire back with their rifles. Glass is attacked and nearly choked to death, but one of his men rescues him. A few men gather their furs and materials toward a boat to make their escape. The Arikaras themselves are looking for the chief's daughter, Powaqa, stolen by unknown white men. The men abandon their boat and start to hike overland to Fort Kiowa. Hawk is antagonized by John Fitzgerald (Tom Hardy) for his race (Hawk is half-Indian on his mother's side), but Glass quickly defends his son and tells him not to retaliate against Fitzgerald. While hunting in the woods, Glass comes across a grizzly bear and her cubs, and he is quickly attacked by the larger bear. The bear claws and bites Glass, throwing him around as Glass tries to defend himself. He manages to shoot the bear, but it doesn't kill her. She attacks again and Glass gets his knife, stabbing it several times as they both tumble down a hill. Glass lands in a gully and the dead bear lands on top of him. The men later find Glass and try to tend to his deep wounds. Meanwhile, the Arikara warriors continue their search for Powaqa. They come across French fur traders and trade the riverside furs for five horses. The men in the hunting party carry Glass on a makeshift stretcher, but he only slows them down. They attempt to carry him up a hill, only for him to slide and bring the other men down. Fitzgerald suggests they need to just kill Glass and put him out of his misery. Henry covers Glass' eyes and almost shoots him in the head, but he cannot bring himself to do it. Henry offers payment of $75 to anyone who will stay behind with Glass. Hawk and Jim Bridger (Will Poulter) volunteer, though Fitzgerald points out that they and Glass will be likely to die. Henry raises the payment offer to $100 so that even Fitzgerald decides to stay with them until Glass expires. Glass is still in great pain and continues to have visions of his wife and the day his home was burnt down. Fitzgerald gets a moment alone with Glass and tries to convince him to let him put him out of his misery so that no one else is slowed down or left waiting to die, including Hawk. As Glass is unable to talk, Fitzgerald suggests Glass should blink if he agrees, knowing that Glass would eventually have to blink, with or without intention to agree to Fitzgerald's offer. Glass holds his eyes open for a long time before closing them, instead of blinking. Fitzgerald intentionally interprets this as blinking and starts to smother Glass. Hawk shows up, seeing Fitzgerald smothering his father. Hawk starts to call Bridger for help, leading to a struggle with Fitzgerald in which the man stabs Hawk in the abdomen, then letting him bleed out as Glass watches helplessly. Fitzgerald gets rid of Hawk's body and tells Bridger he doesn't know where he went. Later that night, Fitzgerald urges Bridger to move on with him, claiming to have seen Ree Indians by the creek. Already having dug a grave for Glass, Fitzgerald forcefully drags him into the hole and partially buries him alive under a pile of dirt as Bridger reluctantly lets him do so. Meanwhile, Henry and the rest of the hunting party have a difficult march by as they head towards Fort Kiowa. As Fitzgerald and Bridger head to meet them, Bridger realizes Fitzgerald was lying about having seen the Ree by the creek. He turns his rifle on Fitzgerald, who takes it from Bridger and turns it on him. He pulls the trigger, but the unloaded rifle clicks on an empty chamber. They continue to move. Glass awakens and weakly struggles to rise from out of the dirt. He starts crawling his way through the woods to find food and warmth. He finds Hawk's body freezing up from the cold. Glass vows to stay by his son's side. He finds a thick bear pelt to take with him to keep warm. As he continues to move through the woods, he feeds off of roots and old bone marrow. He attempts to build a fire for added warmth and uses some of his leftover gunpowder to seal the wound in his throat. Nearby, the Indians are getting closer, so Glass rides down the rapids to escape them. Fitzgerald and Bridger are still walking. They come across a burnt-down settlement with bodies sprawled across the ground. One woman emerges from her burnt hut and sees the men. Bridger quietly leaves some food for her. Glass is getting colder and hungrier. He walks into the river and eats a live fish. He walks up a hill and sees a Pawnee Indian feeding off the carcass of a bison. Glass approaches him cautiously and gestures for food. The Indian throws him an organ, which Glass eats ravenously. In the morning, the Indian observes the bear wounds on Glass' body, which are starting to rot. Glass says his men left him for dead and killed his son. The Indian states that his own family was killed by a rival Sioux tribe. He is seeking out more Pawnee. Fitzgerald and Bridger reach the outpost and rejoin their party. Fitzgerald tells Henry that they couldn't save Glass or Hawk, and he collects his payment. Bridger remains quiet but is upset and refuses a bonus pay. Glass and the Indian move forward. They spend the evening sitting and catching snow in their mouths, the first time Glass has looked peaceful in a while. The Indian gathers materials for a quick sweat lodge and places a feverish Glass inside. Glass starts hearing his wife's voice, and then sees himself walking toward Hawk before they embrace in an old church. The Pawnee performs a healing ritual for Glass' wounds. When Glass wakes up, the Pawnee is gone. A short time later he sees that the Indian has been hanged by the French fur trappers. He infiltrates their camp and witnesses one of the men raping a woman. It is Powaqa (Melaw Nakehk'o). Glass holds the rapist at gunpoint and frees Powaqa. Glass then takes a horse, letting the other horses loose. He rides to a spot in the woods where he builds himself a fire. In the morning, the tribe searching for Powaqa starts to attack. Glass holds them off with his rifle before he mounts his horse and rides away. The tribe follows him on their horses up to a cliff where Glass and his horse fall over the edge. The horse dies, and Glass is injured again. As the night falls and the cold intensifies, he cuts the horse open, removes its organs, and bunks inside its carcass for warmth. When he wakes up, he gets out of the carcass and moves to a snow cave. In there, he carves Fitzgerald killed my son. Sometime later at the outpost, one of the French hunters arrives with Glass' canteen, which Bridger left on the dirt pile after Fitzgerald buried him. Thinking he took it from Hawk, Henry leads a search party through the woods. There, they find Glass, limping towards them. They bring him back to the outpost. Henry finds that Fitzgerald is gone. The French hunter tells him that he heard Fitzgerald was headed to Texas. What's more is that Fitzgerald cleaned out the party's payroll safe. Henry then confronts Bridger with his rifle and beats the young man to the ground and puts him in the stockade. Glass vouches for Bridger's innocence to Henry, stating that he was only following orders. He also tells Henry how he saw Fitzgerald kill his son. Hearing that Fitzgerald is heading for Texas, Glass requests that he seek the man out himself. Henry reluctantly agrees to have Glass join him in the hunt. The two encounter Fitzgerald and split up to get him from opposite sides. Henry finds Fitzgerald first and plans to bring him back to be tried for murder. The two men draw their guns on each other, with Fitzgerald killing Henry. Glass finds Henry's body and puts him back on top of his horse using a branch as a prop. They ride on in view of Fitzgerald, who fires his rifle from a distance. He thinks he's killed Glass, but he just shot Henry's body. Glass gets a shot off and wounds Fitzgerald who runs while Glass pursues. They corner each other in the woods, and Fitzgerald shoots at Glass. Fitzgerald runs down by the creek where Glass finds him and they begin to fight. Fitzgerald nearly stabs Glass, but Glass turns the knife on him. Fitzgerald impales Glass' hand, but Glass overpowers him and nearly finishes him off until Fitzgerald states that killing him won't bring his boy back. On the other side of the creek, Glass sees the Indians that have been pursuing him, now with Powaqa. He decides that revenge is in God's hands, so he pushes Fitzgerald into the water and lets him float over to the Indians. The chief grabs Fitzgerald and kills him with his knife. They spare Glass since Powaqa tells them that Glass freed her. Although he has gotten his revenge, Glass is alone once again, wandering through the cold land. He falls on his knees and sees a vision of his wife once again walking into the light. The final shot is of Glass' eyes filling up with tears.

text: What happens to Beckett at the end of How to Make a Killing? Beckett is a man born into poverty despite being eighth in line for a massive billionaire fortune. Beckett decides to shorten the line of succession by methodically murdering his relatives. From sabotaging photography darkrooms to staging accidents, he successfully climbs the family tree. Beckett successfully secures the fortune, but he loses everything else. The biggest dramatic irony is that Beckett gets away with every murder he actually committed, only to be arrested for the death of Julia's husband, the one person he didn't kill. Having been manipulated by Julia throughout the film, Beckett finds himself framed for a crime he's innocent of. While the authorities remain oblivious to the pile of bodies he left behind. Beckett is left heartbroken and on the verge of tears. He drove away Ruth, the only woman who truly loved him, and is now trapped with Julia, who orchestrated the frame-up to secure the wealth for herself. She blackmails him into a relationship, offering him a fake alibi in exchange for the fortune. Beckett achieved his dream of success, but at the cost of his humanity and true happiness.

text: Scream 7 asked the age-old question that the franchise has posed since its first reboot. How does Ghost Face go on without Sydney Prescott? Welcome back to Scream Crush. I'm Ryan Ary and we're going to break down the loaded ending of the newest Scream installment and explain what may be next for Woodsboro's final girl and her decades old fight against the brutal slasher. Spoiler warning, of course, for the plot of Scream 7. Now, Scream 7 had a bit of a tumultuous road to screen with multiple firings and hirings and a reported $500,000 rewrite and three director changes. It's actually a miracle we ended up with the film that we did. Finally, the project landed in the hands of horror legend Kevin Williamson, and that might have been the best outcome of its initial Rocky production. Williamson, best known for pinning the original Scream as well as parts two and four, returns to the franchise with a deep understanding of what drives these characters and how to continue Sydney's story without too much retreading. Much like the thesis of this film, he goes back to his roots. His familiarity with Sydney and the history of Ghost Face gives the story a sort of confidence that was missing from the initial reboot, making this torch passing feel far more natural than in the 2022. >> Enjoy that torch. Of all the legacy sequels in the franchise, this one feels the most legacy of them all. Nev Campbell returns as Sydney Prescott, not just as a point and you miss it cameo, but as the lead of the film. Now, while it does still include some of the newer characters like Mindy and Chad, they're integrated in a way that feels natural and not just thrown in there as a way to connect to the previous installment. At its core, Scream 7 revisits what fans loved about the original, but it does so with the kind of self-awareness that defined the series in the first place. That's why she always outsmarted the killer in the big chase scene at the end. Only virgins can do that. Don't you know the rules? >> It even begs to ask the franchise's long-standing question. Do the Scream films really need Sydney? Or do we just think that they do? Now, while Scream 7 does exist within the continuity of the soft reboot sequel, it feels like the beginning of a new direction for the franchise. The previous two films took Ghost Face in new directions, literally relocating him to New York and Scream 6. But in doing so, they drifted too far from what made the original films work. Personal connection. The killers in Scream 5 were motivated by fandom, not of the in universe crimes, but of the fictional stab films. >> This time, the fans are going to be the ones who win. >> And the killers in Scream 6 were just related to them. It felt disconnected from the original motivations of Ghost Face. Now, while it reflected modern horror culture, it was far too removed from Sydney's story. But Scream 7 corrects that. Rather than continuing to add in people and lore into the universe, it turns its focus inward, going back into Sydney's past and reconnecting Ghost Face to the original trauma and legacy that all started in Woodsboro. This allows the franchise to give Sydney's story a sense of closure without ending the franchise entirely. The cold open sets the tone for the entirety of the movie. We see a couple arriving at the original Woodsboro house, but it's not as investigators or teens trespassing. They're fans. The boyfriend is obsessed with the 1996 murders, pointing out each death location, playing around with the body outlines, and quizzing his lessinterested girlfriend on trivia about the case. There are plaques along the walls pointing out every person who dies within the house and a shrine dedicated to the in universe stab films. Those are the adaptations of Gail Weather's books. This opening isn't subtle in what it's portraying, and it's not trying to be subtle. This installment shifts the obsession. Instead of targeting crazy stab super fans like Scream 5 did, Scream 7 zeros in on the culture surrounding true crime. Throughout the film, characters interact with Sydney less like she's a survivor and more like she's a character to obsess over. There are multiple references to true crime podcasts. One of the main characters, Lucas, even wants to start his own. And this evolution makes sense. The franchise has always reflected the media landscape of its time. And in today's world, true crime dominates. According to a 2024 Edison Research study, 84% of Americans over 13 consume true true crime content in some form, with the genre's popularity tripling in just over 5 years. Now, Scream has always been about dissecting whatever cultural obsession is most prominent. Here, the fixation is not horror movies, but real life horror packaged as entertainment. After the couple reles the brutal murders that once took place in the house, a new ghost face reminds them of what they're actually romanticizing. He kills them, dousses them in the house in gasoline, and burns it to the ground, erasing the glazed Hollywoodified mythology that was built around these gruesome crimes. He reminds the audience that Ghost Face is not a Halloween decoration or a quirky character to fang girl over. He is a serial killer. And that shift gives the film thematic weight. By reframing Ghost Face as this horrific monster and Sydney as a repeatedly exploited victim, the film puts its real theme into focus, motherhood and legacy. After the opening, the film mirrors the original nearly beat forbeat. We open on a girl in her bedroom and her boyfriend climbing through the window to visit her. This time it isn't Sydney and Billy, it's Sydney's daughter, Tatum. The scene plays out exactly the way it did in the first film. The boyfriend sneaks in and the parent barges in. >> Can you knock? And he has to hide under the bed. They even reuse the music. A cover of Blue Oyster Cults Don't Fear the Reaper. Now, through this parallel, we see how similar Tatum is to Sydney. They share the same rebellious streak and vulnerability. Tatum even admitting to her mother later on that she was afraid to further her relationship with her boyfriend just like Sydney was with Billy. And that similarity is what terrifies Sydney. She keeps her daughter at arms length, not letting her know about her past out of fear for her. She's terrified that the cycle will repeat with Tatum, which they even say as much later in the film. Motherhood and the inheritance of trauma have always been central to Scream. The original murders were rooted in the death of Sydney's mother. In the first film, Sydney spends the entire movie reassessing what she thought she knew about her mom. >> And I can't keep lying to myself about who my mom was. I think I'm really scared that I'm going to turn out just like her. You know, >> that uncertainty shaped her identity in the relationship with the people around her. >> So, you have a few intimacy issues as a result of your mother's untimely death. >> So, it makes perfect sense that decades later, she approaches motherhood with that same fear. Sydney doesn't know how to protect Tatum except by shielding her from the world that made her infamous that turned her into the final girl of the Woodsboro massacre. But her protection of Tatum only drives them further apart. When Cydney tries to connect with her daughter about her past, Tatum throws the same narrative back at her, lashing out about being named after a victim instead of the lone survivor. Again, it connects to how Cydney's whole life has been reduced to the single narrative of the final girl. even to her own daughter. She isn't named after Sydney's lifelong friend Tatum. >> No, please don't kill me, Mr. Ghostface. I want to be in the sequel, >> but instead after the girl who died in the garage. The sensationalizing of true crime has infiltrated every aspect of Sydney's life, not allowing her to simply be a mother to her daughter, but instead the Sydney Prescott and the legacy that she's expected to pass down. Now, like we said earlier, this film follows many of the same beats as the original. Once a teen is murdered at the school, mirroring the principal's death in the first film, the entire town goes on lockdown. We get a near sceneforeen recreation of the original lockdown sequence set to Nick Cave in the Bad Seeds Red Ride Hand. And this isn't just nostalgia bait. It highlights the cyclical nature of Ghost Face and how the publicity surrounding the horrific murders back in the '90s continues to create copycat killers as we have seen in every sequel so far. I mean, hell, Scream 5 didn't even have killers motivated by their original crimes, but by the popular films based on those crimes. The legacy of these murders has been so completely co-opted by Hollywood and the media that the trauma Sydney endured is nearly forgotten in favor of the fame that she unwillingly gained. This film breaks down the glossy facade and returns to where it all started, back to the roots of the franchise. The film's poster even echoes this theme. The tagline, "Face your past," directly calls out what Sydney has to confront, and it visually mirrors the original screen poster. After leaving Woodsboro, Cydney has spent her entire life trying to move on, never fully reconciling with what happened or allowing her daughter to get close to that part of her history, which leads Tatum to resent her. When Tatum decides to take authority for herself, ignoring her mom's wishes to stay out of the Ghostface case, we see history begin to repeat itself. With the help of Chad and Mindy, Tatum gathers her friends at a bar to speculate on potential suspects. And Ghost Face attacks them, picking off her friends one by one until it comes down to a final showdown between Tatum and the slasher. But once again, our expectations are subverted. We are expecting Tatum to step into the role of the final girl like her mom. But as Mindy said in the last film, >> franchises only survive by subverting expectations. >> She's actually overtaken by Ghost Face, completely unprepared to fight a killer like this. Cydney's method of protecting her daughter has been for not. >> By keeping the past from her daughter, she's made her vulnerable. Cydney only became the hardened survivor she is through repeated experience. As we saw in the introduction scene, she and Tatum were nearly identical before Sydney had to fight off Ghost Face again and again and again. This Ghost Face targets Sydney like never before. Not only does he, or it's later revealed, she harass and kidnap her daughter, but she also weaponizes technology to torment Sydney. We've seen updated Ghost Face tech in newer films like voice mimickers. >> Who is this? It's Mother Laura. >> But never to this extent. This Ghost Face uses AI and deep fakes to resurrect figures from the past, including Stew, Dwey, Mrs. Lumis, and Roman. These cameos aren't just nostalgic callbacks. They are another nod to the obsessive parasocial relationship that true crime fans can develop with the people who are actually connected to these cases. The killer is then revealed to be Jessica Bowden, a friend of Sydney's who became so obsessed with the case that when Sydney withdrew from the public eye, Jessica checked herself into a psychiatric facility, determined to bring back the Sydney that she believed she knew. During her monologue, Jessica questions whether Ghost Face can exist without Sydney, a meta nod to Nev. Campbell's absence from Scream 6, Jessica insists that Ghost Face doesn't need Sydney and that it's time for a new beginning for the killer. And for a moment, it did feel like the film might actually kill Sydney off, but I'm glad it didn't. Killing her here would have only continued the cycle that the entire film is trying to break. Billy killing Sydney's mother started this chain of events. Cydney's death would simply pass that on to Tatum. The film also delivers a long-awaited interview between Cindy and Gail. >> It's not answering any questions. All right, just leave us alone. >> It mirrors the off thereord interview in the original film. >> No, Cotton murdered my mother. You're not so sure anymore, are you? Except now the focus isn't on Sydney's mother. It's on Sydney as a mother. It puts her in a very interesting position caught between giving information to help catch Ghost Face or protecting her daughter from the media exposure that Sydney was never shielded from. The film ends with a badass motheraughter team up that has Cydney finally facing her past headon instead of running from it. She's ready to step away from being Cydney Prescott, the woman forever fleeing Woodsboro, and towards simply being Sydney Prescott, a mom. Now, while the film gives us closure on Sydney's story, what is next for Ghost Face's legacy as a whole? Did they truly end the decadesl long battle against Ghost Face? Probably not. According to Variety, an eighth installment is already in development, so Ghost Face isn't going to stay gone for long. We also have a solid group of characters to continue following. Tatum's actress Isabelle May is an upand cominging talent, so I could easily see the franchise building around her in another sequel, and Chad and Mindy are still alive and well. Maybe Mendy could eventually step into the Gail Weather's role within the franchise as they hinted at the end. I do hope we revisit Sam and Terra stories at some point, but who knows? text: The 2026 Canadian horror film Undertone has arrived with a quiet force courtesy of distributor A24 and first-time director Ian Toussaint. Premiering at the Sundance Film Festival before its wide release on March 13th, 2026, this atmospheric nightmare has left audiences both spellbound and deeply [music] unsettled. At its core lies an ending that refuses to hold your hand, instead choosing to abandon you in the dark with nothing but your own imagination for company. Let's walk through what actually happens, what it might mean, and why critics can't seem to agree on whether the finale is brilliant or frustrating. Before we can understand the ending, we need to understand where our protagonist stands when the credits roll. Evie, played with raw vulnerability by an actress whose name deserves more attention, is a woman caught between two massive life events. Her mother lies in a hospital bed slipping away day by day. Meanwhile, Evie herself is pregnant with a child she never planned for and isn't sure she wants. She's exhausted, isolated, and carrying guilt like a second skin. To cope, or perhaps to escape, Evie throws herself into a podcast project with her co-host Justin. They call it The Undertone, and its subject matter is a collection of 10 mysterious audio recordings left behind by a couple named Jessa and Mike. What starts as true crime curiosity quickly becomes something far more personal and far more terrifying. The recordings document the couple's slow descent into supernatural terror, complete with strange sounds, disembodied voices, and ultimately violence. The climax arrives when Evie and Justin sit down to listen to the 10th and final recording. This is the moment everything has been building toward. Through their headphones, they hear the grim conclusion of Jessa and Mike's story. The audio contains sounds that suggest a woman has killed her own child, a moment foreshadowed throughout the film by sinister nursery rhymes and religious imagery. Then comes a voice that doesn't sound human at all. It's dark, ancient, and demonic. Here's where the film makes its boldest choice. As the recording ends, Evie looks up. Something has changed. The entity that lived only in the recordings now feels present in her room, in her space, in her reality. The barrier between the haunted audio and the living world has dissolved completely. We watch Evie realize this. We see the terror dawn on her face, and then the screen cuts away. We never see what happens next. We never see the entity. We never see Evie's fate. The film simply ends, leaving us suspended in that moment of dreadful anticipation. The film never gives the supernatural force a name, and that's entirely intentional. But the clues are scattered throughout like breadcrumbs leading nowhere specific. Religious imagery fills Evie's world from the icons in her mother's house to the themes of corruption and sacrifice that weave through the story. This points toward something demonic, something ancient that understands human guilt and knows exactly how to exploit it. More specifically, this entity seems drawn to mothers. Its victims, both Evie and the woman on the tapes, share that connection. The horror isn't just about death, but about the perversion of the maternal bond, the unthinkable idea of a mother harming her own child. This theme echoes through the film's sound design, which repurposes innocent nursery rhymes into something deeply sinister. But, here's the question the film refuses to answer. Is the entity real, or is it a manifestation of Evie's trauma, grief, and exhaustion? We've watched her spiral throughout the story. We've watched reality bend around her perceptions. By the end, we can't trust our own eyes any more than she can trust hers. That ambiguity isn't a flaw in the film's design. It is the film's design. If you walk away from Undertow feeling unsettled, rather than satisfied, you've understood it perfectly. The ending serves the film's central themes, rather than providing tidy closure. First and foremost, this is a film about the terror of imagination. By refusing to show Evie's fate, the film forces you to imagine it yourself. And your imagination, shaped by everything you've just experienced, will always conjure something more personal and more terrifying than anything the filmmakers could put on screen. It's a horror technique as old as the genre itself, but executed here with uncommon restraint. The ending also speaks to the film's preoccupation with thresholds. [music] Evie exists at multiple crossroads simultaneously. She stands between life and death as her mother fades. She stands between choice and circumstance with her unwanted pregnancy. She stands between reality and delusion as the haunting intensifies. The entity, real or not, finds her at these thresholds because thresholds are where vulnerability lives. The ending traps her and us at the final threshold between survival and annihilation. Then there's the question of guilt and isolation. Evie carries guilt about her mother, guilt about her pregnancy, guilt about feelings she can't control. She's isolated physically in her role as caregiver and emotionally in her inability to share her truth. The film suggests that this combination, guilt plus isolation, creates fertile ground for something dark to take root. Whether that something is supernatural or psychological almost doesn't matter, the damage is the same. If you're planning to watch Undertow or have just finished it and wonder whether you missed something after the credits, you didn't. The film contains no post-credit scene, no mid-credits tease, no final jump scare waiting for impatient viewers. When the story ends, it ends completely. You're free to leave or, better yet, free to sit in the dark for a moment and let the silence do its work. Undertow is a film that trusts its audience to handle uncertainty. Its ending doesn't explain the entity, confirm Evie's survival, or distinguish between supernatural horror and psychological breakdown. Instead, it leaves you exactly where Evie finds herself, standing at the edge of something terrible, unable to look away, unable to know what comes next. Whether that's brilliant storytelling or frustrating evasion depends entirely on what you want from horror. But either way, it's an ending that will stay with you, whispering in the back of your mind long after the screen goes dark. And that's it for me. text: In 1996, a young Cletus Kasady watches helplessly as his love, Frances Barrison, who has the ability of sound manipulation, is taken away from St. Estes Home for Unwanted Children to the Ravencroft Institute. On the way, she uses her sonic scream powers to escape and attacks young police officer Patrick Mulligan. He shoots Barrison in the eye and suffers an injury to his ear due to her scream. Unbeknownst to Mulligan, who believes he killed her, Barrison is taken to the facility, which is hardened against her powers. In the present day, Mulligan, now a detective, contacts Eddie Brock to speak to Kasady, a serial killer who refuses to talk to anyone other than Brock following their interview a year prior. After the visit, Venom, Eddie’s symbiote, is able to figure out where Kasady has hidden the bodies of victims, which gives Brock a huge career boost. Brock is then contacted by his ex-fiancée Anne Weying, who tells him that she is now engaged to Dr. Dan Lewis, much to Venom’s displeasure. Kasady, who was found guilty of his crimes and earlier sentenced to death by lethal injection, invites Brock to San Quentin State Prison, where Kasady is detained on death row, to attend his execution. However, Venom is provoked to attack Kasady via insults towards Brock. Kasady bites Brock's hand, ingesting a small part of the symbiote. Back home, Venom, wanting more freedom to eat criminals, has an argument with Brock, and the two end up fighting until the symbiote detaches from his body and they go their different ways. Kasady's execution fails when a red symbiote emerges and blocks the injection. He introduces himself as Carnage and goes on a violent rampage through the prison, freeing inmates and killing guards. Kasady and Carnage then make a deal: Carnage will help Kasady break out Barrison from Ravencroft, and Kasady will help him eliminate Brock and Venom. Mulligan visits Brock at home and warns him about the situation. In Ravencroft, Kasady frees Barrison, and they travel to their old children's home to burn it down. Mulligan, suspicious of Brock due to his interactions with Kasady before Carnage emerged, takes Brock to the police station. Brock refuses to answer Mulligan's questions and contacts Weying as his lawyer. Brock reveals that Venom has separated from him and needs the symbiote to fight Carnage together. As Venom makes his way through San Francisco by hopping from body to body, Weying finds and convinces him to forgive Brock. She bonds with Venom and breaks Brock out of the police station. Brock and Venom make amends and bond again. Kasady takes Mulligan hostage, and Barrison captures Weying after failing to find Brock. Barrison gives Lewis information on Weying's whereabouts, and he gives it to Brock. Kasady and Barrison plan to get married at a cathedral, where Venom appears and fights Carnage. Barrison seemingly kills Mulligan by hanging him onto a chain. Venom holds his own against his spawn, but he is eventually overpowered brutally by Carnage, and the latter decides to kill Weying atop the cathedral. Venom manages to rescue Weying in time and provokes Barrison to use her powers again; her sonic blast causes both symbiotes to separate from their hosts as the cathedral collapses and a falling bell kills Barrison. Venom saves Brock by bonding with him before the impact. Carnage tries to bond with Kasady again, but Venom devours the symbiote. Kasady states that he only wanted to be Brock's friend, but Venom bites Kasady’s head off. While Brock, Venom, Weying, and Lewis escape, a still-living Mulligan's eyes flash blue. Brock and Venom, now fugitives, decide to take a vacation while they ponder their next steps. As Venom tells Brock about the symbiotes' knowledge of other universes, a blinding light transports them from their hotel room to another room where they watch J. Jonah Jameson reveal Spider-Man's identity as Peter Parker on television.

text: Well, nothing says Christmas like a movie involving nightmares, capitalist greed, and carnies. Carnies? Yes, it's Guillermo del Toro's latest feature, and at least this one doesn't involve having sex with a fish. Nightmare Alley is a neo-noir based on the 1946 novel of the same name by William Lindsay Gresham. And in this video, we'll be taking a look at its ending, its deeper meaning, and proving once and for all that Bradley Cooper can play more than just a raccoon. What? And for those of you who aren't familiar with some of my videos on films just released in theaters, I can only use footage from the trailers and TV spots, so bear with me. Nightmare Alley begins rather cryptically with our protagonist Stanton Carlisle dragging a dead body across the floor of this rural farmstead. The nightmares of Nightmare Alley stem from this event. Throughout the film, we'll get more and more clues as to what actually transpired here, eventually culminating in the revelation that Stanton killed his own father, an alcoholic who he blamed for his mother's abandonment. He takes with him two important items I want you to remember: a wristwatch which his father coveted, and an old radio he could probably sell for cash. With nowhere to go, Stanton joins a nearby traveling circus, eventually befriending a psychic Zeena the Seer and an alcoholic mentalist named Pete. Here he learns the ropes of their psychic scam and hones his own skills of showmanship, but Stanton has dreams of bigger than that of the big top. He wants to be his own showman entertaining the elite in high society. He learns that has a secret book which contains all the secrets to his tricks, including acts that he and Zeena deem morally reprehensible. They call this a spook show in which a mark is conned into believing a loved one is speaking to them from beyond the grave. But as we'll see with Stanton, he has no moral line. All he cares about is money, status, and prestige, and he'll go to extreme lengths to make anyone believe what they want to believe, especially if there's heaps of cash involved. He ends up poisoning Pete and gets away with it with others believing this alcoholic just drank too much. This allows Stanton to swipe his book of tricks, but on a more subconscious level he's taking out another drunk, a drunk who harmed a woman he loved. Zena tells Stanton that Pete breaks her heart. He's drinking too much, thus she suffers like Stanton's mother who also experienced first hand the harm of an alcoholic lover. For this reason Stanton doesn't drink. It's a point of pride for him, but by the end of the film he'll become a full-blown alcoholic. One night the carnival's geek escapes. Back in the 40s when this story takes place, carnival geek shows consisted of a circular ring where a performer would bite the head off of a live chicken and swallow it. These were mainly alcoholics or drug addicts paid in liquor and narcotics. Stanton ends up finding this geek in the carnival's aptly named House of Damnation, a house with mirrors that are captioned "Take a look at yourself, sinner." All of this foreshadows Stanton's continual descent into damnation himself. He ends up beating the geek close to death, which becomes hauntingly ironic since that's who he'll become at the end of the film, a damned alcoholic beast of a man who has to resort to biting the heads off chickens to survive. Is he man or beast? At the same time Stanton is brought under the wing of ringmaster Clem. Clem tells him how he drugs drunks in order to turn them into subservient geeks. The two of them will later have to drop off their at a local hospital where you can see the "Jesus Saves" neon sign, and I can't help but think that it looks rather like "Save us," but maybe that's just me. We also see his collection of pickled fetuses of both the human and animal variety. Of particular note is this one which Clem states is a child whose head was so large the mother died during birth. Notice the protruding eye near the top which conjures images of Stanton's blindfold while performing in the big city. During his time at the carnival, Stanton falls in love with a carny named Molly. Her stage name is Electra and she performs a routine where currents of electricity pass through her body. To win her over, he designs a new routine where they'd fake her death using an electrocution chair of his design. And they say chivalry is dead. As the two perfect the routine, we see just how good Stanton is at reading others when a local police officer threatens to shut down the entire show. Stanton is able to talk the sheriff into letting them continue when he uses his excellent powers of deduction to cold read that the sheriff's mother had passed and that she is talking to him from beyond. We can really see that Stanton's character is a liar and a damned good one at that. So, when he leaves the carnival and promises Molly the world if she comes along with him, it doesn't take too long to realize he's lying to her, too. Two years pass and Stanton and Molly have their own show in the big city. Stanton has finally got what he's wanted, but for him, it'll never be enough. He wants to take his show to the next level and this involves doing what Zeena and Pete warned him never to do. He'll trick some of the city's richest citizens into believing their loved ones are talking to them from beyond the grave in order to amass even more wealth. Of course, Molly is against this, but like every warning Stanton receives, he ignores. This leads him to Dr. Lilith Ritter, a psychologist who attends many of his shows believing he's a con man. The two eventually team up in a rather ingenious plot. Dr. Ritter happens to be a therapist to some of the richest and most influential men in the city and through her recorded sessions, she has a ton of personal information that Stanton can exploit. For example, he finds out that Mrs. Kimball, the wife of a prominent judge, yearns to know more about the death of their son who died in the trenches during World War I. Knowing this, Stanton tells her that her son loves her, that his death was quick, and that one day they'll be reunited. But things get dangerous when Stanton is asked to do a session with unhinged businessman Ezra Grindle. He's wanting to be put in touch with a long-lost love and has been burned in the past by other con men, hence why he has Stanton connected to a polygraph. Stanton beats the polygraph and gains Ezra's trust, and you might be asking yourself, how did he do it? How did he beat the polygraph? The simple answer is that Stanton actually believes in his own lies. That's how far down the rabbit hole he's gone. Earlier in the film, there's a scene between Stanton and Pete in which Pete uses the term shuteye, referring to when a man has lied so much that he ends up believing his own lies. And when those lies end, you see the face of God, and no one can outrun God. But Stanton is full of hubris. When Zeena gives him a bad tarot reading, he simply turns one of the cards right side up. This is symbolized through the Hangman card, which when facing upward represents wisdom, but upside down selfishness. Pretty fitting for our main character. Ezra wants something Stanton has never done before, to make the dead materialize before his very eyes. And Stanton, always dreaming of bigger ways to con those around him, creates a plan to have Molly dress up as Ezra's long-lost love, a woman who died during a botched abortion, one which Ezra made her get. Later in the film, he confides in Stanton that he had been violent to many women in the past, but claims this woman was the one he truly loved. Dr. Lilith says she'll take no part in this plan. She has a great line where she says, "If his foot slips, both of them fall." Even she sees that he's in too deep. But Stanton creates a fake key to later break in and steal Dr. Lilith's information about Ezra. He will do anything to get what he wants. Before the big con, Stanton takes a glass of alcohol from Dr. Lilith and chugs it, symbolic of him changing into the man he so long hated. He used to retch at the smell of alcohol, but now he's downing a glass in one go. Meanwhile, Molly has found Stanton's sketchbook and inside is a drawing of Lilith. She believes him to be cheating on him and it's true. Stanton kisses Dr. Lilith, but it's never explained whether this is because he truly has feelings for her or whether it's all part of his plan to get what he wants. But knowing his character, I think it's pretty obvious. When Stanton later confronts Molly, who leaves him to go back to the carnival, he catches up to her and lies telling her that he never cheated on her will be their last con. You'll notice in this bus station scene Molly is the only one wearing a colorful jacket. It's crimson red foreshadowing the violence to come. Stanton's able to convince her to take part in this final con and it begins. At Stanton's command, Ezra prays and when he opens his eyes in the distance is Molly dressed up as Ezra's dead lover covered in fake blood. But the plan backfires when Ezra rushes over to her and notices it's all fake. I guess Stanton didn't foresee this and isn't the big genius he makes himself out to be. This reveal enrages Ezra who punches Molly, which then causes Stanton to beat him to death. Ezra's bodyguard chases after them but is run over by Stanton's car. To make matters worse, remember Mrs. Kimble, the judge's wife? She's killed her husband and herself in a murder-suicide so that they could be with their dead son just like Stanton told her she'd be with them when they passed. Everything Stanton has done has only led to death and destruction. With Molly leaving for good and the cops on his tail, Stanton needs to escape. So he goes to Dr. Lilith to retrieve the money he stored in her safe, money he wanted to keep hidden from his wife. There he finds out he's the one who's been conned all along. Dr. Lilith has taken his money and set him up incriminating him for her own safety. After a failed attempt on her life, Stanton runs to the train yard nearly escaping captivity and hides in a carriage filled with chickens, the same animal that was killed so violently by the geek at the beginning of the film. Like the chicken, his life has been metaphorically killed. Some time passes as the next we see Stanton, he's gone full hobo rocking a long haggard beard. He even sells his father's coveted watch for a bottle of booze. The film really comes full circle, however, when Stanton attempts to get a job at another carnival. There he sees the radio he took from his father those years ago and alongside it is the one-eyed baby jar Clem had in the background. The carny boss offers him a drink just like Clem would offer a roofie drink to drunks when he knew he could take advantage of them. He's offered the job of the geek and when he's asked if he can handle it, he says, "I was born for it." A little different than what is said in the 1947 film adaptation. Mister, I was made for it. Born for it seems to suggest it was predestined. Made for it that he was crafted. So, I leave it up to you why Del Toro went with this subtle word change. Fun fact, the '47 version has a scene after this where Molly comes in and saves Stanton from his fate because the studio believed without it audiences would think the story too dark. Del Toro went on to tell the LA Times that the ending is, quote, "The revelation of who Stanton really was or the way he really saw himself." That's why you'll see mirror symbolism throughout the film. According to Del Toro, the ending is shot in such a way that you could actually show the final scene first and flashback to all the events that led him there. In this way, the movie is like a circle. I hope you enjoyed my analysis of Nightmare Alley. These videos are super tough to do when you don't have the full footage, so I hope you were able to bear with me. Thanks for watching and if you did like the video, be sure to like and subscribe. You can also follow me on Twitter and Instagram @FilmStoryYT. And remember, daddy loves you very much.
