The Invite may look like a comedy on the surface, but underneath its humorous moments is an emotional story about love, marriage, regret, and whether two people can reconnect after years of drifting apart. Directed by Olivia Wilde, the film follows married couple Joe and Angela, whose relationship has quietly fallen apart long before the story even begins. What starts as a simple dinner with their upstairs neighbors soon forces both of them to confront painful truths they have been avoiding for years. Let's break down everything that happens and explain the emotional ending. The story takes place almost entirely over one evening inside Joe and Angela's apartment. Angela spends the day carefully preparing dinner for their neighbors, Hawk and Piña, while Joe has little interest in entertaining them. The couple already dislikes their neighbors because of the constant noise coming from the apartment above them, and Joe hopes the dinner will finally give him a chance to confront them. However, the evening quickly becomes something completely different. As the conversation grows more personal, Hawk and Piña openly discuss their unconventional relationship and lifestyle. Their honesty surprises Joe and Angela, who begin asking questions out of curiosity. During the conversation, Hawk reveals something that completely catches Joe off guard. He tells Joe that Angela often walks around near the apartment windows without worrying about whether anyone is watching. Angela admits that what began as an accident slowly became something she continued doing because she enjoyed feeling noticed. More importantly, she explains that she no longer felt seen by her own husband. This revelation exposes one of the biggest problems in their marriage. Angela feels invisible. Joe, meanwhile, has become emotionally distant without even realizing how much it has affected their relationship. As the evening continues, Hawk and Piña suggest that both couples spend some private time together in an attempt to help Joe and Angela rediscover parts of themselves they have lost. Instead of solving anything, the idea only highlights how disconnected Joe and Angela have become. Both awkward encounters end almost immediately, making it obvious that their real problems cannot be fixed by a single unusual evening. Afterward, the conversation shifts away from uncomfortable situations and toward something much deeper. Hawk reveals that his real name is Howard and shares the painful story of losing his wife to cancer years earlier. Meeting Piña helped him rebuild his life after overwhelming grief. For a brief moment, everyone lowers their defenses. Even Hawk and Piña admit that their own relationship is not perfect after they argue over small frustrations. Unlike Joe and Angela, however, they quickly apologize and work through the disagreement together. Watching this interaction forces Joe and Angela to look honestly at their own marriage. The discussion becomes increasingly emotional. They admit they have not been physically or emotionally close for more than a year. What was once a relationship built on friendship, laughter, and love has slowly become filled with disappointment and resentment. Joe confesses that he feels like a failure. He dreamed of becoming a successful musician but now teaches students while feeling that his own ambitions have slipped away. Angela believes Joe focuses only on what he has lost instead of appreciating the family and stable life they have built together. Joe responds by accusing Angela of giving up on herself and trying to control every part of their lives. As years of buried frustration finally come pouring out, both admit that they have remained together mainly because of their daughter, Maggie. Piña then offers perhaps the most important observation in the entire film. She tells them that neither of them is actually responsible for the other's unhappiness. Instead, they have spent years blaming each other for disappointments that come from their own unfulfilled dreams. She also suggests that children are often better off with two happy parents living separately than with two unhappy parents living together. After hearing this, Joe and Angela quietly acknowledge something they had been unwilling to admit before. Their marriage may already be over. Soon afterward, Hawk and Piña leave without making a dramatic exit, giving the couple space to process everything that has happened. For the first time in years, Joe and Angela begin discussing practical questions about what separation would mean, including how it would affect Maggie and the family lake house. It feels as though they have accepted that their future together may be ending. But then comes the film's final scene. Unable to sleep, Joe sits down at the piano and begins playing for the first time in a very long time. The music reminds both him and Angela of happier days when they laughed together and genuinely enjoyed each other's company. Angela quietly walks over and sits beside him. The two begin playing the familiar melody together before she simply watches him continue. With tears in her eyes, she gently rests her head on Joe's shoulder. Joe quietly leans his own head against hers. The film ends there without revealing what happens next. That final moment has two very different interpretations. The first is that Joe and Angela have accepted their marriage is over. The piano becomes a final goodbye, allowing them to remember the love they once shared before moving on separately with mutual respect instead of anger. The second interpretation is much more hopeful. The difficult dinner forces them to stop pretending everything is fine and finally confront the pain they have ignored for years. By being completely honest with each other, they may have taken the first genuine step toward repairing their relationship. The piano scene mirrors happier moments from earlier in their lives, suggesting that perhaps the connection they thought was gone still exists beneath years of frustration. The film deliberately refuses to answer which interpretation is correct. Instead, it leaves viewers with one central question. Can two people rediscover the love they once had after finally facing the truth, or does accepting the end of a relationship sometimes become its own form of healing? The Invite never gives a definitive answer because the story is less interested in certainty than in the complicated reality of long-term relationships. What did you think about The Invite? Do you believe Joe and Angela found a way back to each other, or was that final piano scene simply their last goodbye before moving on? Let us know your thoughts in the comments below. The movie begins on Cybertron, in Iacon City.  A miner robot named Orion Pax (Chris Hemsworth) sneaks into an old building and discovers  an archival recording revealing the planet's origin. The first Transformer, Primus, created  Cybertron with his body, and from the planet's core emerged more Transformers, including the 13  Primes. The Matrix of Leadership was created as a powerful source, but when it was lost, the flow  of Energon stopped. Orion is caught by two larger Transformer guards but manages to escape. He meets his best friend D-16 (Brian Tyree Henry), and they head to work in the mines led by  Elita-1 (Scarlett Johansson). An accident occurs in the mine, and despite warnings, Orion and  D-16 save Jazz (Evan Michael Lee) before the mine collapses. Darkwing (Isaac C. Singleton,  Jr) fires Elita, and Orion stands up to him, leading to a scuffle where D-16 gets punched.  They later decide to enter the Iacon 5000 race. During the race, Orion surprises D-16 with jet  packs, and they compete, catching the attention of Sentinel Prime (Jon Hamm) and others. Despite not  winning, they impress Sentinel, who invites them to join him. Instead, they are demoted to smelting  and meet Bee (Keegan-Michael Key) with a distress beacon. They follow the beacon's coordinates  to the surface, where they discover the remains of the Primes and the Matrix of Leadership. They learn from Alpha Trion (Laurence Fishburne) about Sentinel's betrayal and his alliance  with the Quintessons. Trion helps them unlock their true Transformer forms, and they confront  Sentinel, who is revealed to be responsible for the Energon drought and their suppressed powers.  The group transforms and battles Sentinel's goons, with D-16 determined to seek revenge. Airachnid presents Trion to Sentinel, who mocks the fallen Prime for his brothers'  deaths. Trion denounces Sentinel as a traitor once more before being executed. Sentinel  then tasks Airachnid with finding the bots. Orion tries to calm D-16 down, hoping to  use recorded memories as proof of Sentinel's betrayal to Iacon City. However, D-16 refuses to  follow any leader. They, along with Bee and Elita, get captured by the Cybertronian High Guard led  by Starscream, Shockwave, and Soundwave. D-16 challenges Starscream, defeats him, and rallies  the High Guard to follow him against Sentinel. Airachnid, with Sentinel's troops and Quintesson  ships, locates the bots and High Guard, initiating an aerial attack. Despite utilizing new weaponry,  the bots face capture after a siege by Sentinel's forces. The recorded memory is destroyed,  leaving them without evidence. Orion takes responsibility but is encouraged by Elita to seek  help. They return to Iacon City with Shockwave, Soundwave, and the High Guard. Prisoners are brought before Sentinel, where D-16 confronts him. Sentinel  brands himself with the image of Megatronus Prime from D-16's possession. Orion, Elita, and the miners learn of Sentinel's betrayal and unite to stop him. They head into  battle while Airachnid spots them. The hero bots fight Sentinel's forces as he transforms to  face Orion and D-16. Elita subdues Airachnid, who broadcasts Sentinel's admission of guilt, turning  the city against him. D-16, now Megatron, defeats Sentinel, leading to Optimus Prime's emergence. Optimus battles Megatron and banishes him from the city with the Autobots' help. He revives Energon  flow with the Matrix, appoints Elita as commander, and Bee as his right-hand bot, forming  the Autobots. Optimus vows to lead the fight against enemies for Cybertron. In a mid-credits scene, Bee accidentally "decapitates" his fake friends with his  laser-knife hands. In a post-credits scene, Megatron forms the Decepticons for  revenge against Optimus and the Autobots.

Executive Cynthia Utrom from the Techno Cosmic Research Institute dispatches a team to locate the fugitive scientist Baxter Stockman. Stockman has developed a mutagen to bring into being an animal clan of his own, beginning with a housefly. Stockman is suddenly interrupted by a Utrom strike squad and perishes in the explosion that ensues, while the mutagen spills into the sewers of New York City. Fifteen years later, the four turtle brothers Michelangelo, Leonardo, Raphael, and Donatello have been raised by their rodent father Splinter, after being transformed into humanoid mutants due to Stockmans mutagen ooze. Splinter had been chased away by humans, leading to his distrust of humanity. In order to protect them, he taught his sons ninjutsu and instructed them to remain in the sewers. Despite now being teenagers, the Ninja Turtles still wish to experience a normal high school life, which does not please Splinter. The Turtles go on a supply run and come across a gang of thieves. They defeat the gang and find a stolen moped, which belongs to a young woman called April ONeil. During the battle, the Turtles reveal themselves and tell April the story of their origin. April, an aspiring journalist, was determined to overcome the shame of a viral incident of vomiting on camera she was involved in. She has been investigating a series of robberies of TCRI technology committed by a criminal called Superfly. The Turtles were looking to prevent Superfly and, by exposing the situation through April's reporting, gain recognition from the public. When they track down Superfly under the Brooklyn Bridge, they realize he is not only a mutant himself, but also the head of a mutant group which consists of Bebop the Warthog, Rocksteady the Rhino, Wingnut the Bat, Leatherhead the Alligator, Genghis Frog the Frog, Mondo the Lizard, Ray Fillet the Stingray and Scumbug the Cockroach. Thrilled to meet other mutants, the Turtles immediately connect with Superfly and the others. He reveals that Stockman had made them, however they had managed to escape TCRI and were currently residing on an old vessel in Staten Island. Similar to the Turtles, society has attacked them, and Superfly has angrily stolen TCRI technology to mutate all animals on Earth into a new powerful species that will enslave humankind. The Turtles attempt to step in, but the gang manages to flee with the device while TCRI is able to trace them and capture the Turtles. When the Turtles awoke at TCRI headquarters, Cynthia informed them they required their blood to make a potent mutagen capable of creating an army of super soldiers to seize control of the world. Immediately, the machine kicked in and the Turtles endured the agonizing process of having their mutagen extracted. April and Splinter rescue the two turtles as they share their final moments regretting their fate. Splinter scolds his sons for having disobeyed him, and April adds that they had lied. The rat sternly tells them that they must fix the mess and stay in the sewers, where they belong. At the gangs hideout, Splinter and the Turtles explain to most of them that their desire for control will make them no different than the bad people in the world. United, they then turn their attention to Superfly, who questions why they have changed their stance. Angered, Superfly cries out for his followers to continue listening to him. Splinter realised the mistake he had made and assisted the mutants in shoving Superfly towards the machine, successfully demolishing it. Unfortunately, the ooze amalgamated Superfly with the creatures in the vicinity and formed an enormous, whale-like kaiju that began to assault the city. Splinter admitted his error and expressed his wish not to follow Superfly's steps. The man told his sons that they have a chance to stop the menacing mutant and gain the adoration of the people. April then rang and informed them that there was an antidote on her scooter. Upon arriving at the lake shore, the Turtles and the other mutants attempted to confront the mutant, but ended up being seen as monsters by the public. Then it is with Leonardo's newfound leadership that the trio are able to use Michelangelo's improvisational skill, Donatello's smarts, and Raphael's furiousness to drop the anti-ooze canister into Superfly's blowhole. April finally conquers her fear and takes control of a news broadcast to make the public aware of the mutants' goodwill. The New Yorkers quickly come to their aid. Superfly scooped up the Turtles and began squeezing their shells tightly, Splinter watching in terror. The citizens surrounded him and noticed his connection with the Turtles. Splinter, despite deeply despising humans, pleaded with them to assist him in finding the antidote to the ooze. The people responded compassionately and resolved to help. Their actions distract Superfly long enough for the Turtles to escape and hurl the container into him, reverting him back to its original form as a bundle of normal animals. Splinter rejoins the Turtles with April and the mutants, and the city rejoices the victory. Splinter and Scumbug settle underground, and other mutants form a family with them. The Turtles attend April's high school and are welcomed as heroes. What if everything you thought you knew about Robin Hood was a lie? Not a misunderstood hero, not a noble outlaw, but something far darker. And what if the legend you grew up with was actually built on blood? This is exactly what The Death of Robin Hood 2026 dares to show us. A brutal reimagining of the legendary outlaw directed by Michael Sarnoski and starring Hugh Jackman in one of his darkest roles yet. But this is not the Robin Hood you remember. No merry men, no heroic speeches, no stealing from the rich to save the poor. Instead, we open in silence. A cold, empty peat land in 13th century England. Wind cuts through the land like a blade. And there sits Robin Hood, old, worn, covered in mud and scars. Hugh Jackman plays him not like a hero, but like a man who has survived too much violence to ever be called human again. He is alone by a dying fire when something moves in the darkness. A young woman appears, a drifter. She thinks she has found a weak old man, but she is wrong. Robin grabs her instantly and in a chilling moment, he tells her she made a mistake coming close. He could smell her long before she arrived. And then, without hesitation, he kills her. A knife straight through the skull. No music, no mercy, no legend, just death. And in that moment, everything you thought you knew about Robin Hood is gone. Because this is not a hero. This is a man built from violence itself. But what turned him into this? And why does the world still call him a legend? Stay with me, because the truth is only beginning to unfold. After the opening shock, the story pulls us deeper into Robin's broken world. We learn that Robin Hood is not just feared, he is hunted. Not only by soldiers or kings, but by families, by sons, fathers, brothers, all carrying the weight of what Robin has done. Because Robin Hood, as this film reveals, has not stolen from the rich to help the poor. He has stolen from everyone and killed anyone who stood in his way. Bill Skarsgård enters the story as Little John, but even that name feels broken now. He is no longer a loyal companion, but a man trying to survive the same violence that created Robin. And he brings a dangerous offer. One last job. One last act of survival. One last chance at something that might resemble peace. But, Robin does not believe in peace, only escape. The mission goes horribly wrong. Violence erupts in muddy, brutal chaos. Bodies fall. Screams vanish into the wind. And Robin Hood, the legendary outlaw, is finally brought to his knees, mortally wounded. But, death does not take him yet. Instead, something else does. He is carried away to a remote monastery island, a place cut off from war, from revenge, from legend. There, a woman named Sister Bridget appears, played by Jodie Comer. And she does something no one else has ever done for Robin Hood. She saves him. But, healing him may be more dangerous than killing him ever was. Because in this quiet place, Robin is forced to do something he has avoided his entire life. Remember. But what he remembers will change everything. The priory becomes a strange kind of prison, not of walls, but of silence. Robin is weak, injured, stripped of his weapons, and for the first time, he is not feared. He is watched. Sister Bridget tends to him, calm, mysterious, almost unnatural in her peace. Around them, life continues. A dying leper, a silent community, a strange stillness that feels almost unreal. And slowly, Robin begins to change. But not in the way you expect, because this is where the film twists deeper. Robin is no longer the man of legend, and he refuses to even use his name. He becomes Randall, a ghost trying to disappear from history itself. But history does not forget him. Little Margaret, the daughter of Little John, arrives at the priory. A child surrounded by violence, now placed in the care of the man responsible for so much of it. And she begins to bond with him. Strangely, almost dangerously. But she is not the only arrival. A young man appears, one eye damaged, his body marked by violence, and his goal is simple. Revenge. Because Robin Hood did something to him, or to his family, and now he has come to finish the story. Tension begins to rise inside the priory, because peace here is not guaranteed, it feels temporary, fragile, like glass waiting to break. And Sister Bridget, she knows something, something she is not saying. Because this place may not be as safe as it seems, and Robin Hood may not be as changed as he believes. Now everything begins to collapse. The past catches up, not in a battlefield, but in silence. The young man seeking revenge moves closer. The truth about Robin Hood begins to surface, and Sister Bridget reveals something deeper about this place. This priory is not just a sanctuary, it is a test, a place of balance, of judgment, of whether a man like Robin Hood can ever be forgiven or even changed. Robin is forced to confront everything, not just the violence he committed, but the myth built around him. Because in this version of the story, Robin Hood was never a hero. He was a weapon, a man whose legend grew larger than his crimes. And now, at the end of his life, he must face the truth, not through battle, but through acceptance. In the present day, the Waller  family are seeking a new, permanent residence after patriarch Ray Waller has been forced to  retire from his baseball career due to illness. They purchase the former residence of the Fuller  family, but Ray scratches his hand while working to clear out the pool in the back yard. When the  pool maintenance come to inspect it, they reveal that the pool is essentially self-sustaining,  taking its water from an underground spring in the area. As he spends more time in the pool  as part of his therapy, Ray's illness seems to go into remission. However, his wife Eve becomes  concerned at the changes she sees in her husband, and their children Izzy and Elliot each report  being attacked by something in the pool, as well as the family cat going missing. During  a party, the realtor tells Eve about the Fuller's daughter Rebecca drowning in the pool shortly  before Ray seemingly forces a child underwater and almost drowns himself, although this is attributed  to a side-effect of his illness. Tracking down the Fuller family after learning that there is a  long history of disappearances in the house, Eve meets with Kay, Rebecca's mother. Kay explains  that the water that now sustains the pool was once part of a healing spring, but in order to use  the water someone else must be sacrificed to it; Kay was compelled to sacrifice Rebecca to the pool  creature to heal her brother Tommy's illness. Eve is horrified to realise that Ray is now being  healed by the pool but it will take Elliot as a sacrifice. Eve returns to the house to find that  Ray is being directly controlled by the entity, which traps Elliot in the pool. Eve tries to save  her son while Izzy confronts the entity possessing her father, eventually assaulting him with a  baseball bat. Eve manages to retrieve Elliot, and is guided to the surface of the pool by  Rebecca's spirit. Once back in the garden, Izzy's assault and Elliot's condition  help Ray regain control of himself. To stop the entity attacking his children,  Ray sacrifices himself to it. Deciding to remain in the house so that no one  else falls victim to the entity, Eve, Izzy and Elliot make arrangements for the pool to  be filled in to stop such a thing happening again.

feels like poetry in motion and yet somehow it maintains an ingrained sense of realism it offers us a sincere look at a new but growing subculture in america in which people in their 60s and 70s basically a considerable portion of the victims of the 2008 financial crisis are hitting the road in camper vans because they can't afford traditional housing these new age nomads travel across the vastness of their seemingly boundless country looking for temporary jobs the film's protagonist firm played by francis mcdormand is an intimate observer and ardent participant in this lifestyle while serving as the window for the audience into this mobile but tight-knit community she finds a sense of belonging for the first time since her husband's passing nomadland is the cinematic adaption of jessica brouder's 2017 non-fiction book nomad land surviving america in the 21st century here is everything you need to know about its ending warning there are going to be spoilers um my mom says that you're homeless is that true no i'm not homeless i'm just houseless not the same thing right no don't worry about me i'm okay okay so in 2011 the economy of the entire town of empire nevada is decimated after the main source of income for the townsfolk closes its shutters for good fern whose husband beau has recently passed away does several odd jobs to make ends meet she previously worked at the plant along with bo for most of her adult life but now she doesn't have much to show for it empire soon becomes deserted as almost all its residents leave in search of better opportunities fern also realizes that she can't hold on to her home much longer she sells some of her possessions and puts the rest into a warehouse before moving permanently into a van while working at an amazon fulfillment center she learns about nomadic living from her friend and colleague linda initially reluctant fern discovers that it might be the best option for her after her temporary employment at amazon ends and she fails to land any other jobs following linda's advice fern ends up in a desert gathering in arizona where she receives instructions on the basics of how to be a modern nomad from the veterans of that lifestyle including bob wells a real life legend of the community as time passes fern almost seamlessly assimilates into the community she finds that this nomadic life perfectly complements her restless personality it also helps her deal with her grief she carries that grief of her husband's death in her journey throughout the whole film when she eventually returns to empire and the home she and bo shared it signifies that she is finally ready to close that chapter of her life fern is a deceptively complex character she exudes genuine warmth and earnestness when she's with her fellow nomads she demonstrates almost a childlike giddiness when she attends the rv show with her friends on the other hand when swanky tells fern that she has only a few months to live fern is sober supportive and kind however her lifestyle makes these moments of human interactions rare by default most of the time she's on the road alone in nature with her van which she names vanguard as a filmmaker zao truly shines when she depicts these intense moments of loneliness of her protagonist fern seems to thrive in them completely lost in the primal beauty that she encounters in her travel there is a scene in the film in which firm completely nude floats in a remote stream with nothing to invade that absolute privacy fern allows herself to be static even if it's only for a limited time fern's growth in the film is quite subtle she carries a deeply rooted sense of loss wherever she goes from fern's conversation with the boy she meets on the road we learned that she and beau married when they were hardly adults and they remained together for several decades until beau's passing in her marital life with bo she found reasons to overlook her inherent restlessness even though most of them were originally beau's reasons to be an empire he loved working at the plant and loved living in that town and fern loved him and that was enough when bo died that restlessness returned in full extent that she sabotages a potential future with david she declines david's offer to stay with him willingly choosing the nomadic life over a domestic one for the first time and returns to empire her pointed conversation with bob also precedes her return to her home they share stories of loss with each other giving one another glimpses of immense grief that they carry around with themselves bob lost his adult son to suicide a few years ago and it has instilled in him a deep appreciation for nomadic life the nomads don't tell each other goodbyes as there's a sense of finality attached to that word instead they say that they will see the other person down the road according to bob he will see his son again even if it's not in this life fern goes back to empire to say those same words to her husband she sells the stuff she left in the warehouse and visits their home one last time it's her moment of catharsis she is there not necessarily to find closure but to acknowledge her desire to live on she leaves empire because she has nothing that has a hold on her any longer she and beau never had a child and beau's family was not involved in their lives after promising her late husband that they will see each other again she hits the road she chooses not to live only with her memories and is now prepared to make new ones during a conversation between fern and her sister it is fern's marriage with bo grounded her and she was truly happy when she was with him after his death she continues to live in their home until she has no other choice but to leave with david it's beau that woman was perfectly content in sacrificing her own desire for those of her husbands that woman was happy to leave everything behind for love but as fern is now she has experienced all of that to the very end and while she cherishes the memories of her husband she doesn't want to repeat them when fern makes her silent departure she doesn't pick the nomadic life she also chooses herself and that guys is nomadland as i can best explain it let me know what you think about nomad land in the comments below i think nomad land is one of the best movies of the year i wouldn't be surprised if if director chloe's out wins best director in the 2021 oscars but let me know what you think about this movie in the comments below and as always real legends never die [Music]

text: In 1995, Russian undercover agents, super-soldier Alexei Shostakov and Black Widow Melina Vostokoff, pose as a normal family in Ohio with their surrogate daughters Natasha Romanoff and Yelena Belova. When the mission to steal S.H.I.E.L.D. intel is complete, the family escapes to Cuba and rendezvous with their boss, General Dreykov, who has Natasha and Yelena taken to the Red Room for training. Years pass, and Alexei is imprisoned in Russia, while Natasha defects to S.H.I.E.L.D. after bombing Dreykov's Budapest office, apparently killing him and his young daughter Antonia. In 2016, Natasha is a fugitive for violating the Sokovia Accords. She escapes from U.S. Secretary of State Thaddeus Ross and flees to a safehouse in Norway supplied by Rick Mason. Meanwhile, Yelena kills a rogue former Black Widow but comes in contact with a synthetic gas that neutralizes the Red Room's chemical mind-control agent. Yelena sends the antidote to Natasha hoping that she will return to help Yelena free the other Widows. When Natasha unknowingly drives off with the antidote, she is attacked by Taskmaster, who is after it. Natasha manages to escape Taskmaster and realizes that the antidote came from Yelena. The two reunite in Budapest, where Natasha learns Dreykov is alive and the Red Room is still active. Shortly after, they are attacked by Black Widows, and Natasha and Yelena evade the Widows and Taskmaster before meeting Mason, who supplies them with a helicopter. Natasha and Yelena break Alexei out of prison to learn Dreykov's location. He tells them to speak with Melina, who lives on a farm outside Saint Petersburg, where she developed the chemical mind control process used on the Widows. There, Yelena reveals that while they were not a real family, she believed they were so. Melina admits she sent their location to Dreykov, whose agents arrive and take them to the Red Room, an aerial facility. Melina and Natasha use face mask technology to switch places before being captured, allowing Melina to free Alexei and Yelena from their restraints. Meanwhile, Natasha confronts Dreykov, who sees through her disguise. Natasha learns Taskmaster is Antonia, who suffered damage so severe that Dreykov had to put a chip in her head, turning her into the perfect soldier, capable of mimicking the actions of anyone she sees, including several Avengers. Natasha attempts to kill Dreykov but fails to harm him due to a pheromone lock installed in every Widow. Dreykov reveals that he controls Widows worldwide via his desk console. Natasha intentionally breaks her nose, severing a nerve in her nasal passage to negate the pheromone, and then attacks Dreykov. Alexei battles Taskmaster, while Melina takes out one of the facility's engines, and Yelena searches for the other Widows, who are sent to protect Dreykov. Together, Alexei and Yelena lock Taskmaster in a cell. Dreykov escapes as the Widows attack Natasha, but Yelena creates an antidote bomb that releases the Widows from the mind control. Natasha gets into the control desk and copies the locations of the other Widows worldwide as the facility begins to explode and fall. Natasha retrieves the two surviving vials of the antidote and frees Taskmaster from the locked cell. Melina and Alexei escape via a plane just as Yelena takes out Dreykov's helicopter, killing him. Natasha gives Yelena a parachute before battling Taskmaster in freefall. After landing, Natasha uses the antidote on Taskmaster, freeing her from servitude. The freed Widows arrive as Yelena, Melina, and Alexei say goodbye to Natasha. She gives Yelena the last antidote vial and the portable drive, telling her to find and free the other, still mind-controlled, Widows. As they leave with Antonia, Natasha awaits Ross and his men, who have arrived to apprehend her. Two weeks later, Natasha reunites with Mason, who supplies her with a Quinjet. She leaves, intending to free the imprisoned Avengers. In a post-credits scene set after Natasha's death, Yelena encounters Contessa Valentina Allegra de Fontaine at Natasha's grave. De Fontaine assigns Clint Barton, whom she claims is responsible for Natasha's death, as Yelena's next target.

text: Thanks for sitting until the end of the video I've been P...oh crap I've started at the end again. Welcome to the Heavy Spoilers show I'm your host Paul aka the guy whos not backwards in coming forward and tomorrow I'll make the Tenet Video that you're watching right now. Since August I've done a tonne of videos on the movie and I've compiled the most asked questions to clear up any confusion over the film. This includes why the future version of the Protagonist shot at himself, what the Algorithm is, why Kat didn't need a mask on the boat and a lot lot more If this is your first time here then please click the thumbs down button and make sure you unsubscribe from the channel to never see a video. With that out the way, thank you for clicking this, now let's get into the breakdown. Ok so Tenet opens with an Opera scene that pretty much throws you into the movie at the deepend. But what exactly is going on here? Well on the surface it seems like The Protagonist is part of a CIA operation to infiltrate the Opera during a siege so that he can secure the algorithm. This fails and instead he's drafted into the TENET organisation after being double crossed, having his teeth pulled out and also choking down on what he believes is a cyanide pill. Sounds like my kinda night at the Opera. But what exactly was going on here, well The Protagonist was actually given this intel by the future version of himself and this was so that he could not only ensure that he handed the Algorithm over to Sator but also make it so that he not only met Neil, but also showed he was willing to lay his life on the line. Before the finale we learn from Ives that the splinter team mission is meant to be one that nobody returns from. Ives even says that they can't afford having anyone left alive who knows what the algorithm is and the fact that the protagonist takes the pill shows that he's willing to lay down everything if needs be. Now why the future version made sure that Sator got a piece of the algorithm is hinted at by Priya who refuses to change telling his past version about where the algorithm is. Do try and keep up. She says that they actually need Sator to bring all of the pieces together so that they can then snatch them and then split them up. The entire point of the finale is to trick Sator into believing that his mission in burying the Algorithm is successful so that his future version won't change anything and will continue collecting the pieces in order to bring them together and carry out the plan that will allow the algorithm to be stolen. This is why the Tenet team allow the explosion to go off so that the past version of the character believes that his future forces succeed in completing their mission. In the car chase we saw how the antagonist learning the truth about certain events helped him to play them to his advantage and thus his past version has to believe that he will win. In actuality, the Tenet team now have everything they need to divide up the algorithm and take it to their graves. But what is the algorithm exactly? Well it's probably the plot point that we learn the least about but from what we discover we can piece certain things together. From Priya we learn that the algorithm was developed in the future by a scientist that discovered a way to fully invert the world. This would allow things like global warming and climate change to be reversed so that future generations would not suffer because of the sins of the past. The algorithm is pretty much a bomb that when detonated will cause a massive spike in reverse radiation across the planet that forces the past to fold in on itself wiping out all life beyond the consciousness of the future. Contrary to the Grandfather clock theory, the people of the future believe that it is possible to change things in the past whereas we learn throughout the film that it's not. However, because the people of the future always tried to change things they always will make the algorithm and attempt to send it back so we can see the events of the movie play out. The Scientist realised that in destroying the past they would destroy themselves and thus she seperated the algorithm and buried it which is where it was found by Sator. Upon believing he's won Sator says that someday in the future a man in a tower will flip a switch and armageddon will be both created and avoided. Now the armageddon he is referring to is creating it in the past in order to avoid it in the future. He believes that once the algorithm is planted and then detonated that all life in the past will be wiped out. However, what the Tenet team do is basically along the same lines as the Scientist and they seperate the algorithm, invert it and place it somewhere so that it can never be found. By doing this at no point in the future can these pieces of the algorithm be put together so they can't be used. But who is the scientist exactly? Well the movie tells us very little but as we only ever meet one scientist and they happen to be female I believe that this is the same person that becomes the oppenheimer of her time. We learn that Laura has been studying the reverse radiation for quite some time and that though the people in the past haven't figured out how to do it, one day they will. I think that Laura is actually the person who discovers the formula for inverting things and the only time we meet her she says that she was assigned to the project and has been studying it. This close proximity to the time inverted objects makes her the perfect person to figure it all out and they we'll never know for definite, movies tend to give us the answers even if they don't always point them out. Because this is the only possible person we meet who fits the role I think it's the case and ey...if the shoe fits. Also I was gonna keep this video really tenet and actually give the answers before asking the questions but I thought that would be too confusing. Now this idea of everything being pre-determined has put a lot of people off the movie and made them say "what's the point." Well as Neil says before he goes off to his death, they have faith in the laws of the universe and by carrying out things the way they're supposed to it shows that there is actually a grand plan to it all. Tenet is a fatalist film and I'm sure many of us look back on bad things that happened to us and see that they actually led to a positive outcome years down the line which this film seems to also be hinting at. Now though lots of people die along the way, that doesn't mean that Tenet doesn't have somewhat of a happy ending and though we don't know if The Protagonist goes off with Kat and Max at the end I think the movie is hinting to us that he does. Before going away for the...the last mission and I swear I'm not crying...you're crying...Neil asks The Protagonist if he's going back to London to check in on Kat and he replies by saying no it's far to dangerous. Neil then says "not even from afar" which the Protagonist also denies. However we know from the finale that he did go back to London to check in on her from afar so this was indeed a lie. Now we've already done a big breakdown on why we think that Neil is actually Kat's son Max which will be linked at the end of the video but I think Neil asked these two specific questions because he knows that The Protagonist did indeed meet the pair after killing Priya. Speaking of there were several questions surrounding why they didn't just hang around at the turnstile after she was shot and then revert her there. However, we do know that before this moment Sators men owned it and operated there so this would cause issues with the past had they hung around. They're only able to move then and there because Sator is out on the highway so they have to travel back to the turnstile that they know will be accessible at the airport during their heist. I've also had a lot of people ask why Kat didn't need to wear a mask on the boat at the end. I'm never sure of exactly what boat they mean as she's on several in the finale but if it's the TENET one it's because she's in a sealed room which has a regular supply of Oxygen so the mask isn't needed and if it's when she's on Sators it's because she's reverted back to normal at this point so isn't feeling the effects of inversion. Many of you wondered where Kat went after the boat scene at the end and the simple answer is that she hid away whilst her past version continued on the same path that she did. All Kat would have to do was lie low until the inversion scene in which that version of her goes to the past and then she could pop out as there is no duplicates and continue living life like normal, aware that she succeeded and that her husband doesn't exist beyond this point. Outside of the airport the characters are actually very good at avoiding themselves and we even see that The Protagonist passes the windmill that he was in at the start of the movie, well aware that his past self is hidden out of view so they won't come face to face. Now the next question is why can't anyone understand what anyone is saying in any of the movie. That's because the movie was mixed during the pandemic on some Iphone headphones and the score was so good that Nolan told them to turn it up to 11. Bass in the ride had the car going like. Nah but seriously I have seen a lot of people asking why the Protagonist shot at himself at the airport. The first time we see this fight scene it seems like the attacker is trying to kill him, however in hindsight we know that this is actually the future version of the character who is just trying to make it to the turnstile. The reason that he fires the gun at his past self isn't to kill him it's actually to unload the entire thing so that it can't be used against him. From his POV we can clearly see that he knows it won't hit his head and thus he is deliberately missing on purpose. The past version even grabs it from him from the end of the fight and rather than trying to snatch it back he dismantles it to make sure that no matter what he won't be shot. Speaking of Turnstiles a lot of people are confused about why people have to see themselves exiting the turnstile before going into it. This is simply because if they know they got out the otherside then they will get out but I don't think it's completely imperative to their operation beyond simply knowing that things will be ok. Now most of the ops to do with the turnstiles are led by Ives and many of you have been asking who he is. We don't actually know but we do know that he was hired by TENET in order to basically be the cavalry for The Protagonist at the Turnstile and also be the person that leads the final op. Ives was clearly very close to The Protagonist if he was picked to be someone who will guard the algorithm but beyond that we know very little. Now that is the main point of the movie and it's pretty much said that the Tenet ops should know very little about each other which is why we don't actually learn who he is. I think that's all of the major questions that I haven't cleared up in my previous videos but I will be doing one in the coming weeks which talks about why no one actually dies in the film. It's difficult to post that without spoiling things but I will get to work on it and drop it after I think enough people have had the time to see the movie. Don't forget that on the 30th of December we're giving away three copies of the Lord Of The Rings 4k box set to our subscribers. With that out the way thank you for sitting through the video, I’ve been Paul and I’ll see you next time. Take care, Peace

He sees Johanna as not just a challenge he's eager to surmount, but an eager and curious spirit who complements his own desire to share his knowledge with the rest of the world. We don't know what awaits them in the future, but it's clear from the film's final scene that Kidd is a changed man. When we meet Kidd, he's making his living as a professional reader of news, but his job is about more than merely reading from a newspaper. He's a curator, an orator, and a showman, and his interest in the kinds of stories he wants to tell shifts along with the film, as he delivers everything from delightful romps to hard news. "Ladies and gentlemen, my name is Captain Jefferson Kyle Kidd and I'm here tonight to read the news from across this great world of ours." So what does that mean for Kidd's professional future? By the end of the film he's happily news-reading with Johanna by his side, but he also mentions his past as the owner of a printing company, something it seems like he'd be very good at with the right financial backing. We know from history that men who get paid to deliver the news don't go away. They just evolve with the technology. So will Kidd evolve his news-reading to change with the times? Will he go back to printing? The young girl known as Cicada to her Kiowa family and Johanna to her German family is an intriguing puzzle throughout News of the World. And yet we do get to see an arc unfolding through her nonverbal communication as Johanna shifts from being desperately sad to lose her Kiowa family to confused and angered by her German family to eager and happy to be with Kidd for the rest of her life. Still, the question remains what exactly Johanna's future truly holds. Given that she's essentially the child of two worlds, it would not be hard to see her as an advocate for Native American rights as an adult, fighting for social justice with her adoptive father's passion for knowledge supporting her along the way. Even if that's not the path she takes, though, she has a bright and loving future ahead. "See all those words? Put them all together and you have a story." News of the World is set in 1870, five years after the end of the American Civil War, in a state that's found it particularly difficult to keep up with the reconstruction era. Violent racism remains rampant, roads everywhere are dangerous, and people are willing to do just about anything to survive or to profit off others. Very early on in the film, Kidd tells us that he is a part of this aftermath in a no small way, having been a soldier in Texas who didn't surrender until weeks after the death of Abraham Lincoln. He is a product of this time, and he suffers for it. But of course, we know the history of Reconstruction. What the film is more interested in showing us is an intimate look at the human cost, because as Kidd later explains, he was off fighting a war on behalf of other people, and all he got for his trouble were some scars and the fact that he wasn't there for the death of his wife. There was a tremendous economic, political, and social cost to the American Civil War, some of which we still feel today. But it also left a more human carnage behind, psychological scarring that wasn't easily healed. News of the World is, at its core, a story of two people who have both lost their family. Johanna is, as Kidd eventually learns, an orphan two times over, having lost her birth parents when she was too young to really remember them and then losing her adoptive parents at the hands of people who thought they were saving her. Kidd, for his part, is also without a family, traveling around and making plenty of friends across Texas even as he refuses to go home to reckon with the loss of his wife. Both of them are on a journey of reconciliation, one that truly picks up steam when Johanna makes a choice. Faced with the prospect of rejoining a group of Kiowa who just happen to be traveling nearby, she instead asks them for a horse, brings it back to Kidd, and keeps traveling with him. It takes a little longer for Kidd to catch up to her emotional wavelength, but the message is clear. This is the moment when she decides that he is her family, and because he ultimately makes the same choice, they can both find their taste for familial love again. The entire movie hinges on that choice, when she asks to stay rather than to go, and it perfectly sets up the final moments of the film. Check out one of our newest videos right here! text: In 1979, Texas NWA heavyweight champion Kevin Von Erich worries that his father, WCCW owner Jack "Fritz" Von Erich, is pushing his youngest brother Mike away from his musical ambitions. Their brother David makes his wrestling debut with Kevin in a tag-team match against Bruiser Brody and Gino Hernandez, where Kevin meets and starts a relationship with a woman named Pam. He tells her about the "Von Erich curse" that killed his oldest brother Jack Jr., supposedly brought on by Fritz changing his last name from Adkisson to his mother's, whose family had suffered constant tragedy. Kevin fights world champion Harley Race to put himself in the lead for the championship contender, but he is brutally beaten and only wins when Race attacks the referee and is disqualified. A disappointed Fritz is delighted when David displays a natural talent for showmanship while trashing Race. The 1980 Summer Olympics boycott dashes Von Erich brother Kerry's hopes of competition, so he moves back home. Fritz presses him to fight alongside Kevin and David, while Pam helps the boys sneak Mike out to play a gig against his parents' wishes. By 1983, the trio defeats the Fabulous Freebirds for the six man tag team championship title, and Fritz volunteers David over Kevin to fight current world champion Ric Flair. Kevin and Pam get married, and he reveals at the wedding to an ill David that he will soon be a father. A week before the match, David, while touring in Japan, dies of enteritis. Both Kevin and Kerry volunteer to fight Flair in his place, and Kerry is chosen by a coin flip, beating Flair and winning the title. Still despondent, he goes out for a motorcycle ride and loses his foot in an accident. Kevin begins training Mike, who badly injures his shoulder during a match and goes into a toxic shock-induced coma during surgery. Fearing the curse, Kevin has his newborn son legally surnamed Adkisson. Mike narrowly emerges from his coma, but when Fritz presses him to get back in the ring, he commits suicide and Kevin starts to distance himself from Pam and their son. He fights Flair for the championship, but is disqualified when he ignores the referee and grapples him with the signature Von Erich "iron claw" move for too long. Kerry remains the only Von Erich wrestling with his new prosthetic foot, while Fritz has given Kevin the task of running the WCCW as he focuses on life with Pam and their two sons. Kerry gives Fritz a new gun for Christmas but becomes upset when he puts it away instead of firing it, later calling Kevin and telling him that the curse's constant presence has made him consider suicide. He hangs up before Kevin can learn his location, so Kevin calls Fritz and begs for help. Kevin arrives at the Von Erich house the next morning just in time to hear Kerry commit suicide with the gun, and he briefly strangles Fritz in a rage. In the afterlife, Kerry leaves behind the coin that decided that he would face Flair and reunites with Jack Jr., Mike (carrying his guitar), and David (wearing the champion belt). Some time later, Kevin sells the WCCW to Jerry Jarrett, his mother has given up her housewife duties to pick her hobby of painting back up, and Pam is pregnant again. Kevin weeps while watching his sons play football, telling them he misses having brothers when they try to comfort him. They promise to be brothers to him, and he gets up and plays with them. Closing titles reveal that the Von Erichs were inducted into the WWE Hall Of Fame in 2009, and Kevin and Pam bought a ranch where their large family lives to this day.

text: Sixteen-year-old homeschooled Cady Heron moves back to the United States from Kenya with her mother and attends North Shore High School. Cady befriends outsiders Janis 'Imi'ike and Damian Hubbard, who introduce her to the various cliques, and warn her to avoid the "Plastics", who consist of the doubtful Gretchen Wieners, unintelligent Karen Shetty, and 'queen bee' Regina George. Regina invites Cady to join the Plastics; Janis uses this as an opportunity to convince Cady to infiltrate the group for her. Cady becomes attracted to Aaron Samuels, a senior in her calculus class and Regina's ex-boyfriend. Cady tells Gretchen and Karen that she likes Aaron, who warn her that he is off-limits as he has dated Regina. Cady goes to Regina's house with the Plastics, and Regina's mom finds her old "Burn Book", a scrapbook the Plastics filled with cruel content about students and staff at the school. Cady tells Janis and Damian about the Burn Book, and they explain that Janis and Regina were once friends, but fell out after Regina outed Janis as a lesbian to the school. Cady begins to intentionally fail math to get closer to Aaron, who invites her to his Halloween party. Regina discovers Cady's crush on Aaron and, in a fit of jealousy, flirts with Aaron before kissing him in front of Cady. Realising Janis was right about Regina, she agrees to commit to her plan to ruin Regina's reputation. Cady tricks Regina into eating weight-gain Kälteen Bars to lose weight and replace her face cream with lard. The trio target Gretchen's insecurities by having a Candy Cane-Gram sent to Cady on Regina's behalf, making Gretchen think Cady is her new best friend. Gretchen reveals Regina's secrets to Cady, including her cheating on Aaron with football player Shane Oman. Regina's reputation takes a further hit after a disastrous performance at the Winter Talent Show leads to viral embarrassment. With Regina's social status plummeting, Cady becomes the new 'queen bee’. Janis invites Cady to her art show, but Cady tells her she has to travel with her mom on a business trip. However, Cady later convinces her mom to let her stay home and secretly throws a house party, where she drunkenly admits to Aaron that she has been deliberately failing math to get closer to him. Aaron rebukes Cady for becoming as manipulative as Regina and storms out. Cady follows him out and is confronted by Janis, who confronts her on being as catty as Regina. Cady accuses Janis of being in love with her and Janis responds that Cady has become fully Plastic, renouncing their friendship. Regina discovers she was not invited to the party and that Cady lied about the Kälteen Bars. She adds herself into the Burn Book and deliberately drops it in the school hallway. Upon the discovery, a riot breaks out among the junior girls over the rumors in the book. Principal Duvall and math teacher Ms. Norbury organise the junior girls into the gymnasium to find the source of the book. Ms. Norbury stages a cathartic intervention, encouraging the girls to apologize to each other about their treatment of others. Janis speaks out and reveals the whole plan to take revenge on Regina, who storms out in anger and, during a confrontation with Cady, is hit by a bus. Cady realizes the damage she has done and takes full responsibility for the book, leading her to be suspended for three weeks. Ms. Norbury offers Cady a way to earn extra credit by joining the Mathletes at state championships and Cady redeems herself after helping the team win. At the Spring Fling, Cady reconciles with Regina and is elected Spring Fling Queen, but snaps the plastic crown and gives pieces out to the girls, telling them they are all special in their own way. Cady apologizes to Janis and Damian, who accept her back as their friend, and makes amends with the Plastics. Cady also makes up with Aaron as they kiss.
