text: Near the start of ‘The Holdovers’ there’s a key scene that I think sheds light on the themes of the rest of the movie. Ollerman had ratted out Kountze for being the one that started the fight. “It was Kountze!” In retaliation Kountze grabs one of Ollerman’s gloves and throws it in the river. The one remaining glove has instantly become a holdover, baggage from Ollerman’s immediate past. “My glove’s gone! Twisted fucker orphaned that glove on purpose. Left you with one so the loss would sting that much more.” And in Ollerman’s reaction we see a microcosm of the whole movie that’s going to unfold. Ollerman thinks, then runs back to sacrifice his other glove into the river. Poetically the glove floats off downstream, Ollerman watches it disappear, he lets it go, and the river of life flows on. So what are we witnessing here? This is the ancient Greek philosophy of Stoicism in action. The same philosophy that Paul gifts to everyone in the form of the stoic classic Meditations by Marcus Aurelius. “for my money it’s the bible, the koran, and the bhagavad gita rolled up into one” One of the key teachings of Stoicism is to accept things that are beyond our control. Instead of reacting emotionally to uncontrollable events, the Stoics encourage us to think about what we can control and to act with wisdom, courage, justice, and self-discipline. This, they teach, is the way to stave off disruptive emotions and prevent us from falling into the abyss. It’s a guide to living a good life. Instead of feeling sorry and over the lost glove Ollerman chooses to let go of his attachment to both gloves. In this way, he’s rationally taking control of the situation, he’s refusing to be a victim. He’s choosing dignity over victimhood. Welcome to Cinema Detective. There will be spoilers in this video so if you haven’t seen ‘The Holdovers’ now is the time to leave. “I’ll go pack!” While the film’s title nominally refers to the students that are holding over at Barton Academy over christmas it could equally refer to the found family of Paul, Angus, and Mary who are each holding on to baggage from their past. The three main characters all have elements of Charles Dickens’ Scrooge in their character but in this Christmas Carol, there are no ghosts of Christmas past. Instead, Paul, Angus, and Mary each become each other's teachers. Each character learns to overcome their struggles and emotional barriers, leading to a renewed sense of purpose and connection with others. Three broken people come together and manage to become more whole. Like Ollerman losing his glove, something cruel has happened to each of them, and they must combat the destructive emotions that they’re feeling by doing the right thing even when it’s tough, by making choices they can be proud of, by standing up for what they believe in, and treating other people with kindness. “So who got stuck with it?” “Who do you think?” “That poor walleyed bastard” Paul Hunham is an ancient civilizations teacher who is struggling with life. His room paints a picture of a man not taking care of himself. He’s reading the memoir ‘Fear Strikes Out’ by American baseball player Jim Piersall. It’s a book about struggle with mental illness. He’s listening to “There’s A Place For Us’ from West Side Story, a song about longing for a place to belong. He’s got hemorrhoids and athlete's foot. There’s an unmade bed with a glass of whisky on the bedside table, and an opened bottle of Jim Beam on his desk. He’s drinking too much… “Are you kidding me? It’s only eleven and he’s already lit. I can smell the whiskey on him.” And on top of all that he’s got a wonky eye that veers off in the wrong direction and he stinks of fish! “You smell… like fish” Angus Tully is a troubled rebellious young man, but not without cause. We meet him packing to go on a trip to St Kitts, a luxury holiday destination island in the Caribbean. In the student dorm they’re listening to the raucous ‘The Time Has Come Today’ by The Chambers Brothers. The lyrics include “I have no place to stay”,”I have no home” which is apt for this group of boarding school students. “Little christmas orphan needs his pot and porn” As the film progresses we learn about the absence of Angus’ father due to mental illness and the St Kitts trip isn’t going to happen because his mother abandons him to spend time with the new man in her life. “I know it’s last minute, and I’m absolutely heartbroken about it, devastated really, but could you please see your way to staying at school over break?” Life has dealt him a few knocks at an early age and he’s desperately in need of guidance to keep him on the straight and narrow. Mary, is the manager of the cafeteria, toiling away to feed the school, who is taken aback by the sight of the snow falling outside the window. This moment here is one of the many scenes that will surely win Da’Vine Joy Randolph best supporting actress at the 2024 Oscars. It’s a look that says so much. The sight of snow falling jolts her back to the realization that she has lost her son and they won’t be spending Christmas together. For a lot of people Christmas is one of the hardest times of the year. “My little sister Peggy and her husband invited me to go visit them at Roxbury, but I feel like it’s too soon. Like Curtis will think that I’m abandoning him.” Paul has been lumbered with the responsibility for looking after the students during the Christmas vacation. “Thank you again for doing this Hunham” "Well ‘Non nobis solum nati sumus’ I suppose” Paul’s response… it’s part of a longer quote - “Not for ourselves alone are we born; our country, our friends, have a share in us" But Paul says it in a somewhat jaded way. This statement encapsulates a central tenet of Stoicism, which emphasizes the importance of community and social responsibility. The Stoics believed that all humans are manifestations of the same universal spirit and should live in brotherly love and readily help one another. Our actions should not be directed towards personal gain, but rather towards benefiting others. “Let us remember the poor and the helpless, the cold, the hungry and the oppressed” Paul understands all this and the importance of self-integrity. These are the principles he wants to teach and to uphold but he’s struggling in an environment where money and privilege are holding too much sway. It’s making Paul bitter… “At least pretend to be a human being” Paul gleefully whistles Ride Of The Valkyries by Wagner when handing out all the bad exam results. He’s taking a little too much pleasure in failing these students. “I can’t fail this class” “Oh don’t sell yourself short Mr Kountze I truly believe that you can” Only Angus manages a reasonable grade of B+. Angus is insubordinate. “Honestly it’s a little absurd” Causing the group to lose the chance of resitting the examination. Paul isn’t nice. “Latitude is the last thing these boys need” But as Director Alexander Payne has commented, there is a difference between being nice and being kind. Paul is kind in a way, because he is trying to give the students a first class education, “As Dr. Green used to say, our one true purpose is to produce young men of good character” But he is perhaps going about things in the wrong way. At the chapel we learn of Mary Lamb’s grief and the death of her son Curtis Lamb who I think is named Lamb as in “Lambs to the slaughter”. Unlike some of the other privileged kids at Barton Academy, Curtis couldn’t afford to further his education so he had no chance to defer the draft by using student status. “He had the grades, but I didn’t have the money. Even with financial aid it wasn’t enough. So when he got called up, no student deferment, off he went.” “I suspect that like me this is not how you wanted to spend your holidays, but such are the vicissitudes of life” Paul is teaching the students a lesson right out of the Stoic playbook. “As Barton men, we learn to confront our challenges with heads held high and with a spirit of courage and good fellowship” And we see with Angus slamming down his suitcase that he’s taking this situation without that spirit of courage and without his head held high. “Adversity builds character Mr Tully” As the students move into the infirmary we learn that Paul Hunham used to be a student at Barton Academy. “You know he used to be a student right?” And we also learn that Angus could be sent to Fork Union Military Academy if he is expelled from Barton Academy. “I just don’t want to end up at Fork union” Angus is 17 years old and military school could set him on a path eventually leading to Vietnam like Curtis Lamb. After Kountze stole Angus’ photo in revenge for the theft of his cigarettes Angus is projecting his own insecurities on to Kountze: “Your parents don’t want you around because your a fucking insecure sociopath… who’d want you for a son?” Which leads to a fight and Kountze sitting alone at dinner without a plate. When Kountze insensitively remarks about Mary: “I know she’s sad about her son and everything but still, she’s getting paid to do a job” Paul struggles to contain his rage: “you have no idea what that woman has been through” And criticizes his privilege ”Like is like a hen house ladder, shitty and short, you were born lucky” We’re getting insight into Paul’s deep desire to be an educator, not just facts and figures, he wants to raise fine young men. “Maybe someday you entitled little degenerates will appreciate that and if you don’t, I feel sorry for you, and we will have failed to do our jobs.” Paul doesn’t know The Newlywed Game, one of the top-rated TV programs of the period “You don’t know the Newlywed game? What planet have you been living on?” He’s been living an isolated life. It’s an opportunity for Mary to teach Paul a few things. When Paul says that the students have had it easy their whole lives Mary rebukes him: “You don’t know that! Did you?” And reminds him to be compassionate: “Everybody should be with their people on Christmas” Of course, Mary won’t be with Curtis this Christmas, so her mind has been focused on what is truly important. Paul is highly educated but Mary is more worldly wise than Paul, she’s got life experience. “Those two are going to get a divorce” Mary has suffered two tragedies in her life, Curtis’s father died before he and Mary could be married. The scale of the injustice that Mary has suffered is revealed. The social and economic disparities of the time influenced who ended up serving in Vietnam and African Americans, along with other minorities, ended up being disproportionately drafted as well as suffering higher casualty rates due to being assigned more dangerous combat roles. “my Curtis in the cold ground and those boys safe and warm in their beds” How can Mary possibly find the strength to carry on? “How’d you say it? Like is like a henhouse ladder” As the story progresses, we see that Angus isn’t a bad kid, he empathizes with YE-Joon helping him hide his wet bed sheets. Then we have the helicopter turning up to take most of the students away, and the movie shifts gears forcing a more intimate setting between Paul, Mary, and Angus. And we have Paul saying: “Let’s make the best of it shall we?” It’s another little line embodying the stoic philosophy that Paul is struggling to uphold. And now we have the beginnings of our “found family”. Paul, Mary, and Angus are all gathered round the tv together. Mary questions Paul’s rationalization of his life as: “I like being alone. I’ve always found myself drawn to the ascetic. Like a monk.” “Spiritual goals? You?” She doesn’t buy it. And she coaxes Paul into revealing his buried ambitions to travel to: “Greece, Italy, Egypt, Peru, Carthage, Tunisia now of course” And his desire to write a monograph rather than book is something else that Mary criticizes: “You can’t even have a whole dream, can you?” Paul has grown bitter, disillusioned, and is lying to himself, and Mary’s dose of the honest truth will be a catalyst that helps Paul heal and grow. As Angus steals the keys, drinks wine and eats ice cream, we hear a segment of Crying, Laughing, Loving, Lying by Labi Siffre. It’s a song that can easily be viewed through a Stoic lens. Crying never did nobody no good, no how That's why I don't cry Laughing sometimes does somebody some good somehow That's why I'm laughing now The stoics don’t expect people to be emotionless, they encourage people to replace negative emotions that never do nobody no good with rational actions that will do people good. And laughing, since it’s logical to do things that make you feel better, would qualify as a rational action. Although there are times where crying does do people good and we’ll get to that later. Maybe Mary is beginning to get through to Paul. He shares his Christmas cookies with Mary and Angus. “Well, I’m trying” And this makes Mary laugh, which as the song said should do her some good. So Paul’s presence is having a positive effect on Mary, even if he’s just amusing her at the moment. Angus is desperate to leave and Paul catches him trying to book a hotel room in Boston. In a lot of ways Angus is a typical teenager, rebelling, challenging authority and being mischievous and sarcastic. This leads to lots of funny moments in the film like when Paul chases Angus and he’s throwing Paul’s own lines back at him: “Without exercise, the body devours itself” And he’s intelligent, and Paul warns him that “This is your rubicon. Do not cross the rubicon” Angus retorts by quoting Julius Caesar: “Alea Jacta est” The die is cast. It’s the point of no return. This rubicon moment forces Angus and Paul to become accomplices. Paul’s job will be under threat if his boss finds out what happened. And Angus will probably face suspension and being sent to military academy. So it’s at the hospital that Angus first has a lesson to teach Paul. Paul says… “Barton men don’t lie” But Angus lied to protect Paul and protect himself. The moment is significant as it shows Paul’s growth from a rigid, traditional teacher to someone who is willing to bend rules for the well-being of his student. They’re now partners in crime, they’ve bonded, “Okay, then. This all remains entre nous.” Angus also has an altercation and mocks a Vietnam veteran missing his right hand. I think this could be a call back to Ollerman’s right glove that Kountze stole. It’s another stoic teaching opportunity for Paul. He tosses Angus the car keys forcing Angus to catch them with his right hand, the hand the Veteran is missing. “How many boys do you know who have had their hands blown off? Barton boys don’t go to Vietnam. No they go to Yale or Dartmouth or Cornell, whether they deserve to or not.” Paul is encouraging Angus to think rationally about what has just happened. Sure, Angus could react emotionally, call them assholes, get riled up, and end up in a fight. Or Angus can think rationally, view the veteran with empathy, understand why there might be a reason for his aggression, reflect on his own privilege, control his own emotions, and avoid a nasty scene. It’s a much more healthy situation for everyone involved, all for the cost of a beer. I want to mention Paul’s awkward football throw. Aside from being funny, it’s humanizing him, it’s a little mirror for Paul stepping outside his comfort zone and foreshadowing his personal growth. And then we see Paul is peeling potatoes, something he’s not used to doing. But he’s finding it “theraputic”, again it’s just a little sign that Paul is having new experiences that are changing him. Mary continues to push Paul out of his comfort zone: “Mr. Hunham, if you’re too chickenshit to go to that party, then just say so. But don’t fuck it up for the little asshole! What’s wrong with you? It’s just a party.” Angus’ shaving scene is symbolizing him growing up, he’s transitioning from being an adolescent to a young man. And his kissing scene at the party serves the same purpose but he’s still got some growing up to do. Because at the party he steals the Christmas snowglobe. His fascination with the snowglobe reflects his longing for simplicity, nostalgia for happier times with his father, and protection from the harsh realities of the complexities of his life. Paul’s dream was to make a difference as an educator. He wants to raise fine young men. “I guess I thought I could make a difference. I used to think I could prepare them for the world, even a little -- provide standards and grounding, like Dr. Green always drilled into us. But the world doesn’t make sense anymore. It’s on fire, the rich don’t give a shit, poor kids are cannon fodder, integrity’s a punch line, trust is just a name on a bank.” Paul is failing to live up to the stoic ideals he cherishes. He’s focused on the problems of the world that he can’t control, the inequalities that exist in the world. His sense of defeat and loss of purpose is a lapse of the stoic virtues he preaches. “Well, look. If that’s all true then now is when they most need someone like you.” This is the rational thought that Paul needs to process. What can he control? Where can he make a difference? “I thought maybe you were doing something special for Angus… you should!” Paul’s baggage is his unfulfilled potential, as an educator, as an author. He’s only ever read about the places he’s so fascinated by in books. And he’s retreated into his teaching role as a safe space. Barton is his comfort zone. “Like catches up to them so fast… them… ha… us!” This fear of living is perhaps the reason that he is depressed, takes pills, and drinks heavily. We see his longing for a relationship with Ms Crane, until her boyfriend shows up and bursts his bubble. Because Paul can’t be whole until he fixes himself. And Paul’s interaction with Angus represents his opportunity for his redemption. It’s his chance to become the kind of man he believes in but is failing to realize. Throughout most of ‘The Holdovers’ Mary carries herself with a quiet dignity, she is the moral compass of the film and guides Paul and Angus through her words and through her actions. She has lost her son but she hasn’t stopped being a mother. Da’Vine Joy Randolph’s performance is exceptional. Mary is written as a stoic character in the flawed modern sense of the word, as in, she’s emotionally bottled up. And yet Randolph effectively conveys Mary’s subtle emotional depth through her facial expressions and interactions, and we’re well aware of her profound sadness long before the party scene. Her breakdown at the party contrasts with her usual display of dignity and strength. It’s pivotal in her character arc, she can no longer contain her suppressed emotions. The death of a child is perhaps the greatest challenge to the stoic philosophy. How can you expect someone to act rationally, check their attitude, and focus on actions with controllable outcomes in the face of such profound grief? It’s one thing dealing with the loss of a glove… “It’s gone, my gloves gone” But what nonsense is this? To act rationally, keep calm, and focus on what you can control after such a cruel and devastating blow? But Mary’s situation is a little different from Angus and Paul because acknowledging and expressing her pain is a crucial step in her healing process. But remember, stoicism isn’t about suppressing all emotion it’s about avoiding futile negative emotion. For Mary, letting out her grief is the rational step forward, and it’s not something that she can reasonably control. I think the party with its festive atmosphere is simply too much for her. She breaks done and confronts her harsh reality. “He’s gone” This crying isn’t futile. It’s a cathartic release, a necessary step towards healing and understanding. It aligns with Stoic thought by emphasizing the importance of facing reality as it is. And with Mary we again see constructive negative emotion when she scolds Paul on the walk to the car. “You don’t tell a boy who’s been left behind at Christmas that you’re aching to cut him loose. That nobody wants him. What the fuck is wrong with you?” So don’t misunderstand stoicism. It isn’t about the suppression of all emotion, it’s about the suppression or redirection of negative emotion about uncontrollable events in particular where the emotion won’t make any difference. But Mary can influence Paul. And she does. With Mary and Ms Cranes words no doubt ringing in his ears, Paul wakes up the next morning and goes out to buy a Christmas tree. He’s taking positive action in areas that he can control. He can’t fix all society's problems, but he can heed Ms Crane's advice and try to do something special for Angus and Mary on Christmas day. And he agrees to bend the Barton rules to go on a road trip to Boston. Mary’s little sister is pregnant and Mary is staying in the nursery that’s being decorated for the new baby that’s on the way. It’s in this scene that we discover what’s in Mary’s box. Mary has packed up Curtis’s old baby clothes, a bottle and a pair of his little shoes. She’s putting them in the drawer for her niece or nephew. And later we learn that Mary is going to be saving up for college for the new member of the family. She’s focusing on what she can do with the rest of her life. Where she can make a difference. She can support her family. Nothing will ever allow Mary to get over the loss of her child, but she has reconnected with her sister and found purpose in saving for the education of her sister’s child. I’m a little worried that viewers might be put off by the ancient Greek philosophy that I’ve tried to highlight in this review. Don’t be: “before you dismiss something as boring or irrelevant, remember that if you truly want to understand the present, or yourself, you must begin in the past. You see history is not merely the past it’s an explanation of the present” When it comes to human psychology there’s nothing new under the sun and perhaps these ancient thinkers have something to teach us about our lives today. “See, when you say it that way, and throw in some pornography, it’s a lot easier to understand. You should try doing more of that in class and less yelling. You know, most of the kids pretty much hate you. Teachers, too. You know that, right?” This prevents him from doing what he wants to do… to teach. And with this comment by Angus Paul is visibly humbled. He is listening. When Paul and Angus run into Paul’s old university acquaintance. Paul lies about where he is teaching: “I’m currently posted in Antwerp” Angus rolls with the lie, pretending to be Paul’s nephew and claiming that Paul is a published author. “I’m his nephew, Leonard” He’s got his back, he doesn’t understand what’s going on but he plays along and blows Paul’s trumpet for him… And this interaction that allows us to learn why Paul is so antagonized by privilege, we’re getting to the crux of his problems. “That blue-blooded prick’s family had allies on the faculty… I mean their last name is on a library for Christ’s sake.” Paul was kicked out of Harvard for being falsely accused of cheating. The privileged kid got away with it. It’s another shared secret bringing Angus and Paul even closer together. Mr Hunham never graduated college, he got his job as a favor from Dr Green and he’s kinda been trapped in Barton ever since. Paul should have been an Ivy league professor but due to the incident he was held back in life. It was an event beyond his control and as something that’s part of his past he can’t change what happened. But he’s been frustrated by it ever since, he’s been unable to move past it. He reacts emotionally to privilege, and it clouds his judgment, and prevents him from being the effective educator he desires to be. This anger is what’s stopping him from living up to Stoic ideals, and it’s plagued him his whole life. There are a lot of similarities between Paul and Angus, they mirror each other, they’ve both got similar problems. Angus’ fear and anger is preventing him from thriving as a student. They’re both on Librium. They both make nazi jokes. And at the bowling alley we have Paul sarcastically reflecting Anguses criticism back at him: “You’re a pretty good teacher, kid. Too bad everyone dislikes you. Pretty much hates you. But you must know that, right?” They’re learning from each other. The girls smiling at Angus draw attention to his growth, people are starting to notice his positive transformation. Angus is becoming a man. Outside of Barton Paul is like a fish out of water, which is probably an appropriate phrase since he smells of fish due to his unfortunate medical condition. His mini-lecture to the drunk Santa is highlighting his social awkwardness and how much growing Paul still has to do. “My son” At the cinema Paul and Angus are watching “Little Big Man” a 1970 western film about a white man “Little Big Man” that is raised by Cheyenne Native Americans. In the western the Cheyenne chief is a father figure to his adopted son “Little Big Man’. He says “I have thought and talked and smoked on this matter,.....and my decision is… Little Big Man has returned.” At that exact moment we see Paul, the chief, with pipe billowing with smoke, and his thoughts have turned to HIS adopted son… Angus. Little big man has returned, Angus is a big man, almost an adult, but as someone caught between adulthood and childhood he’s still little and still capable of doing childish things. Angus is saying he is going to the toilet and then running off! The same thing he did earlier! “He used to be fine. He was better than fine. He was great. He was my dad” And now we come to the crux of Angus’ issues. His history doesn’t have to dictate his destiny, but he’s not realized it yet. He’s caught up in his own sad story, he’s at risk of being consumed by it, the same way Paul was, he needs to learn he can control his narrative. “You are not your father, you’re your own man” It’s Paul saying you are not a victim to external circumstances. You have the ability to focus on your own choices and actions. Mary embodies the stoic principles. Take the PAPRIKA scene. Something out of Mary’s control happened, her colleague added too much paprika, and Mary’s response wasn't rage, she just came up with the logical solution to fix it by adding more water. She’s a natural stoic. Paul has the textbook knowledge but he’s not always successful when it comes to putting what he knows in theory into practice. Paul learns from Mary the missing ingredient… empathy, understanding, and compassion. Which allows Paul to finally teach Angus what he wanted to teach. Not through words, but through example, through action. And speaking of missing ingredients… Let’s take a closer look at the Cherries Jubilie scene. Angus is refused the desert because of the alcohol. And we see that Paul reacts emotionally, losing his self-control. Failing to live up to the stoic ideal. “Christ on a crutch what kind of a fascist hash foundry are you running here?” But Mary calmly asks to buy cherries and ice cream as take out to make their own dessert. She’s ignoring what they can’t control and focusing on what they can control effortlessly embodying the principles of Stoicism. Refusing to be victims to circumstance. “Presto! Cherries Jubilie” Back at Barton we get the firecracker scene symbolizing how Paul loosening up. “We’re gonna light this sucker off in the kitchen!” “Congratulations Mr Tully, congratulations Danny, Mary… congratulations” We see that Paul has relaxed a bit because he’s allowing the students to retake the exam after all. He says: “Omnia ex scrineis vestris praeter stilum” Which means “everything off your desks except your pen. It’s another stoic metaphor. Everything can be taken away from you except your intellect, your rationality, your pen, which cannot be taken away. When Mary takes Angus’ hand it’s showing that despite her loss she can still play a mothering role. She still has something to offer life and life still has something to offer her. I read some reviews of The Holdovers and some people said they didn’t like the ending because Paul lost his job. This job and this environment had been holding him back for years. In sacrificing his job to save Angus, “It was my idea” “I don’t give a shit. I said I don’t give a shit. You two were unreachable, he was all alone at christmas” Paul’s has finally found a way to embody the ideals he cherishes. He’s lost his job but gained his self-integrity. He’s become the man he always wanted to be. Yes it’s bittersweet but it’s also the reason why Paul is finally able to say to Angus: “It’s this one… This is the one you should look in…” So don’t feel sorry for Paul, he’s not a loser here, this ending is his triumph and his redemption. He’ll be okay. Paul spits out that ridiculously expensive cognac, which represents privilege, because he doesn’t need the alcohol anymore and he’s letting go of the hold that his resentment for privilege has held on him all these years. I’m sure you don’t need to look far to find people around you who are enraged and angry about things they have no control over and where their anger and rage won’t change anything. We all spend a lot of time howling at the moon, wrapped up in our own tales of injustice to little effect. This type of victim mentality often doesn’t achieve anything. It’s pointless to bang your head against a brick wall even if you rightly think the brick wall has no right being there. There’s a well known phrase, “if life gives you lemons, make lemonade”. You make lemonade by thinking through your problems and deciding the best course of action, not getting caught up in anger, rage, resentment, fear, envy, or jealousy. Paul, Angus, and Mary move towards tranquility and contentment, not because their circumstances have changed but because their perspective and reactions to their circumstance have been changed. And that is the greatest lesson that we can all take from ‘The Holdovers’. If you liked this video then please consider subscribing to the channel. We’re getting close to 1000 subscribers and I’d like to thank everyone that’s supporting the channel. I find the YouTube comments section to be a bitter and complicated place and it seems to feel the same way about me. Don’t get me wrong, you’re a gigantic pain in the balls but I’d love to hear all your comments whether you’re a Stoic sage or a genuine troglodyte!

text: Murders that will live on in infamy, a twisted love story that actually happened, and an entire alternate screenplay? Here's what the ending of "Killers of the Flower Moon" really means. "Killers of the Flower Moon" opens with the Osage people in Oklahoma striking oil. By the 1920s, the discovery had turned them into the wealthiest group of people in the world — except that racist laws require white "guardians" to handle their wealth. Many Osage are being murdered, and the police are doing nothing to solve the cases. William King Hale is one white man using this situation for his own benefit, and ropes his war veteran nephew Ernest Burkhart into an elaborate criminal scheme: Marry into an Osage family, then kill the members off one by one until the oil money is all theirs. Ernest actually falls in love with his new wife Mollie, but still partakes in the violence against her family due to a combination of greed and his uncle's manipulations. "I do love that money, sir." Mollie is diabetic, and gets prescribed the new, rare, and extremely expensive synthetic insulin. Distrusting the doctors, she has her husband perform the shots for her. Unbeknownst to her, Ernest is following the doctors' orders to mix the insulin with a poison to "slow her down," gradually sickening her. Afraid she's going to die, Mollie uses what little strength she has left to travel to Washington D.C. to plead to President Calvin Coolidge for an investigation into the unsolved murders. It works: Agents from the Bureau of Investigation led by Tom White, come in and arrest Ernest. Hale casually turns himself in, confident he'll be ruled innocent. In the final act of "Killers of the Flower Moon," Ernest wavers back and forth on whether to testify against Hale. Ernest makes confessions only to take them back and claim he was forced to by the BOI; He shows up in court without realizing he and his uncle have the same lawyer, W.S. Hamilton, who works further to scare him off from testifying. In jail, Ernest learns his youngest daughter has died of whooping cough, but surprisingly, Mollie is still alive and has gotten help recovering from the poisoning. Ernest has an emotional reunion with his wife. The trials continue to unearth evidence of the conspiracy despite Hale's best efforts to suppress it, and Ernest ultimately testifies and pleads guilty to killing Rita and Bill Smith by blowing up their house. But he won't confess to everything — in his last scene, he lies to Mollie, still saying the shots he gave her were just regular insulin. The film continues into an epilogue of sorts, where the story of the Osage murders is presented via a live performance of a true crime radio play. The energetic fast-paced deliveries and wacky sound effects make it easy to miss all the details, but this epilogue describes what happened in the aftermath of the story. We hear how Ernest and Hale both ended up free on parole despite their life sentences and, in a cameo from director Martin Scorsese himself, how Mollie's obituary made no mention of the murders. The final shot of the film shows a massive Osage drum and dancing circle from overhead. Like Scorsese's past crime films, "Killers of the Flower Moon" is about the all-consuming power of greed in the American capitalist system. Here, this theme also plays into the reckoning with the mass genocide of Indigenous people. Ernest makes for a particularly complicated protagonist because on the one hand, he seems to genuinely love his wife — but on the other, he's both so greedy and so easily manipulated that this love ultimately means nothing. More than anything, Ernest is a weak man, and the way he's pulled back and forth over the course of the trial in the film's final act serves to emphasize that weakness. "I just love money. I love it as much as I love my wife." The scene in which Hamilton brings Ernest to a meeting with the oil company execs to put the fear of God into him evokes Ned Beatty's scene in "Network," another film about the forces of the market doing everything to suppress dissent. You might watch the final act of "Killers of the Flower Moon" hoping for Ernest to find the strength to stand up to Hale and acknowledge his crimes, but his confession offers little catharsis. Ernest's final interactions with Mollie only serve to emphasize his dishonesty and cowardice. Mollie never really trusted him, identifying him as a "coyote" from the beginning, but nonetheless chose to spend her life with him. By the end of the film, she fully sees through his charming facade, wanting nothing more to do with him. On the most basic level, presenting the final facts of the story in the form of a live radio show offers a more entertaining alternative to the standard practice of closing historical films with informational title cards. The choice to present this information so entertainingly, however, comes with its own layers of commentary on the nature of the true crime genre as a whole and on Scorsese's own responsibilities with "Killers of the Flower Moon" in particular. For one thing, there's the question of entertainment as a distraction. After over three hours of methodically paced storytelling, suddenly getting bombarded with a presentation so fast and so silly makes it harder to take in the sadness of the story being told. This radio show is specifically stated to be associated with FBI director J. Edgar Hoover, which raises questions about the propagandistic use of such stories. The images of the theater audience recall how Scorsese ended "The Wolf of Wall Street," forcing the viewer to reflect on their own attraction to such stories in the first place. Not letting himself off the hook either, Scorsese appears onstage as part of the radio show — but when he's talking about Mollie's divorce, remarriage, and death, the bells and whistles fade away. He wants us to take this in. That's what "Killers of the Flower Moon" is trying to accomplish: To offer serious reflection on tragedy within the apparatus of mass entertainment. Whereas Ernest is the sort of villain who lacks any serious sense of right or wrong, Hale is the kind who's convinced himself he's in the right — which is what makes him so scary. He's convinced the Osage Nation he's their ally, and he can talk at length about the virtues of their culture. Yet he still wants to take everything from them because he views their fall as a historic inevitability. "The Osage. They're gonna go. Their time is over." It's an even more extreme parallel to Ernest professing love for the same woman he's slowly poisoning. Speaking to Ernest in jail, Hale delivers a chilling monologue affirming his confidence that history will vindicate him, because all the anger people hold towards him now will end up forgotten. To some degree, this confidence was scarily well-founded: He and the other convicted killers were eventually let free, while other killers weren't caught or convicted at all, and the broader culture generally forgot about this story for a long time. Yet even if white America forgot, the Osage Nation did not forget -- when Hale was let out of prison, his release was met with protests. And though it's taken far too long, the existence of "Killers of the Flower Moon" as both a book and a movie is also a rejoinder to Hale's view of history: What might have once been forgotten is now being remembered on a large scale. As with the radio epilogue, the closing shot of "Killers of the Flower Moon" seems to serve two primary purposes: one stylistic and one thematic. The stylistic purpose of the final shot is the sheer visual splendor of it all. With a reported budget of $200 million, this production had plenty of resources for stunning scenes with massive crowds and fancy camera work, but Scorsese restrains those more grandiose instincts for much of the film in favor of a more intimate focus on character drama. The ending offers a place where such a spectacle fits comfortably. Thematically, the final shot returns the central focus of the film to the Osage people. Trying to navigate the issue of perspective was one of the challenges of making the film. Most of the significant Native American characters are killed midway through the film, and Mollie, the main exception to this rule and one of the most important characters, still has to spend a large chunk of the film bedridden while the white male exploiters take center stage in the drama. Presenting the Osage perspective on this tragedy, however, was one of Scorsese's priorities in telling this story. The movie opens from their perspective, and after the radio drama segment entirely about white America's viewpoint, the closing shot returns the movie to them. The start of the credits solidifies this, with the film's title displayed in the Osage language before it is shown in English. Scorsese's thoughtful direction continues even beyond the end of the narrative into the credits themselves. Pay attention to the sounds in the background: They're the sounds of nature that Mollie teaches Ernest to listen to at the start of their courtship. When Sight and Sound pointed this out in an interview with Scorsese, he responded, "The music comes from there. It always did. That's how music originated, from imitating animals and the sounds of insects. And so you get the goat singers, you get the ancient world, the tragedy, again, from that. And that's for us to go back to and to find comfort in. I think." Well before the release of "Killers of the Flower Moon," Osage Nation Principal Chief Geoffrey Standing Bear, who advised Scorsese on the film's cultural depictions, discussed the filming of the film's closing shot. He revealed that it was a relatively late edition, telling Tulsa World that, "I heard that Mr. Scorsese and the producers are going to come back and try to get a better ending by showing everyone who was an extra in a social dance where everyone's having a good time." Speaking to Vogue during the movie's premiere at the Cannes Film Festival, Gladstone made sure to inform people of one of her favorite details in the true story that wasn't included in the film: "It's not in this film, but it's important to me that people know that Mollie, once she divorced Ernest, she didn't just cut and run — she went back and got the money from him that he'd embezzled from her." In an Interview Magazine talk with director Kelly Reichardt, Gladstone described using quotes from those later court cases to base her performance of the film's ending scenes on, saying, "I don't want harm to befall my husband. But I want the truth to come out for what it is." Closer to release, Scorsese has talked more about aspects of the film's final act in interviews. He told The New Yorker that the film's ending was harder to write than the beginning, explaining, "The first two hours, we were moving along. The second two hours, boy, is this getting a little long in the tooth, as they say." The "Killers of the Flower Moon" movie captures much of the book's content but is completely different in terms of structure. The book is divided into three major sections or "chronicles." The first chronicle, "The Marked Woman," is centered around Mollie and her account of the crimes against her family. The second, "The Evidence Man," follows Tom White and the BOI as they uncover Hale's big conspiracy. Finally, "The Reporter" shifts the focus to the book's author, David Grann, as he personally investigates the case further and uncovers the extent to which the BOI overall failed to bring about justice. "When this money start coming, we should've known it came with something else, cause it's the white man's money." Even if Scorsese's film adaptation had stuck closer to the structure of the book, there was almost no way the book's ending could be directly adapted. To even attempt that, the film would either have to shift to a documentary format or there would need to be a big, meta framing device involved. Scorsese gets a bit meta with the radio show epilogue, but that's different from making the whole third act about a writer living nearly a century later. As far as we know, "Killers of the Flower Moon" didn't have an alternate ending filmed. There is, however, an entire alternate screenplay. Eric Roth's original draft was closer to the mystery structure of the book as well as to more traditional Westerns, with Tom White as the primary viewpoint character. As Roth and Scorsese worked on developing the script, they realized they had to completely start over for multiple reasons. Putting the focus on the BOI made it too much of a white savior story, and with Hale so obviously a villain with Robert De Niro in the role, the BOI-centric version failed as a compelling mystery. DiCaprio, who was originally going to play White, reportedly questioned Scorsese, "Where's the heart in this movie?" Scorsese determined that the heart was in the twisted romance between Ernest and Mollie, a topic which only became more interesting to him while doing research and speaking with members of the Osage who claimed the love between the couple was real despite how badly Ernest was hurting Mollie. DiCaprio switched roles from White to Ernest, and the movie that exists today came into being.

text: “Peeping Tom” also known as “Face of Fear”, was a movie way ahead of its time, directed by Michael Powell and starring Karlheinz Böhm and Anna Massey. The film was released in theaters a month before Alfred Hitchcock’s “Psycho” (and overshadowed), but both movies are about men killing off beautiful women in horrific ways. While Psycho maintains some suspense over the nature of the killer, Peeping Tom has him front and center, presenting a compelling and conflicting examination of his mind. Böhm plays Mark Lewis, a shy, lonely and quiet man with a dark secret. He's a serial killer who murders women while using film cameras to record their dying expressions. The expression “peeping Tom” describes a voyeur, and that's what he is, and it's kind of what we, as audience, turn into watching him be cruel to these women. Helen, his neighbor, befriends Mark, who reveals through home films that he was used as a guinea pig for his father's psychological experiments on fear and the nervous system. He also claims to shoot documentaries with his camera, to get away with his crimes, but after the two get closer, he begins screening his latest snuff film with her still in the room. Helen senses how emotionally disturbed he is, but Mark reassures her that he will never photograph or film Helen. In the end, he attempts to kill her, but instead impales himself on the knife with his camera running, providing the finale for his “documentary”. The last shot shows Helen crying over Mark's dead body as the police enters the room.

The long-awaited Inside Out 2 was finally released in theaters on June 14th, introducing old and new audiences to Riley's teenage years. In the throes of puberty and on the cusp of starting a new high school, Riley and her five core emotions are left to navigate through a time of uncertainty. However, now that Riley is growing up, she begins to experience new and intense emotions spurred on by recent experiences. The film introduces new emotions like anxiety and how they significantly impact Riley's life. In today's video, we'll fully recap everything that unfolded during Inside Out 2. Boy, are we so lucky we ran into you guys. In the film's opening, Joy and the other emotions prepare to watch Riley during her championship game with the Foghorns. They help her navigate the game together until Riley is sent to the penalty box. During this, Joy updates the audience on various changes throughout the passing years, like Riley's new friends, Grace and Bree, her kind and goofy personality, her recent birthday, and her sense of self. The sense of self is a new function in headquarters as a sub basement now connects to Riley's stream of consciousness. When memories enter this location, they can manipulate Riley's perception of herself, creating a sense of self. With the sense of self, Riley forms morals, beliefs, and critical decision-making skills. At the film's beginning, Riley believes wholeheartedly that she is a good person. However, her positive self-image is due to Joy preventing negative memories from influencing her sense of self. She uses a machine to throw bad memories, like Riley entering the penalty box, into the recess of her mind to be forgotten. After winning her championship game, Riley is offered the chance to attend a 3-day summer camp with her best friends. Run by the coach of Riley's dream team, the Firehawks. That night, the emotions are abruptly woken from sleep by the sound of the puberty alarm installed at the end of the first film blaring. As they try to quiet the alarm and eventually throw it from headquarters, the sound marks the arrival of the mind workers who begin to make additions and update the control panel. They leave headquarters unfinished by foreshadowing the arrival of new emotions. The following day, the effects of puberty impact Riley as the emotions can hardly touch the control panel without causing an emotional outburst. She calms on her way to camp with Grace and Bree, but is devastated to learn they're assigned to a different high school, meaning they won't attend school the following year or play on the Firehawks together. Riley's emotions are surprised by the arrival of anxiety in headquarters, an energetic emotion eager to help but constantly worried about what could go wrong in Riley's future. They're then introduced to four other emotions, Envy, Embarrassment, Ennui, and Nostalgia. However, the latter is sent away due to arriving years too early. Once at the summer camp, Riley runs into her idol, Valentina Ortiz, who made the Firehawks team during her first year. text: The film opens in Italy, with two fishermen riding their boat out into the water at night. Their record player is then taken underwater by a sea monster. The creature gets caught in their net but manages to free himself, leaping out over the boat before disappearing from the mens’ sight. Under the ocean lives Luca Paguro, a young sea monster who lives with his parents Daniela and Lorenzo plus his Grandma. He must round up some fish that act like sheep while also hiding from a boat that passes above the surface. Despite his parents’ warnings to avoid the surface, Luca has always had some interest, and Grandma even encourages his curiosity. Luca comes across the record player from before. As he approaches it, a figure in a diving suit goes near Luca. Thinking it’s a human, he hides in a cave. The figure pulls off their helmet to reveal the other sea monster from earlier, a boy around Luca’s age named Alberto Scorfano. Luca watches as Alberto goes up to the surface and changes into a human boy, and when Luca is pulled up out of the water, he does the same. He is initially freaked out, but he soon joins Alberto on the land once he learns how to use his new legs. Alberto takes Luca to his hideout, filled with other human trinkets that he has collected. Luca sees a poster for a Vespa, which both boys are impressed by. He then spends the next couple of hours helping Alberto create a makeshift Vespa until he has to go home. Over the next few days, Luca joins Alberto on the surface, although his parents are both becoming suspicious when he comes home late and they don’t see him tending to the sheep fish. The boys try to do a jump with their Vespa, but it keeps breaking apart until they manage to create a more durable one. When Luca continues to show fear and hesitance, Alberto tells him that he has a voice in his head, a “Bruno”, and he must get over his fear by declaring “Silenzio Bruno!” Unfortunately, when Luca gets home, Daniela and Lorenzo reveal that they know he has been going off to the surface, so they plan to send him off with his senile Uncle Ugo for the rest of the summer. Luca tells Alberto of their predicament, and his solution is to retreat to the nearby town of Portorosso and find a way to get their own Vespa and be free. The boys manage to get into town in their human forms and spot other humans in the plaza. Luca kicks a ball toward some children playing, only for the ball to bounce and hit a Vespa belonging to local bully Ercole Visconti. He is accompanied by his lackeys Ciccio and Guido, and Ercole goes to antagonize Luca and Alberto. He tries to drag Luca into the fountain, almost revealing Luca’s scales, but the boys are saved by a girl named Giulia Marcovaldo. Luca and Alberto briefly follow Giulia as she mentions that she hates Ercole because he always picks on everyone and taunts her for losing a local triathlon, The Portorosso Cup, the previous year because she got sick. After learning that the grand prize is money, Luca tells Alberto that they can use the money to get a Vespa and fulfill their goal. Giulia tells them that she races alone, but Luca convinces her to let him and Alberto create a team. She brings the boys back to her house where she lives with her father Massimo (Marco Barricelli), a one-armed sea monster hunter. The boys try to hide their sea monster forms from him as he feeds them pasta, which they love. Their cat Machiavelli is less welcoming to the boys and attacks Luca more than once. The next morning, Luca and Alberto join Massimo on the water as he fishes, while both trying to continue hiding their underwater forms. Afterward, they go with Giulia to sign up for the race, only to find Ercole there to taunt them. After Luca compares him to a catfish (a bottom feeder with whiskers), Ercole’s pride is hit and he decides to let the boys enter the competition just so he can rub it in their faces when he wins. The kids then train for the three main parts of the race: swimming a lap, eating a bowl of pasta, and then doing the final bike ride. Giulia takes on the swimming task, while Alberto must devour countless bowls of pasta in preparation, and Luca practices bike-riding. Daniela and Lorenzo realize Luca is missing, so they go to the surface world and take on their human forms to find their son. Since they have never seen his human form before, they go through the kids in the plaza by making them fall into the fountain and seeing that none of them are Luca their son. At night, Luca talks to Giulia, who says she feels like an outsider because everyone thinks she’s weird, which Luca relates to. She also tells him about the stars in the sky, which Alberto previously told him were fish. She brings Luca to a neighbor’s telescope to see them more closely, and Luca is amazed. However, Alberto notices that Luca is spending more time with Giulia and he starts to get jealous. Giulia tells Luca about the school that she goes to in Genova when she stays with her mother, which piques Luca’s interest. However, Alberto tells Luca that other kids would not accept them because of who they really are. The boys are then found by Ercole and his minions, as he has become suspicious of the boys. He threatens them and even punches Alberto in the stomach before saying he wants them out of town. When the kids try to practice the bike ride through the town, Alberto takes Luca with him to spite Giulia, leading to them careening through the streets out of control until they ride the bike off a ledge into the ocean. The boys argue, but Giulia finds them once they turn human again. After Luca tells Giulia he wants to go to school in Genova with her, Alberto then decides to reveal his true form to Giulia. Unfortunately, Ercole and his goons are nearby and throw harpoons at Alberto, who sadly flees after Luca hides his own identity and calls Alberto a sea monster. Luca goes back to Giulia’s house, but when he won’t explain things to her, she throws water on him and finds out he is also a sea monster. She is not horrified, but rather concerned that the other people out there might hurt him since Portorosso is a fish-hunting town. Luca then leaves to find Alberto at his hideout. There, Alberto reveals that his father left him and never came back, and he has been living on his own ever since. Even though Alberto tells Luca to go away, Luca wants to go through with the race anyway for the sake of their friendship. The day of the Portorosso Cup arrives. Giulia decides to compete by herself, but Luca shows up and does the same. He wears Alberto’s diving suit for the swimming portion as Ercole tries to get Ciccio to go faster by dumping olive oil on him, but it only attracts fish that bite Ciccio. The others make it to the pasta portion, with Giulia and Luca gaining momentum, while Ercole stuffs the pasta into Guido’s face to get him to finish. As the bike portion begins, it starts to rain. Luca can’t get far enough without risking revealing himself, but Alberto soon runs toward him with an umbrella. Ercole knocks Alberto down, revealing his sea monster form to everyone. As they start to go for Alberto, Luca rides his bike and reveals his true form as well to save his friend. They then race to the bottom of the hill as Ercole deliberately tries to kill the boys with a harpoon. Giulia rams her bike into his to save her friends, leading to her taking a hard tumble down the hill. The boys cross the finish line but run back to help Giulia up. The townspeople then surround the boys, until Massimo defends them and declares they are the winners since their bike did make it past the line. Ercole protests and orders his goons to do something, but Ciccio and Guido have had enough of his behavior, so they toss him into the fountain. Daniela, Lorenzo, and Grandma all arrive and reveal their sea monster forms as they embrace Luca. Two elderly women seen throughout the film also reveal that they are sea monsters. Everyone celebrates at Giulia’s house, and the boys buy a cheap, worn-out Vespa. Daniela and Lorenzo wonder if they have been too hard on Luca’s curiosity and think maybe he could go off to school with Giulia. Grandma says that while not everyone will accept him, Luca is smart enough to know who to trust. Luca and Alberto go to the train station as Giulia is set to leave for Genova. Alberto then tells Luca that he sold the Vespa so that he could buy Luca a train ticket so that he can join Giulia at school. Daniela and Lorenzo come out to state that they talked it over with Giulia’s parents so that Luca can stay with her and her mom. Although Luca wants Alberto to go, he tells Luca that he is going to stay with Massimo, helping him with work in exchange for a place to stay. The two boys hug each other goodbye, and Luca says farewell to his family as he stands outside the train in his sea monster form. The credits show drawings of Luca and Giulia having fun in Genova while keeping in touch with Alberto, Massimo, and Luca’s family. Then After the credits, Uncle Ugo is shown talking nonsensically to one of the sheep fish.

text: The movie starts by showing us a secret world inside the Earth called Hollow Earth, which is full of huge and powerful creatures. One day when Kong pursued by giant Wartdogs, Kong cleverly leads them into a trap by stopping near a hill's edge, fooling his chasers into falling in after him. He then cleverly makes a rock fall, which opens up a hidden deep crack in the ground. This trap catches many of the creatures, making them fall into the deep hole. During the confusion, Kong fights one of the creatures and beats it very skillfully. This makes him look so strong that the other creatures run away scared, making it clear that Kong is the boss of Hollow Earth. After everything calms down, Kong stands alone, watching over this underground world from a hill. Meanwhile, on Earth’s surface, we are introduced to Dr. Ilene Andrews, a dedicated scientist monitoring the global threats posed by titans. She uses a complex system to watch where they go and what they do. Godzilla, who is also a giant creature, surprisingly acts as a protector, stopping other titans that might harm people. Right now, Godzilla is living deep in the ocean, quietly watching for any threats from the sea or land. One day in Rome, where a scary giant Scylla suddenly appeared, causing panic and disorder. So Godzilla, came up to fight this dangerous creature. They had a massive fight, and Godzilla used his strength and smart tactics to win. In the end, Godzilla used his powerful atomic breath to defeat the giant Scylla once and for all. After getting rid of the threat, Godzilla went back to the sea, leaving the city safe. After that, we see Ilene is in office, feeling worried and uneasy as she examines strange and unsettling signals coming from Hollow Earth. These signals are very troubling to her. At the same time, in Jia’s school, something unusual is happening. Jia, who is the adopted daughter of Ilene, starts having intense daydreams. She’s overwhelmed with strange ideas that make her fill her desk with detailed drawings. This sudden and strange behavior makes her teacher and classmates very confused and worried. Later, Ilene is called to Jia’s school quickly because there’s a problem. In school Jia tells her that she’s confused and scared by the weird visions she keeps seeing. Every time she blinks, she sees a bunch of strange and disturbing pictures. It turns out that Jia has a special gift because she’s the last known survivor of the Iwi tribe from Skull Island, who can talk to Kong. This special bond might be the reason behind the odd things happening to him. At night, Jia started having scary visions again, which made her feel very afraid. She was so upset that she went to Ilene for help, telling her she was sure that Kong was in danger in the mysterious Hollow Earth and that she needed to contact him right away. Ilene spoke to her in a calming way, saying she understood Jia’s worries and would take care of them, but also told Jia that you go to sleep now. In her room, Ilene was thinking deeply about the drawings that Jia, who was very upset, had made. She suddenly understood that the mysterious signals she had picked up from Hollow Earth looked a lot like Jia’s drawings. Knowing she had to act fast, she went to find Bernie Hayes, a specialist who could figure out if these signals were coming from a giant creature like Kong, or something else. While Bernie found out something surprising after looking into it: the signals didn’t come from a giant creature or Kong. They were actually sent by people, which is unusual for Hollow Earth. These signals sent by humans were strange because they were different from anything known before, suggesting that there’s a big secret happening deep inside the Earth. At this time, Ilene gets a scary message while everyone is already on edge: Godzilla has woken up from his sleep in the water. This is serious and means there’s a big threat coming soon, something Godzilla was expecting. The story then tells us that Godzilla has moved to a new place in Europe after leaving the ocean. But story gets more interesting when Kong comes out from the underground world of Hollow Earth to the surface of the Earth. Ilene and Jia are with him when he comes out. Then, Kong shows that he has a problem that’s bothering him a lot: a really bad toothache. To treat his tooth, Ilene calls for a team member named Trapper to help with Kong’s tooth problem in a not-so-normal way. Trapper bravely hangs from a plane and ties a rope around Kong’s bad tooth. Then, they carefully go back up into the plane and use the plane’s power to pull out Kong’s tooth, which helps him feel better from his tooth pain. After fixing Kong’s tooth with a fake one, Ilene goes back to her office and talks to Bernie about a shocking find: the signals they’ve been getting are actually made by people, and this could mean trouble for Hollow Earth. So Ilene decides to face this new threat head-on. She puts together a small group of experts, including herself, Bernie, Trapper, Jia and a pilot named Mikael. This team, along with Kong, bravely sets out to the center of the Earth, into the mysterious world of Hollow Earth. The journey to Hollow Earth was very dangerous and difficult, really pushing the team to their limits. But even though it was risky, they made it to the beautiful world of Hollow Earth. Kong found comfort in the cave of his ancestors, and the people with him went on to the place they had set up as their base. On the surface of Earth in a high-tech control room, Hampton were watching Godzilla closely, Godzilla departs from Rome and travels north, attacking a nuclear plant in France to absorb radiation and strengthen himself. Monarch believes he is preparing for an imminent threat. Meanwhile, Ilene found something very sad and serious in Hollow Earth: the Monarch outpost, which used to be a place full of smart human inventions, was completely destroyed, showing just how powerful the titans are. At the same time, Kong felt a strange new kind of energy that seemed to come from a titan no one could see. Getting ready for a fight that was sure to happen, he picked up his axe. While Kong walks around this underground place and came out from a waterfall. There Kong found a new place where he saw a big, scary shadow in the smoke. When it got closer, it turned out to be a small gorilla named Suko. Kong tried to be friendly and reached out his hand, but Suko bit him instead. Then Suko runs away and Kong chases after it. Suddenly, Kong is surrounded by other big gorillas like him, which he has never seen before. They quickly catch him, but Kong easily breaks free. When Suko shows up again, Kong grabs it and uses it to fight off the others. Kong fights fiercely and beats all the other gorillas, proving he’s the strongest and the leader among them. The fight was intense, showing Kong’s strength and instinct to survive, and he’s left standing as the clear winner. After everything that happened, Kong asked Suko to show him where his tribe was, but Suko didn’t respond to Kong’s request. Still, the group didn’t give up and kept going. At the same time, deep in Hollow Earth, Ilene’s team was busy trying to understand the strange signals. While they were looking, one of the team members Mikael warned everyone that the place was very dangerous because of all the Titans around. He said that they would only be safe if they followed his advice. But just as he was trying to convince them, a Titan that was hiding by looking like a tree suddenly ate him. Seeing this, they all ran from that place; only then Jia discover an ancient symbol that seemed very important. When everything was calm, a butterfly landed on a rock, and when Jia touched it, water suddenly started flowing from a little tunnel. They were so curious that they decided to follow where the water was going, and it took them to a secret, protected place that was hidden by something like an invisible shield. So Jia opens the invisible shield with her hands, and they found a completely new place that was secret and waiting to be explored. Meanwhile, we see Kong and Suko. Kong wants to find his tribe, but Suko has different plans and tricks Kong into going to a river. Kong doesn’t know that there’s a gigantic serpent monster hiding in the river, but Suko does. Suddenly, as if it was meant to happen, a water-dwelling gigantic serpent monster attacked Kong. Kong, fighting to stay alive, hit the creature in the mouth with his axe, which made the creature even angrier. The creature tried to drag Kong under the water, and it looked like Kong was going to lose. Seeing how scary the situation was, Suko got scared and ran away. While running away, Suko saw something really shocking: the head of the gigantic serpent monster that Kong had just defeated. This horrible sight showed without a doubt that Kong was not just an ordinary gorilla. As they moved on, they ate gigantic serpent monster's meat that Kong had kill. After that, we see Monarch follows Godzilla's path until he reaches Tiamat, the underwater Titan who emerges from hibernation to battle Godzilla. Despite Tiamat wrapping herself around him, Godzilla overpowers her. And then, with his powerful atomic breath, Godzilla completely destroys the threat, and absorbs Tiamat radiation energy before submerging to prepare for the next battle. At the same time, deep inside Hollow Earth, Ilene and her team find a new area they’ve never seen before. While they’re exploring this place, they’re suddenly attacked by some people. These attackers are from the Iwi tribe, who can communicate with Kong and are the ones who sent the strange signals that Ilene was getting. During the fight, a girl from the Iwi tribe sees Jia and feels like she belongs with them. They bring Jia to the leader of the Iwi tribe to check if this is true. The leader holds hands with Jia and finds out that Jia really is part of their tribe. This discovery makes it clear that Jia has an important place in the story, connecting Kong with people. Now Ilene used this chance to ask about the scary signals that were sent up to the Earth’s surface. The tribe’s leaders told her something shocking: there are many gorillas like Kong living in Hollow Earth, and they all follow one ruthless leader known as Skar King. Now Skar King wants to take over the world above Hollow Earth too. But Godzilla, who keeps things in balance, had stopped Skar King before and made him go back to Hollow Earth. Now, this strong enemy is a danger to the world again. Meanwhile, Kong goes after Suko and finds where all the big apes are, which is a big shock for him. They’re all being made to work hard by Skar King. Kong notices one of Skar King’s bullies beating another elderly gorilla. Kong gets angry when he sees this cruel thing happening. He faces the one responsible and hits them hard, showing that he’s the strongest and shaking up the way things are usually done. When Kong stood up, it made Skar King come out. Skar King, who had been stopped by Godzilla before, didn’t get mad at Kong but laughed because Kong has metal teeth, but the laughter didn’t last long. Suddenly Skar King gets angry about being laughed at and does something terrible—he throws the gorilla into a pit of lava, which makes Suko very sad. Seeing this, Kong can’t keep quiet and shouts out in anger. This makes Skar king attack him quickly with a whip made from another Titan's spine and a sharp crystal on it. Kong almost gets hit badly, but he manages to dodge most of it hits. However, the crystal still cuts his hand, showing that the fight between Kong and Skar king is getting worse. At a tense point, Skar king managed to catch Kong’s neck with his whip, and it looked like he might kill Kong. But Kong, using all the strength he had left, kicked Skar king hard to the ground. This changed everything in the fight, and Skar king, realizing he might lose, ordered his goons to stop the lava from flowing. Just then, an ice Titan named Shimo, joined the battle because it was connected to Skar king by a crystal on his whip. Skar king used this crystal to make Shimo attack Kong with icy breath. When Kong tried to block this icy breath attack with his axe, both his axe and hand got covered in ice. When things were looking bad, Suko showed Kong a way out, and Kong took the chance to run away. Seeing the Kong fleeing, Skar King tells his gorilla goons to chase the Kong and kill him. So a bunch of gorillas ran after him, but Kong tricked them into a trap he had set before. Some of the gorillas got caught in the trap, but the smarter ones figured out what Kong was doing and avoided it. However, Suko stopped them by throwing a lot of stones at them to help Kong, showing that they were now on the same side. After all that had happened, Kong felt better when Suko came for aid, which was a sign of their new friendship and how they both stayed strong together. Then scene shift to Godzilla, who has just defeated Tiamat and is absorbing Tiamat radiation energy. At the same time, deep underground in Hollow Earth, Ilene watches her daughter Jia, who is happy being with her own tribe. Seeing this beautiful moment, Ilene decides it’s best to let Jia stay with her tribe while she goes back up to the surface world by herself. During these emotional times, suddenly Iwi tribe quickly open a hidden entrance to their place as Suko arrives with the injured Kong. But they weren’t the only ones who knew about this secret door; another gorilla who had been following them saw this. After everything that happened, Kong was knocked out. While he was out, the gorilla who saw the secret door went to tell Skar king about it. He told Skar king about a special door that could take him up to the surface of the Earth, where Skar king wanted to rule. Skar king was excited about this and rode his Ice Titan Shimo like a horse to go and take over. But Godzilla, who always keeps an eye on things to make sure they’re balanced, knew Skar king was up to no good. Since Godzilla had sent Skar king and his Ice Titan Shimo away to Hollow Earth before, he knew he had to stop them from getting out. As Godzilla was getting ready for a big fight. Meanwhile, Ilene and her team were taking care of Kong’s injuries. They found out that Kong’s hand was broken because of all the fighting he had been through. They decided to make him strong again by getting a metal hand made for him from the surface world, which would be a mix of high-tech and Kong’s own power. After they put on Kong’s new metal hand that has special energy boosters, Kong starts to feel strong again and forgets the pain from his old fights. At the same time, Suko sees Skar king coming their way, riding on his Ice Titan Shimo. Suko quickly tells Kong, who remembers that he lost to this huge ice monster before. Knowing he can’t win this fight alone, Kong tells Ilene and her team to get out of there. Then, feeling the need to act fast, Kong heads to the edge of the Earth to ask Godzilla for help. Godzilla felt that a fight was about to happen and came to Earth, watching Kong closely. Thinking Kong was coming to fight, Godzilla started fighting him. They both clashed in a huge battle that seemed like a misunderstanding because they thought they were enemies. But Kong didn’t want to fight and was actually trying to warn Godzilla about the danger that was coming. But Godzilla got it wrong and thought Kong wanted to fight, so he attacked with his dangerous atomic pink breath. Kong had no choice but to fight back, and they both ended up in an epic battle showing their great strength. At the same time, something magical happened with the Iwi tribe. Jia’s spirit joined with Mothra, a god-like creature, and they flew off to stop Godzilla and Kong from fighting. She quickly stepped in to explain the real danger they all faced. Then, the Iwi tribe did something special: they poured a red liquid into the water, which caused crystals to rise from deep within the earth. These crystals came together, signaling that something big and unknown was about to happen. As the crystals moved into place, the doorways to Earth were almost shut for good. But suddenly, Skar king showed up with his giant Ice Titan Shimo. The Ice Titan Shimo used its power to freeze the stones, stopping the doorways from closing. Right then, Jia, who had joined with the spirit of Mothra, appeared. Godzilla and Kong both rushed into the fight. Kong, now stronger with his new metal hand, started a tough battle with Skar king. With his new power, Kong was a tough match and fought Skar king with a lot of power. In the middle of all the action, Godzilla was fighting hard against the ice titan Shimo, which had caught him in its icy breath. Mothra came just in time to break the ice and free Godzilla so he could fight again. The fight kept going, with Mothra taking on Skar king’s soldiers. Suddenly, there was no gravity, and everyone started floating and spinning around, heading towards a doorway that led to the surface of the Earth. Skar king didn’t stop trying to take over, and he told the ice titan Shimo to start unleashes ice powers on the world, freezing buildings and firing an ice blast skyward. As the Earth was almost destroyed by icy apocalypse. Soon Godzilla and Kong came back to Earth and start fight against Skar king’s freezing attacks. Skar king threw a big brick at Kong, but Kong, now stronger with his metal hand, broke it easily. Then Kong hit Skar king really hard, showing his incredible fighting spirit and how strongly he and Godzilla are connected to the Earth they were defending. Soon Godzilla took a chance to take the crystal off Skar king’s whip, which was controlling the ice titan Shimo. Kong wanted to break the crystal, but Skar king attacked him from behind. Right when Skar king was about to get his crystal back, suddenly Suko stepped in with Kong's axes and broke the crystal with a strong hit of axes, which freed the ice titan Shimo from Skar king’s control. Without his ultimate weapon, Kong grabs Skar king and tosses him toward Godzilla, who whips him back with his tail towards Kong like a volleyball. After that, Kong holds Skar King in the air as ice titan Shimo turns on her former master and freezes him. It looked like they had won, but Kong saw a tiny bit of life left in Skar king’s eye that wasn’t frozen. So, with one last powerful smash, Kong made sure Skar king was completely defeated. After the big battle, Godzilla used his powerful atomic breath to melt the ice that was covering the sky and the sun. This started a reaction that melted all the ice on Earth and made things right again. On the other hand, in Hollow Earth where Ilene and Jia was. Now that the danger is over, it’s time for Ilene to go back up to the surface with her friends. She didn’t want to take Jia away from the happiness she found with her tribe, but then Jia says she’s not happy in Hollow Earth and really wants to go with Ilene. Because Jia feels that being with Ilene is like being at home. Ilene is really happy to hear this and agrees, so they get ready to leave for the surface together. Later, Mothra, who is like a god to the Iwi tribe, works to fix the Earth by closing up the broken parts and doorways. Meanwhile, we see Godzilla, who is very tired, taking a break after all the fighting. At the same time, Kong goes back to Hollow Earth, where the gorillas welcome him as their king.

text: Civil War, Alex Garland's brand new film for A24. It might not be what people were expecting, but it's a devastatingly powerful piece of work. In this video, we're going to press into its deeper themes and symbolism, and what it has to say about the human condition. The film is a bleak road trip movie. A ragtag group of four journalists are making their way from New York to Washington D.C. to photograph and interview the president in the midst of a civil war. Our protagonist, Lee Smith, is a renowned war photographer. She shoots in color with a digital camera. The cold, unflinching, immediate quality of her photos reflects something of her character. She has been hardened by years of frontline action. She says it as it is, and she shoots it as it is. Lee is idolized by Jessie, a 23-year-old up-and-coming photographer who manages to wriggle her way onto this expedition. Jessie shoots on black and white film, hand developing her photos on the go. She keeps the bottle of developer stored against her skin. Apparently, it's just right when it's at body temperature. So, Jessie's photos are more organic and stylized. Whereas Lee captures the cold brutality of the events, Jessie memorializes them. And you could see this as a reflection of the naivety that we see in Jessie when we first encounter her. We're going to enter spoiler territory. During an early fuel stop, she is profoundly distressed by the sight of two captive men hanging from a ceiling. Their bodies bloodied and barely alive. The captor asks her for an opinion. What should he do with them? Shoot them? The mortified Jessie has no answer and finds herself unable to take a photograph.
